C1.justification: The principal contribution remains selective momentum updates for forgetting mitigation. v3's introduction adds an explicit no-additional-memory-overhead advantage, while its conclusion narrows the performance claim from surpassing traditional fine-tuning to achieving comparable default fine-tuning performance with less forgetting.

C2.justification: The original proximity and attractor interpretation remains. v3 adds substantive hypotheses about temporal update stability and avoiding second-moment normalization, interprets proxy-subset tuning, and explains the use of IFEval to avoid medical overlap with MMLU. Section 5 newly identifies fixed update fractions and the supervised fine-tuning scope as limitations.

D1.justification: v3 substantially expands v1's brief implementation appendix with evaluator metric identifiers, MMLU inference precision, warm-up settings, LoRA configurations, hyperparameter grids, partition and distance calculations, proxy-tuning instructions and training times. These include newly disclosed details, not necessarily changed implementations. Hardware and the stated TRACE training schedule remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v3 removes dedicated Code-Alpaca fine-tuning and adds PMC-LLaMA medical fine-tuning with PubMedQA, MedMCQA and MedQA evaluation. It also adds IFEval instruction-following tests, RedPajama loss evaluation and an UltraFeedback timing workload. MetaMathQA, TRACE, FLAN/Pile and HumanEval retention evaluations remain.

E2.justification: v3 newly evaluates LoRA, HMA, CoFiTune with and without soft masking, vanilla soft masking, EWC, Lion and additional MV/GV filtering comparators. TRACE gains EWC and EWC+MoFO but loses the MTL upper bound. Full FT is renamed Default FT; L1/L2 comparisons remain in the Pareto analyses.

E3.justification: The reported MetaMathQA subset changes from 33,000 to 39,500 examples, both described as 10%; retained scores do not establish reruns. Added experiments introduce chat/Gemma configurations, Llama-3-family timing configurations, medical preprocessing, baseline hyperparameter sweeps and proxy-subset tuning protocols (Appendices D–G).

E4.justification: v1 already studies update fractions, random/gradient selection and model proximity. v3 expands these with Pareto tradeoff studies, distance–forgetting correlations, proxy-based fraction selection, MV/GV filtering and update-stability analyses, alternative partitions and efficiency measurements. The original Pythia proximity experiment is retained in Appendix G.1.

E5.justification: v3 adds numerical correlation estimates for distance versus RedPajama loss and MMLU accuracy, reported as 0.97 and -0.79 in Figure 2; v1 provides qualitative proximity comparisons. Neither version reports repeated-seed variability, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Many original entries remain, including MoFO's 47.7 GSM8K and TRACE OP/BWT of 41.3/-5.4. New results include medical MedQ/general-average scores of 54.3/43.1 and EWC+MoFO OP/BWT of 43.2/-4.4. The retention-sweep peak shifts from 10% in v1 Figure 3 to 15% in v3 Figure 9. Code-Alpaca results and MTL's 50.8 OP are removed.

M1.justification: The central momentum-filtered Adam procedure remains. v3 adds adaptations within LoRA's trainable space, a Lion variant and attention-head partitioning (Appendices F.2, G.4–G.5). Algorithm 1 also omits v1's epsilon denominator term, without establishing a corresponding experimental implementation change.

P1.justification: The introduction, motivation and theoretical narrative are extensively rewritten. Theory becomes a standalone section; related work moves to Appendix A; dataset, implementation and exploratory material are reorganized into specialized appendices. The conclusion gains explicit limitations, alongside terminology and author-list edits.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. v3 adds Pareto and distance plots, expands the fraction-sweep display, and pairs several new tables with scatterplots. Retained tables lose accuracy-change subrows, toy landscapes are reorganized, and the original Pythia landscapes move from Figure 2 to Figure 11.

R1.justification: v3 substantially broadens research positioning through optimization-based and model-averaging approaches, including soft masking, CoFiTune, HMA, FetchSGD and concurrent masking work. It more explicitly positions MoFO as greedy BCD adapted to Adam and adds relevant optimizer, theoretical and dataset references (Appendix A and associated discussions).

T1.justification: v1 proves convergence only for a gradient-descent surrogate. v3 replaces this with full-batch momentum MoFO analysis at O(log(T)/sqrt(T)), specifying momentum constraints and diminishing learning rates. It also introduces an L1-based filtered norm, additional lemmas and a higher-dimensional forgetting-mitigation theorem with proof (Section 3; Appendix B).

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited theoretical coverage and baseline evidence through full-batch momentum analysis, tuned Pareto comparisons, broader evaluations and clearer implementation documentation. These gains outweigh losing Code-Alpaca and MTL comparisons. Reporting weaknesses remain: Appendix F.1 claims a 0.3-point IFEval decline although Table 4 shows 41.4 to 38.6, and Figure 9 has unexplained discrepancies with retained tables.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MoFO. Their complete main texts and appendices, including algorithms, proofs, figures and tables, support comparison. Retained material can be matched across substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds medical evaluations, model and optimizer comparisons, supplementary analyses and measured training times.

before.justification: v1 reports original instruction fine-tuning, continual-learning, loss-landscape and ablation results, including Tables 1–5.

results.title: MoFO: Momentum-Filtered Optimizer for Mitigating Forgetting in LLM Fine-Tuning

C1.justification: The central claim of a simple RE defense with favorable privacy–utility trade-offs remains. However, v2 makes feature-space mismatch and the distinct roles of Partial Erasure and Random Location central claimed contributions in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion. The claim of preserving or improving utility in some high-resolution settings already appeared in v1.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes reduced information exposure and localized features producing false-positive reconstructions. v2 develops a different, more detailed account involving mismatch between reconstructed and private-image features, preserved class separation, partial erasure reducing joint-feature exposure, and random locations restoring utility through diversity. It also attributes adaptive-attack failure to optimization fluctuations and discusses inpainting's computational cost. The classification-only and image-domain limitations remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit project/code access address, identifies evaluation architectures and their accuracies in Table A.1, and documents PCA and parameters for new analyses. These improve documentation without establishing changes to the retained experiments. The existing hardware description and much of the dataset-processing and attack-configuration guidance remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds VGGFace2 evaluation through MIRROR and attacker-aware erasure scenarios in Appendix D.5. CelebA, FaceScrub, Stanford Dogs, FFHQ, and AFHQ Dogs remain represented. The occluded-private-test evaluation from v1 Appendix B.1 disappears. Coverage changes are bounded extensions and removals within the existing image-classification and inversion domains.

E2.justification: The comparison set expands substantially beyond NoDef, MID, and BiDO. v2 evaluates NLS, TL-DMI, and MI-RAD variants RoLSS, SSF, and TTS in corresponding comparisons, and adds actual DP result rows for PPA. CutMix, random cropping, and Gaussian blur are also evaluated against MIDRE. MIRROR and IF-GMI receive reported attack evaluations.

E3.justification: v2 adds high-resolution experiments with maximum erasure 0.8 alongside 0.4, additional model configurations and 160×160 inputs, and distance/FID metrics. The low-resolution user study changes from 150 pairs across 20 identities with two raters and forced choice to 150 identities with three raters and four response options. A 530-identity high-resolution study and controlled erasure/adaptive-attack protocols are also introduced.

E4.justification: v2 adds feature-space analyses, partial-versus-entire and random-versus-fixed erasure controls, alternative augmentations, pixel/multiple-patch masking, aspect-ratio tests, defense combinations, adaptive attacks with loss curves, and inpainting experiments. The original masking-value and area-ratio ablations remain in Appendix D. Conversely, v1's occlusion-likelihood histograms and Grad-CAM false-positive analysis are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report selected low-resolution attack results with ± values and high-resolution results mainly as point estimates. Neither introduces explicit run counts, seed information, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Changed uncertainty values belong to results; the additional human ratings change study sampling rather than uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial MIRROR, IF-GMI, baseline-comparison, combination, adaptive-attack, and user-study results. Retained results also change: MID's KedMI attack accuracy is 41.73±4.59 in v1 Table 2 versus 53.33±4.97 in v2 Table B.2. The original user-study counts of 153 versus 147 are replaced by 221 versus 108 under a redesigned protocol, so these are not directly comparable improvements. v1's standalone Stanford Dogs Table 5(a) entries disappear, although Dogs remains in Figure 2.

M1.justification: The core procedure remains random square erasure of every training image, ImageNet-mean filling, and ordinary classification training. v2 additionally implements combinations with BiDO and NLS in Section 4.4 and an inpainting-based replacement for masked pixels in Appendix D.6. These are limited procedural extensions to the retained defense.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten. Analysis becomes a standalone section, high-resolution comparisons take priority, and original low-resolution results, algorithm, metric descriptions, and masking ablations move into reorganized appendices. The author list and publication header also change. This is substantial restructuring beyond simply inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: Figure 1 expands from three to six panels; feature-space, privacy–utility, masking-strategy, and adaptive-loss plots are added. Figure 2 is redrawn and its setup composition changes. Original accuracy and KNN tables are consolidated, while IF-GMI reconstructions replace the earlier PPA illustration. The user-study interface gains four choices, and the document adopts a different journal layout.

R1.justification: v2 expands positioning from a comparison centered on regularization-based MID/BiDO to a broader account of loss-based, transfer-learning, and architectural defenses. NLS, TL-DMI, and MI-RAD receive substantive discussion in the introduction and Appendix G.2. New citations also cover IF-GMI, PPDG-MI, VGGFace2, and inpainting; the author–year citation conversion itself is only presentational.

T1.justification: The underlying MI objective, RE masking construction, and trade-off calculation retain their mathematical meaning. v2's feature notation and named properties support empirical explanations through visualizations and experiments; they do not introduce substantive formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the paper's evidence through broader defense comparisons, controlled tests of the proposed mechanism, adaptive attacks, and experiments validating complementarity that v1 mainly asserted. These address important gaps in the original support for MIDRE. Reporting weaknesses remain: Tables B.11–B.12 reverse the prose's both/none vote labels, and the entire-erasure protocol is described inconsistently. These limit particular findings but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in experimental scrutiny and support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MIDRE research despite the changed title. All 19 pages of v1 and 33 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable and support comparison of text, equations, tables, and figures.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds feature-space analyses, defense combinations, adaptive-attack evaluations, and revised user studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-inversion experiments, masking ablations, qualitative analyses, and an Amazon Mechanical Turk study in Appendix A.2.

results.title: Random Erasing vs. Model Inversion: A Promising Defense or a False Hope?

C1.justification: The exploratory demonstration on three Navier–Stokes models becomes a broadly positioned attribution framework claiming diagnostics beyond residual inspection. New headline contributions include systematic loss-component analysis and recurring differences in initial-condition dependence across five time-dependent PDEs, substantially expanding the abstract, introduction, and conclusion claims.

C2.justification: Beyond v2's warning that passing an indicator does not establish correctness, v3 interprets temporal symmetry and persistent initial-condition dependence, distinguishes sensitivity from physical causality, and discusses Hessian conditioning and sign cancellation. Appendices C.3–C.4 explicitly qualify monotonicity and show that accurate SOAP solutions can have low indicators, limiting their interpretation as universal accuracy measures.

D1.justification: V3 provides per-PDE configuration tables, Arnoldi settings of 200 iterations and 50 retained eigenvectors with damping 0.001, and CPU, timing, and memory measurement details. However, v2's explicit Hammersley sampling statement and Navier–Stokes test-set counts are omitted. The code-availability statements identify the same repository.

E1.justification: V2 evaluates only steady Navier–Stokes flow around a cylinder. V3 retains that problem and adds five time-dependent problems—Heat, Allen–Cahn, Burgers’, Drift-Diffusion, and Wave—and a steady Poisson problem with a localized source, substantially broadening the represented physics and task requirements.

E2.justification: V3 adds one attribution comparator, Grad-Dot (Charpiat et al., 2019), to the leave-one-out and local fine-tuning validation experiments in Tables 5–6. V2 evaluates no competing attribution method. The PINNACLE, gradient-alignment, and causal-training comparisons in v3 Table 10 are conceptual rather than additional evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The retained Navier–Stokes setup reports tanh instead of GELU activations, and its stated inflow formula gains a factor of four. New evaluation protocols include relative L2 errors, Spearman correlations, 30 individual point-removal trials, 1000-step L-BFGS fine-tuning, and controlled data-quantity and optimizer sweeps. The inflow revision alone does not establish whether implementation or documentation changed.

E4.justification: V3 adds Hessian-recovery and attribution-fidelity checks, computational scaling studies, continuous data-quantity sweeps, and NNCG/SOAP optimizer analyses. Additional diagnostics test downstream regional influence, Wave symmetry, and Burgers’ shock locality. Conversely, v2's deliberately incorrect-physics Navier–Stokes model is no longer evaluated.

E5.justification: V2 reports averages over test locations without repeated-run uncertainty. V3 specifies ten random seeds and systematically reports means, standard deviations, and shaded uncertainty bands. Appendix B.2 also discloses excluding failed well-trained Allen–Cahn runs, leaving the effective retained count unclear despite ten-seed table captions.

E6.justification: V3 adds PDE-error, temporal-attribution, fidelity, and computational-cost results absent from v2. Tables 5–6 distinguish near-zero retraining correlations from local fine-tuning correlations of 0.08–0.77. Navier–Stokes directionality and regional scores are also revised, but changed model settings, run aggregation, and regional targets prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: V3 adds normalized loss-component contributions, a cancellation score, and temporal diagnostics to the existing point/region influence framework. Influence computation also changes from the NaiveInfluenceFunction specified in v2 to a modified low-rank Arnoldi implementation in v3 Appendix A.2.1. These extend the diagnostic procedure beyond additional explanation.

P1.justification: V3 extensively rewrites the abstract, motivation, contribution statements, and conclusion; separates related work and methodology; and reorganizes the supplement into Appendices A–C. The Navier–Stokes study moves to the appendix, while a practitioner’s guide and dedicated limitations discussion reshape the narrative. Title and authorship information also change.

P2.justification: V3 changes the main text to two columns, introduces a framework schematic and diagnostic overview table, and adds structured validation, configuration, and cost tables. Influence visualizations are redesigned and supplemented with loss-fraction curves and uncertainty bands; Navier–Stokes displays are rearranged and expanded within the appendix.

R1.justification: V3 adds a substantial related-work section and methodological comparisons with training-time diagnostics and alternative attribution approaches. New discussions of influence-function fragility, PBRF validation, efficient influence estimation, and interpretable architectures establish a much more developed research position than v2's brief contextual citations.

T1.justification: The stationary-point lemma and generalized first-order influence derivation already appear in v2 Appendix A.1. V3 refines the Taylor-remainder and finite-addition/removal formulation, adds formal definitions for loss shares, cancellation, and temporal indicators, and supplies computational complexity bounds. These extend the retained mathematical foundation without replacing its central argument.

improvement.justification: V2 offers a narrow demonstration without directly checking influence-estimate fidelity. V3 substantially addresses this deficiency through perturbation validation, uncertainty reporting, and tests across PDEs, data quantities, and optimizers. Reporting failed leave-one-out prediction and accurate-but-low-indicator SOAP cases makes the applicability limits more informative. Although the original incorrect-physics control is lost and Allen–Cahn seed selection remains incompletely quantified, the stronger validation and more qualified interpretation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present PINNfluence and share its influence-function framework and Navier–Stokes study. The text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support matching retained material despite v3's substantial expansion.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices A–C report original experiments across seven PDE problems, including attribution validation, data-quantity sweeps, optimizer analyses, and computational measurements.

before.justification: Section 3, Table 1, and Appendix A.3 report original diagnostic scores, predictions, errors, and influence maps for three trained Navier–Stokes PINNs.

results.title: PINNfluence: Interpreting PINNs through Influence Functions

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion expand the claimed demonstrated applicability from small-scale SimCLR image classification to ImageNet-pretrained SimCLR and BYOL models and object detection. This broadens the empirical contribution, while the central claim of aligning pre-training and fine-tuning through bilevel optimization remains.

C2.justification: v3 qualifies the duration finding as holding after sufficient pre-training and adds an interpretation of greater stability across runs. It removes v2's Future Work discussion, including uncertainty about larger setups and the requirement for full pre-training-data and pretext-task access. The central information-sharing and feature-alignment explanations remain.

D1.justification: v3 documents BYOL's target decay and prediction-head architecture, replaces and expands the dataset-specific hyperparameter tables for both pretext methods, and adds detection implementation details in Appendix B.6. It also changes the code/model-weight repository pointer. These substantially revise the reproducibility information, without establishing external repository accessibility.

E1.justification: ImageNet-1K replaces STL10U in the main pre-training experiments, although STL10U remains in the duration study. v3 adds VOC07+12 object detection and BYOL pretext training. Downstream classification retains twelve datasets but removes STL10L and FashionMNIST.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates only the SimCLR-pretrained Only FT baseline. v3 adds an evaluated BYOL-pretrained Only FT baseline alongside SimCLR in Tables 1 and 6. BYOL was already cited in v2, but was not an evaluated comparator there.

E3.justification: The main backbone changes from ResNet-18 to ResNet-50, baseline pre-training decreases from 600 to 500 epochs, and the fine-tuning search decreases from 200 to 100 configurations. v2 approximately matches total pretext epochs; v3 instead shares the baseline's 500-epoch checkpoint and adds about eight BiSSL pretext epochs. Detection introduces AP50 evaluation, 50-epoch fine-tuning, batch size 16, and a separate 50-configuration search.

E4.justification: The existing pre-training-duration and latent-feature analyses are revised rather than replaced by new analytical questions. v3 changes the Flowers duration curves and presents updated feature visualizations under its revised main setup. The STL10L and DTD visualization cases from v2's appendix are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions specify ten fine-tuning models with different random seeds and report means and standard deviations. Both mark significant results in bold without specifying a significance-testing procedure. v3's discussion of lower variability does not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: The main classification results are replaced under different conditions: CUB200 top-1 scores change from 47.1 versus 45.7 in v2 to 59.2 versus 49.6 for SimCLR in v3, so these are not same-setting gains. v3 adds BYOL results and detection AP50 scores of 60.6 versus 59.6 for SimCLR and 56.7 versus 54.6 for BYOL. The Flowers duration curves also change.

M1.justification: v3 replaces the gamma-weighted downstream loss term with unit weight and removes Algorithm 1's periodic upper-backbone mixing update. Algorithm 2 replaces Hessian-vector averaging over five stored batches with a single-batch calculation. Appendix B.6 additionally adapts the parameter partition for detection by assigning ResNet-50 layers beyond C4 to the pretext head. These change the procedure despite retaining the core bilevel framework.

P1.justification: The title and selected abstract, introduction, experimental, and conclusion passages are rewritten, while the overall section sequence and much explanatory prose remain. Future Work is removed, a generic Impact Statement is added, and the experimental and appendix subsections are adjusted for detection and separate top-5 reporting.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch to a two-column layout. The main results table is transposed and grouped by pretext method, with top-5 results moved to Appendix Table 6. The two-panel duration figure becomes separate main-text and appendix figures, detection gains a table, and feature plots and captions are extensively revised.

R1.justification: v3 removes the related-work discussions of Chen et al. (2023) and Somayajula et al. (2023), adds references including Lorraine et al. (2020) and Ren et al. (2015), and prunes future-work citations. Its principal distinction from prior SSL and meta-learning approaches remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The upper-level objective definition and its derivatives in equations (2), (4), and (7) change through removal of gamma weighting. Appendix A.1 otherwise retains the same implicit-gradient derivation and assumptions concerning fixed pretext-head parameters, convexity, and Hessian invertibility; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v2 Section 5.1's explicit uncertainty about larger setups and tasks beyond small-scale classification. ImageNet/ResNet-50 experiments with two pretext methods and the detection results materially strengthen support for BiSSL's applicability, with accompanying implementation details. The main comparison now shares starting checkpoints but gives BiSSL additional pretext updates, and the full-data-access limitation is omitted. These qualifications temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gain in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BiSSL research work and contain readable main text, equations, algorithms, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C. The experimental replacements and relocated material can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v3 reports original SimCLR/BYOL classification results in Tables 1 and 6, object-detection results in Table 2, and duration and feature-visualization experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original downstream classification results in Table 1, pre-training-duration experiments in Figure 2, and feature visualizations in the main text and Appendix C.

results.title: BiSSL: Enhancing the Alignment Between Self-Supervised Pretraining and Downstream Fine-Tuning via Bilevel Optimization

C1.justification: The central claims remain the λ = 1 tightness threshold, the effect of loading on local maxima, two projection-free solution approaches, and strong density/scalability performance. The expanded discussion of the AAAI predecessor explains contributions already present in v2.

C2.justification: Section 4.6 qualifies the explanation attributing AdamW's higher cost to PyTorch versus NumPy as particularly relevant under CPU-only execution. The existing landscape interpretations, loading tradeoffs, and tightness limitations are otherwise retained.

D1.justification: Section 3.3 adds quickselect as an implementation option for top-k selection, and Section 4.3 revises the documented iteration limits. Hardware, initialization, preprocessing, AdamW's learning rate, and the code URL remain unchanged; the URL is relocated.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same densest-k-subgraph task on Facebook, web-Stanford, com-Youtube, soc-Pokec, as-Skitter, and com-Orkut. Table 1 statistics and the plotted subgraph-size coverage are retained.

E2.justification: Figure 5 includes Greedy in the Facebook runtime comparison in v2 but omits its curve and legend entry in v3. Other comparator membership is retained, including the existing omission of Greedy from Facebook's density panel.

E3.justification: Section 4.3 increases Frank–Wolfe's reported iteration cap for baseline comparisons fivefold, from 200 to 1,000, while AdamW remains at 200. This substantially revises the optimization budget underlying the main density/runtime comparisons. Other stated settings remain stable; the PDFs do not establish the rerun history.

E4.justification: Figure 2 revises the λ = 0.1 traces in the existing Facebook diagonal-loading sensitivity experiment, particularly solution sparsity. The tested loading values and analytical question remain unchanged, and Figure 3's step-size experiment is retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty bands for its experimental results.

E6.justification: Figure 5 revises runtime curves across the six networks, notably Frank–Wolfe's relative efficiency: on com-Youtube it now exceeds EXPP's runtime at some larger k. These results accompany a revised iteration cap, so they do not establish a same-setting slowdown. Figure 2's λ = 0.1 sparsity at iteration 200 changes from approximately 0.29 to 0.36, and Section 4.3 newly reports integral convergence within 1,000 iterations. Figure 4's density results are largely retained.

M1.justification: The diagonal-loading objective, Frank–Wolfe updates and step-size options, and constraint parameterization solved with AdamW are retained. The added quickselect discussion concerns an equivalent implementation of the existing top-k operation.

P1.justification: The introduction and related-work prose are revised, the AAAI comparison is expanded, and Section 2 gains separate tightness and landscape-analysis subsections. Most method, experimental, and appendix prose and the overall section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: The entire document changes from an IEEE two-column layout to a single-column layout, with different margins, equation flow, algorithm formatting, table-caption placement, and figure placement and sizing. Figures 2, 4, and 5 are redrawn with revised title, axes, and legend arrangements; the same five figures and dataset table remain.

R1.justification: V3 adds Matula and Beck (1983) for k-core peeling and expands the comparison with the cited AAAI paper, explicitly discussing its restricted tightness guarantee and the reuse of Theorems 3 and 4. The remaining cited works are retained despite reference reordering and metadata updates.

T1.justification: Appendix B corrects stationarity calculations to use the loaded objective g instead of f and derives g(x'') − g(x*) = 2λt², repairing a central proof step. Appendices A and C correct edge-term subtractions. Section 3.3 changes the Frank–Wolfe complexity bound from O(m + k log n) to O(m + n + k log n) and adds an average O(m + n) bound using quickselect. The theorem conclusions remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V3 repairs an important deficiency in the theoretical foundation: Appendix B now applies stationarity to the objective actually being maximized and supplies the missing valid derivation. Together with the corrected rounding/local-maximizer proof expansions and complexity bounds, this substantially strengthens support for the central guarantees. Revised iteration and runtime reporting also makes the empirical evidence clearer, although the larger budget prevents interpreting changed timings as same-setting performance gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. The text, equations, five figures, dataset table, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison despite extensive reformatting.

after.justification: Section 4 retains original graph-mining experiments, revises plotted results, and additionally reports integral convergence within the stated iteration budget.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original diagonal-loading and step-size experiments, plus subgraph-density and runtime comparisons on six real-world networks.

results.title: On Densest $k$-Subgraph Mining and Diagonal Loading: Optimization Landscape and Finite-Step Exact Convergence Analysis

C1.justification: The central spectral GP/RKHS and calibration contributions remain. v3 frames the empirical contribution as improved uncertainty quantification with competitive effect estimation and explicitly extends its practical claims to a large real dataset; v2 emphasizes state-of-the-art uncertainty quantification and CBO performance on simulations and the healthcare example.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands discussion of surrogate-likelihood validity, Gaussian approximation limitations, and the restrictions of calibration within a chosen spectral family. It explains ORF's limitations through its linear treatment-response model and explicitly treats 401(k) as a plausibility and feasibility study without ground-truth causal effects. These qualifications go beyond v2's brief surrogate-model explanation.

D1.justification: v3 supplies extensive 401(k) loading, preprocessing, training, calibration, covariance-computation, and resource-measurement details. It adds ORF configuration and documents the already evaluated Continuous DR baseline's fixed-B=0 adaptation and nuisance-estimation procedures. The latter is newly disclosed information, not evidence of changed implementation. The code-access information is retained.

E1.justification: v3 adds the 9,915-observation 401(k) dataset, evaluating income-dependent effects of binary pension-plan eligibility on financial assets. It also adds toy scenarios with Student-t outcome noise and skewed Beta treatment sampling. The original toy, synthetic causal graph, and healthcare-simulator coverage is retained.

E2.justification: v3 adds orthogonal random forests, implemented with DMLOrthoForest, to the synthetic benchmark comparison in Table 2 and Figure 4. Continuous DR, Sampling GP, and BayesIMP remain; the original toy and CBO comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: v3 adds interval-score evaluation, including IS95 in Tables 1–2 and IS90/IS95 in robustness tests. New protocols include ORF response-curve reconstruction with an oracle intercept and the 401(k) experiment's standardization, minibatch training, and income-quantile evaluation grid. These additions do not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained calibration, sample-splitting, and BayesIMP ablations, v3 adds sensitivity to bootstrap replication counts and kernel choice, plus heavy-tailed-noise and limited-support robustness tests (Tables 6–8). These examine additional questions about calibration stability and model misspecification.

E5.justification: v3 adds explicit seed-zero disclosure for the 401(k) experiment and examines calibration bootstrap counts of 10, 20, 50, and 100. The existing 50-trial experiments and 100 bootstrap replications for calibration-summary uncertainty remain; no increase in repetitions for the original results is established.

E6.justification: v3 adds ORF scores, interval scores, sensitivity and robustness results, and 401(k) effect and computational findings. For example, Table 2 reports IS95 of 2.27 for IMPspec and 2.99 for BayesIMP. Existing main-table RMSE/calibration values are largely retained with rounding. Table 2 drops explicit out-of-support calibration averages, although Figure 4 retains the corresponding curves.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 corrects the coverage check from each bootstrap posterior mean falling inside its own interval to a fixed plug-in estimate falling inside bootstrap intervals. This aligns the pseudocode with the separate plug-in estimator already described in v2's appendices. The GP priors, posterior formulas, training objectives, and principal inference procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method explanations, related work, and experimental narrative. It adds a Discussion section, consolidates evaluation-metric explanations, and moves experimental appendices ahead of the mathematical proofs. This is substantial restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: v3 changes document and plot typography, reformats algorithms, restructures Tables 1–2, and adds the 401(k) figure and several tables. Figure 4 gains ORF curves. The existing CBO convergence plot moves from v2's appendix Figure 7 to main-text Figure 5; it is not a new experiment.

R1.justification: Section 6 broadens Bayesian causal-inference context with Alaa and Van Der Schaar, Hahn et al., and Oganisian and Roy, and adds ORF-related positioning. It removes the previous GP predictive-calibration discussion and associated citations. The central relationship to Singh et al. and BayesIMP remains unchanged.

T1.justification: New Appendix A.4 derives posterior chi-squared, total-variation, and moment-error bounds under likelihood-ratio moment control, separating surrogate-likelihood error from Gaussian approximation error. Appendix C.2.5 also adds an argmin-consistency argument for calibration grid search. The original posterior-moment and calibration-estimator proofs are largely retained after relocation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evaluation of its central uncertainty claims through interval scores, misspecification and support tests, and documented real-data feasibility. Appendix A.4 and the Discussion also make approximation limits more explicit. Some qualifications remain: 401(k) cannot validate causal coverage, and Table 8's claim of best interval scores overlooks Sampling GP's slightly better limited-support IS90. These issues do not outweigh the broader gains in validation and transparency.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IMPspec research by the same authors. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds robustness and sensitivity results, plus a 401(k) data analysis with runtime and memory measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original simulation results, causal Bayesian optimization experiments including a healthcare simulator, and appendix ablations.

results.title: Interventional Processes For Causal Uncertainty Quantification

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add nearly tight constant-k junta-testing guarantees and a conditional improvement for AC0 learning. V2 also explicitly claims proper classical learning and a quadratic runtime improvement over ABR16. The original three main learning bounds and address-function lower bound remain.

C2.justification: V2 explains that the proposed AC0 improvement depends on open Question 24, identifies its potential polynomial-sample DNF consequence, and describes the restricted supporting case. Remark 9 acknowledges the classical learner's output-validity issue. The abstract also corrects 'juntas' to 'close to juntas' for QAC0, while retaining the earlier size-regime limitation.

D1.justification: Remark 9 newly documents O(2^k) output postprocessing and total runtime O(n^k 2^k k log(n)/ε²). Section 1.1 also explicitly specifies that circuit size counts multiqubit gates. These add computational details without documenting experimental implementation changes.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or experimental test scenarios for training or evaluation. The added junta-testing and AC0 problems receive theoretical treatment only.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates comparison methods. Table 1 retains the same theoretical comparisons against ABR16 and NPVY23; the newly cited methods support theoretical arguments.

E3.justification: Neither PDF reports empirical evaluation protocols or experimental settings. Sample and copy requirements describe theoretical algorithms rather than executed evaluation budgets.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, sensitivity analyses, or robustness tests. The spectral-concentration robustness argument and address-function example remain theoretical; new special-case proofs are assessed under T1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Concentration inequalities and success probabilities are mathematical guarantees rather than uncertainty reporting for observed results.

E6.justification: Table 1 retains the same three theoretical learning-complexity comparisons, and neither PDF contains measured performance results. New testing guarantees and revised theorem constants are theoretical changes assessed under T1.

M1.justification: V2 introduces a junta-state tester that enumerates k-qubit subsets, performs tomography, and certifies the reconstructed product states (Theorem 15). Remark 9 also adds clipping and normalization to produce a valid distribution from the classical learner. The existing Fourier-thresholding and classical-shadow learning procedures are retained.

P1.justification: V2 reorganizes the introduction into nested results subsections and expands Section 2 with quantum-information and Fourier/Pauli background. QAC0 background moves from v1 Section 4.1.1 to v2 Section 2.4, while its results become standalone Section 5. Repeated theorem statements, widespread prose edits, and the added author further revise the exposition.

P2.justification: The single-column design, Table 1's structure and caption, and both boxed algorithms are retained. V2 changes title typography and author layout and repositions existing displays as the text reflows. No figures or additional tables are introduced.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands connections to quantum certification and tomography through BOW19 and OW16, and to AC0 Fourier concentration through Håstad and the Kindler–Safra literature. It also adds a substantive comparison with ZLK+24, distinguishing its pure-state junta definition and bounded-gate learning guarantees.

T1.justification: V2 adds a distance proxy and its factor-two equivalence (Proposition 12), junta-testing upper and lower bounds with proofs (Theorems 15 and 17), and a conditional AC0 derivation with an epsilon = exp(-D) special case (Section 6). Remark 9 adds output-validity and runtime arguments. V2 Theorem 11 also tightens v1 Theorem 9's squared-error guarantee from 2ε²/4^n to ε²/4^n, although its proof still concludes the earlier bound.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens theoretical completeness: Remark 9 supplies the missing valid-distribution output construction, and Section 4.2 establishes the exponential copy requirements of constant-k junta testing alongside inexpensive promised-junta learning. Expanded preliminaries improve accessibility, and the AC0 extension clearly identifies its unproved dependency. The new constant-factor statement/proof mismatch in Theorem 11 is a limited rigor regression, but the substantive gains outweigh it while the original asymptotic learning bounds remain supported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Fourier/Pauli-based learning work. All 18 pages of v1 and 25 pages of v2 are readable, including the proofs, equations, Table 1, and references. Neither PDF contains an appendix.

after.justification: V2 adds mathematical results on junta testing and conditional AC0 learning, but reports no original empirical outcomes.

before.justification: V1 reports theoretical algorithms, complexity bounds, and proofs, without original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

results.title: Learning Junta Distributions, Quantum Junta States, and QAC$^0$ Circuits

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion add normalization against training-time distribution shift as a core contribution. The claimed state-of-the-art coverage expands from MNIST/Fashion-MNIST to include CIFAR10 and DVS Gesture. Earlier claims about stable training, early firing and average pooling are retained.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of distribution drift after initialization and the representational constraint addressed by affine parameters. It discusses dataset-dependent decoding choices and vanishing-gradient risks from strong temporal decay. It also qualifies CIFAR10 comparisons against larger conversion models and explains propagation-mode and GPU limitations relevant to hardware efficiency.

D1.justification: Appendix Tables 6–7 newly document dataset-specific losses, epoch budgets, augmentation and detailed layer dimensions. v2 also explains affine initialization and inference fusion, but omits v1's explicit Atan surrogate and warm-up/cosine schedule description. Appendix E newly claims accompanying code, weights and logs; their availability cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. v2 retains these and adds CIFAR10 natural-image classification and DVS Gesture event-based recognition, substantially expanding the represented visual and temporal domains.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 expands the retained benchmark comparisons with methods including Mostafa, Comsa, Göl tz, Sakemi and STiDi-BP, and introduces conversion comparators such as TTFS clamped, LC-TTFS and T2FSNN. v1's STDBP is retained under the label Zhang et al.; it is not a new comparator.

E3.justification: The reported MNIST/Fashion-MNIST optimizer changes from Adam to AdamW, and the Fashion-MNIST CNN changes from SCNN1 to SCNN5. v2 adds a MNIST CNN evaluation, depth experiments spanning 5–11 layers, and test-set-averaged inference stopping time as a latency metric. The added datasets also receive distinct training protocols.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the initialization/pooling analyses with normalization-induced distribution stability, separate normalization and affine ablations, and deeper-network tests. Figure 9 and Appendix Table 4 supply decay-function and gamma sweeps that v1 mentioned without reporting results. Appendix Table 5 extends component analyses across three datasets; v1's firing-rate-versus-iteration plot is not retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. The plotted distribution variances describe network signals, and v2's moving-average training curves do not introduce uncertainty estimates across runs.

E6.justification: v1 Table I lists 99.2% MNIST accuracy, conflicting with 98.2% in its prose; v2 reports 98.67% for the MLP and 99.48% for the CNN. Fashion-MNIST CNN accuracy changes from 91.61% to 92.90% with a different architecture. New results include CIFAR10 at 90.56%, DVS Gesture at 95.83%, and extensive latency, decoding and component results in Tables 2–5. Method and protocol changes preclude treating these as uniform same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: v2 adds weight normalization during training and a learnable affine transformation that is fused into synapses for inference (Section 3.3). It also replaces v1's Gaussian initializer with a uniform initializer having the same target variance. The renamed AMOS neuron retains the earlier firing-mask mechanism.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and substantial method and experiment prose are rewritten. Neuron background and derivations are reorganized into appendices, experiments receive separate accuracy/latency and component-analysis subsections, and terminology changes to AMOS and ETTFS-init. These changes substantially reshape the narrative beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v2 merges the separate benchmark tables into a wide comparison table and adds latency, decoding, settings and architecture tables. It redesigns the overview and diagnostic plots, adds a propagation schematic, and redraws or relocates existing explanatory figures, including the neuron diagram moved to Appendix A. Typography and page layout also change throughout.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises research positioning around neural coding and layer-by-layer versus step-by-step propagation. It adds relevant initialization, normalization and TTFS literature, and gives more specific limitations of earlier initialization approaches. v1's separate survey of SNN learning algorithms, including online training, is removed.

T1.justification: v2 revises the default-initialization premise and predicted current variance from 2/T in v1 Equation 12 to 1/(3T) in v2 Equation 13, and adds normalization/fusion formulas. The central one-spike variance derivation and target weight variance T/N remain, with much existing derivation material relocated to Appendix B.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for training stability and low latency through quantitative latency comparisons, deeper-network tests, and separate normalization/decoding ablations. CIFAR10 and DVS Gesture address v1's narrow empirical coverage, while the settings appendix improves implementation disclosure. These gains outweigh reporting defects, including Appendix C's linear/exponential decay mix-up and conflicting SCNN6 widths in Table 7, which still limit precision and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ETTFS research framework. Their text, equations, figures and tables support comparison. All pages were inspected, including v2's Appendices A–F; v1 contains no appendix.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification, latency and ablation results across four datasets, including additional analyses in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original MNIST and Fashion-MNIST classification results, training diagnostics, and initialization/pooling ablations.

results.title: Efficiently Training Time-to-First-Spike Spiking Neural Networks from Scratch

C1.justification: v3 replaces the speculative chain-of-flows contribution with multimask flows and empirical claims of up to eightfold fewer inference steps for BoW flows at comparable generative perplexity, plus improved multimask generation without reduced diversity. The single evaluation-bound contribution expands to two bounds supporting training and evaluation (abstract, introduction, and conclusion).

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of multimask benefits and expected computational scaling, and qualifies its evaluation claims: OT-coupled bound estimates are heuristic because the implicit coupling is inaccessible, and realistic-scale bound tightness remains unmeasured (Appendices C.3 and C.5). These qualifications go beyond v1's general discussion of source similarity and training stability.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-access statement, three implementation algorithms, and a detailed experimental recipe covering architecture, tokenization, schedules, AdamW settings, warm-up, clipping, hardware, and training time (Appendices B–C). For example, it specifies a 12-layer, 12-head, 768-dimensional transformer and H200 training. v1 lacks these implementation and access details.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates no datasets. v3 adds Morse-converted and character-level Shakespeare experiments, OpenWebText training and text generation, and perplexity evaluation on LAMBADA, WikiText2, WikiText103, PTB, and LM1B. Appendix C.5 additionally evaluates a small synthetic discrete distribution.

E2.justification: v3 introduces comparisons with SEDD and GPT-2 in Table 2, SEDD Absorb in Table 6, and standard-training controls and masked DFM-O/N/S variants in Table 3. DFM-S uses the MD4 loss; MD4 is not a separate additional row. v1 contains no evaluated baseline comparisons.

E3.justification: v3 adds experimental protocols absent from v1: 100k-step Shakespeare training, 400k-step OpenWebText training, batch and sequence-length controls, and comparisons across 8–1024 generation steps. Generation quality is evaluated on 10,240 samples using GPT-2 Large and Llama 3.1 8B, alongside perplexity bounds, entropy, jump counts, and timing measurements.

E4.justification: v3 tests sensitivity to OT regularization, solver choice, and OT batch size; investigates bound tightness through simulation and analytic examples; and checks agreement between dynamic and Kantorovich costs (Section 5 and Appendix C). It also adds diversity and metric-correlation analyses and qualitative generated samples. These investigations are absent from v1.

E5.justification: v3 introduces uncertainty reporting across the empirical evaluation, including plus/minus values for jump counts and standard deviations for generative perplexity, entropy, and ablations (Tables 1, 5, 10–12, 14, and 16). v1 has no such reporting. Repeated-training-run counts, seeds, and the procedure used to estimate these deviations are unspecified.

E6.justification: All empirical results are newly reported in v3. Examples include 85.47 versus 74.87 Morse-code jumps without versus with OT (Table 1), and GPT-2-Large generative perplexity of 141.92 for DFM-MMLM-OT versus 146.54 for DFM-O at 1024 steps (Table 3). Some duplicated BoW scores disagree between Tables 3 and 10; these are internal discrepancies, not changes from v1 results.

M1.justification: The original minibatch-OT formulation is retained, but v3 adds multimask flows with 50,257 special mask tokens distinct from data tokens and independently adjustable mask embeddings, enabling nontrivial OT couplings for masked-style generation (Section 3.2). It also introduces bound-based masked training variants alongside cross-entropy training (Section 5.2 and Appendix C.2).

P1.justification: Beyond adding scientific content, v3 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, and explanatory narrative. It moves Markov-chain background to Appendix D and the original bound derivation to Appendix A.2, relocates training stability into Section 7, removes the chains-of-flows section, and reorganizes the paper around theory, experiments, related work, and structured appendices.

P2.justification: v1 contains no results tables or graphical figures. v3 introduces 17 numbered tables, three formatted algorithms, and seven boxed generated-sample listings. It also changes typography, headers, text width, and appendix navigation, substantially revising how methods and evidence are displayed.

R1.justification: v3 adds a dedicated related-work section and substantially expands research positioning. It distinguishes its path-length objective from Shaul et al.'s kinetic-energy approach, acknowledges their concurrent bound derivation, and connects its bounds to Haxholli et al. and Shi et al. It also discusses newer block-diffusion and scaled masked-diffusion work.

T1.justification: The original transport identity and KL upper bound are retained, with the latter becoming Theorem 4.2. v3 adds an exact forward/reverse-velocity KL identity, an entropy identity and second perplexity bound, precise-likelihood expressions, masked-bound equivalence derivations, and a proof of multimask predictive time independence (Theorem 4.1, Propositions 4.3–4.4, and Appendices A.3–A.6).

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the practical case left untested in v1: controlled language experiments assess generation benefits, computational overhead, bound usefulness, and sensitivity to implementation choices. New proofs and detailed implementation information also improve scrutiny and reproducibility. Inconsistent duplicated BoW scores, unexplained standard-deviation estimation, and heuristic OT-bound evaluation limit precision, but do not outweigh the substantial gain in evidence and technical completeness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, title, transport formulation, and original perplexity bound. The complete main texts and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 reports original language-model experiments, computational timings, ablations, and a Monte Carlo simulation in Section 5 and Appendix C. Appendix E supplies generated text samples.

before.justification: v1 presents theoretical formulations, proofs in Appendix A, and proposed future work. It reports no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

results.title: Minibatch Optimal Transport and Perplexity Bound Estimation in Discrete Flow Matching

C1.justification: The abstract retains the exponential-separation claim, but the introduction substantially strengthens its quantitative scope: a near-linear classical query lower bound for fixed k, constant precision, logarithmic conditioning, and 3-sparse matrices replace the weaker original parameters.

C2.justification: Section 2 newly explains why both reductions are retained: k-Forrelation gives stronger bounds, whereas the random-walk argument is described as simpler, more self-contained, and potentially useful for its graph insights. The original interpretation of the graph construction remains.

D1.justification: Neither version provides implementation, hardware, experimental runtime, or code/data access information. The new circuit parameters specify the mathematical reduction rather than an implemented experiment.

E1.justification: Neither version uses datasets or tasks for training or empirical evaluation. The newly introduced k-Forrelation problem serves as a theoretical reduction source.

E2.justification: Neither version experimentally evaluates comparison methods. The analytical benchmarks from Costa et al. and Shao and Montanaro remain unchanged in equations (1) and (2).

E3.justification: No experimental protocols are reported in either version. The changed precision, sparsity, conditioning, and query counts concern theoretical constructions and guarantees.

E4.justification: Neither version contains empirical ablations, robustness tests, or case studies. The retained spectral analyses and newly added approximation analysis are mathematical proof material.

E5.justification: Neither reports experimental repetitions, seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical estimates. Section 3's independent samples, Hoeffding inequality, and failure probabilities establish theoretical algorithmic guarantees.

E6.justification: Neither version reports measured performance or empirical findings. The strengthened asymptotic query bounds are theoretical results assessed under T1.

M1.justification: v3 uses a graph-adjacency construction and oracle simulation for its hardness reduction. v5 retains this and adds a different algorithmic reduction in Section 3: encode a k-Forrelation circuit using HHL's block-matrix construction, simulate sampling/query access, and recover circuit-output information through sampling.

P1.justification: Most original prose is retained. v5 adds transitions accommodating two reductions, introduces Section 3, and reorganizes v3 Sections 2.2–2.4 into Sections 4.1–4.3. This is a focused structural revision rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: The page format changes from US Letter to A4, with corresponding whitespace and page-break changes. Equations and references are redistributed while the single-column presentation remains. Neither version contains figures or tables.

R1.justification: v5 adds references to Aaronson–Ambainis, Bansal–Sinha, Sherstov–Storozhenko–Wu, and Simon, and explicitly builds on HHL's circuit reduction. Most existing positioning remains. The introductory reference to reducing from Simon's problem is inconsistent with the k-Forrelation proof actually presented.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 changes from an Ω(n^(1/12)) lower bound with κ≤c ln² n, 4-sparsity, and ε≤1/(c ln^(2.5) n), to c^(-1)n^(1-1/k) with κ≤c ln n, 3-sparsity, and ε≤2^(-ck). Section 3 adds the k-Forrelation/HHL reduction and an approximation-to-total-variation argument. The earlier random-walk lemmas and auxiliary proofs remain.

improvement.justification: The additional circuit reduction supplies substantial support for stronger fixed-k separations and removes v3's requirement that precision shrink with matrix size, while preserving the original proof material. These are substantial theoretical gains. Corrections remain necessary: page 12 contains incorrect intermediate normalization equalities, and Theorem 1's uniform-in-k constants are not fully reconciled with Section 3's fixed-k analysis. These defects limit the statement as written but do not erase the substantial fixed-k advance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same linear-systems separation result and are readable throughout, including all auxiliary proofs and references. Neither contains a separately labeled appendix; no essential comparison material is missing.

after.justification: v5 remains entirely theoretical. Its additional circuit construction and probabilistic sampling analysis are proof arguments, not reported empirical experiments.

before.justification: v3 reports mathematical reductions, spectral analysis, and proofs, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

results.title: An Exponential Separation Between Quantum and Quantum-Inspired Classical Algorithms for Linear Systems

C1.justification: The core claims about generating complete solutions through RL and using a Transformer-based GNN remain. v3 adds theoretically grounded learning and search strategies to the explicit contributions and strengthens the larger-dataset accuracy claim from roughly a 1% gap to below 1%.

C2.justification: v3 introduces substantial interpretations of reward bias, neighborhood size, and the different feasibility/quality roles of MPNN and Transformer components. It removes v1's detailed ablation-specific explanations of critic spikes and phase-layer failures, along with the conclusion's continuous-variable extension discussion. Integer-only evaluation and the lack of optimality guarantees remain acknowledged elsewhere.

D1.justification: Appendices C and E add training pseudocode, hardware and software versions, RMSprop hyperparameters, 64-instance concurrent training, component depths, and implementation-source links. These substantially expand reproducibility information. The generation parameters in v3 Table 4 were already supplied in v1 Table 1.

E1.justification: v3 adds D50×20 and D300×100 alongside the retained D9×18 and D100×50 datasets. These extend the tested problem-size regimes, while retaining the same synthetic generation family and optimization task with exclusively integer variables.

E2.justification: v1 Table 2 compares against Gurobi, M_MLP, and M_CNN. v3 Table 1 retains these comparators and adds classic local search, initialized with the RL agent's first feasible solution to compare subsequent search performance.

E3.justification: Main comparisons retain a 100-second limit, but v3 includes a 600-second Gurobi reference when defining the best-known objective and introduces #win. D9×18 training increases from 500 to 5,000 updates. Added experiments vary β and action magnitudes; the neighborhood study uses 300 seconds and 10,000 updates.

E4.justification: v3 adds reward-bias sensitivity experiments and a neighborhood-size study testing movement magnitudes. Table 3 also replaces v1's eight PE/PT/SL combinations with a revised selection that additionally removes the Transformer and MPNN separately, testing their respective contributions to solution quality and feasibility.

E5.justification: Neither version reports seeds, repeated-training-run counts, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Both use 100 test instances per dataset; the added result rows do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Results are substantially replaced and expanded. On D100×50, v1 Table 2 reports a 1.33% gap for the proposed solver; v3 Table 1 reports 0.55%, 0.38%, and 0.34% for β = 1, 0.6, and 0.3. M_CNN feasibility changes from 100% to 0% across those later settings. These accompany method and protocol changes, so they are not same-setting performance gains or losses.

M1.justification: v3 substantially replaces both phases' rewards with violation-based and objective-dependent terms controlled by β. Transformer/Critic inputs change from objt to objr and objb, training gains a phase1 warm-up, and phase2 search accepts only feasible, nonworsening moves. These change training and inference procedures, beyond the added pseudocode.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, methodology, and results discussion are extensively rewritten. v3 introduces nested background/method subsections and explicit research questions, shortens the conclusion, and redistributes reward explanations, search pseudocode, and generation details into appendices. This is substantial narrative reorganization beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: v3 restructures the main results into a wide table with dataset columns and β groups, redesigns the ablation table, and adds a neighborhood-results table. The architecture figure changes its inputs, the reward diagram is revised and moved to Appendix B, and a new two-panel reward plot is added. Headers, typography, and appendix layouts also change.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations supporting rounding, LP theory, local search, and neural optimization, including Cont and Heidari, Shaw, and Son et al., while removing the Zhang et al. 2023 survey. The related-work taxonomy remains, while the novelty statement becomes more specifically framed around full end-to-end RL for integer MILP.

T1.justification: v3 adds Proposition 1 and Appendix A's formal feasible-set proof of objr ≤ objopt ≤ obj′ < objb, extending the interval argument used informally in v1. It also corrects the equilibration-scaling justification from a nonnegative to a positive multiplier. The theoretical addition does not establish convergence or optimality of the solver.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important gaps in v1's validation: local search supplies a direct search control, while bias, neighborhood, and MPNN/Transformer studies test specific design choices. Appendices C and E substantially improve training transparency and reproducibility information. These gains outweigh the loss of some earlier ablation discussion, although evaluation remains confined to synthetic integer MILPs and lacks run-level uncertainty reporting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RL-MILP solver. Their complete text, equations, figures, and tables support comparison, including v3 Appendices A–E. v1 has no appendices, and material moved into v3's appendices can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 Section 4 and Tables 1–3 report original solver comparisons, reward-bias and neighborhood experiments, and architectural ablations.

before.justification: v1 Section 4 and Tables 2–3 report original experiments comparing solvers and ablating architectural components on generated MILP instances.

results.title: RL-SPH: Learning to Achieve Feasible Solutions for Integer Linear Programs

C1.justification: V5's conclusion claims theoretically guaranteed feasibility. V7 instead emphasizes theoretical reward–feasibility alignment and empirically observed 100% feasibility. Its introduction also expands the stated contributions to comparisons against seven baselines, cross-problem generalization, distribution shifts, and MIPLIB evaluation, substantially revising the scope and qualification of the central claims.

C2.justification: V7 adds interpretations of baseline failures, reward prioritization, and training efficiency. It discusses poor solution quality on scpk4 and bppc8-02, implications of unseen constraint types, excessive reward bias, and computational bottlenecks at extreme scales. The earlier solver-integration suboptimality caveat is retained, while applicability boundaries and future optimality improvements receive substantial additional treatment.

D1.justification: V7 adds model parameter counts, explicitly lists the 15 diving and six rounding implementations, explains Transformer token construction more fully, and supplies implementation references and training details for the added baselines. The existing hardware, software versions, optimizer settings, principal training budgets, and RL-SPH training times are retained.

E1.justification: The five synthetic problem families are retained. V7 adds cross-problem IS/MVC training and transfer, 17 MIPLIB instances including mixed variable types, BA-to-ER graph distribution transfer, and SC tests at unseen sizes and densities. These substantially broaden the evaluated populations and generalization scenarios.

E2.justification: V7 adds standalone comparisons with DDIM, DiffILO, and PAS, with PAS evaluated on CA and IS, plus Gurobi comparisons in Appendix H.3. Diving and Rounding are merely renamed DHF and RHF with the same constituent families. The earlier SCIP and PAS+SCIP comparison is retained as Table 16.

E3.justification: V7 introduces first-feasible-solution timing, new E2EPH evaluation budgets of 300/300/30 seconds for SC/CA/IS, controlled joint training with MVC resized to 1,500 variables, and 100-second MIPLIB evaluations. It also changes the reported NBI objective-coefficient generator from randint[-10,1] to randint[-10,-1]. This documents a setting revision without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained architecture ablation, v7 tests whether feasibility-aware variable selection accelerates feasibility and whether trajectories satisfy the theoretical reward conditions. It adds presolving ablations, transfer and robustness tests, neighborhood-ratio and movement-magnitude sensitivities, attention and training analyses, and extends the reward-bias comparison from alpha=1,2 to alpha=1,2,5.

E5.justification: V7 replaces several asymmetric, zero-truncated spreads with symmetric reporting, such as IS primal gap 0.14 with +0.59/-0.14 becoming 0.14±0.59. It also removes v5's explicit statement identifying the spreads as NumPy standard deviations. SCIP randomization remains zero; no increase in independent repetitions is documented.

E6.justification: V7 adds extensive timing, comparator, transfer, MIPLIB, and sensitivity results while retaining the original binary benchmark means and SCIP integration results. Newly reported direct IS/MVC transfer fails at 0% feasibility, whereas joint training achieves 100%. Headline averages change from 44×/2.3× to 28.6×/2.6× for primal gap/integral under expanded comparisons, and bias-ablation values are revised; these do not demonstrate same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The core two-phase actor–critic and Transformer search remains. However, v7 revises phase-one reward gating from nonnegative to strictly positive constraint improvement, corrects bound conditions, and changes Appendix C's training pseudocode to retain the stay flag until Tstay. Appendix I.7 also introduces tested larger action-space variants; naming the architecture ILP-GT alone is not a method change.

P1.justification: The introduction and contributions are extensively rewritten, the architecture receives the ILP-GT name, and the methodology is reorganized. Background and related work move into Appendices D and E, the solver comparison moves to Appendix H, and substantial main-text and appendix discussion sections reshape the narrative around standalone feasibility.

P2.justification: V7 adopts a two-column main-text layout, redraws explanatory diagrams, expands Table 1 with timing and NBI rows, and adds optimization curves, trajectory plots, attention heatmaps, and training curves. Retained material is also reformatted: the architecture ablation changes table orientation, while solver results and reward illustrations are relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: Appendix E substantially expands the former related-work section with DDIM, DiffILO, and NeuRewriter, among other additions. It positions RL-SPH relative to solver-independent feasibility methods, neural local rewriting, and LNS, and explains complementary initializer roles. This changes the research positioning beyond bibliographic updates or relocation.

T1.justification: Appendix A substantially replaces the central proof: v5 infers convergence to zero from monotonicity, whereas v7 introduces a claimed minimum positive increment delta and a finite bound T=ceil(-D0/delta). Appendix I.4 adds a search-complexity derivation. The minimum-increment justification remains incomplete for the generally real-valued coefficients permitted by the formulation.

improvement.justification: V7 substantially addresses v5's limited validation of standalone feasibility through direct comparisons with newer learning methods, empirical checks of reward-condition adherence, and transfer tests that expose failures as well as successes. These strengthen the evidential basis and clarify applicability beyond the original benchmarks. The feasibility claim is also better qualified. The proof's minimum-increment justification remains incomplete, and uncertainty reporting becomes less explicit, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical scrutiny and disclosure.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RL-SPH research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v7 retains original empirical results and reports additional baseline comparisons, generalization experiments, MIPLIB evaluations, and sensitivity analyses in Section 4 and Appendices H and I.

before.justification: v5 reports original benchmark comparisons, SCIP integration experiments, architecture ablations, and reward-bias experiments in Section 4 and Appendix F.
