E3.justification: V2 introduces paired pre-discussion validation trials with Full Profile accuracy at least 80% and Hidden Profile accuracy at most 20%, plus model-size and reasoning-budget comparisons such as GPT-5 Minimal versus Medium Reasoning. Existing task inputs also change: Table 1's mudslide blocks the driveway in v1 but walking trails in v2, limiting direct comparison of the revised evacuation results.

E4.justification: The five cooperation–contradiction interventions are retained, while v2 adds zero-shot chain-of-thought and explicit information-asymmetry tests in Table A2. Section 4.3.1 also extends the conversation analysis with early-consensus timing for LLMs and human discussion-length information.

E5.justification: The cross-model benchmark changes from 30 Hidden and 50 Complete Profile repetitions in v1 Section 5.2 to 10 per condition in v2 Section 5.2. Fisher tests and mean ± s.e.m. reporting remain, but uncertainty presentation changes: v2's aggregate model chart includes error bars, whereas Table A1 omits the prompting uncertainty previously shown in v1 Figure 4.

E6.justification: Under the respective evacuation setups, GPT-4.1 Hidden Profile post-discussion accuracy is 0.200 in v1 and 0.233 in v2; Full Profile pre-discussion accuracy is 0.433 and 0.733. These are revised-setting results, not established same-setting gains. V1's steadily increasing tone-series accuracy is replaced by nonmonotonic results in Table A1, including 0.017 for Conflictual. V2 additionally reports 57/200 successful task validations and extensive new aggregate benchmark results.

M1.justification: V2 Section 5.1.2 adds an automatic benchmark-construction procedure: GPT-4.1 generates candidates, evaluates their Full and Hidden Profile solvability, and filters them using accuracy thresholds. V1 constructs and adapts tasks without this generation-and-selection pipeline. The underlying multi-agent discussion framework remains broadly similar.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion around HiddenBench. The framework/setup/experiments sequence becomes a formalization followed by Study 1 and Study 2; mathematical exposition is condensed, terminology changes from Complete to Full Profile, and the appendix is extensively reorganized and expanded.

P2.justification: V2 substantially redesigns Figure 2 and replaces v1's task-by-model heatmaps with an aggregate horizontal-bar comparison containing performance-gap columns. It adds a generation-pipeline diagram, combines the earlier tone instructions and plotted experiment into Appendix Table A1, and adds Table A2. The document template and appendix presentation also change extensively.

R1.justification: The Hidden Profile and social-psychology foundations remain. V2 adds Lu et al.'s meta-analysis, Stasser and Titus (1987), Wei et al. (2022), and newer multi-agent framework/scaling references. It removes Lewis et al. (2022) and much of v1's exploration–exploitation and human–AI future-work bibliography, updating the supporting literature without replacing the central intellectual grounding.

T1.justification: The central information-distribution model, Hidden Profile condition, and average/majority aggregation rules are retained in condensed form. V2 Figure 4 introduces an explicit mathematical criterion for strong collective reasoning: Yfull > 0.8 and Ypost − Ypre > 0.4 × (Yfull − Ypre). No new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The decisive gain is the documented generation-and-screening procedure: v2 explicitly checks generated tasks for high Full Profile and low Hidden Profile accuracy, strengthening the separation of individual task difficulty from distributed-information failure. Complete generation instructions and broader evaluations make the benchmark substantially more reusable and diagnostically useful. These gains outweigh lost per-task and implementation detail. A material weakness remains: Section 4.3.2 dismisses informing agents about asymmetry despite Table A2 reporting 0.367 accuracy versus the default 0.233, without uncertainty supporting that dismissal.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Hidden Profile research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, mathematical content, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

after.justification: V2 reports original human and LLM experiments, task-generation validation outcomes, expanded benchmark evaluations, and additional prompting results in Appendix A.2.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments across six LLMs and nine tasks, a 96-participant human study, and prompting experiments in Sections 4–5.

results.title: Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information in Multi-Agent LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's new fourth contribution, and conclusion explicitly add the claim that HIDDENBENCH can guide a practical communication protocol that substantially improves collective reasoning. This expands the central contribution beyond the retained benchmark and failure diagnosis.

C2.justification: Section 6.2 replaces the broadly presented Goldilocks interpretation with model-dependent effects, including harmful dissent for Gemini-2.5-Flash. Section 6.3 replaces the specific inference that ineffective summarization rules out forgetting with an interpretation acknowledging model-dependent summarization benefits and integration ability. Section 3.1 also adds an argument for real-world applicability without new real-world evaluation.

D1.justification: Section 4 replaces the anonymous repository link with named GitHub and Hugging Face links for the benchmark, evaluation suite, and generated corpus. Section 4.2 clarifies threshold averaging, and a new footnote explains that Reveal-All mechanically appends facts to first-round messages. These clarify existing implementation rather than establish procedural changes.

E1.justification: The 65-task benchmark, human-study scenarios, and group-size task variants remain. The expanded diagnostic experiments sample existing HIDDENBENCH tasks; the real-world examples added in Section 3.1 motivate applicability without adding evaluated domains or task requirements.

E2.justification: The main benchmark model roster and existing comparison procedures remain. Table 5 retains the same dissent compositions, and Table 6 retains Baseline, Reveal-All, and Secretary. Additional model backbones expand the experimental settings; the new proposed protocol is compared against the existing unstructured baseline.

E3.justification: Table 6 replaces the three-task GPT-4.1 evaluation with 18 tasks, comprising three manually crafted and 15 randomly sampled tasks, evaluated using GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash. Table 5 expands to five model backbones. Section 6.4 adds a four-agent, three-model evaluation on the same 18-task sample.

E4.justification: Dissent sensitivity is investigated across five models instead of GPT-4.1 alone, and disclosure versus summarization receives broader testing. New Section 6.4 tests whether the diagnosed failures can guide an effective communication intervention without explicitly revealing information asymmetry or forcing complete disclosure.

E5.justification: The reported ± uncertainty values disappear from Tables 5–6, and new Table 7 reports only point estimates. Section 6.4 specifies five runs per task for its new experiment. Existing benchmark session counts, Figure 3 standard errors, and verification significance tests remain; this does not establish reduced runs for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Table 5 retains GPT-4.1 mean accuracies and adds four models' results. Table 6 replaces three-task GPT-4.1 baseline/Reveal-All/Secretary accuracies of 0.233/0.967/0.100 with 18-task values of 0.037/0.926/0.241, so these are not same-setting performance changes. New Table 7 reports structured accuracies of 0.800, 0.727, and 0.743 for GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Flash-Lite, alongside baselines of 0.037, 0.173, and 0.043.

M1.justification: New Section 6.4 introduces an Exchange-then-Decide communication procedure: two rounds of sharing decision-relevant facts and challenging the leading option, followed by evidence and uncertainty summaries before voting. This adds a substantive coordination mechanism beyond v3's dissent, disclosure, and summarization interventions.

P1.justification: Several introduction, benchmark-motivation, interpretation, and conclusion paragraphs are rewritten. Section 6.4 and acknowledgements are added, and affiliation ordering and publication-header text change. The overall section sequence and all appendix text remain substantially stable.

P2.justification: Tables 5–6 are restructured to display results across models, Table 7 is added, and existing tables shift within the ablation section. The three figures and Table 1 retain their displays, and the basic document layout remains unchanged.

R1.justification: Sections 2–3 add connections to multitask transfer, distributed knowledge, transactive memory, and real-world coordination, citing works including Wu et al., Fagin et al., and Wegner. Pathak et al. and Dibangoye and Buffet are removed. The central positioning of HIDDENBENCH relative to previous evaluations remains.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2's information partitions, decision functions, aggregation rules, and Hidden Profile conditions are unchanged. Added conceptual motivation and removal of the introduction's informal policy-misalignment statement do not change formal reasoning or proofs.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the central diagnostic evidence: previously narrow GPT-4.1 ablations gain broader model testing and an 18-task bottleneck evaluation, revealing exceptions that qualify the earlier interpretations. Section 6.4 also demonstrates a practical intervention without forced disclosure, strengthening the benchmark's usefulness. Clearer implementation explanations and resource links help reproducibility. Removing uncertainty from Tables 5–6 and omitting it from Table 7 weakens statistical reporting, but the broader, better-qualified evidence and constructive validation provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable 19-page versions of the same HIDDENBENCH paper. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison; Appendices A.1–A.4 are unchanged.

after.justification: v4 retains the original human and LLM experiments and reports expanded diagnostic studies and a new structured communication experiment in Sections 6.2–6.4.

before.justification: v3 reports original LLM benchmark and ablation results, plus human experiments involving 96 participants described in Appendix A.3 and analyzed in Section 3.2.

results.title: Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information in Multi-Agent LLMs

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes a theoretical uncertainty-reduction contribution and results for one LLaMA student–teacher pair. V3 emphasizes cross-family state-of-the-art performance, robust self-correction, sample efficiency, and approaching or exceeding SimpleRL-Zero with 60x less compute. The formal-proof contribution disappears, while answer-format preservation and deployment without additional inference overhead remain central claims.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations linking attention to planning and execution, smaller gradient norms to optimization efficiency, balanced feedback to avoiding indiscriminate agreement, and model differences to receptivity and alignment data. It acknowledges that counterfactual robustness has not been investigated at scale. The limitations discussion is substantially rewritten, reducing v1's explicit dataset-generalization and critique-generation-bias caveats.

D1.justification: Appendix A newly documents ZeRO-3, AdamW, batch size 64, cosine scheduling, warmup 0.1, sequence length 8192, and a default single epoch. Appendix C explains diagnostic computations and attention aggregation. Appendix E describes a code.zip archive, configurations, scripts, LLaMA-Factory integration, and README instructions. The supplied PDFs establish this disclosure, but cannot verify the archive's availability or contents.

E1.justification: The original training datasets and benchmark coverage are retained. V3 adds AIME24 in Table 3 and OpenMathInstruct2 diagnostics in Appendix C, including testing with factual versus irrelevant critiques. These extend mathematical evaluation and self-correction scenarios within the existing reasoning focus.

E2.justification: V3 introduces an RL comparison against SimpleRL-Zero in Table 3, substantially broadening the comparison beyond supervised and critique-based fine-tuning. It explicitly uses the comparator's official reported scores, rather than claiming a new replication. Table 8 also adds direct teacher-model reference results; the original SFT, Distilled SFT, and CFT comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce S1.1, Mixtral, and OLMo configurations, a base-LLaMA RL comparison, fixed-size 25K correctness-mixture controls, and training curves across five epochs. Appendix C introduces 500-sample entropy/gradient probes and 50-sample attention analyses with critique-containing inputs. These are new experimental designs; newly disclosed default hyperparameters do not establish changes to the retained original experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained critique-removal and learning-rate ablations, v3 adds student/teacher sensitivity studies, correctness-mixture controls, epoch and loss trajectories, entropy/gradient diagnostics, attention analyses, and a counterfactual-critique case study. Figure 4 extends critique removal to S1.1, and Appendix D adds an isomorphism example. The original MetaMathQA results and qualitative examples are retained elsewhere.

E5.justification: V1 provides point estimates without seed counts or formal uncertainty reporting. V3 newly states that performance is averaged over three random seeds, adds paired t-tests in Table 9, gradient-norm standard deviations in Table 10, and 95% confidence intervals over 50 samples in Figure 9. This establishes expanded reporting, not an explicit increase in training runs.

E6.justification: The original benchmark tables retain their scores, but v3 adds extensive results: S1.1 achieves 61.8 versus CFT's 49.6 on MATH500, and the new base-model RL comparison reports averages of 11.9 versus 10.6, while CGD trails on AMC23. New diagnostic results and some revised LLaMA no-critique bars also appear. Gains are not universal: Table 1 gives S1.1 general averages of 33.4 for CGD and 33.5 for Distilled SFT.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and Equation 1 retain the same student-answer generation, teacher critique and refinement, and negative-log-likelihood training on the full input triplet. V3 explicitly clarifies prompt-only, single-pass deployment; the PDFs do not establish a procedural change from v1's already claimed deployment without additional inference cost.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contributions, method explanation, results narrative, limitations, and conclusion receive substantial rewriting. Section 3 becomes an overview and training-objective presentation, limitations precede the conclusion, and the supplement is organized into setup, experiments, diagnostics, examples, and code instructions. Existing Bayesian discussion and MetaMathQA results are relocated rather than deleted.

P2.justification: V3 relocates the overview and method-comparison diagrams, removes the optimization cartoon, redraws the benchmark plots, and expands the critique ablation into two student panels. Table 1 gains student blocks, Table 2 wraps beside prose, and new result tables, training curves, attention plots, and heatmaps substantially change the visual presentation. Headers, typography, captions, and appendix layouts also change.

R1.justification: Although much of the related-work section remains, v3 substantially repositions CGD as an efficient alternative to RL, adding discussion of DeepSeekMath, DeepSeek-R1, and SimpleRL-Zero. New model and alignment-data references support its architectural interpretations. The Swamy et al. likelihood reference disappears with the formal analysis; the corrected CFT bibliography still denotes the same prior work.

T1.justification: V3 removes v1's Lemma 1, its Jensen-based proof, and the associated KL optimization derivations in Equations 2–9. The proof's concluding inequality reverses the implication of its displayed Jensen step. The Bayesian equation is retained in Appendix C.5, with an added unnormalized-scoring interpretation; it is not a replacement proof of the removed guarantee.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially improves scrutiny of student/teacher dependence and training robustness, supplies previously missing reproducibility details, and introduces statistical reporting. Removing v1's flawed KL proof also resolves an important theoretical defect. These gains outweigh significant qualifications: critique-conditioned diagnostics do not establish the mechanism of prompt-only deployment, some new performance summaries overstate their tables, and the abstract's 60x compute claim lacks transparent reconciliation with Section 4.2.1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CGD research work despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V3 retains those original experiments and adds student/teacher comparisons, controlled ablations, and quantitative diagnostics. Its separately attributed SimpleRL-Zero scores are not the sole empirical evidence.

before.justification: V1 reports original CGD and baseline experiments across mathematical reasoning and general-capability benchmarks, with ablations and qualitative examples.

results.title: Critique-Guided Distillation for Robust Reasoning via Refinement

C1.justification: The central claims of transform-general, complex-valued IG and its axiomatic guarantees remain. The introduction refines the contribution as a unified transformed-coordinate framework, explicitly claims six instantiated transform families, and adds the claim that domain choice affects quantitative behavior.

C2.justification: The new Discussion interprets varying benchmark rankings as evidence for task-dependent domain choice and explicitly distinguishes masking-based faithfulness from semantic usefulness to practitioners. Most baseline, integration-path, invertibility, and domain-expertise caveats already appeared in v2 and are expanded or relocated.

D1.justification: v3 specifies Haar wavelets and the cepstrum transform for new evaluations, and expands the LLM-use disclosure to include minor coding assistance. It removes standalone real-domain pseudocode. Existing complex-domain algorithms, FastICA settings, synthetic-signal generation details, hardware disclosure, and code-access information remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds classification evaluations on PAM, Boiler, Epilepsy, Wafer, and Freezer, plus AudioMNIST digit and gender classification. This substantially expands coverage beyond the retained PPG, Siena EEG, and synthetic mechanistic/forecasting examples.

E2.justification: New comparisons include TIMEX++ and TIMING in Table 2, and FreqRISE plus VIL-based LRP and IG in Table 3. Table 3 explicitly sources comparator scores from prior work. Figure 6 also adds a direct CDIG/VIL attribution comparison; the original time-IG and random controls remain.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include CPD with average and zero substitutions, and AudioMNIST faithfulness/complexity benchmarking across four explanation domains. The existing PPG intervention percentages and EEG single-component insertion/deletion procedures are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds systematic comparisons testing how explanation-domain choice affects faithfulness and complexity: Fourier versus Cepstrum in Table 2 and four domains in Table 3. Appendix E also adds an empirical CDIG/VIL equivalence illustration. The earlier mechanistic probe and case analyses remain.

E5.justification: Unlike v2's point estimates and subject-averaged scores, v3 Table 2 reports means and standard errors over five random repetitions. This reporting is limited to the new CPD comparison; it does not establish additional runs of the retained experiments.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 add extensive CPD and AudioMNIST results. For example, PAM average-substitution CPD is 1.183 for Cepstrum versus 0.463 for TIMING. Domain rankings vary across datasets and tasks. The numerical contents of v2 Tables 1–2 are retained in v3 Tables 4–5.

M1.justification: The transformed-coordinate IG procedure, complex-gradient formulation, integration path, and baseline approach remain unchanged. Additional transform choices instantiate the existing general framework; removing standalone real-domain pseudocode does not establish removal of that functionality.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, and contribution list are substantially rewritten. Applications become qualitative subsections within Experiments, quantitative evaluation receives dedicated main-text treatment, and a Discussion section is added. The validation overview is condensed and appendices are reordered.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout, with widespread figure resizing and relocation. Figure 1's panels are rearranged, three tables and a VIL comparison figure are added, and the formerly rotated EEG plots are displayed horizontally together. Existing result tables are retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v3 substantially revises positioning by acknowledging MIX's transformed-coordinate IG and Schröder et al.'s latent-feature motivation. It adds TIMING, FreqRISE, FlexTIME, and a transform-coverage comparison table. The generic saliency-method overview and its Bach/GradCAM++ references are removed.

T1.justification: Appendix F adds the explicit transform definition T(x)=F^{-1}(log(F(x))), and Remark 4.4 identifies the Haar-DWT specialization with MIX's view-space IG. The complex-IG proof, completeness argument, CNN derivation, and DFT/VIL equivalence derivation remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v2's limited comparative validation by adding broader benchmarks, named competing methods, and repeated-run uncertainty reporting. Clearer acknowledgment of prior transformed-coordinate IG and the distinction between faithfulness and semantic utility also improve assessment of the contribution. New benchmark implementation details remain sparse, and real-domain pseudocode is lost, but these limitations do not outweigh the stronger evidence and positioning.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Cross-domain Integrated Gradients work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds five-dataset CPD comparisons and AudioMNIST digit/gender attribution benchmarks.

before.justification: v2 reports original mechanistic probes, cross-domain attribution examples, and quantitative PPG and EEG insertion/deletion results, including in Appendix F.

results.title: Time series saliency maps: Explaining models across multiple domains

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: adaptive motif tokenization, lightweight conditional decoding, and meaningful token representations. The headline 36% forecasting improvement, 1990% efficiency improvement, and up-to-44% decoding improvement are unchanged. New experiments primarily support existing claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations linking noise resistance to coarse quantization, the Weather ablation disadvantage to unusually high compression, and handling unfamiliar patterns to single-sample fallback. It also discusses non-stationary applicability and possible overfitting with higher-order decoding. Some new robustness wording overgeneralizes: Figure 17 shows that superiority over Chronos depends on dataset and noise level.

D1.justification: v2 largely refers readers to Chronos hyperparameters. v3 Table 8 explicitly lists model dimensions, layers, heads, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, dropout, batch size, and training steps. Appendix B additionally identifies A6000 profiling hardware, inclusion of tokenization in timing, CPU memory use, pipelining guidance, and expanded computational budgets. These are substantial disclosure improvements, not evidence that retained training settings changed.

E1.justification: The Chronos training corpus and five forecasting benchmarks are retained. v3 Appendix C.6 extends their test scenarios with Gaussian noise on all five benchmarks and linear/exponential trends and transients on Electricity. This expands input conditions within the existing task and domains.

E2.justification: v3 substantially expands the central comparison by adding patch-based Chronos models with patch lengths 4 and 8 across five model sizes in Table 3. It also evaluates discretization-only models in Table 13. Earlier comparators are retained, including Moirai, spelled Morai in v2.

E3.justification: New protocols include non-overlapping patch baselines trained with MSE loss, a 37-bin control without motif discovery, Gaussian noise up to sigma 0.3, trend perturbations up to absolute alpha 0.5, and transients with 1% probability and amplitude 3. These substantially extend experimental controls and testing procedures; retained forecasting horizons and splits are unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds an ablation separating discretization from motif representation in Appendix C.2, controlled noise/trend/transient robustness tests in C.6, and motif-hierarchy analysis in C.5. These address new questions about the source of forecasting gains, behavior under disturbances, and vocabulary structure. Earlier preprocessing, token-occurrence, training-size, and embedding analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 provides no across-seed uncertainty estimates. v3 Appendix B reports six-seed training experiments and MSE standard deviations for selected small motif-based, single-sample Chronos, and patch-based Chronos models. It also discloses seed 2024 and profiling with two warm-up and two measurement runs per batch, reporting timing standard deviations below 2%. These checks do not cover every configuration.

E6.justification: Headline results and existing comparator scores are retained, while Tables 3 and 13 and Appendix C.6 add substantial comparison, ablation, and robustness findings. For example, Table 17 reports clean/transient MSE of 0.261/0.398 for Chronos and 0.170/0.203 for the proposed method, with compression falling from 3.95 to 3.38. These are newly reported perturbation results, not performance changes between versions.

M1.justification: The quantization-plus-BPE tokenizer, T5 next-token objective, and analytic conditional decoder remain unchanged in Equations (1)–(6) and Appendix A. The added patch-based and discretization-only models are experimental comparators. Newly explaining fallback to individual samples does not introduce a new algorithmic step.

P1.justification: v3 locally restructures Section 5.2 into patch-based Chronos and broader literature comparisons, tightens the representation discussion, clarifies decoding terminology, removes the Outlook, and adds an Impact statement. The main section sequence and much of the existing prose remain, so this is a limited narrative revision.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout with extensive display repositioning. Figure 1 is redrawn, Table 3 expands substantially, and new uncertainty, ablation, robustness, hierarchy, and motif displays appear. Figure 4 loses its Weather panel, retained in Appendix Figure 10; the shortened Table 5 retains its full original contents in Appendix Table 16.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds classical time-series symbolization and pattern-discovery references, including Lin et al. and Berndt and Clifford, alongside newer foundation models. It qualifies the unexplored area as the proposed data-dependent tokenization for machine-learning-based analysis and changes the categorization of wavelet tokenization. Removing the Outlook also removes its associated references; the overall related-work framework remains.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.2 adds an explicit O(n) sequence-length complexity assertion without an accompanying proof. Existing mathematical definitions, quantization bounds, and conditional-decoding derivations are retained. Naming the first-order Markov assumption clarifies conditioning already present in v2's equations.

improvement.justification: The new same-backbone patch controls and discretization-only ablation substantially strengthen attribution that v2's confounded patch comparisons could not provide. Repeated-seed evidence and explicit training/profiling details also materially improve assessability and reproducibility. Some new noise-robustness prose overstates Figure 17, and uncertainty checks cover selected small models, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial strengthening of the empirical evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, algorithms, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds patch-based comparisons, a discretization-only ablation, repeated-seed measurements, and controlled robustness experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original forecasting and efficiency measurements, conditional-decoding experiments, and tokenizer analyses in Sections 4–5 and Appendix C.

results.title: Byte Pair Encoding for Efficient Time Series Forecasting

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction raise the claimed forecasting improvement from 36% to 40%, efficiency boost from 1990% to 2314%, and conditional-decoding improvement from up to 44% to 48%. These update quantitative claims under broader evaluation; the three central contributions and conclusion remain substantively stable.

C2.justification: v4 explicitly interprets target-data conditional decoding as domain adaptation (Section 5.3), attributes matched-input gains to motif expressiveness (Appendix C.2), and discusses marginal higher-order benefits versus parameter growth (Appendix C.3). Existing robustness interpretations and limitations are largely retained.

D1.justification: v4 documents the Fev-bench dataset selection and filtering, specifies vocabulary-creation order for motif iteration in Algorithm 2, and reports that estimating conditional-decoding distributions generally takes under 10 seconds. Existing training hyperparameters, hardware, and access information are retained.

E1.justification: v4 retains Chronos training and the five original evaluation datasets, adding Solar photovoltaic forecasting and 37 selected Fev-bench datasets spanning cloud, economy, energy, mobility, and retail (Appendix B, Table 8). This substantially broadens evaluation coverage.

E2.justification: Table 3 adds Time-MoE base and large models and LightGTS to the existing patch-based Chronos, MOMENT, and Moirai comparison. The sample-based Chronos and non-foundation comparator sets elsewhere are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix C.2 adds a controlled comparison using 384 time-series samples for both Chronos and motif models, alongside the retained 128-token comparison. New protocols cover Fev-bench sequence filtering and aggregation, higher-order decoding, and post-processing patch-model forecasts. The original training budgets and forecast horizon remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether longer inputs explain forecasting gains (Table 15), whether conditioning on additional previous samples helps (Table 17), and whether conditional decoding benefits continuous-output patch models (Table 18). The noise, non-stationarity, transient, and embedding analyses already appeared in v3.

E5.justification: Both versions report the same six-seed, five-dataset MSE standard deviations for selected small models (v3 Table 9; v4 Table 10). The stated training seed, timing warm-up and measurement counts, and timing uncertainty reporting are also unchanged.

E6.justification: The original five-dataset results are retained, while v4 adds benchmark, baseline, and controlled-analysis results. Section 5.1 changes reported average MSE reduction and acceleration from 36.1% and 19.90× to 39.8% and 23.14× under expanded coverage, not identical settings. The new Solar result is internally inconsistent: Tables 2–3 report 0.439 without conditional decoding, whereas Table 12 reports a best value of 0.493.

M1.justification: The BPE tokenizer, T5 training objective, and default first-order decoder are retained. Appendix C.3 adds second- and third-order decoding variants and a procedure that quantizes continuous patch-model forecasts before conditional decoding. These are localized procedural extensions.

P1.justification: Changes include local copyediting, more consistent sample-based terminology, expanded explanations, and updated affiliation and publication-header text. The main section structure and appendices A–C.9 remain, with limited reordering within Appendix C.2.

P2.justification: v4 expands Tables 2, 3, and 12, adds Tables 8, 15, 17, and 18, and adds panels to Figures 9 and 10. Table 3 gains comparator columns, while appendix body text increases from approximately 9 to 10 points, producing widespread reflow and relocation of retained material.

R1.justification: v4 adds citations for Fev-bench, Time-MoE, and LightGTS. Related work now discusses predefined multiple patch lengths and dominant-frequency-based patch selection, positioning motif tokenization against their limitations in capturing arbitrary-length patterns within a sequence.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 refines tokenization complexity from O(n) to O(|Ψ|·n), explicitly accounting for vocabulary size. The quantization-error bounds and analytical first-order conditional-decoding derivation are retained.

improvement.justification: The equal-input-length control in Table 15 addresses an important ambiguity in v3 about whether gains arose from longer raw contexts. Broader domain coverage, additional contemporary baselines, and the higher-order ablation substantially strengthen the empirical support and design justification. Explicitly identifying target-data decoding as domain adaptation improves interpretation. These gains outweigh the localized new Solar reporting inconsistency between Tables 2–3 and Table 12.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–C.9 are readable and support reliable matching despite additions and layout changes.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds benchmark evaluations, an input-length control, and further conditional-decoding experiments.

before.justification: v3 reports original forecasting accuracy and inference-time experiments, tokenizer ablations, robustness tests, and representation analyses in Section 5 and Appendix C.

results.title: Byte Pair Encoding for Efficient Time Series Forecasting

C1.justification: v3 drops the claim to be the first such benchmark and narrows the abstract's encoder-failure statement to weak encoders. It explicitly emphasizes synergy between expanded context and long-prompt training. The central benchmark contribution and claims about compositional failures and declining adherence with prompt length remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of advanced encoders, unified architectures, and Nano Banana 2's positional and attribute-binding failures (Appendices O–Q). It develops arguments about evaluator-family bias and smaller-evaluator viability, and explicitly bounds the benchmark as a proxy for professional constraint-intensive prompts. Sections 4.4–4.5 also make more assertive mechanistic and training interpretations.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 documents the new connector, frozen components, training-data construction, and caption compression. Appendices E and V add verification prompts and worked filtering examples. The embedded code link changes from Data-Juicer's DetailMaster branch to Qirui-jiao/DetailMaster. Existing hardware, timing, and core inference disclosures are retained.

E1.justification: v3 newly evaluates short-prompt generalization on T2I-CompBench, covering attribute binding, spatial and non-spatial relationships, and complex composition (Appendix U). The original source datasets, 4,116-prompt benchmark, four evaluation dimensions, and 800-prompt mini-benchmark are retained.

E2.justification: The twelve original generators remain. Table 2 adds SANA, Qwen-Image, Janus-1.3B, JanusFlow-1.3B, Janus-Pro-1B, Lumina-Image-2.0, and BAGEL-7B-MoT; Appendix Q additionally evaluates Nano Banana 2. Qwen-Image also enters the cross-evaluator comparison, substantially expanding the evaluated methods.

E3.justification: v3 adds a controlled 2×2 design varying 77/512-token limits and short/long training captions, with two million sampled training pairs and short captions compressed to at most 30 tokens (Appendix C.2). Additional protocols include T2I-CompBench evaluation and a 3B evaluator. Nano Banana 2 uses model-chosen resolution rather than the fixed resolution specified for earlier comparisons.

E4.justification: New analyses test training versus context capacity, short-prompt generalization, missing attributes in source captions, Qwen-Image evaluator-family bias, and smaller-evaluator robustness. Figures 7–8 extend length-sensitivity analysis to seven additional generators. Existing detector/cropping ablations, difficulty analysis, and illustrated case studies are retained.

E5.justification: The same three listed evaluator runs for five generators at temperature 0.8 remain in v2 Table 10 and v3 Table 13. No new uncertainty intervals, significance tests, or seed-reporting practices appear. The additional smaller-evaluator Kendall correlations reuse an existing reporting approach.

E6.justification: The original twelve-model Table 2 scores and matched appendix tables are unchanged. v3 adds substantial results, including Qwen-Image's 60.04% relationship accuracy, controlled ablation outcomes, T2I-CompBench scores, missing-attribute rates, evaluator comparisons, and additional length curves. Nano Banana 2's Table 18 scores are new results under its variable-resolution setting.

M1.justification: v3 introduces an ablation-specific SD-XL adaptation combining T5 and CLIP through a Timestep-Aware Semantic Connector, training only the connector while freezing the backbone and encoders (Appendix C.2). The benchmark construction and main evaluation algorithms remain unchanged; expanded filtering descriptions document the existing pipeline.

P1.justification: v3 substantially rewrites the abstract and introduction, revises related-work and conclusion passages, and reorganizes contributions and model categories. Existing conditional-attribute analysis and evaluator-bias discussion move into appendices. The appendix organization changes extensively, and the standalone contents page and Limitations heading disappear, with several underlying caveats retained elsewhere.

P2.justification: The main text switches to a two-column conference layout. Table 2 is reorganized into five model groups; new tables and Figures 7–8 appear; Figure 6 receives standardized vertical axes; and old Table 3 becomes appendix Table 20. Existing case-study images are rearranged from 4×3 to 6×2 grids.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds ConceptMix, LongBench-T2I, T2I-CoReBench, and OneIG-Bench, expanding positioning beyond v2's DensePrompts/DPG-Bench discussion. It develops new distinctions concerning synthetic prompt sources, physical plausibility, constraint density, and evaluation granularity. References supporting newer generator architectures and proposed research directions also expand.

T1.justification: Appendix B retains the same region coordinates, 75% coverage criterion, and spatial-assignment reasoning. No substantive mathematical revisions or proofs are added. The prompt/constraint notation introduced in Appendix G restates the existing prompt-conditioned evaluation objective.

improvement.justification: v2's training-versus-context argument relied on comparisons between heterogeneous generators. v3 adds a controlled SD-XL ablation and short-prompt transfer testing, substantially strengthening this central argument, alongside broader generator and evaluator validation. Some interpretation remains overstated: Table 3's 77-token long-trained configuration trails the 512-token short-trained configuration on background and style despite the claim of consistent superiority. This qualification limits the conclusion but does not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DetailMaster and provide readable text, tables, figures, and complete appendices. Content can be reliably matched despite substantial reformatting and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains these original results and adds generator evaluations, controlled training experiments, short-prompt testing, and evaluator analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of twelve generators, human assessment of benchmark quality, and pipeline ablation and robustness experiments.

results.title: DetailMaster: Can Your Text-to-Image Model Handle Long Prompts?

C1.justification: The central method, probabilistic generalization, and superiority claims for the original 13 tasks remain. However, the conclusion changes from saying effectiveness was validated only with matched-cancer teachers to asserting that pretraining on one cancer fails to improve downstream performance on other cancers. This substantively revises the claimed applicability, although Table 18 presents a more mixed picture.

C2.justification: v4 replaces an untested cross-cancer limitation with interpretations of teacher mismatch, fine-tuning transfer, and direct out-of-domain prediction. It also adds explanations concerning supervision strength, limited-data robustness, GRN uncertainty, and pathway-specific biological meaning. Some summaries overgeneralize: Table 4 contains settings below GRACE, and Table 18 preserves lung-to-breast fine-tuning performance despite the conclusion's broad transfer-failure statement.

D1.justification: v4 documents the link-prediction decoder, sigmoid scoring, and BCE loss, plus patient averaging, g:Profiler use, and small-cluster exclusion for enrichment. It corrects GOOtools to GOATOOLS and removes the placeholder code-availability sentence. Existing preprocessing, hyperparameter, hardware, and timing details are largely retained; neither PDF establishes a usable code release.

E1.justification: The original three cancer cohorts and 13 downstream tasks remain. Appendix F.6 adds masked-edge link prediction on breast cancer GRNs, and Appendix G adds mismatched-teacher pretraining, cross-cancer fine-tuning, and direct prediction on unseen cancer types. These substantially expand task and test-scenario coverage without adding new cancer cohorts.

E2.justification: The original five baselines remain in Tables 2–3. v4 additionally evaluates GCA, AFGRL, and SimGRACE against SupGCL on breast cancer hazard and BP tasks in Table 16. Table 17 adds a GCLink-style comparator adapted to the estimated GRNs for link prediction. These are substantive evaluated additions, not merely new citations.

E3.justification: Original benchmark splits, architecture, hyperparameter tables, and fine-tuning protocols are retained. New protocols include link prediction using 500 positive and 500 negative samples with an 80:20 split and masked target edges; temperature and encoder comparisons; patient/teacher subsampling; alternative GRN filtering thresholds; and quantitative clustering and enrichment evaluation. These substantially extend the experimental design.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained PCA and embedding-dimension analyses, v4 tests supervision temperature, Graph Transformer versus GAT within GRACE, cross-cancer transfer, patient and teacher sample sizes, and GRN filtering thresholds. Figure 3 adds quantitative clustering assessment, while Appendix I adds gene-cluster balance and GO/KEGG enrichment analyses. These address supervision, robustness, and biological interpretability questions largely untested in v3.

E5.justification: v3 reports means and standard deviations across folds or seeds without specifying formal significance tests. Appendix F.4 in v4 adds Student's t-tests with Bonferroni correction at 5%, reports four significant comparisons, and states that most comparisons are nonsignificant. The new link-prediction experiment specifies ten seeds, 0–9. Additional repetitions of the original experiments are not established.

E6.justification: The original main and supplementary score tables retain identical means and standard deviations. Substantial new results include temperature, comparator, transfer, robustness, and enrichment findings. For example, Table 17 newly reports SupGCL link-prediction accuracy of 0.763±0.028 and F1 of 0.855±0.018; Figure 3 adds SupGCL NMI/ARI values of 0.117/0.150. These are added evaluations, not improvements over v3 under matched settings.

M1.justification: The shared encoder, masking operations, joint loss, and Algorithm 1 are retained. However, Equation 6's description changes from a Frobenius inner product to cosine similarity via that product, while the pseudocode still shows inner products. The PDFs do not resolve whether the procedure's normalization changed or the wording corrects an existing implementation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction's motivation, and related-work narrative are substantially rewritten. Related work gains two focused subsections, the main results narrative is reorganized, and node-level discussion is consolidated in the appendix. An appendix contents page, revised subsection hierarchy, and separate appendix references substantially change navigation and document organization beyond copyediting.

P2.justification: Figure 3 becomes graph-only and gains NMI/ARI annotations; node-level panels are consolidated and redrawn in Figure 4. Figures 7–8 and numerous tables add clustering, enrichment, ablation, transfer, and robustness displays. Existing plots, captions, legends, float placement, title formatting, and page headers are also revised, producing substantial visual changes.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially reframed around augmentation-free GCL and representation learning from known GRNs. v4 adds discussion and citations for AFGRL, SimGRACE, CancerGATE, and additional GRN literature, while sharpening distinctions from already-cited MuSe-GNN and GCLink. SupGCL is positioned as exploiting measured within-modality perturbations, with explicit separation from multimodal learning and GRN inference.

T1.justification: The stated mathematical definition of simF around Equation 6 changes from a Frobenius inner product to cosine similarity via that product. Theorem 1, its independence assumption, Corollary 1, and the Appendix A derivation remain unchanged. The new explanation motivating independence does not introduce another formal result.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens the evidence for biological usefulness and applicability, which v3 supported mainly through downstream scores and embedding plots. Relevant comparator tests, biological enrichment, Bonferroni-corrected significance tests, and transfer/robustness experiments make important benefits and boundaries assessable. The gains are tempered by overstatements: Table 4 contradicts the claimed advantage over GRACE in all settings, and Table 18 is more mixed than the conclusion suggests. Nevertheless, the added biological evidence and explicit exposure of statistical and transfer limitations provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SupGCL, with matching authors, core equations, datasets, and original benchmark results. The main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds temperature ablations, comparator evaluations, link prediction, cross-cancer experiments, robustness tests, and biological enrichment analyses.

before.justification: v3 reports original downstream experiments on TCGA/LINCS-derived GRNs in Tables 2–3, with additional metrics, embedding analyses, and dimension experiments in Appendix F.

results.title: Supervised Graph Contrastive Learning for Gene Regulatory Networks

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central claims: randomized benchmarks permit evaluation without fully disclosing true answers and enable contamination detection through a Bayes-accuracy ceiling. The conclusion additionally mentions theoretical support, without redefining the principal contribution.

C2.justification: V2 explains the estimator's precision cost, difficulties distinguishing small performance gaps, why benchmark-generated randomness suffices, and reasoning's role in instruction compliance. It newly qualifies disclosure-allowed defenses as addressing benign leakage and acknowledges stronger answer-recovery attacks. It also revises the canary-completion interpretation and softens eliminating a second private test set to potentially reducing that need.

D1.justification: V2 adds explicit reverse-engineering and prompt-variation templates (Tables 7–8), detailed canary query and temperature settings, H100 hardware information for 14B models, and MMLU-Pro access information. Existing dataset-access and model-merging implementation references are retained; these are bounded additions to reproducibility documentation.

E1.justification: V2 adds an adversarial answer-recovery scenario across eight benchmarks, supplying models with randomized answers and transformation rules (Table 3). It also includes MMLU-Pro and GPQA-diamond in the expanded evaluations. The recovery task substantially extends the tested requirements, while the existing QA domains and six-language coverage remain.

E2.justification: The competing contamination detector remains the BIG-bench canary-string approach, evaluated through log probabilities and GUID completion. Additional LLMs are evaluation subjects, and the new reasoning and unphished conditions are controls. The revised canary sampling procedure changes evaluation settings rather than comparator membership.

E3.justification: GUID completion changes from one temperature-zero completion per prefix to 1,000 queries at each of 11 temperatures, counting any successful completion (v1 Appendix B.2; v2 B.3). Model-progress tracking changes from full benchmark sizes to samples of at most 1,024 and expands from three Llama models to eleven models. V2 also adds 14B configurations, correlation metrics, and protocols for the new controlled analyses.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained Bayes-accuracy sensitivity and cross-language experiments, v2 adds reverse-engineering attacks, reasoning versus no-reasoning analysis, nine prompt variants, training on original versus phished data, and checks for ignored randomization instructions (Table 3, Appendix B.2, and Figures 16–18). These test previously unexamined robustness and mechanism questions.

E5.justification: V2 adds Kendall rank-correlation estimates and associated p-values for individual benchmarks and aggregate performance (Table 6). Both versions retain the stated three-seed mean/standard-deviation convention and the 5% binomial detection test; no increase in independent experimental runs is stated.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial ranking, scaling, recovery, and diagnostic results. Table 6 reports aggregate Kendall's tau of 0.96, but GPQA has tau 0.35 and p=0.16; new Table 3 reports GPQA recovery accuracy of 47.87% versus 37.82% with original prompts. GUID-completion curves are replaced under the expanded sampling protocol. The pretraining and model-merging values in Tables 1–2 are unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3 adds an explicit sample-based estimator that converts phished answer matches into an estimate of original accuracy. This is a limited scoring extension; the benchmark randomization procedure and binomial contamination detector are retained.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose are retained. V2 locally rewrites methods and results passages, presents practical strategies as bullets, and adds appendix subheadings. The private-evaluation rewrite also introduces an unfinished 'underlying xxx' placeholder.

P2.justification: The model-progress bar charts become scatterplots with model and release-date encodings. V2 adds reasoning, robustness, and control plots plus recovery, correlation, and prompt tables, and expands or rearranges model panels. The existing dataset-size table is expanded and renumbered from Table 3 to Table 5, rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against memorization audits, membership inference, and dynamic evaluation. New discussions distinguish dataset-level detection from example-level membership inference and answer randomization from question regeneration, citing work such as Carlini and Panda's canary research, VarBench, DyVal, DARG, and KIEval.

T1.justification: V2 derives an unbiased original-accuracy estimator, adds Theorem 2 giving its variance and mean squared error, and supplies its proof in Appendix A.2. Theorem 1, Corollary 1, and their proofs are retained. The algebraic description of Z/KZ is also corrected from a finite field to an additive group.

improvement.justification: Theorem 2 and its proof quantify a previously unexamined precision cost, while the expanded ranking study replaces a three-Llama demonstration with broader quantitative evidence. New controlled analyses probe instruction-following and concealment failures, addressing central validation gaps in v1. Attack-resilience conclusions remain limited by the simple attacks tested, and an unfinished private-evaluation passage reduces polish, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in analytical and empirical scrutiny.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PhishBencher work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments on answer recovery, reasoning, prompt sensitivity, and additional model configurations.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on contamination detection, model-progress tracking, cross-language contamination, pretraining, and model merging in Section 4 and Appendix C.

results.title: CapBencher: Give Your LLM Benchmark a Built-in Alarm for Test-Set Overfitting

C1.justification: The central benchmark, species-range, aggregation and multimodal contributions remain. v3 adopts a more explicitly bioacoustic framing and adds conclusion-level claims about transfer to real-world settings and audio geolocation being substantially harder than image geolocation.

C2.justification: The new Discussion develops explanations involving environmental sounds, broad species ranges and acoustic similarity across distant locations. Added appendices discuss resampling failures, limited month-supervision benefits, embedding confusions and confident prediction errors, while noting possible Perch training/evaluation overlap. The Impact Statement expands qualifications about geographic bias, evaluation overestimation and privacy.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents regression-coordinate normalization, existing dataset subsampling details and settings for added training variants. It replaces separate benchmark/code links with one project link and states an XCDC license. Availability statements are inconsistent: the introduction says models/code are available, whereas the Impact Statement promises release upon acceptance. Core hardware and training details are retained.

E1.justification: v3 adds WABAD passive acoustic monitoring evaluation in A.9/Table A3. This substantially extends external testing to recordings collected under monitoring conditions, beyond iNatSounds focal recordings and curated XCDC dawn choruses. The original datasets and movie cases are retained.

E2.justification: Table A5 substantially expands the bioacoustic comparison set with BirdMAE, ProtoCLR and Perch 2.0, alongside frozen-MobileNet and Taxabind retrieval probes. These are actual evaluated alternatives, supplementing the unchanged original comparator sets. Table A10 also introduces a from-scratch comparator for species-identification transfer.

E3.justification: The original geolocation thresholds and core training settings are retained. Added protocols include frozen-encoder linear probes, ResNet50/ViT-B16 configurations, weighted training-data sampling, month-loss weight sweeps, top-1/top-5 species-identification transfer evaluation and entropy-ranked evaluation subsets. These substantially broaden the experimental design.

E4.justification: Appendices A.14–A.20 add taxonomic breakdowns, encoder and architecture ablations, geographic/species resampling tests, month-supervision sensitivity, representation analyses and checklist-uncertainty diagnostics. These investigate several previously untested failure mechanisms. The species-count distribution panel accompanying v2 Table 4 is removed, although its principal weekly-group observation remains in prose.

E5.justification: A.20/Figure A12 newly quantifies predictive uncertainty through normalized SINR-checklist entropy and reports error as uncertain recordings are excluded. Existing three-run mean/standard-deviation reporting and 100-run species-subset uncertainty bands remain unchanged; no increase in repeated-run counts is documented.

E6.justification: Scores in the retained Tables 1–4 and A1–A2 are unchanged. Substantial new results include WABAD AG-CLIP performance of 3439 km median error and 3.23% regional accuracy, a ResNet50 configuration reporting 935 km and 18.86%, and species-identification top-1 scores of 48.4% from scratch versus 50.7% after geolocation pretraining. These concern newly evaluated conditions.

M1.justification: The default AG-CLIP architecture, checklist supervision and retrieval procedure remain unchanged. Appendix A.18 adds an experimental variant with a 12-way month-prediction head and auxiliary cross-entropy loss, constituting a limited extension to the training objective.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction and conclusion undergo extensive revision. Problem setup and methodology are merged, regression/classification descriptions move to the appendix, and dedicated Discussion and Impact Statement sections are introduced. The appendix narrative is also substantially expanded and reorganized.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout, Figure 1 moves above the abstract, and Figure 3's legend/colorbar arrangement changes. Table 4 is reordered and loses its species-diversity panel. New Tables A3–A10 and Figures A9–A12 substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: The benchmark-survey paragraph is replaced by a Species Identification subsection distinguishing geolocation from location-conditioned identification and auxiliary geolocation pretraining, including MetaPerch. References to newer bioacoustic encoders and passive monitoring are added. The principal positioning relative to image geolocation and soundscape mapping remains.

T1.justification: A.20 introduces a quantitative definition of checklist uncertainty: entropy of predicted classwise probabilities normalized by the number of predicted positives. This extends the mathematical definitions used for analysis. The underlying geolocation formulation is retained, with no new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the benchmark's empirical credibility. WABAD tests passive-monitoring generalization, while Table A5 addresses v2's limited comparisons with specialist bioacoustic encoders. Added diagnostic and negative-result analyses clarify the method's applicability and weaknesses. These gains outweigh the removed diversity plot and inconsistent release statements, although some new causal interpretations remain speculative and reporting details for added experiments are limited.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same iNatSounds/XCDC benchmark and AG-CLIP research, despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, appendices, tables, equations and rendered figures support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds WABAD evaluation, bioacoustic encoder comparisons, training variants and representation analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original geolocation experiments on iNatSounds and XCDC, component ablations, spatiotemporal aggregation results and multimodal case studies.

results.title: Bioacoustic Geolocation: Species Sounds as Geographic Signals

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same model-mis-specification dichotomy, possible online-DPO advantage, and sparsity-based statistical separation. The new proofs support existing central claims rather than redefining them.

C2.justification: v5 adds a sparsity rationale supported by cited examples and explicitly states that the statistical theorems do not directly extend to three or more tokens. It also discusses applicability to other random-utility models and qualifies the single-prompt versus multi-prompt comparison with Nika et al.

D1.justification: v4 Appendix C and v5 Appendix D provide the same code/data access information, preprocessing template, hyperparameters, sampling implementation, hardware, memory requirements, and runtimes.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same PKU-SafeRLHF QA, prompt, safer, and better data, the same model-capacity scenarios, and the same bandit simulations. Newly cited applications motivating sparsity are not additional evaluations.

E2.justification: The comparisons remain online DPO versus RLHF/RL for model mis-specification and DPO versus reward modeling for statistical efficiency. The pairwise-regression implementation of RL and the appendix simulation comparators are unchanged.

E3.justification: Section 5 and the implementation appendices retain the same data splits, GPT-2-large-774M models, freezing controls, reward scales, sample-size sweeps, training budgets, and evaluation procedures. The new proofs analyze the existing simulation settings.

E4.justification: The reward-scale, model-capacity, and sample-efficiency analyses are retained, as are both numerical bandit examples. The added analytic proofs strengthen theoretical support without adding an empirical ablation or robustness test.

E5.justification: Both versions report three seeds in Section 5.1 and display the same shaded uncertainty bands. No new run counts, uncertainty-estimation procedures, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: v4 Figures 2–5 match v5 Figures 1–4, including all ten experiment and simulation panels. The curves, rankings, numerical examples, and original empirical findings are unchanged.

M1.justification: The RLHF/DPO objectives, online samplers, token-level parameterization, and sparse estimators are retained. The reward-modeling discussion moves from Appendix A to B without changing its proposed procedures.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact. Changes include moving much of related work to Appendix A, adding focused explanatory passages and an Impact Statement, clarifying RLHF terminology, and updating affiliations and conference front matter.

P2.justification: v5 converts the main text and references to a two-column conference layout and replaces v4's Venn-style Figure 1 with a matrix-style Table 1. Existing plots are enlarged and relocated, and appendix layout and equation wrapping change substantially.

R1.justification: v5 adds Ackermann et al. on off-policy reward correction and references supporting preference-learning foundations, token-level parameterization, and sparsity/low-rank motivation. It refines the comparison with Nika et al.; the existing broader survey is retained in Appendix A.

T1.justification: v4 Appendix B.8–B.9 explicitly relies on numerical verification of Propositions 4 and 7. v5 Appendix C.8–C.9 adds analytic proofs deriving gradient signs, fixed points, and value inequalities for the same constructions, substantially strengthening the mathematical support for the online-DPO dichotomy.

improvement.justification: v5 replaces numerical-only support for two central online-DPO propositions with analytic proofs in Appendix C.8–C.9, resolving an important rigor gap in this primarily theoretical paper. The added qualifications about the two-token statistical construction also improve interpretive precision. These gains strengthen the existing contributions while retaining the empirical evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RLHF–DPO study. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, references, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: v5 retains the original experiments in Section 5 and numerical simulations in Appendix C.8–C.9.

before.justification: v4 reports original GPT-2-large experiments on PKU-SafeRLHF in Section 5 and numerical bandit simulations in Appendix B.8–B.9.

results.title: Understanding the Performance Gap in Preference Learning: A Dichotomy of RLHF and DPO

C1.justification: The unified-attribution and Grokking-alignment claims remain. v4 expands the principal validation claim to a 1.7B language model and introduces EuroLLM's two-phase pretraining dynamics as a main contribution in the abstract, introduction and conclusion. Attribution across granularities was already claimed in v2.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations connecting EuroLLM's phases to early MLP representation building and later attention-based refinement, and connects first-moment oscillations to unstable local learning dynamics. It also develops substantive qualifications concerning weak counterfactual data attribution, run-specific influences, unavailable example-level momentum attribution at sparse checkpoints, and reconstruction-fidelity versus computation tradeoffs (Section 7, Appendices F.4 and G.1-G.2).

D1.justification: v4 documents the MNIST architecture and optimizer settings, EuroLLM checkpoint and batch construction, approximately 15-minute H100 computations per checkpoint, and subset-retraining and subsampling procedures. Existing model details remain. Code-access documentation becomes inconsistent: Appendix A promises release upon acceptance while the main text retains the GitHub link; v2 explicitly stated that code was available.

E1.justification: v2 evaluates CIFAR-2 and modulo-113 addition. v4 retains these and adds MNIST digit recognition, multilingual language-model loss analysis using EuroLLM, and counterfactual training-subset prediction evaluations on MNIST and CIFAR-2. These substantially broaden the represented data and task requirements.

E2.justification: The random and Li et al. (2017) pruning comparisons remain in Figure 2. v4 additionally evaluates single-model TRAK and TracIn against ExPLAIND for causal data attribution on MNIST and CIFAR-2 (Appendix G.1, Figure 7); these methods were only cited in v2.

E3.justification: The existing CIFAR-2 and modulo-113 settings remain. New protocols include MNIST training on 5120 samples with 1024 test samples, a separate five-epoch trajectory for subsampling analysis, LDS evaluation using 1000 random training subsets at multiple retention fractions, and simulated single-update EuroLLM evaluations at 37 checkpoints using batches of 3072 sequences of length 4096.

E4.justification: The existing Grokking layer-swapping, reinitialization and cyclic-geometry analyses are retained. v4 adds a sensitivity analysis of reconstruction fidelity versus retained training steps (Appendix G.2, Figure 8) and a EuroLLM case study examining parameter type, layer depth, regularization and first-moment influences (Figures 6, 14 and 15).

E5.justification: Five-run mean and standard-deviation reporting for pruning and Grokking reinitialization remains unchanged. v4 additionally summarizes EuroLLM reconstruction-error variability across checkpoints and displays subsampling error bars in Figure 8 without specifying their statistical meaning or run count. These additions do not establish increased replication of the retained experiments.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 values and Table 2 Lasso coefficients remain unchanged. Added results include MNIST EPK agreement of 0.998/1.0 at 10/100 integration steps, EuroLLM simulated-update reconstruction error averaging 4.46e-8, and CIFAR LDS of 0.06 versus 0.05 for both TRAK and TracIn. New findings concern EuroLLM learning phases, generally stronger MNIST LDS for TRAK except the reported leave-one-out case, and high reconstruction agreement retaining 60% of steps. The aggregate-model heatmaps from v2 Figure 6 are omitted.

M1.justification: The tensor-accumulation framework remains. v4 refines the published training-feature and atomic-score formulas and adds concrete adaptations: loss-change-ranked checkpoint selection and separate attribution of stored first-moment effects under checkpoint subsampling (Section 4.2, Appendices F.4 and G.2). v2 only proposed general subsampling and early accumulation.

P1.justification: v4 updates the abstract, contribution list and conclusion, streamlines theoretical exposition, and edits retained prose. Pruning and efficiency exchange order, while reproducibility and LLM-use statements move to appendices. The overall theory-to-framework-to-case-study organization and much of the original Grokking narrative remain.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column conference layout. Figure 1 is rearranged and moved to the opening page, Table 1 gains MNIST columns, and Figures 6-8 and 14-15 are added. Existing figures are resized and relocated; v2 Figure 6 becomes v4 Figure 9 with revised labels, a visible color scale and removal of the aggregate Model row.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds bounded substantive comparisons with DualXDA's input-feature/data attribution and LCA/POLCA's loss attribution. Additional references support MNIST, EuroLLM, Llama and the stability interpretation. The central positioning relative to EPK, TracIn and prior Grokking research remains; numerous publication-metadata updates concern already cited works.

T1.justification: v4 substantially revises the AdamW and momentum derivations, introducing weighted batch losses and explicit differentiability assumptions, including the previously omitted stability constant, and keeping time-dependent loss gradients inside the momentum sum. It corrects the parameter summation for regularization, extends Corollary 3.3 to differentiable output functions, and adds detailed composition, activation and partition-accumulation proofs (Appendices F.1-F.4).

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens mathematical justification and empirical validation. Revised optimizer and loss-gradient derivations repair important weaknesses in v2, while EuroLLM and subsampling experiments test previously speculative scalability. Causal data-attribution comparisons also expose an important applicability limitation. EuroLLM conclusions remain bounded by simulated local updates, and code-release wording is inconsistent, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in rigor, evidence and clarity about applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ExPLAIND research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial additions and reformatting.

after.justification: v4 retains those experiments and adds MNIST validation, EuroLLM checkpoint analysis, causal data-attribution comparisons and checkpoint-subsampling results.

before.justification: v2 reports original model-reconstruction results, CNN pruning experiments, and Grokking analyses including layer interventions and Lasso regression.

results.title: ExPLAIND: Unifying Model, Data, and Training Attribution to Study Model Behavior

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same central claims: proxy-free IRL-derived guidance, robustness through indirect use of edge rewards, faster convergence and improved sample quality. The added theory and experiments do not redefine those contributions.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly treats Oracle-GFN as an online reference and qualifies canonical recovery in Remark B.6. It adds interpretations of FM robustness and soft-guidance sensitivity while removing the standalone oracle-surpassing hypotheses. Existing limitations concerning adversarial IRL, trajectory quality and continuous/stochastic extensions remain.

D1.justification: v3 adds a TD-GFN source-code and reproduction-script link, ML1M construction instructions, and disclosure that biosequence baseline checkpoints were selected to balance reward and diversity. This checkpoint statement adds documentation without establishing a changed procedure. Original architecture, hyperparameter and hardware information is retained.

E1.justification: Appendix E.1 adds MovieLens 1M recommendation using real user-interaction trajectories to generate six-item slates. This introduces a new domain and permutation-invariant set-generation task on a general DAG, extending the retained Hypergrid, peptide and molecular-design coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds BraVE to the molecular reward and mode-discovery comparisons (Table 1 and Figure 7). Figure 19 additionally compares naive offline Dataset-GFN variants using DB, TB and SubTB objectives. These differ from v2's retained experiment applying TB within TD-GFN.

E3.justification: Added evaluation designs include ML1M user filtering, six-item slates and average/max reward and coverage metrics; a 256×256 Hypergrid with 100 training trajectories; post-hoc top-100 molecular Tanimoto similarity; and offline objective comparisons using SubTB with lambda 0.9. These supplement the retained original settings rather than establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses of widely separated Hypergrid modes, molecular structural diversity, the adequacy of naive offline GFlowNet objectives and biosequence training stability (Appendices E.3 and E.10–E.12). The earlier rebalancing, pruning, backward-sampling and threshold-sensitivity studies remain.

E5.justification: Both versions specify seeds 0, 1 and 2 and use mean/standard-deviation reporting and shaded uncertainty bands. Best-seed reporting for molecular offline-RL baselines is retained and extended to BraVE. Additional result entries do not introduce a new statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: New Table 4 reports TD-GFN's ML1M average reward of 1.988±0.006 and coverage of 186.8±6.3; Table 6 adds molecular similarity of 0.531±0.022. BraVE becomes the lowest-trajectory molecular comparator at 6,450 trajectories. New Figures 10, 19 and 20 add further findings, while existing molecular reward values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and Equations (4)–(7) retain the same trajectory reweighting, adversarial edge-reward extraction, pruning and prioritized backward sampling. The theoretical analysis and additional objective comparisons do not specify a revised TD-GFN procedure; soft guidance remains a future direction.

P1.justification: The abstract and much of the main-text prose are extensively rewritten, and the introductory motivation is reorganized. Appendix organization changes around the new theory section, the supplementary contents page disappears, and the discussions are revised. This exceeds simple renumbering or additions of scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column layout. Hypergrid panels are redistributed, the biosequence chart becomes vertically arranged, and the pipeline diagram is redrawn. v2's introductory summary plot is removed, new tables and figures are added, and Table 1 visually separates reference methods from offline comparators.

R1.justification: v3 adds BraVE (Landers et al., 2025) and FlowRL (Zhu et al., 2025), while dropping the trajectory-example references to Cobbe, Khazatsky and van der Kamp. The substantive related-work discussion is largely retained; several other citation changes merely update publication metadata.

T1.justification: v3 introduces Theorems 3.1–3.2 and Appendix B with formal assumptions and proofs concerning reweighting invariance, canonical-gauge reward recovery, backward-policy perturbation, pruning survival and target-distribution distortion. v2 contains background formulations and training objectives but no corresponding theoretical development.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens justification and validation: Appendix B supplies explicit conditions and proofs, while ML1M extends real-data evidence beyond v2's tree-structured peptide task to user trajectories in a general DAG. Added diversity and stability analyses and clearer comparison disclosures improve scrutiny. The guarantees remain conditional, and Section 4.1's DB/SubTB compatibility assertion lacks corresponding results in Appendix E.8, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TD-GFN work. Their main text, equations, algorithms, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and additions.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds recommendation results, further Hypergrid tests, molecular-diversity measurements and supplementary comparisons.

before.justification: v2 reports original Hypergrid, biosequence and molecular-design experiments, including component ablations, sensitivity analyses and training-resource measurements.

results.title: Beyond the Proxy: Trajectory-Distilled Guidance for Offline GFlowNet Training

C1.justification: The central contributions remain the learning-rate-controlled bias trade-off and the insufficiency of either bias alone to explain generalization. v2 qualifies increasing norm as an overall trend and presents the theoretical contribution more explicitly as particular scenarios and counterexamples.
