C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion newly position RedDebate explicitly as an inference-time complement to existing safety alignment. The central automated debate-and-memory contribution and headline HarmBench reduction claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive qualifications concerning untested memory poisoning, disabled reasoning mode, hybrid-memory over-refusal, weaker Socratic guides losing context, and early stopping sacrificing useful feedback. It also interprets cumulative adapter training as mitigating forgetting and semantically similar retrievals as cushioning retrieval misses. These considerably expand the applicability and mechanism discussion.

D1.justification: v3 newly discloses four 80GB A100 GPUs, disabled thinking/reasoning mode, and detailed inference-time and Socratic-agent overhead information. Disabled reasoning is newly documented, not an established change from v2. Existing LoRA settings, prompt templates, memory implementation details, and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: Appendices C.3 and C.6 add Aegis-2, WildJailbreak, and XSTest, covering broader safety categories, diverse jailbreak prompts, and safe requests resembling unsafe ones. They also test memory transfer to unseen benchmarks. HarmBench, CoSafe, and TriviaQA are retained.

E2.justification: v3 adds unguided Self-Revision to the HarmBench/CoSafe comparisons in Tables 1–2 and Best-of-N independent sampling to the HarmBench comparison in Table 3. Standard Prompting and constitution-guided Self-Critique remain. These additions substantially strengthen controls for isolated revision and additional sampling.

E3.justification: Added protocols include Best-of-N with N=3 and 5 and best/average/worst aggregation, single-round memory-transfer tests, a frontier-scale PReD triad, and replacement of the Socratic guide. v3 also adds retrieval evaluation at K=5/10 and one- and two-round conditions to the existing round-count ablation.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses of memory transfer, frontier-scale generalization, Socratic-guide dependence, targeted over-refusal, retrieval reliability, wall-clock costs, and early stopping. It extends the round-count ablation and adds a conservative-agent case study in Figure 14. Earlier evaluator, instruction-tuning, diversity, and agent-count analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The existing 2,104 ± 228 token-usage summary is unchanged; new result tables do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include Qwen's WildJailbreak error rates of 41.5% without memory and 6.5% with transferred HarmBench TLTM (v3 Table 6), and hybrid-memory XSTest compliance losses of 14 and 8 points for Mistral and Phi (Table 10). Retained CoSafe totals also change: Standard Prompting for the second triad rises from 7.9% to 8.1% in Table 1, and first-triad SReD with Unified memory changes from 2.4% to 2.5% in Table 2.

M1.justification: Section 5.3 introduces an optional early-stopping variant that terminates debate when all agents produce safe responses in a round. The three principal debate strategies, four memory configurations, core algorithms, and agent prompts otherwise remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose remain. v3 revises the introduction and Self-Critique explanation, standardizes abbreviations, collects cost discussion into Section 5.3, moves limitations into Appendix A, and removes the separate LLM-use statement. These are localized narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: v3 converts the main text and references to two columns, redraws framework Figures 1–2, and revises the vulnerability figure's labels and caption. It adds seven tables and Figure 14, expands existing comparison and round-ablation tables, and redistributes retained appendix figures and prompt displays.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially expands discussion of training-time alignment, distribution shift, reward hacking, and alignment faking, adding works such as Ouyang et al. (2022), Casper et al. (2023b), and Greenblatt et al. (2024). Section 5.1 explains the complementary positioning and exclusion of training-based comparators. New benchmark, model, sampling, and guardrail references further broaden the literature coverage.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(5), including the ER and AGR definitions, are unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs; the added metric descriptions and mechanism discussions do not introduce substantive mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: Beyond v2's Self-Critique and token-budget comparisons, v3 adds controls for unguided revision and independent sampling, tests unseen-benchmark transfer, and directly examines over-refusal and guide dependence. These address important gaps in the evidence for interaction benefits and generalization. Some broad prose still overstates the findings, especially helpfulness despite hybrid-memory compliance losses in Table 10, but the stronger controls and newly exposed limitations substantially improve the paper's overall evidential quality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RedDebate. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and added experiments.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds benchmark-transfer, frontier-model, over-refusal, retrieval, baseline, and efficiency experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original HarmBench and CoSafe experiments, memory and debate ablations, TriviaQA evaluations, and validation against human safety annotations.

results.title: RedDebate: Safer Responses Through Multi-Agent Red Teaming Debates

C1.justification: The abstract and central claim about synchronizing curriculum and model growth remain stable. However, the introduction and discussion extend the contribution to 20B-token training and domain-adaptive code pretraining, beyond v1's low-budget experiments. MMLU-STEM-specific claims are removed, and the reported average advantage is revised for the reduced benchmark set.

C2.justification: v2 adds a depth-related inductive-bias explanation for the perplexity/downstream-performance discrepancy and qualifies that discrepancy by training budget. It interprets new stage trajectories, seed variability, and code-transfer results in terms of knowledge transfer, stability, and domain adaptation. The MMLU-subfield interpretations disappear, while the existing half-depth recommendation remains.

D1.justification: v2 adds MIDAS weight-copying clarification, the code-transfer mixture schedule, and measured training times on four H100s: 5h53m for CGLS versus 5h39m for the baseline. Existing optimizer, learning-rate, and hardware details remain. It removes dataset/model license disclosures and the GPT-2 three-layer-start curriculum weights, although that configuration remains in the perplexity plot.

E1.justification: v2 adds a general-web-to-Python-code training scenario using DCLM and StarCoder2, evaluated on HumanEval (Section 5.1, Table 3). It removes MMLU evaluation, including the STEM column and full appendix breakdown. The 20B-token experiment expands training scale within existing DCLM coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparison retains the randomized and curricularized baselines, layer-scaling-only, MIDAS, and pretrained references. Locally, the starting-depth comparison changes: v1 Table 4 includes a randomized-baseline reference, whereas the replacement depth-sweep plot in v2 Figure 2 shows only CGLS configurations.

E3.justification: v2 adds 20B-token training and a 4B-token code-transfer experiment with HumanEval pass@8/16/32/64 evaluation. Appendix A.2 introduces matched zero- and five-shot evaluations using PMI accuracy. The retained main experiments preserve their settings, but their 1B aggregate now excludes MMLU. Figure 2 inconsistently labels the depth-sweep budget as 2B tokens in its title and 2.5B in its caption.

E4.justification: v2 expands the existing starting-depth analysis with 4- and 12-layer starts, adds a final-stage budget sweep, and reports validation trajectories across training stages (Figures 2 and 5). It also tests general-text-to-code distribution shift. The MMLU category analysis is removed; the existing per-domain perplexity plots are retained rather than newly added.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-run counts or uncertainty estimates. v2 Table 7 newly reports three training runs per method at the 1B/2.5B-token scale, with means and standard errors; Appendix A.4 discusses the higher variability of CGLS. This establishes new uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Shared main-table task scores and existing perplexity plots are unchanged. New results include 20B-token average accuracy of 42.30% for CGLS versus 38.41% for the randomized baseline, and HumanEval pass@8 of 6.67% versus 3.56% (v2 Tables 2–3), plus few-shot, replication, and trajectory results. MMLU and some configuration-specific entries disappear. Changed main-table 1B averages reflect removal of MMLU, not same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The curriculum mixture, progressive addition of randomly initialized layers, frozen-weight initialization phase, and subsequent full-model tuning are unchanged. Defaulting to the previously evaluated half-depth configuration and clarifying MIDAS implementation do not introduce a new CGLS procedure.

P1.justification: Most abstract, introduction, method, and setup wording is retained. v2 promotes related work to a separate section, simplifies CGLS configuration names, edits results and discussion, and reorganizes the appendices around the expanded analyses. The MMLU, broader-impact, and licensing sections are removed, without an extensive rewrite of the retained exposition.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template, headers, typography, and citation presentation. It relocates curriculum tables and existing perplexity plots, removes the MMLU table, replaces the depth-comparison table with plots, and adds four experimental tables plus budget/depth and stage-trajectory figures. Table 4's caption still describes the omitted three-layer-start configuration.

R1.justification: v2 adds Du et al. on stacking, Heineman and Hwang et al. on evaluation practice, Ouyang et al. on fine-tuning, and two Tay et al. studies supporting the depth/perplexity discussion. The MMLU reference is removed. The central positioning as a combination of curriculum learning and progressive model growth is unchanged.

T1.justification: The curriculum-mixture definition and parameter-transfer equation remain unchanged, with no added or revised theorems, proofs, or derivations. Removing the standard PMI scoring formula alongside the MMLU description changes evaluation exposition, not substantive mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence was confined to low-token-budget experiments without reported run-to-run uncertainty. v2 tests the method at 20B tokens and under code-domain transfer, adds three-run uncertainty estimates, and directly examines budget allocation and learning trajectories. These address important gaps in generality and reliability. Removing MMLU detail and licensing information reduces transparency, and appendix inconsistencies remain, but the expanded validation substantially strengthens the paper's empirical foundation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CGLS research work. All 15 pages of v1 and 16 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable; the text, equations, tables, and rendered figures support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original pretraining results and adds 20B-token training, code-domain transfer, few-shot evaluation, replicated runs, and training-stage analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original compute-matched pretraining experiments at GPT-2-Small and Llama-3.2-1B scales, including downstream accuracy, perplexity, starting-depth comparisons, and MMLU analyses.

results.title: Curriculum-Guided Layer Scaling for Language Model Pretraining

C1.justification: The central computational contribution is recast from two new consistent estimators to a subsampled computation and an exact single-shot factorization with quadratic memory. The introduction also qualifies the best-achievable mitigation claim under hidden confounding by excluding valid proxies. The overarching SAM, causal-stability, and competitive debiasing claims remain.

C2.justification: Section 2.2 adds overlap failure conditions, selective treatment of useful mediators, and proxy-based exceptions to hidden-confounder limitations. Section 6 explicitly discusses observed bias-label requirements and distinguishes visually assigned sex labels from gender; the skin-tone/race caveat already existed. Waterbirds background bias is described as mediation instead of collider bias, while its generating equation remains unchanged.

D1.justification: V3 replaces the anonymized code placeholder with a concrete repository address and adds the TinyBERT checkpoint, IRM/Fishr adaptation details and grids, and runtime hardware, preprocessing, workers, and precision. It newly mentions label noise and specifies YaleB's selection vector, without establishing changed experiments. V2's dedicated reproducibility statement describing frameworks and automated configuration files is removed.

E1.justification: V3 adds MNLI three-way sentence-pair classification with negation-based shortcuts, extending evaluation from vision to language. The original five datasets and both dSprites counterfactual scenarios remain; relocating their descriptions does not constitute new coverage.

E2.justification: IRM and Fishr become evaluated comparators on the retained FairFace and Waterbirds benchmarks and on MNLI (Table 2), using adaptations to target/bias groups. V3 also evaluates naive DISCO in its new runtime comparison. The regression counterfactual comparison drops DISCOm, which appeared alongside sDISCO in v2.

E3.justification: The new MNLI experiment uses TinyBERT and worst-group accuracy for selection and evaluation on biased data. V3 also introduces a controlled runtime protocol across batch sizes 64–1024 and IRM/Fishr search grids. Appendix H.4 revises the counterfactual R² normalization, without establishing whether those experiments were rerun. Existing methods' appendix hyperparameter grids are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix H.5 adds a substantial scalability analysis comparing epoch times and out-of-memory failures across nine methods and four batch sizes, directly testing computational claims previously unsupported by such measurements. The existing counterfactual studies remain, with revisions to the regression comparison rather than an entirely new causal analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report benchmark means ± standard deviations across unspecified runs, without seed lists, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V3 retains this practice for added results. Its timing table reports means and OOM outcomes without introducing an uncertainty estimation procedure; hyperparameter-grid run counts describe configurations.

E6.justification: Table 2 replaces the corrected implementation's sDISCO results: dSprites R² 0.619→0.687, Blob 0.788→0.751, YaleB balanced accuracy 0.694→0.770, FairFace 0.854→0.850, and Waterbirds 0.863→0.874. MNLI, IRM/Fishr, and runtime/OOM results are added. The counterfactual sDISCO row changes from (0.067, 0.6474) to (0.058, 0.7181), exactly v2's DISCOm values; that numerical match is unexplained.

M1.justification: V2's sDISCO uses globally weighted centering and normalization. V3 replaces this with an exact factorization computing all local covariances and averaging their correlations (Section 3.2, Appendix G). Appendix B explicitly confirms a corresponding implementation correction. This changes a central estimator; DISCOm and the general regularized prediction objective are retained.

P1.justification: The introduction and method narrative undergo substantial explanatory rewriting, including the counterfactually stable-effect terminology and expanded assumptions discussion. Dataset equations move from the main text into Appendix H.1. Appendices are reorganized around corrections, contextualization, proofs, and experiments, and a limitations section replaces the previous reproducibility section.

P2.justification: V3 changes the single-column preprint main text to a two-column conference layout. Figure 3 becomes a multirow arrangement, and v2's combined Figure 4 becomes a separate table and graph. Tables gain benchmark columns and comparator rows, an archival results table and runtime table are added, and retained appendix graphics are resized and relocated.

R1.justification: New Section 1.1 and Appendix C substantially position the work within discriminative causal representation learning with observed biases. They expand comparisons with Makar, Veitch, and Puli/NURD and add discussion and citations concerning generative learning, latent confounding, causal discovery, and proxies. Wang et al.'s existing V-statistic decomposition receives a more explicit role in defining sDISCO's computational novelty.

T1.justification: V3 replaces the earlier sDISCO consistency sketch with an exact factorization theorem, derivation, and memory-complexity analysis in Appendix G. DISCOm consistency now requires m to grow rather than permitting fixed m. V3 also corrects the main-text spurious-effect sign to match the appendix and adds an explicit positivity assumption. Renaming the stable pathway alone is not a mathematical change.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses an acknowledged error in a central estimator with an explicit factorization and proof, corrected implementation results, and transparent preservation of earlier scores (Appendices B and G). The revised consistency condition, scalability measurements, and clearer applicability boundaries substantially improve technical reliability and evidential support. Its blanket stronger-performance wording exceeds the mixed replacement scores, and the counterfactual table's numerical reassignment remains unexplained, but these reporting limitations do not outweigh the central improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SAM/DISCO research work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting and renumbering.

after.justification: V3 reports original experiments across six datasets, corrected sDISCO results, counterfactual analyses, and a new runtime and memory study in Appendix H.5.

before.justification: V2 reports original experiments across five datasets in Table 2 and original counterfactual analyses in Section 4.4 and Appendix E.4.

results.title: DISCO: Mitigating Bias in Deep Learning with Conditional Distance Correlation

C1.justification: The principal claims remain linear-cost ENN/TuRBO-ENN, comparable optimization quality with one-to-two-order proposal-time reductions up to 50,000 observations, and PBO convergence. The abstract's added 'without sacrificing solution quality' wording repeats claims already present in v2's contributions and conclusion.

C2.justification: V3 qualifies timing comparisons by contrasting its single-core allocation with multicore/GPU resources in cited studies. Appendix C interprets neighbor radius as controlling bias and squared weights as controlling effective noise averaging, and frames its PBO result as surrogate-side conditions for an auxiliary acquisition. Section 6's practical limitations remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: Anonymous package and repository placeholders become the named ennbo package and an identifiable source location. V3 newly discloses one CPU core per run and specific fitting configurations, including sparse-GP inducing-point counts. These disclosures do not establish a hardware change for retained experiments.

E1.justification: V3 adds a distinct regression and held-out predictive-quality evaluation track on Ackley, Sphere, Booth and Rosenbrock (Section 5.4 and Appendices A–B). These functions already appeared among v2's optimizer tests, but the regression task is new. The five principal optimization tasks and their natural/frozen-noise coverage remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 and Figures 3, 6 and 7 add actual comparisons with SMAC, DNGO and GP-UCB, although several attempted settings time out. Appendix A adds turbo-one-nds and turbo-one-ucb controls. Appendix B also evaluates two sparse-GP configurations, including the capped-inducing-point SVGP_linear variant.

E3.justification: New protocols include synthetic regression with independent training/test sets, Gaussian noise, predictive-error/log-likelihood metrics, fitting-size sweeps to one million observations, and normalized-rank evaluations. Appendix A.1 uses 1,000 training and 1,000 test points; Figure 8 uses 100 test points. Table 1 revises natural-noise LunarLander N from 300 to 10,000, matching v2 Figure 3's existing axis; this does not establish that additional optimization runs occurred.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained turbo-zero ablation, Appendix A tests K/P sensitivity in surrogate prediction and optimization, and isolates acquisition choice by replacing Thompson sampling with NDS or UCB while retaining TuRBO's GP. Tables 2–5 and Figures 9–15 provide substantial new evidence about parameter sensitivity and component effects.

E5.justification: The optimization experiments retain 30 runs and mean ± two standard errors. The new fitting protocol explicitly reports 10 replications with ± one standard error in Figure 8, shared with Figures 16–17; the new sensitivity tables also report uncertainty. There is no stated increase in repetitions for retained experiments.

E6.justification: V3 adds predictive-quality, fitting-time, sensitivity and acquisition-ablation results throughout Tables 2–5 and Figures 8–17. Existing timings also change: frozen-noise LunarLander's ENN proposal time changes from 0.6 to 0.9 seconds and its tabulated speedup from 89 to 58; frozen-noise Hopper's CMA-ES time changes from 7.0 to 5.2 seconds. Natural-noise LunarLander timings are replaced alongside the revised N entry, preventing a straightforward same-setting comparison.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the precision-weighted ENN surrogate, subsampled fitting, incumbent selection, RAASP candidates, noisy UCB and fitting-free NDS acquisition. The revised scalarization and variable-neighbor analysis in Appendix C are theoretical constructions, not documented changes to the implemented method.

P1.justification: The former seven-part PBO appendix is extensively rewritten and reorganized into a four-part surrogate-theory exposition, alongside separate ablation and fitting appendices. Section 5 is reorganized into Simulators, Noise Handling, Results and Pure Fitting Tasks, with rewritten results prose. Acknowledgements and an impact statement are also added, while much of the introduction and method exposition remains.

P2.justification: Table 1 is transposed and expanded with comparator rows and explicit timeout entries. Figures 3–7 are redrawn with revised legends, comparator curves and placement. New sensitivity tables and fitting/acquisition displays substantially expand the visual presentation; Figure 8 redisplays the Ackley portion of the Appendix B fitting results.

R1.justification: V3 adds Lindauer et al. (SMAC3), Regis and Shoemaker (2013), and Wang et al. (2019, million-point exact GPs), including a discussion of hardware differences in the latter comparison. Snoek's neural-network work and Hutter's random-forest work were already cited in v2; the overall positioning remains similar.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix A is substantially reworked into v3 Appendix C. V3 replaces the full-K-neighbor radius argument with a bound on distant-neighbor weights, adds approximation and spacing bounds, and formalizes improvement properties for a shifted scalarization. New Theorems 2–3 provide conditional noisy weighted-kNN bias–variance/rate results and fitted-parameter stability transfers. V2's final algorithmic-consistency theorem is not retained.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses important validation gaps in v2 through held-out surrogate-quality tests, GP-based acquisition controls and systematic K/P sensitivity analyses. It also improves the local-consistency reasoning, adds conditional noisy-estimation theory and identifies the implementation. These substantially strengthen the paper's evidential support. Remaining inconsistencies limit the gain: Section 3 still says neural-network/random-forest methods are excluded, and the main text retains a convergence claim broader than Appendix C establishes.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Taking the GP Out of the Loop and the same TuRBO-ENN research. Text extraction and visual inspection cover all 14 pages of v2 and 21 pages of v3, including figures, tables, equations and appendices.

after.justification: V3 retains original optimization results and adds surrogate-fitting benchmarks, hyperparameter sensitivity experiments and acquisition ablations in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V2 reports original scaling experiments and optimization results on five simulation or hyperparameter-optimization tasks, including repeated runs under natural and frozen noise.

results.title: Taking the GP Out of the Loop

C1.justification: The central MEAL/JAX novelty claim remains, but v2 broadens the claimed benchmark contribution to controlled observability and agent count. Its conclusion adds claims about curriculum benefits, reward design, and centralized-critic interference. It drops the handcrafted-layout contribution and v1's assertion that parameter-isolation methods fail to scale.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantial mechanism explanations involving cumulative versus decayed Fisher penalties, centralized-critic interference, team-size non-stationarity, role bottlenecks, and multi-head protection against plasticity loss. It removes the fully observable/two-agent applicability restriction while retaining domain and continual-setting limitations. Some concluding interpretations are stronger than the evidence: individual rewards have positive aggregate forward transfer in Table 5 despite the conclusion's negative-transfer claim.

D1.justification: The detailed implementation appendices largely persist. V2 adds optimizer and activation settings, AGEM memory/projection sizes, task-boundary handling, observation-window dimensions, and role-assignment instructions. Listing 1 now returns soup counts rather than counts multiplied by 20; this does not establish a rescaling of reported scores. Hardware, seed identifiers, and the code-access link remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate all three Overcooked difficulty levels; higher difficulties already appear in v1 Appendix C.1. V2 adds evaluated scenarios with one and three agents, partial observability, heterogeneous roles, and individual or sparse rewards. These extend sensing conditions, agent capabilities, and task requirements.

E2.justification: AGEM joins the five existing CL comparators in v2 Table 2. Higher-difficulty comparisons expand from v1's EWC analysis to the full six-method set. V2 also evaluates MAPPO against IPPO in Figure 8 and introduces independently trained IPPO as the explicit forward-transfer reference.

E3.justification: V1 states that task identity is hidden at evaluation and evaluates previously seen tasks; v2 specifies known evaluation identities and evaluation on all sequence tasks. V2 replaces the primary plasticity metric with baseline-relative forward transfer, averages forgetting over final windows, and removes the replay prohibition. Appendix E adds an equal-budget curriculum comparison. Appendix B.1 narrows the stated MLP depth from {2,3} to two layers. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original five-component ablation and repeated-task plasticity study remain. V2 adds tests of agent-count effects, reward design, partial observability, designated roles, and curriculum ordering. Appendix I and Figure 13 add qualitative failure cases involving single-pot fixation, deadlock, and role collapse.

E5.justification: Five seeds and the existing Level 1 average-score and forgetting intervals are retained. V2 explicitly identifies the appendix table intervals as 95% confidence intervals. However, Figure 7 drops v1 Figure 6's explicit ±1 standard-error specification for plasticity bars, leaving their convention less clear under the general confidence-interval statement. No increase in runs is documented.

E6.justification: V2 replaces primary plasticity-score entries with forward-transfer results and adds extensive comparator and scenario results. The newly tabulated Level 3 comparison ranks Online EWC at 0.306 above EWC at 0.178 in average score. Existing Level 1 average-score and forgetting entries remain identical. Separately, plasticity FPR changes from 1.228 to 0.906 for three repetitions and from 0.896 to 0.866 for ten repetitions (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 4), with its definition retained.

M1.justification: V2 extends the benchmark with direction-aware observation masking, individual rewards, and chef/waiter roles that restrict permitted interactions and can switch across tasks (Sections 5.6–5.7; Appendices D and H). These substantively change observations, capabilities, and reward assignment. The core layout generator and existing actor–critic framework largely persist.

P1.justification: Much of the original exposition is retained. V2 consolidates baseline and forgetting discussions, moves normalization into Section 4.5, and relocates the old appendix difficulty/plasticity analyses into Appendices F and G. Local explanations and the conclusion are rewritten, and authorship and acknowledgments change.

P2.justification: The layout examples and generator illustrations are redrawn and reordered. V2 combines existing and new panels in Figure 3, expands per-task plots in Figure 16, restructures Table 2 across difficulties, and places full uncertainty tables in Appendix J. New trade-off plots, observability illustrations, failure examples, and experimental tables substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: V2 retains the earlier references and adds ten works supporting AGEM, curriculum learning, partially observable benchmarks, and reward/cooperation discussions. The dedicated related-work discussion and the central positioning as a CMARL benchmark with end-to-end JAX acceleration remain largely intact.

T1.justification: Section 4.5 revises mathematical evaluation definitions: endpoint forgetting becomes window-averaged forgetting, and mean current-task performance is replaced by normalized AUC-based forward transfer. Section 3 also relaxes the restriction on retaining past data. The soup-bound derivation, generator/validator complexity arguments, and appendix plasticity definitions remain substantially unchanged; no new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's diagnostic value. V1's evidence centered on homogeneous, fully observable two-agent learning; v2 directly tests coordination through agent-count, visibility, reward, and role controls, including roles that prevent solo task completion. Broader comparators and explicit single-task references better distinguish retention from transfer. These address important gaps in support for the CMARL benchmark claim. Less explicit plasticity uncertainty reporting and overstatement of individual-reward negative transfer remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MEAL, with matching core benchmark, methods, and experiments. All 18 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds results concerning agent count, observability, rewards, curriculum learning, and designated roles in Section 5 and the appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original continual-learning baseline results, architectural ablations, difficulty comparisons, and repeated-task plasticity experiments in Section 5 and Appendix C.

results.title: MEAL: A Benchmark for Continual Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: v1 presents a definition and diagnostic of a sufficient world model. v2 centers its contribution on intent comprehension, explicitly identifying this with latent-state recognition rather than the entirety of world modeling (Remark 2.2). Its abstract and introduction also restrict size-related conclusions to the evaluated LLaMA/Gemma models and within-family patterns.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly treats size trends as descriptive rather than causal, adds interpretations involving training-family differences and overfitting, and discusses prompt-dependent credit-decision thresholds. New qualifications concern subjective scoring and zero-variance tasks; Appendix E develops the relationship to correctness. The first/second-moment limitation and multiple sources of model uncertainty were already discussed in v1.

D1.justification: v2 adds lme4::lmer/pymer4 implementation information, detailed answer-generation and paraphrase-filter prompts, loan-profile generation instructions, and a 125-attempt sampling limit. v1's 600-token answer cap is no longer reported. Exact reconstruction remains limited by conflicting v2 task counts: 24 across domains in Section 4, 24 per domain in Appendix F, and 100 in Figure 7.

E1.justification: The five broad domains remain, but v1's everyday scenarios, such as prednisone duration and moving-box logistics, are replaced by a broader generated suite covering nutrient content, expenditure, infrastructure and population estimates (v1 Appendix C; v2 Appendix J). v2 also evaluates binary loan approval and five-level credit-risk rating.

E2.justification: Both evaluate LLaMA 3.2 3B Instruct, LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct, LLaMA 3.3 70B Instruct, and Gemma 3 12B-IT and 27B-IT. v2's categorical and temperature comparisons use this same set. ProSA and FORMATSPREAD remain related-work citations rather than evaluated competing methods.

E3.justification: The reported main sampling grid changes from 3 intents x 50 paraphrases x 50 responses to 12 x 10 x 25. Generation/extraction models change, v2 requests a single numeric estimate, and Appendix F adds removal of estimates beyond three standard deviations. New temperature tests use 0.2, 0.5 and 1, with Gemma 27B at 0.55 instead of 0.5. ICI is added as an evaluation metric.

E4.justification: v2 adds human audits of paraphrase fidelity and numeric extraction, using 200 items per audit and two annotators, plus temperature sensitivity tests (Appendices B and H). These directly examine pipeline validity and decoding sensitivity. v1's survey-generation comparison and two-task response-density case studies are removed.

E5.justification: Reported output draws per cell decrease from 50 to a target of 25, and bootstrap replications from 500 to 100. v2 documents nested task/prompt/response resampling and REML estimation, specifies percentile confidence intervals for categorical results, and adds raw agreement and Cohen's kappa for human audits. Statistical estimation and reporting are substantially expanded and revised.

E6.justification: New numerical-suite, ICI, credit-decision, temperature and validation results replace v1's detailed 15-task results and survey experiment. v2 Figure 3 reports higher aggregate MVS for the two smaller LLaMA models, whereas v1 Figure 4 generally favored 70B within domains; these concern different tasks and protocols. Appendix B newly reports annotator fidelity rates of 95%/91% and extraction correctness of 94%/91%.

M1.justification: The variance decomposition, MVS and categorical entropy analogue remain, with PS renamed IS. Section 3 adds ICI, the harmonic mean of IS and MVS, extending the diagnostic's output. Appendix D specifies REML estimation, but v1 does not identify its estimator, so an implementation switch cannot be established.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around intent comprehension, alongside substantial explanatory and results/discussion rewrites. Experimental detail moves into Appendix F, references precede the appendices, and the appendix organization expands from A–D to A–K. The narrative restructuring extends well beyond terminology changes.

P2.justification: v2 adopts two-column formatting and redesigns the results presentation. v1's density case studies and five detailed result tables disappear; aggregate/ICI plots, task-distribution violins, credit-decision and temperature plots, and human confusion matrices appear. The conceptual illustration is retained. The new Appendix K example table overflows the right page boundary.

R1.justification: Positioning shifts from world models and the stochastic-parrot critique toward intent recognition, pragmatics and inverse planning. v2 adds foundations including Grice, Baker et al., Qin et al., and Louvan and Magnini, plus model-training references. It removes v1's benchmark-critique and stochastic-parrot discussions and associated citations, while largely retaining the DFA/world-model comparison.

T1.justification: v2 adds the formal ICI definition, a finite-sample bias derivation and Gaussian nested random-effects specification (Appendix D), and correctness, acceptability and hybrid valuation definitions (Appendix E). The original consistency/sensitivity conditions and entropy chain-rule decomposition remain mathematically equivalent despite renaming.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidential foundation by directly auditing two previously unvalidated pipeline assumptions, testing temperature sensitivity, and empirically demonstrating the categorical extension that v1 only derived. Narrower intent-comprehension claims and explicit finite-sample analysis improve interpretation. Conflicting task counts, loss of precise task-level tables and Appendix K's overflow impair reproducibility and presentation, but the validation and conceptual gains outweigh these shortcomings. Changed performance values alone do not establish improvement.

A1.justification: These are versions of the same work, retaining the core decomposition, invariance criteria and evaluated models despite retitling. Both main texts and appendices support comparison; text extraction also recovers v2's visually overflowing Appendix K table.

after.justification: Section 4 and Appendices A.2.1, B and H report original numerical-estimation, categorical credit-decision, human-validation and temperature-sensitivity results.

before.justification: Section 4, Figures 2–5 and appendix Tables 1–5 report original model-response experiments, including an alternative survey-style paraphrase experiment.

results.title: Measuring Intent Comprehension in LLMs

C1.justification: The central two-component optimizer and 35–45% memory claim persist. v2 reframes the research question from minimal optimizer states to minimal modifications to SGD and extends the abstract's 7B superiority claim from APOLLO to APOLLO and Muon. The contribution as a minimalist baseline remains in the conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 attributes poor row-wise normalization to extreme LM-head gradient values and hypothesizes that column normalization balances learning across frequent and rare tokens (Section 2.1, Appendix A.9). It adds an interpretation of architectural generality and explicitly qualifies fine-tuning applicability: pretraining remains the target, replacing PEFT is not expected, and combining SCALE with PEFT is future work. These explanations and boundaries were absent from v1.

D1.justification: v2 documents the four-H100 throughput setup and the Newton-Schulz surrogate used for unavailable SWAN throughput measurements. It also supplies diagnostic iteration and tokenizer details and fine-tuning selection procedures. Existing SCALE learning rates, momentum coefficient, vector-parameter handling, and code link remain unchanged; much of Appendix A.2 simply consolidates previously disclosed settings.

E1.justification: v1's task evaluation concerns C4 language-model pretraining. v2 adds RoBERTa-base fine-tuning on six GLUE tasks: RTE, CoLA, MRPC, STS-B, SST-2, and QNLI (Appendix A.6, Table 11). This substantially expands data and task coverage. The additional decoder architectures still use C4 and constitute configuration changes.

E2.justification: The main comparator roster largely persists, but Table 6 adds Muon to the previously APOLLO/APOLLO-Mini-only 7B comparison. Table 2 drops Muon, while Table 3 replaces its Muon reference row with Adam and Adam (Stable-SPAM). Stable-SPAM's renaming does not introduce another method. The original 1B SWAN comparison survives in v2's Table 5 caption.

E3.justification: Table 5 changes the 1B training budget from 13.1B to 20B tokens. v2 also introduces Qwen2-500M, GPT2-M, and Gemma-2B configurations, 350M training at 15.6B and 31.2B tokens, a tokens-per-second evaluation on four H100 GPUs, and fine-tuning with learning-rate search and best-epoch selection. Existing LLaMA sequence length, batch size, precision, and scheduling settings are retained and relocated to Appendix A.2.

E4.justification: v2 adds mixed-normalization ablations holding last-layer momentum fixed (Table 12), LM-head gradient histograms and token-column diagnostics (Figures 3 and 7), training-budget sensitivity (Table 10), and training-throughput analysis (Table 7). The original learning-rate sensitivity and layer-variance analyses remain. The small comparison without Muon-style learning-rate scaling reported in v1 Appendix A.2 is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without confidence intervals, significance tests, or documented seed replication. The single-run disclosure for 7B SCALE is retained and extended to the added Muon result using the same reporting practice. Gradient-distribution diagnostics do not add uncertainty estimates for experimental performance.

E6.justification: The 1B results are replaced under a longer budget: SCALE reports 14.25 perplexity at 13.1B tokens in v1 and 13.49 at 20B in v2, rather than a same-setting improvement. Table 6 retains SCALE's 12.59 and adds Muon's 12.72. Tables 7–12 add substantial results, including SCALE throughput of 44,728 tokens/second and GLUE averages of 85.51 for SCALE versus 85.68 for Adam.

M1.justification: SCALE retains column-wise normalization and first-order momentum restricted to the output layer. Adam updates for vector parameters and Muon-style scaling for the 1B model were already documented in v1. Algorithm 1 now consistently uses the already-defined mini-batch gradient, repairing notation without establishing a different optimization procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten, related work is reorganized, and the normalization exposition is recast from an explicit steepest-descent formulation into a direct list of normalization schemes. A main-text proof sketch is added, experimental settings move into Appendix A.2, and existing appendix analyses are reordered. These changes substantially revise the exposition while retaining the main section sequence.

P2.justification: v2 adds diagnostic Figures 3 and 7 and Tables 7–12. The original 1B training-curve Figure 4 becomes Figure 6 with a longer iteration axis and additional comparator curves. Table 4 is restructured, and several main-text tables are resized and placed beside prose. The original variance and learning-rate plots are retained rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 adds SM3, CAME, a SWAN variant, and a connection to Kunstner et al. (2024) on class imbalance, alongside references supporting the new architectures and tasks. Sophia and standalone SPAM discussion and references are removed, while Stable-SPAM remains. The central positioning as a minimalist memory-efficient optimizer is retained.

T1.justification: The convergence assumptions, bound, and appendix proof are retained; the new main-text proof sketch restates existing arguments. However, v2 defines the gradient in Eq. (2.8) as a stochastic sample gradient, whereas both appendix proofs define it as the full-loss gradient before Eq. (A.10). This changes the stated stationarity quantity and introduces an internal mathematical inconsistency.

improvement.justification: v1 primarily supported SCALE through LLaMA/C4 experiments and isolated normalization timings. v2 substantially strengthens practical-efficiency, generality, and design-justification evidence through training throughput, additional architectures, longer training budgets, GLUE evaluations, mixed-normalization ablations, and the 7B Muon comparison. These gains outweigh the localized theorem-definition inconsistency. Run-level uncertainty remains absent, so small performance margins still provide limited support for broad superiority claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCALE optimizer study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across renumbering and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds training-throughput measurements, additional model configurations, overtraining experiments, GLUE fine-tuning, and mixed-normalization ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original SCALE pretraining results, normalization and momentum experiments, timing measurements, and gradient-variance analyses. Some comparator scores are explicitly attributed to earlier work.

results.title: Memory-Efficient LLM Pretraining via Minimalist Optimizer Design

C1.justification: The abstract's Byzantine contribution changes from an O(sqrt(f/(n-2f))) upper bound to an Omega(sqrt(f/(n-2f))) lower bound. V2 centers its contributions on formal convex SMEA separation for f>=n/3 and withdraws v1's nonconvex contribution.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly identifies the unresolved order of the gap for f<n/3 and explains why poisoning regularity improves generalization bounds without improving already-tight optimization guarantees. New Appendix H substantially expands discussion of practical relevance, other optimizers, multiple local steps, locally poisonous models, and targeted attacks, distinguishing these extensions from established results.

D1.justification: V2 documents revised attack triggering logic and an explicit lower-bound attack construction, while removing empirical robustness-coefficient estimation instructions. Experimental parameters, worker identities, and epsilon=0.001 are retained. New Algorithm 1 contains a threshold inconsistency: its g1<=C condition does not distinguish the unperturbed value C from the smaller perturbed value described in the proof.

E1.justification: Both numerical studies use the same constructed one-dimensional linear-loss task with honest and corrupted workers. No evaluated dataset, domain, or task is added or removed; v1's removed nonconvex coverage was theoretical.

E2.justification: Figure 1 removes the numerical no-attack reference. Optimal poisoning and tailored Byzantine comparisons remain, with the latter using a substantively revised attack. CWTM was not an evaluated empirical baseline in either version.

E3.justification: Figure 1 switches from uniform stability to generalization error using the documented factor 1/[4(n-f)]. Both versions retain n=15, m=1, T=5, learning rate and Lipschitz constant equal to 1, and f ranging from 1 to 7.

E4.justification: V1 Appendix E.1 estimates empirical robustness coefficients and substitutes them into the Byzantine upper bound to examine tightness. V2 removes this diagnostic and instead compares numerical errors with its new Byzantine lower bound for f>=n/3.

E5.justification: Both numerical validations use deterministic GD and display point values without repeated-run statistics, error bars, or significance tests. V2 omits v1's caption explanation for not reporting variance, but the statistical reporting practice is unchanged. Appendix G contains theoretical probability bounds in both versions.

E6.justification: The poisoning curve is unchanged after accounting for the stated rescaling. The Byzantine curve changes beyond rescaling under the revised attack, while retaining the finding of greater error than poisoning. No-attack results and the empirical-coefficient bound series are removed; these revisions do not establish a same-protocol performance gain.

M1.justification: The robust GD/SGD updates and SMEA aggregation rule are retained. The tailored Byzantine procedure changes: v1 Algorithm 1 starts with a poisoning step and subsequently branches on the parameter sign; v2 Algorithm 2 immediately selects extremal updates using the pivot worker's initial gradient.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statement, and Sections 3–4 are extensively rewritten. SMEA's definition moves into the preliminaries, GD/SGD upper-bound proofs are consolidated, cryptographic implications move to the conclusion, and the appendices are reorganized around the two threat models.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main text and references with redesigned headers and appendix formatting. Figure 1 changes its axis, curves, legend, and regime markings; Table 1 and a Byzantine-construction diagram are added. V1's two CWTM illustrations are removed, and the attack pseudocode displays change.

R1.justification: V2 adds Bousquet, Klochkov and Zhivotovskiy (2020) as the source for Appendix G's probability bounds, replacing Lugosi and Neu (2022). Several background and nonconvex-analysis references are removed, including Charles and Papailiopoulos (2018) and Le Bars et al. (2024). The principal positioning against robust optimization and decentralized stability work remains.

T1.justification: V2 adds a constructive Byzantine stability lower bound in Theorem 3.2 and Appendix C.3, plus the generalization-separation theorem 4.2. Lemma 4.1 generalizes the calculation already present in v1 Appendix E.2. Conversely, v1's nonconvex theorems, CWTM properties and counterexample, and trace-based robustness results are removed rather than relocated.

improvement.justification: V1 relied on upper-bound comparisons and numerical evidence for Byzantine tightness. V2's constructive lower-bound argument and generalization-separation theorem substantially strengthen the central scientific justification, while explicit regime qualifications clarify what remains unresolved. Removing nonconvex/CWTM coverage narrows the paper, and Algorithm 1 retains a localized threshold inconsistency, but the central convex analysis is substantially better supported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work despite the changed title and organization. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, figures, and tables are readable and support comparison.

after.justification: Section 4 and Figure 1 report original numerical generalization-error results under optimal poisoning and a revised tailored Byzantine attack, with experimental details in Appendix E.2.

before.justification: Section 4 and Figure 1 report original numerical measurements of robust GD stability under poisoning, a tailored Byzantine attack, and a no-attack reference condition.

results.title: Tight Stability Bounds for Robust Distributed Learning: Byzantine Failures Hurt Generalization More than Data Poisoning

C1.justification: The inference-only, logarithmic DUS contribution remains, but v4 adds hybrid complementarity as an explicit main contribution and claims instruction-following effectiveness and up to 5.8× measured wall-clock acceleration. Its conclusion removes v3's explicit framing around a path toward surpassing AR models in both efficiency and performance.

C2.justification: v3 argues that the spacing bound holds throughout decoding; v4 says it is informative mainly in coarse iterations and explicitly declines to claim late-stage conditional independence. It discusses strong long-range dependencies, treats fast mixing as an analytical device, recommends moderate blocks, acknowledges adaptive samplers' higher-accuracy operating points, and reports task-dependent skip benefits and occasional hybrid regressions.

D1.justification: v4 adds a dedicated DUS code-access link, full hybrid-filter pseudocode, explicit default settings and parameter ranges, and detailed runtime hardware and measurement information. It also clarifies that standard DUS runs without the optional skip heuristic. These materially extend v3's existing harness, hardware, prompting, and dataset disclosures.

E1.justification: v4 adds IFEval, extending evaluation to instruction-following requirements while retaining all six original math, code, and knowledge benchmarks. Additional model configurations, block sizes, and parameter sweeps reuse existing task coverage.

E2.justification: EB-Sampler, discussed but not evaluated in v3, and CB-Sampler become substantial empirical comparators in v4. Qwen-3-8B is added, and token-by-token and Llama-3-8B comparisons expand beyond v3's Figure 1 references into Tables 1–2 and runtime evaluation. The original confidence and random planner comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Original benchmark splits, prompting, and generation lengths are retained. New evaluation designs include Dream-Instruct and additional block sizes on BBH/MMLU-Pro, single-block decoding, threshold and spacing sweeps, IFEval budgets of 1024 and 256 tokens, spatial metrics on 150 samples per row, and timing on 105 samples after five warmups.

E4.justification: v4 adds skip-threshold, single-block, dilation-base, and level-skip analyses; sampler-overhead profiling; token-spacing analysis; hybrid-filter ablations; and qualitative trajectories across five benchmarks. These test sensitivity, mechanism, computational cost, and failures. The original parallelism ablation and fixed-budget block-size analysis are retained, the latter moving from Appendix A.2 to B.1.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v4 identifies some baseline results as author reruns, but this supplies provenance without documenting repeated-trial or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: The original Table 1 confidence/DUS scores, overlapping Table 2 entries, and original ablation results remain unchanged. v4 adds extensive results for new comparisons and analyses. For example, Table 4 newly reports LLaDA-Instruct HumanEval pass@1 of 24.4% for EB versus 37.8% with spacing, with NFE increasing from 35 to 59. Table 12 adds measured DUS wall-clock speedups of 3.9× and 5.8× over token-by-token decoding.

M1.justification: The core deterministic DUS schedule and previously described skip mechanism remain. v4 introduces a distinct hybrid procedure: a score-ordered spacing filter for EB/CB selections that defers nearby candidates and relaxes its minimum gap as the block fills (Section 4.4, Algorithm 1). This extends the proposed method to adaptive samplers.

P1.justification: v4 extensively rewrites the introduction, related work, and method exposition, clarifying the denoiser/planner distinction and entropy objectives. Experimental setup moves from Section 4.1 to 3.7, and the appendix is reorganized into setup/background, experiments, theory, and qualitative trajectories. This is substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain baseline columns and expanded comparison structure. v4 adds multiple ablation, hybrid, and runtime tables, new comparison plots, and colored generation panels. v3's Figure 2 is retained as appendix Figure 3, while Figure 1 moves off the opening page. The document also adopts a different conference layout.

R1.justification: v4 substantially repositions dilated spacing as complementary to adaptive EB/CB sampling, adds Fast-dLLM and newer diffusion-versus-AR research, and explains why JYS is unsuitable for the reported comparison. The theoretical references shift from Asoodeh and Renyi to Bradley and Zhang. These changes go beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v3's first-order Markov and maximal-correlation argument is replaced by finite-order variable-length Markov chain assumptions and geometric-mixing derivations. v4 also introduces explicit optimal-estimator and planner-objective assumptions, block-wide bounds for grouped sampling, and a formal entropy-gap decomposition with proofs in Appendix C. These substantially revise the mathematical framework.

improvement.justification: Adaptive-sampler comparisons, measured latency, sensitivity studies, and code/pseudocode substantially address v3's limited evidence for practical acceleration and reproducibility. v4 also better qualifies applicability and accuracy–compute tradeoffs. These gains outweigh unresolved weaknesses: Table 7's supposedly matching default gives 16.8% versus Table 1's 19.2% for LLaDA-Base on MATH500 at B=16, and Appendix C.2 invokes conditional mutual-information decay without establishing it from the unconditional bound in Lemma 3.6.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DUS research work with the same title and authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and newly added material to be matched reliably.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds IFEval evaluations, adaptive-sampler comparisons, hybrid experiments, runtime measurements, sensitivity studies, and generation examples.

before.justification: v3 reports original evaluations on math, code, and general-knowledge benchmarks, including planner and block-size ablations in Table 3 and Appendix A.2.

results.title: Plan for Speed: Dilated Scheduling for Masked Diffusion Language Models

C1.justification: The encoderless, any-manifold representation-learning claim remains. However, v2's contribution list and conclusion substantially extend the main claims to high-dimensional scalability and numerical stability relative to variational alternatives, together with broader predictive and generative utility. Higher-dimensional scaling was presented principally as future work in v1.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new training trajectories as evidence that noise helps internalize the prescribed geometry, and qualifies utility/generation evaluations as sanity checks. It removes v1's explicit warning that optimized test latents favor RGD reconstruction comparisons and its detailed cross-study benchmarking caveats. The limitation of memory growing with dataset size remains.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly documents training initialization and selection among test-time starting points. Section 4.4 specifies the timing experiment's CPU allocation and decoder layers, and a reproducibility statement describes configurations and scripts. Existing general hyperparameters and hardware are retained. Appendix A also introduces an inconsistent argument order between the noise-function call and definition.

E1.justification: The three datasets remain, but evaluation substantially expands beyond reconstruction and geometric correspondence. Section 4.4 and Appendices I–J add cell-generation discrimination, cell-stage classification, cyclic-phase regression, and mitochondrial-DNA classification of geographical region and two haplogroup resolutions.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in Tables 1–2 remain. v2 adds RGD with Lee and Park's explicit intrinsic-curvature penalty to runtime and alignment comparisons, includes a Euclidean ΔVAE timing variant, and evaluates P-VAE against RGD in mitochondrial-DNA downstream prediction.

E3.justification: New protocols include discriminator training/evaluation on separate halves of the cell-cycle test set, supervised latent-feature prediction, and full-gene timing at 5, 50 and 500 latent dimensions. Appendix C also revises baseline settings from approximate architectural matching and additional-parameter defaults to identical backbones with model/dataset-specific tuning. This reported revision does not establish that retained tables were rerun.

E4.justification: The original noise and curvature sweeps are retained. Appendix K adds a targeted analysis of distance-correlation trajectories during training with noise, without noise and with explicit curvature regularization. Table 4 additionally examines computational robustness as latent dimensionality increases.

E5.justification: Table 4 newly reports runtime means and standard deviations across 100 post-warmup epochs. Figure S5 specifies five runs for RGD conditions but one prematurely stopped explicit-regularizer run. Existing five-initialization and three-run reporting remains; the new utility and generative-fidelity tables report point estimates without uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the earlier mitochondrial-DNA training entries retain their numerical values. Substantial new results appear in Tables 3–4, Tables S1–S3 and Figure S5. For example, new rCRS region-classification XGB accuracies are 0.97 for regularized hyperbolic RGD, 0.85 for Euclidean RGD and 0.65 for P-VAE. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v1 scores.

M1.justification: The per-sample manifold latents, decoder, RiemannianAdam optimization and metric-scaled noise procedure remain. Replacing MLE terminology with MAP clarifies the already prior-containing objective. Newly documented initialization strategies do not establish that the underlying procedure changed.

P1.justification: v2 adds an explicit contribution list and reproducibility/LLM statements, clarifies MAP terminology and optimization, and condenses several results discussions. Appendices are expanded and reorganized, but the main Background–Methodology–Results sequence and substantial existing exposition remain.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, with extensive resizing and repositioning of displays; Figure 2 changes from a 2-by-2 arrangement to one row. The old Table 3 becomes expanded Table S1, and the duplicated mutation histogram remains only as Figure S1. New utility/runtime tables and Figure S5 substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds Huang et al. (2022) to the dimensionality-reduction motivation and Lee and Park (2023) as a substantive curvature-regularization comparison. It contrasts their explicit derivative-based penalties with its noise-induced regularization. The broader related-work coverage and relationship to the Deep Generative Decoder remain.

T1.justification: Section 2.1 adds parameter priors to the formal background MAP objective, and Section 2.2 introduces the mathematical expression for Lee and Park's explicit curvature penalty. The proposed noise regularizer and curvature-versus-noise derivation remain substantively the same; their expanded presentation does not constitute a new proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of practical usefulness and computational feasibility, which v1 left largely untested. Held-out mitochondrial-DNA results, downstream prediction, high-dimensional timing and the regularizer comparison provide evidence beyond low-dimensional visualizations and reconstruction correlations. Removing the test-time comparison caveat is a regression, and uncertainty reporting for new utility results is limited, but the added evidence addresses important validation gaps and yields a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Riemannian generative decoder research. All 14 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2, including appendices, were readable. Textual and visual inspection supports matching retained, relocated and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds downstream prediction, generative-fidelity discrimination, runtime measurements, held-out mitochondrial-DNA results and training-trajectory analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on cell-cycle expression, synthetic branching diffusion and human mitochondrial DNA, including baseline comparisons and noise/curvature ablations.

results.title: Riemannian Generative Decoder

C1.justification: The central bilevel-planning, TWNM, and closed-loop adaptation claims remain. V3 removes the claim to be the first bilevel framework, adds empirical validation as an explicit contribution, and foregrounds live-API generalization. The abstract replaces the 'up to 17 points' headline with an average 13.1-point complex-task gain.

C2.justification: V3 adds a local KL-projection interpretation and explicitly excludes characterization of the full evolving TWNM process. It also interprets the new ablations as complementary component benefits and distinguishes pruning's avoidance of failing APIs from reactivation's recovery of useful tools. Earlier interface, dynamic-environment, and heuristic-runtime limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix E.5 newly documents asynchronous local updates, tool insertion, and offline graph retraining with hot-swapping on a single NVIDIA P40. Appendix C clarifies the retrieval request and illustrates dependency-tree serialization; Table 4 clarifies that the static graph excludes historical invocation data. Existing fine-tuning details and prompts are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use ToolBench, API-Bank, and 50 real APIs covering the same seven domains. V3 adds a distinct changing-availability scenario in Appendix F.2, with API outages followed by recovery. The larger real-API query count changes sampling rather than domain or task coverage.

E2.justification: V3 adds evaluated ToolNet and ToolPlanner comparisons to both the ToolBench comparison in Table 1 and the real-API comparison in Table 2. These substantially broaden comparison with graph-based and structured planners beyond the retained ReAct, ToolLLM, and alpha-UMI baselines; both added methods were already cited in v2.

V3 also introduces component-removal controls and a 50-query, two-phase outage/recovery protocol with explicit pruning and reactivation settings. Existing benchmark splits, metrics, and fine-tuning settings are retained.

E4.justification: V3 adds tests separating the effects of bilevel planning, graph access, and search strategy (Table 3); removing clarification and merging retrieval with execution (Appendix H, Table 11); and enabling pruning/reactivation under changing API availability (Appendix F.2, Table 8). These extend the retained TWNM-variant and decision-pattern analyses substantially.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. V3's additional results and average timings do not introduce a different uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V3 adds comparator, ablation, recovery, and maintenance-cost results, including 44.0% versus 48.0% TSR without versus with pruning/reactivation. Real-API NaviAgent TSRs change from 36.7/53.3/63.3% to 37.4/54.4/64.6% across the three backbones under the expanded query set, not identical settings. Retained ToolBench comparison rows, benchmark-variant tables, and runtime values match v2.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.4 adds periodic probing and reactivation of recovered APIs alongside pruning. The four-action agent, HGT architecture, losses, and search procedures remain substantially unchanged. The three named recovery strategies mainly elaborate v2's existing path-recombination description.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, baseline description, and results narrative undergo substantial rewriting. Real-API evaluation moves from Appendix F.1 into a dedicated main-text section, and ablations are reorganized. The title and author information change, with acknowledgements and an impact statement added.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column preprint layout to two-column conference formatting. Earlier Figures 1–2 are replaced by a conceptual comparison, an architecture/recovery overview, and a redrawn evolution diagram. Comparison tables and plots expand, new ablation tables appear, and the real-API table moves into the main text.

R1.justification: V3 removes Qu et al.'s 'From Exploration to Mastery' reference and moderates the first-framework novelty claim. The introduction more explicitly distinguishes action-mode selection from standard planner–executor formulations. Most related-work discussion and cited works remain unchanged.

T1.justification: New Section 3.4 and Appendix I introduce context-dependent feasible action sets, a KL-minimal projection theorem with a support assumption and proof, an idempotence proposition, a hard-rule corollary, and a possible soft extension. This formal analysis is absent from v2; the existing HGT and loss equations remain mathematically equivalent.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central orchestration and adaptation claims by adding relevant graph-planner baselines and direct component, action, and outage/recovery controls that v2 lacked. The expanded live-API evaluation and maintenance-cost disclosure also improve practical assessment. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses: uncertainty estimates are still absent, and configurations underlying some new ablation rows are not fully reconciled across Tables 3, 4, and 11.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NaviAgent, with matching core methods and experiments despite title and formatting changes. The complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains original benchmark results and reports expanded real-API evaluation, additional component and action ablations, API outage/recovery experiments, and graph-maintenance measurements.

before.justification: V2 reports original ToolBench and API-Bank experiments, component analyses, link-prediction results, and a 60-query evaluation on real APIs in Appendix F.1.

results.title: NaviAgent: Graph‑Driven Bilevel Planning for Scalable Tool Orchestration

C1.justification: Despite renaming and stronger emphasis on associative memory, both versions claim that sparse, self-routed rank-1 experts improve knowledge reuse, reduce interference and forgetting, and preserve generalization efficiently. The memory interpretation already appears in v2; the new experiments support these retained core claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of replay compatibility, order robustness and aggregated routing patterns, and explicitly discusses linear storage growth and pruning trade-offs. It distinguishes static weight-memory keys from dynamic attention keys and adds application, bias and misuse discussion. The central specialization and forgetting explanations remain.

D1.justification: v3 adds a TRACE implementation recipe covering hyperparameters, context length, epoch schedule, DeepSpeed ZeRO-2, BF16 and four H100 GPUs, plus the post-pruning procedure. Existing experiment recipes remain. v2's promise to release source code upon acceptance is removed without replacement access information.

E1.justification: v3 adds TRACE's heterogeneous continual-learning stream, including MeetingBank summarization, Py150 code generation and 20Minuten multilingual simplification, and adds SuperNI evaluation. This substantially broadens language-task coverage beyond the retained classification streams and single-stage CodeAlpaca fine-tuning experiments.

E2.justification: New evaluated comparators include FIX(ICL), OGD, GEM, DualPrompt, HiDeLoRA and TreeLoRA in TRACE Table 2, and SAPT and C-LoRA in SuperNI Table 13. Earlier comparison sets remain; the renamed routing-ablation variants correspond to their v2 counterparts.

E3.justification: TRACE introduces three backbone configurations, 5,000 training and 2,000 testing examples per task, a variable epoch schedule, task-specific metrics and OP/BWT evaluation. SuperNI adds protocols with and without generated replay. These are settings for added experiments; the stated settings of retained experiments are unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds tests of the storage–accuracy trade-off from post-pruning (Table 19), order sensitivity using existing task-order results (Table 14), and whether illustrative rank-reuse patterns hold across entire task test sets (Figure 5). Earlier routing, sparsity, temperature and activation analyses remain.

E5.justification: Table 14 newly reports standard deviations across the three existing task orders, including 77.6 ± 0.26 for MoRAM. This measures order variability rather than additional random-seed runs. The earlier three-run X-TAIL uncertainty reporting remains unchanged; TRACE follows the same mean-and-standard-deviation practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial TRACE, SuperNI, pruning and activation results. For example, TRACE reports LLaMA-2-7B-Chat OP 44.54 ± 0.9 and BWT 1.37 ± 0.3; Table 19 reports Last accuracy of 79.5 with pruning versus 80.9 without it. Retained benchmark values match v2. A small inconsistency appears in new Table 14: L2P's mean is 61.0, while retained Table 8 still gives 60.7.

M1.justification: The core rank-1 experts, self-activation, top-k masking, temperature scaling and inference thresholding remain unchanged. v3 additionally specifies and evaluates optional storage pruning after each task, retaining atoms covering 99% of cumulative training activation (Section 3.3.4 and Appendix A.10), beyond v2's per-input activation pruning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten around the MoRAM terminology. Methods are reorganized into Sections 3.3.1–3.3.4, standard language-classification discussion moves to the appendix, and impact and funding statements are added. These are substantial narrative changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v3 adds TRACE, SuperNI, order-robustness and post-pruning tables and an aggregated activation heatmap. It relocates the main-text T5 summary to Appendix Table 8, revises Figure 1's routing illustration and changes title-page, table and page formatting. Earlier activation and sensitivity plots remain under matched numbering.

R1.justification: v3 adds targeted positioning against TreeLoRA, HiDe-PET and SAPT, references TRACE and SuperNI, and adds fine-grained MoE literature. It removes model-editing references such as Bau et al. and Meng et al. The broader relationship to LoRA, MoE and classical associative memory remains substantially intact.

T1.justification: Definition 1 and the reorganized method equations restate the existing associative-memory factorization and sparse rank mixture. Redundant algebra is condensed, and standard OP/BWT formulas explain the added evaluation metrics. No substantive new theoretical result, proof or mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: TRACE substantially strengthens support for language-model continual learning by testing heterogeneous generative and multilingual task streams across three backbones, beyond v2's mainly classification-based sequential evaluations. Post-pruning results and test-set-wide activation analysis also address storage costs and the representativeness of illustrative examples. These gains outweigh limited reporting drawbacks, including underspecified SuperNI settings, the inconsistent L2P mean and removal of the code-release pledge.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same continual-learning framework, renamed from MoRA to MoRAM. The complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated content.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds TRACE and SuperNI evaluations, post-pruning experiments and aggregated activation analysis.

before.justification: v2 reports original CLIP and language-model experiments, code-generation and generalization results, routing ablations and activation analyses.

results.title: Little By Little: Continual Learning via Incremental Mixture of Rank-1 Associative Memory Experts

C1.justification: The central contribution remains partner-specific in-context adaptation without parameter updates. V3's abstract, introduction and conclusion broaden the claimed demonstrated applicability from Overcooked to higher-dimensional GRF coordination with multiple partners. The fundamental contribution is retained rather than replaced.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantial interpretations of cross-episode conditioning versus behavior cloning, stale-context effects, meta-RL failures and reward-shaping controls. It introduces limitations concerning larger teams, communication, embodied perception/control, cold-start costs and within-episode compounding errors. V2's explicit lack-of-mutual-adaptation limitation is no longer stated in the conclusion.

D1.justification: V3 adds reward-event tables, GRF configuration, DPP implementation details, context-masking documentation, baseline adaptations, coding prompts and all 144 human comments. Computational accounting expands, with total reproduction cost changing from approximately 300 to 800 GPU hours. A demo link is added, but v2's explicit scripts/configuration availability statement and human-score outlier-trimming disclosure disappear. Some new descriptions conflict with retained appendix settings.

E1.justification: V3 adds Google Research Football's 3-vs-1 with Keeper scenario, where CooT coordinates with two simultaneous partners using higher-dimensional observations. This substantially extends coverage beyond two-agent Overcooked. The five evaluated Overcooked layouts and the human-study population are retained.

E2.justification: V3 adds BC-RNN and an adapted PACE to the main Overcooked comparison. Appendix F adds GAMMA comparisons on Coord. Ring and Counter Circ., PLASTIC on Coord. Ring, and sparse-reward HSP/MEP variants. Conversely, the fine-tuning comparison drops its no-fine-tuning column from v2 Table 11 to v3 Table 17.
