after.justification: v3 reports revised benchmark results and additional behavioral, ablation and expert analyses, while retaining the wet-lab results.

before.justification: v2 reports original benchmark experiments, ablations, expert evaluations, multi-step predictions and two wet-lab syntheses.

results.title: Retro-Expert: Collaborative Reasoning for Interpretable Retrosynthesis

C1.justification: The introduction changes the higher-order contribution from selected checks finding no contradictions to a claimed proof of completeness at all orders. The abstract and contribution list also add a general multi-input numerical implementation and its demonstrated predictive accuracy, substantially extending the stated contributions.

C2.justification: Appendix K.1 newly explains why full-kernel plots can conceal inaccuracies in first-order corrections and why width-rescaling amplifies sampling noise at larger widths. The existing interpretations of criticality, scale invariance and the restriction to MLPs are largely retained.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's inputs, estimators and GPU timings, v3 documents the existing NTK parameterization, a SymPy-to-NumPy/SciPy recursion implementation, integration simplification and caching, JAX sampling procedures, integration tolerances, numerical precision and CPU timings (Appendices B, J and K). This substantially expands reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Both versions study initialization statistics using synthetic Gaussian inputs, single and distinct inputs, and MLPs with ReLU, LeakyReLU, identity and GeLU activations. The added convergence experiments retain this coverage; different input realizations, dimensions and widths are setting changes.

E2.justification: The infinite-width kernels computed with neural-tangents and the existing theoretical stability predictions remain the reference methods. The added finite-width curves evaluate the proposed framework; no new competing method is introduced.

E3.justification: Section 6.1 and Appendix K.1 add a substantial recursion-validation protocol: four-layer GeLU networks, four specified four-dimensional inputs, widths up to 220, double-precision sampling, numerical integration and width-rescaled kernel deviations. These are new experiments alongside the retained stability and activation studies.

E4.justification: v3 adds systematic checks of whether the first-order terms explain finite-width deviations. Appendix K.1 isolates the corrections by multiplying deviations by width and tests convergence of V, A, B, D and F against solved recursions. v1 primarily tested depth stability and the presence or absence of corrections.

E5.justification: The new tensor-convergence studies specify 100 repeated Monte Carlo estimates for their means and error bars (v3 Figures 6–10). Existing experiments retain their repetition counts and uncertainty conventions; the addition does not establish increased repetitions for the earlier studies.

E6.justification: v3 adds corrected-kernel agreement with sampled networks at widths above approximately 20, isolated-correction results and tensor-convergence results (Figures 1 and 4–10). Existing stability fits also change: B0101 changes from 0.01ℓ^3.78 to 0.21ℓ^3.34 under the same stated settings (v1 Figure 8; v3 Figure 16).

M1.justification: The diagram-construction procedure and MLP model remain. However, v3 corrects the computational specification by explicitly centering the cubic-vertex quantity ΔΩ and adding a factor of 1/8 to the V contribution in the NTK-mean correction (v1 Equation 72; v3 Equation 75).

P1.justification: Sections 4–5 are reorganized around numbered theorems, with substantial application derivations moved into Appendices H–I. Appendix material is regrouped into proofs, implementation details and experiments, and the experimental narrative now begins with solving the recursions. This exceeds local language editing.

P2.justification: v3 adds an introductory corrected-kernel comparison, extensive multi-panel convergence figures and additional theoretical diagrams. It also splits v1 Figure 2 into v3 Figures 3 and 22, moving the NNGP panel to the appendix, and substantially rearranges diagram and figure placement.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for SymPy, NumPy and SciPy and claims novelty for implementing the general multi-input recursions. The related-work discussion and positioning against earlier NTK and Feynman-diagram research otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.3 and Appendix E.4 add an all-orders completeness argument beyond v1's selected higher-order checks. Appendix I adds an explicit all-orders argument for the diagonal NTK mean. Mathematical corrections include centering ΔΩ and the factor of 1/8 in the mean recursion. Many earlier derivations are retained under new theorem labels.

improvement.justification: v1 tested qualitative stability and vanishing-correction predictions without numerically validating the solved finite-width recursions. v3 addresses that important gap through direct Monte Carlo comparisons, isolated-correction checks and tensor-convergence studies, supported by detailed implementation instructions and corrected formulas. These substantially strengthen empirical support and reproducibility. Section 7 still uses tentative higher-order wording despite the new all-orders theorem, but this inconsistency does not outweigh the concrete gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and visual inspection supports matching equations and figures across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical studies and adds numerical solutions of the finite-width recursions compared with sampled networks in Section 6.1 and Appendix K.1.

before.justification: v1 reports original Monte Carlo experiments on MLP kernel statistics, depth stability and activation-dependent finite-width corrections in Section 6 and Appendix H.

results.title: Finite-Width Neural Tangent Kernels from Feynman Diagrams

C1.justification: v1 presents a method to determine the correct L0. v2 reframes this central contribution as a proxy that guides the search, particularly by detecting excessively low L0, and explicitly rejects treating it as a perfect guide. Its architectural scope also expands beyond BatchTopK, while retaining the central claim that insufficient L0 encourages feature mixing.

C2.justification: v2 adds hypotheses about per-latent thresholds explaining JumpReLU's high-L0 behavior and simultaneous excessive and insufficient firing across BatchTopK latents (Section 4.2; Appendix A.10). It discusses elbows versus global minima, uncertain differences between diagnostic metrics, and limitations concerning nonlinear features and unbalanced correlations. These substantially qualify and extend v1's interpretations.

D1.justification: v2 Appendices A.1–A.3 substantially expand training-loss, pseudo-gradient, learning-rate schedule, and JumpReLU hyperparameter documentation; the code link is unchanged. Reproducibility gaps remain: toy batch size is stated as 500 in Section 3 but 1024 in Appendix A.2, and v1's explicit N(1.0, 0.15) magnitude specification is no longer supplied. These disclosure differences do not establish actual batch-size or magnitude-setting changes.

E1.justification: v2 adds five-feature synthetic scenarios isolating positive and negative correlations (Section 3.1), extending v1's randomly correlated 50-feature setup. The Pile training corpus and the same sparse-probing task suite remain; additional model and layer configurations are settings changes.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates BatchTopK SAEs and ground-truth toy controls, without evaluated JumpReLU comparisons. v2 introduces extensive direct BatchTopK–JumpReLU comparisons on Gemma-2-2b layer 12 (Figures 10, 15, and 18), establishing an architectural comparison absent from v1. Appendix A.5 also evaluates decoder cosine similarity as an alternative diagnostic.

E3.justification: The Gemma-2-2b layer-12 comparison uses 1B training tokens in v2 Section 4.1, versus 500M in v1 Section 4. New protocols cover Gemma layer 5, Llama-3.2-1b layer 7, JumpReLU sparsity-coefficient sweeps, and the decoder-cosine metric. The MSE control is now described as a constructed ground-truth SAE rather than the correctly trained SAE; that description alone does not establish a rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of signed correlations using ground-truth initialization, JumpReLU sparsity sensitivity, alternative-metric agreement, decoder-projection histograms, and encoder-bias/threshold dynamics (Sections 3.1, 3.6, 4.2; Appendices A.5 and A.10). These substantially expand investigation of failure mechanisms. The earlier sparsity–reconstruction and L0-transition analyses are retained, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: v1 reports no seed counts or uncertainty bands for its experimental sweeps. v2 specifies five seeds per L0 for the BatchTopK toy sweep and three for the additional LLM sweeps, introducing standard-deviation bands (Figures 7, 9, 13, and 14). This establishes new uncertainty reporting, without establishing how many runs underlay v1.

E6.justification: v2 adds results on signed feature mixing, JumpReLU's stronger high-L0 sparse-probing performance relative to BatchTopK, and cases where diagnostic minima disagree with probing optima. LLM projection and F1 curves are expanded or replaced under revised configurations and budgets, so they do not establish same-setting gains over v1. The MSE example remains 2.73 versus 4.88, and the Neuronpedia survey results are retained.

M1.justification: v2 adds an alternative L0-selection diagnostic based on mean absolute pairwise decoder cosine similarity (Appendix A.5). This extends the approach while retaining the original nth decoder projection calculation and automatic L0 optimization procedure, moved from v1 Appendix A.4 to v2 Appendix A.6.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the introduction and background, expands explanations of features, latents, and toy models, and reorganizes the experimental narrative. The former appendix sparsity–reconstruction analysis becomes Section 3.4, while the discussion and appendix organization are extensively revised.

P2.justification: v2 adds correlation heatmaps, an explanatory projection histogram, architecture comparisons, and diagnostic plots, while redrawing sweep figures with uncertainty bands. Metric and probing panels are vertically aligned for comparison, and existing appendix figures move into the main text. Captions and the document template also change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 adds positioning around superposition and the linear representation hypothesis, nonlinear features, Anthropic's training procedure, and AxBench, citing Elhage, Park, Engels (2025), Conerly, and Wu, among others. Templeton et al.'s Scaling Monosemanticity reference is removed. The central relationship to feature hedging and absorption remains.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix A.5 introduces a mathematical definition of the decoder-cosine diagnostic, averaging absolute cosine similarities over distinct latent pairs (Equation 6). The original projection definition and automatic-L0 finite-difference updates remain unchanged. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on one SAE architecture and one LLM layer through controlled correlation tests, JumpReLU comparisons, additional LLM configurations, and seed-based uncertainty reporting. The expanded evidence exposes failures of the global-minimum interpretation, and v2 correspondingly narrows its diagnostic claims, improving their credibility. Although conflicting toy batch-size disclosures and omitted magnitude parameters weaken reproducibility, the stronger empirical support and better-calibrated conclusions provide a clear substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching analyses moved between sections.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds controlled correlation experiments, JumpReLU comparisons, additional LLM configurations, and diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic SAE experiments, Gemma-2-2b sparse-probing evaluations, and an analysis of open-source SAE sparsities.

results.title: Sparse but Wrong: Incorrect L0 Leads to Incorrect Features in Sparse Autoencoders

C1.justification: The central contributions remain low-rank attention outputs, their association with dead features, and ASI with SparseAdam. However, the abstract's quantitative claim changes from roughly 60% of directions capturing 99% of variance to roughly 60% effective rank. It also qualifies the output projection's role from inducing the phenomenon to strongly shaping it.

C2.justification: v3 substantially extends interpretation: Appendix N argues that feature quality and dead-subspace reconstruction are preserved and proposes weak signal or absent standalone features as explanations for dead-subspace behavior. Section 6 suggests architectural changes to mitigate rank collapse, while Appendix I links remaining dead features to fixed-subspace-dimension mismatch. Existing qualifications concerning unresolved causality and high-initial-L0 failure remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix O supplies a detailed Lorsa recipe, including head/QK-group dimensions, optimizer settings, learning-rate schedule, 2048-token sequences, training budget and initialization distributions. SAE settings and pseudocode are also revised, and dataset-component selection is clarified. Some ambiguity remains because ASI-specific Q/K copying in Section 5.4 is not clearly distinguished from the general Xavier initialization described in Appendix O.2.

E1.justification: Appendix I.2 adds actual ASI evaluation on fineweb-edu, and Appendix N introduces blinded semantic-consistency evaluation beyond reconstruction and dead-feature measurement. Existing general-text, code, scientific-text and Chinese coverage remains. Github and Arxiv already appear in v2; the clarified SlimPajama subset names do not establish new coverage.

E2.justification: The Lorsa comparison expands from Base versus ASI in v2 Figure 8 to TopK, AuxK and ASI in v3 Figure 9, adding AuxK within that experiment. The principal SAE/scaling comparators, random-subspace baseline and JumpReLU Pre-Act Loss comparator were already evaluated in v2.

E3.justification: The principal dimensionality metric changes from a 99%-variance threshold to entropy-based effective rank. Outside scaling, stated SAE defaults change from batch size 32768 and Adam learning rate 2e-4 to 4096 and 4e-5. The earlier 2.5B-token scaling budget becomes an 800M-token general specification. Lorsa's layer sweep becomes a middle-layer sparsity sweep, and additional model/site configurations and blinded feature scoring are introduced. These reported changes do not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds SVD sample-stability analysis, dictionary-size/sparsity controls for the rank–dead-feature relationship, broader ASI robustness evaluations, and monosemanticity/dead-subspace analyses in Appendices C, F, I and N. Random-subspace, near-full-rank and high-initial-sparsity ablations are retained under new appendix labels. The variance-threshold sensitivity sweep in v2 Appendix F is removed.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports three-seed means and standard deviations for Figures 6–7 and Table 4, 15 independent seeded trials with one-sided Welch tests in Appendix H, and five SVD samples with coefficients of variation in Appendix C. v2 does not provide these uncertainty procedures or corresponding run counts, so an increase over known v2 repetition counts cannot be inferred.

E6.justification: v3 replaces dimensionality estimates and revises SAE/Lorsa result displays while adding extensive numerical results in Tables 1–10. For example, the new Qwen3-8B/fineweb-edu layer-8 comparison reports normalized MSE of 0.31228 for Base, 0.28849 for AuxK and 0.28533 for ASI. Table 10 adds dead-subspace MSE of 0.00350 versus 0.00334. The headline 87%-to-below-1% result remains; changed metrics and budgets limit direct cross-version performance comparisons.

M1.justification: The ASI and SparseAdam framework remains, but the initialization routines change. Appendix I in v2 initializes SAE weights using random subspace coefficients; Appendix K in v3 instead projects the full decoder matrix through V_active V_active^T. Lorsa switches from output-side SVD and decoder-to-encoder tying to input/value-side SVD and encoder-to-decoder tying. These are procedural refinements within the existing approach.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled, dimensionality terminology is revised throughout, and substantial related-work, quantification, initialization and discussion passages are rewritten. Experimental settings receive a separate subsection, and existing appendices are extensively reordered around the new analyses. Author contributions are added and the earlier LLM-use declaration is removed.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column to two-column layout. Most plots are redrawn or rearranged, the introductory illustration is relocated and numbered, the rank–dead-feature display gains a scatter panel, and ten tables are introduced. These changes substantially alter the visual presentation beyond figure renumbering and numerical updates.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds representation-collapse literature, including Hua, Tian and Jing, and reframes the linear-representation discussion around superposition while qualifying claims of empirical validation with Sharkey et al. New references support effective rank and feature evaluation, while Guth et al. is removed. The core positioning relative to attention-pattern approximation, compression and single-head rank bottlenecks remains.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 replaces the variance-threshold dimension definition with Definition 4.1, effective rank computed from the entropy of normalized singular values. The attention variance factorization and head-subspace bound remain substantively unchanged. Appendix B states the formula for the existing loss-recovery metric; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence that was limited in v2: repeated-seed estimates and significance tests establish reliability, additional layers and Qwen3/fineweb-edu evaluations test ASI's generality, and feature-quality/dead-subspace checks address whether reducing dead features sacrifices useful representations. These additions materially support the practical contribution. Changed metrics and budgets complicate cross-version score comparisons, and Lorsa initialization remains partly ambiguous, but those limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same attention-rank and Active Subspace Initialization study despite the changed title. All 22 pages of v2 and 27 pages of v3, including figures, equations and appendices, support comparison. Changed metrics and experimental settings can be identified separately.

after.justification: The paper retains original empirical results and adds SVD stability measurements, further SAE evaluations, statistical tests and blinded feature-quality assessments.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 and the appendices report original activation-spectrum analyses, SAE and Lorsa training results, scaling experiments and ablations.

results.title: Dimensional Collapse in Transformer Attention Outputs: A Challenge for Sparse Dictionary Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion replace the claim that compact architectures consistently outperform larger models and challenge typical scaling laws with a protocol-qualified account: REVE leads on average, compact models remain competitive, and scale alone does not explain transfer. The central multi-task claims also explicitly acknowledge negative transfer.

C2.justification: Section 4.6 replaces the interpretation that architectural bias outweighs scale with an account allowing scaling benefits while acknowledging objective, architecture and adaptation confounds. v3 adds substantive discussion of pretraining overlap, protocol-dependent rankings and limited public EEG data for further scaling. Section 6 also identifies model-specific adaptation constraints, while retaining limitations already discussed in Appendix F.

D1.justification: Appendix B.6 newly documents model-specific amplitude normalization, including BENDR's min-max scaling and REVE's window-level z-score approximation. The reported hardware changes from two A800 GPUs to one; PCA rank 6 and Figure 1's data-volume estimation basis are also specified. These disclosures improve reproducibility without establishing that the newly described normalization procedures changed.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 14 datasets across 10 paradigms, with matching dataset descriptions and Table 1. Additional SEED-VII classifier-head results extend an existing experiment within already represented task coverage.

E2.justification: Both evaluate BENDR, BIOT, LaBraM, EEGPT, CBraMod, CSBrain and REVE, alongside Mantis and Moment. Tables 7–8 retain the same four head-ablation comparators: LaBraM, CBraMod, CSBrain and REVE.

E3.justification: v3 excludes LaBraM–SEED and EEGPT–SEED/PhysioMI pairs from Figure 1's aggregate performance. The reported CountSketch dimension changes from 6 to 1024, and the warm-up learning-rate factor changes from 0.1 to 0.5. These are limited protocol revisions; splits, metrics and the 30-epoch budget remain unchanged, and the PDFs do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Tables 7–8 add SEED-VII to the attention-pooling and large-MLP classifier-head ablations, extending evidence about decoder capacity. Existing adaptation and pretraining ablations receive revised outcomes, while the gradient, representation and qualitative case-study analyses retain their scope.

E5.justification: Both versions report performance means and standard deviations across five independent runs and diagnostic statistics across ten random seeds. No new uncertainty-estimation practice, confidence interval or significance test is introduced.

E6.justification: Numerous entries in Tables 2–8 change, and Section 4.6 switches the overall leader from EEGPT to REVE. For example, Table 3 replaces REVE's PhysioMI balanced accuracy of 30.63±0.06 with 58.82±0.45, and EEGPT's BCIC-2a value of 50.52±0.93 with 39.23±1.48. Tables 7–8 also add SEED-VII results. These are revised reported outcomes, not established same-setting performance gains, given the changed settings and aggregation.

M1.justification: The benchmark retains its model adapters, fine-tuning strategies, task setups, classifier heads and diagnostic algorithms. Newly documented normalization conventions do not establish a method change; the revised numerical diagnostic settings concern evaluation protocol.

P1.justification: The abstract, introductory findings, substantial experimental discussion and conclusion are rewritten to present more conditional interpretations. v3 adds main-text Section 6 and Appendix C.1, while retaining Appendix F. Correspondence, publication headers and bibliographic wording are also updated; the benchmark pipeline and most appendix prose remain recognizable.

P2.justification: The figure and table inventory and overall visual design remain intact. Figure 1 and several radar charts are rescaled or redrawn, Figure 5 moves, Figure 10 gains a SEED-VII spoke, and Tables 2–8 gain overlap markers. Tables 7–8 add corresponding rows, while diagnostic and case-study figures remain visually unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 adds Markiewicz et al. (2021) on OpenNeuro to support discussion of the available pretraining-data supply. Most other reference changes update publication metadata for existing works, including REVE, CBraMod and CSBrain; the related-work coverage is otherwise retained.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(12) and the definitions of gradient alignment, conflict, subspace affinity, CKA, RSA and classification metrics are retained. Specifying projection dimension and PCA rank changes experimental documentation rather than mathematical theory or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important weaknesses in the benchmark's central comparisons by flagging pretraining overlap and excluding affected pairs from Figure 1. It replaces v2's categorical scaling conclusion with protocol-qualified interpretations consistent with the revised tables and documents checkpoint-specific normalization. Together, these changes substantially improve comparison transparency, reproducibility and the defensibility of the main conclusions; higher reported scores alone are not the basis for this assessment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EEG-FM-Bench. Their text, equations, tables, figures and Appendices A–F are readable and support reliable matching despite revisions and page shifts.

after.justification: v3 reports revised benchmark results, additional classifier-head results and retained original diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original classification experiments in Section 4 and Tables 2–9, plus gradient, representation and qualitative analyses in the appendices.

results.title: EEG-FM-Bench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for the Systematic Evaluation and Diagnostic Analyses of EEG Foundation Models

C1.justification: Both versions claim that a lightweight compressor optimized using downstream task feedback preserves or improves QA accuracy while greatly reducing context, retaining the headline 3% compression ratio and 3.3-point average EM gain. v4 foregrounds the existing distillation stage and changes the title without materially changing the central contribution.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands applicability and efficiency discussion: Section 3.4 proposes task-specific rewards for generation, summarization, and dialogue, while Appendix B develops training, inference, and retraining-cost arguments. Section 4.7 qualifies cross-dataset transfer as nearly lossless despite degradation relative to target-dataset training. The alpha discussion also narrows improvement to the majority of cases. Open-ended applicability remains proposed rather than experimentally demonstrated.

D1.justification: v4 replaces the promised code release with a repository URL and newly specifies greedy decoding, validation-based alpha selection over 0.2, 0.5, and 1.0, and approximately five hours of RL training on eight H20 GPUs. Most implementation settings are retained or relocated. Conversely, Figure 3 replaces v3's explicit few-shot QA examples with an Examples placeholder, reducing prompt specificity.

E1.justification: v4 adds LongBench evaluation on MuSiQue and long-context variants of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultihopQA (Appendix D.1). Their context lengths and document construction differ from the retained retrieval benchmarks. It also adds NQ evaluation with shuffled irrelevant passages. These substantially extend the represented inputs and test environments.

E2.justification: v4 adds evaluated LongLLMLingua and QGC baselines to both the five-document and ten-document comparisons in Table 1, materially broadening the principal compression comparison. Existing comparators remain, and the corresponding downstream-LLM transfer and alternative-compressor tables retain their comparator sets.

E3.justification: New protocols include training on NQ and evaluating on HotpotQA, evaluating LongBench using HotpotQA-trained compressors with F1 and token counts, and constructing noisy NQ inputs from three DPR passages plus seven random Wikipedia passages followed by shuffling. The original benchmark splits, retrieval setup, model configurations, and training budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 4.7 adds cross-dataset transfer analysis, and Appendix D.2 tests resistance to irrelevant, shuffled context without noise-augmented training. Figure 4 adds F1 sensitivity curves alongside the existing EM analysis. The original stage ablations, compressor-size comparisons, downstream-LLM transfer analysis, and two case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated evaluation runs, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The retained five GRPO rollouts per sample describe training, not repeated experimental evaluations.

E6.justification: Shared table values and case-study outputs are unchanged. v4 adds baseline scores, F1 sensitivity curves, LongBench results, cross-dataset transfer results, and noisy-NQ results. For example, CORE/full-context scores are 38.94/38.41 F1 on LongBench MuSiQue and 38.19/35.21 EM on noisy NQ. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over matched v3 results. The prose changes the five-document EM-gain range from 1–7 to 1.5–6.9, although unchanged Table 1 implies 0.68–7.08.

M1.justification: Both versions use DeepSeek-V3 distillation with the same filtering rules, followed by GRPO optimization using EM plus weighted F1 rewards and a frozen downstream LLM. Greedy decoding is newly documented, while the open-ended-task discussion proposes possible extensions without establishing an implemented method change.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodology, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work moves before methodology, experiments and appendices are reorganized, and inference receives a dedicated subsection. The title, author information, and disclosures also change. This is substantial editorial restructuring beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v4 changes the document from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout. Figures are redrawn or relocated, the two appendix prompt figures are merged into main-text Figure 3, and Figure 4 gains an F1 panel. Table 1 gains baseline rows and shaded groups, and three new experimental tables are added.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands to discuss soft compression, including xRAG, and prompt compression methods including LongLLMLingua, DAC, and TACO-RL. It develops new distinctions between generative compression and token deletion, and between training a fixed-generator compressor and training the generator itself. Earlier citations to RA-DIT, REPLUG, and RAFE are removed.

T1.justification: Equation 1 expands the previously stated cross-entropy loss into token-level log probabilities, and Equation 2 introduces shorthand for the existing probability ratio. The filtering conditions, GRPO objective, and reward definitions are mathematically retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important gaps in v3's evidence by extending five- and ten-document evaluations to much longer LongBench contexts, injected retrieval noise, and cross-dataset transfer, including a documented transfer limitation. Additional relevant baselines and implementation disclosures strengthen evaluation and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of explicit few-shot examples and the inaccurate revised EM-gain summary. Statistical uncertainty and measured inference-latency comparisons remain absent, but the empirical support for applicability and robustness is substantially stronger.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CORE compression framework despite the changed title. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds LongBench evaluation, cross-dataset transfer, noisy-context experiments, and additional baseline comparisons.

before.justification: v3 reports original QA accuracy and compression results, training-stage ablations, compressor comparisons, downstream-model transfer experiments, and case studies.

results.title: Less Is More: Elevating RAG via Performance-Driven Context Compression

C1.justification: v1 centers its contributions on the first fast SNGD/SPRING guarantees for least-squares and strongly consistent least-quadratics. v2 claims a systematic framework based on SVS as an alternative theoretical proxy, global guarantees without independent mini-batches, and an explicit alpha/gamma characterization of subsampling. The retained SPRING connection becomes one component of this broader contribution.

C2.justification: v2 substantially develops the interpretation of SVS as an analytical proxy, including its impractical row-access costs, limitations of extending guarantees beyond SVS, and unresolved bounds on gamma. It also explicitly discusses SPRING's lack of improved dependence on the Hessian condition number. v1's explanation of regularization through negative-eigenvalue divergence is removed.

D1.justification: v1 provides dimensions, condition numbers and brief tuning statements. v2 Appendix F specifies matrix construction and normalization, spectral profiles, consistency construction, Monte Carlo budgets, rate fitting and logarithmic hyperparameter searches. It also newly states that code accompanies the supplementary information, although that resource's availability cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: Evaluation remains confined to synthetic linear least-quadratics. Within that coverage, v2 tests independently constructed Jacobian and Hessian matrices, contrasts flat and decaying spectra, and adds a non-Gaussian scenario with one Jacobian row inflated by 100 (Appendices E–F). Neither version evaluates actual neural wavefunction or PINN tasks.

E2.justification: v1 Figures 1 and 4 compare SGD, SNGD and SPRING. v2 Figure 5 retains SNG versus SPRING but omits SGD, while Figures 2 and 6 newly compare directly implemented SVS-SNG, independent two-mini-batch SNG and uniform single-mini-batch SNG. These substantially change the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: The experimental design changes substantially. v1's main optimizer comparison uses m=10,000 and n=100; v2 uses m=1,000 and n=100, introduces regularization and step-size sweeps evaluated after 1,000 iterations, and reports fitted convergence rates against relative batch size. Its spectral-scaling experiment fixes the step size at 1, while the SPRING comparison retains independent hyperparameter tuning.

E4.justification: v1's eigenvalue-based instability and regularization studies are removed. v2 adds sampling-proxy sensitivity tests, a 100-fold row-outlier robustness test, and analyses of alpha/gamma scaling and flat versus decaying spectra (Figures 2–4 and 6). The batch-size question from v1 Appendix D is retained but investigated with new experiments in v2 Figure 5.

E5.justification: v1 reports eigenvalue distributions over 1,000 random problems per panel. v2 drops that study and introduces documented Monte Carlo estimation of gamma, including draw counts, and regression-based convergence-rate estimates (Appendix F). Neither version reports seeds, confidence intervals or optimizer-run error bars; the Monte Carlo draws are not repeated optimization runs.

E6.justification: The earlier optimizer trajectories and eigenvalue results are replaced. v2 newly shows that SVS generally tracks uniform single-batch SNG more closely than the two-batch proxy, and reports superlinear alpha/gamma and empirical convergence-rate scaling under spectral decay (Figures 2–4 and 6). Figure 5 reports new SNG/SPRING rates retaining the shrinking acceleration gap at larger batch sizes. Different settings prevent direct cross-version performance comparisons.

M1.justification: The SNGD update, renamed SNG, and SPRING momentum update are retained (v1 Algorithm 1; v2 Equations 8 and 23). The squared volume sampling distribution in v2 Equation 14 already appears as k-DPP sampling in v1 Proposition 9, Equation 37. Its expanded theoretical and experimental role does not introduce a new optimizer.

P1.justification: Most main-text exposition is rewritten and reorganized. The least-squares-to-least-quadratics narrative becomes sections on analysis without decoupling, small-sample insights and principled acceleration. Contributions receive a separate section, background explanations expand, and appendix proofs are regrouped. The title changes and SNGD becomes SNG throughout.

P2.justification: The main text and references change to two columns. v1's pseudocode block, equivalence table, green summary boxes and eigenvalue scatterplots disappear; v2 introduces a contribution matrix and new proxy and scaling plots. The batch-size comparison changes from multiple iteration-error trajectories to a convergence-rate-versus-sample-size display using new results.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around squared volume sampling and sketch-and-project analysis, adding discussions of Mutny et al., Rodomanov and Kropotov, Gruhlke et al., and Xiang et al. It removes v1's proximal-point and interpolation-related discussion and revises the comparison with previous stochastic-preconditioning analyses. Retained works' publication updates alone do not constitute these changes.

T1.justification: v2 adds an exact SVS expected-update identity and a global stationarity guarantee beyond quadratic losses (Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.2). Theorem 5.1 replaces v1's strong-consistency and alignment framework with an SVS analysis allowing ordinary consistency and rank deficiency, and revises gamma. New bounds and compatibility results receive appendix proofs. v1's divergence criterion and explicit SGD comparison proof are removed, while the SPRING equivalence is generalized.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central analysis: the exact SVS identity enables ordinary-consistency LLQ results without v1's restrictive range-containment assumption, plus a global stationarity theorem. Targeted experiments test proxy validity and spectral-scaling mechanisms, and Appendix F materially improves reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of direct SGD comparisons and eigenvalue diagnostics. Dependence on the SVS proxy and the unresolved general SPRING guarantee remain explicit limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' analysis of subsampled natural gradient algorithms. All 21 pages of each version, including equations, figures and appendices, support comparison despite the changed title and extensive revision.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on sampling proxies, convergence constants, spectral decay and SPRING acceleration, including the non-Gaussian experiment in Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic optimization experiments comparing SGD, SNGD and SPRING, plus eigenvalue simulations in Appendix C.

results.title: A Sketch-and-Project Analysis of Subsampled Natural Gradient Algorithms

C1.justification: The contributions shift from a cross-attention U-Net and comprehensive topography visualization to DiT/DDIM generation, joint visual/text conditioning and learnable spatio-temporal encoding. v4's conclusion additionally claims consistent superiority over evaluated existing methods and effectiveness of the newly introduced components. This substantially redefines the claimed technical contributions and comparative performance.

C2.justification: v4 adds interpretations connecting caption alignment to generation performance and regional ablations to the importance of occipital processing. It retains the inter-subject variability concern already discussed in v1, but drops v1's optimistic EEG generalization interpretation based on small MSE standard deviations. The hardware-limited model-capacity limitation and detailed discussion of acquisition noise and anatomical variability are removed.

D1.justification: v4 Appendices B–G add channel-region assignments, padding instructions, explicit preprocessing, training/inference pseudocode, DiT and CLIP dimensions, diffusion scheduling and baseline descriptions. This substantially expands technical documentation beyond v1's U-Net configuration and preprocessing citation. However, v1's explicit 50-epoch training count disappears, and v4 does not reconcile its per-region padding instructions with the patch totals reported in Appendix E.

E1.justification: The brain-signal coverage remains THINGS-EEG2 with ten participants and THINGS-MEG with four participants, evaluated within and across subjects. v4 Section 4.3 and Appendix I additionally evaluate image-caption generation and semantic alignment on the same images, providing a limited auxiliary task extension without introducing another neural dataset or population.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates Addition and Concatenation conditioning variants but no external encoding baselines. v4 Tables 1–2 add Güçlü and Van Gerven, Yamins et al., and an M/EEG adaptation of SynBrain; Tables 5–6 additionally compare VisualGLM and MiniGPT-4 caption generators. The original Addition/Concatenation comparison is removed.

E3.justification: v4 restricts cross-subject evaluation to training on Subject/Participant 1, replacing v1's all-source/all-target design. Brain-signal evaluation expands from MSE and PCC to include cosine similarity and synchronization likelihood. New caption analyses use CLIPScore over 16,740 EEG-dataset images and 22,448 MEG-dataset images. Expanded preprocessing documentation does not establish that the retained datasets were processed differently.

E4.justification: v1's fusion-strategy ablations are replaced by tests removing text, brain-region or temporal embeddings. v4 also adds alternative-caption-generator comparisons, caption-quality distributions and an example, and regional channel-removal analyses. Conversely, v1's all-subject training/test/generated topography analyses are reduced to two cross-subject training-versus-test comparisons without generated-signal topographies.

E5.justification: v1 Tables 2, 4, 9 and 10 report source- and target-wise standard deviations across subjects; v4's aggregate performance tables omit this dispersion reporting. Neither version reports repeated-training run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. This is a reporting loss, not evidence that fewer independent training runs were performed.

E6.justification: Reported within-subject mean MSE/PCC changes from 0.217/0.188 to 0.109/0.425 for EEG and from 0.763/0.122 to 0.663/0.379 for MEG. These are results for the revised system, without an established identical experimental protocol. v4 adds external-baseline, cosine/SL, caption and component/region results, while removing individual-subject scores and most cross-subject pair entries.

M1.justification: v1's CLIP-image-conditioned U-Net with DDPM sampling is replaced by a Diffusion Transformer with DDIM sampling. v4 additionally introduces Qwen2-VL-generated captions encoded by CLIP, combined image/text conditioning, and learnable brain-region and temporal embeddings with region-aware patch construction. These substantially change the architecture, conditioning and inference procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, method exposition, experimental narrative and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work gains numbered subsections; dataset and implementation descriptions move into appendices; the appendix is reorganized from A.1–A.3 into A–I. The title and authorship also change, and a separate impact statement replaces part of the former discussion/conclusion structure.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn for the caption-conditioned DiT architecture. Subject-wise and cross-subject matrix tables are replaced by compact method-by-metric displays, while caption examples, score distributions and regional-ablation charts are introduced. The extensive earlier topography panels are replaced by two cross-subject views, and the main text changes from a single-column to a two-column layout.

R1.justification: v4 expands positioning through dedicated diffusion-model and LLM subsections, adding DDIM, DiT, captioning models, established neural-encoding research and SynBrain. M1.justification: The spectral estimators and scalar OP-GF procedure are retained. Although v3's main text uses separate depth factors, its Appendix C already gives the scalar flow used throughout v4; reconciling those descriptions does not establish a new learning procedure.

P1.justification: The document is extensively reorganized: ridge analysis and model extensions move into appendices, related work is consolidated, and proofs receive a new hierarchy. The introduction, discussion, mathematical explanations, terminology, and cross-references are substantially edited.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and reformats the five empirical figures with revised labels, legends, captions, and sizing. Figures 3–5 move into appendices, while v3's unnumbered eigenvalue-ordering schematic is removed.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands positioning against balanced spectral cutoffs and early stopping, adding Blanchard, Stankewitz, and Hucker–Reiss references, alongside Canatar's alignment measure. It explicitly identifies the classical bias–variance crossing as an antecedent rather than the novelty. The existing PCR survey is relocated and refined.

T1.justification: v3 Theorem 6.2 becomes v4 Theorem 5.2 with corrected concentration scales, an additional log n in the endpoint time, explicit learned-spectrum margin conditions, and a reconstructed proof in Appendix G. v4 also adds source-ellipsoid worst-case sharpness and assumption-verification proofs, supplies fixed-quota minimax upper bounds, and revises correlated-noise, RKHS-range, and ridge boundary definitions.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important mathematical deficiencies: fixed-quota estimators supply explicit minimax achievability arguments, the adaptive theorem gains matching conditions and a substantially repaired proof, and the source-condition example becomes a proved worst-case embedding. RKHS boundary cases and Figure 4's inconsistent documentation are also corrected. Although the adaptive guarantee is narrower and changed simulation curves are only partly explained, the stronger mathematical support and clearer applicability limits constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ESD framework and contain readable main texts, figures, equations, and complete appendices. Relocated and renumbered material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v4 reports original simulation outcomes in Section 6 and Appendices B.4, C.4, and D.2, including Figures 1–5.

before.justification: v3 reports original simulations for sequence models, fixed-design regression, RKHS regression, and deep linear networks in Figures 1–5.

V1 described guardrail and pooling components but did not report these as separate comparators; SPI was discussed without an empirical comparison.

Figures S6–S10 and S18 examine questions beyond the retained simulation sweeps and trimming experiments.

V1 already reported repeated trials and standard deviations for the interpretability study. Stated repetition counts for retained experiments remain unchanged.

Figure S14 adds majority-vote findings, including little evidence favoring K = 64 over 16. Guardrail, Synth+Real, SPI, and matched-error results further expand the evidence.

However, Appendix H.1 changes the prescribed tolerance from ε = rδ/(n+1) − α to ε = 1 − α − rδ/(n+1), altering the stated tuning rule for that conformal specialization. This does not establish a change to the experimental implementation.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten around practical choices, validity, utility, and the tolerance tradeoff. The main experiments are reorganized around classification, proteins, and multiple outlier testing; LLM comparisons move to Appendix C. Related-work organization and the experimental appendices are also restructured.

P2.justification: V2 adds classification plots, matched-error curves, majority-vote displays, and per-class tables. Existing plots gain comparator series and revised legends; protein panels are regrouped, and the main outlier figure incorporates an ROC display. Appendix J redisplays many experiments with Synth+Real. The protein visualizations are retained.

Prediction-powered inference discussion largely moves to Appendix A. FLUX's renamed author attribution and SPI's publication update refer to existing works.

T1.justification: Localized mathematical corrections include composite one-sided nulls and their binomial-test justification, the meet condition in F.1, changing > k to ≥ k in Appendix G's k-FWER definition, the ε formula in H.1, and replacing TV with KL inside the Pinsker bound in I.7. The principal theoretical framework and proofs are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the empirical case beyond comparisons against a more conservative real-only procedure. New classification evidence, standard errors, and mathematical corrections further improve the paper. These gains outweigh Appendix J's overbroad claim that pooled and synthetic-only baselines consistently perform similarly.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GESPI research work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical studies and adds classification experiments, majority-vote comparisons, and further controlled analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulations and experiments involving protein structure prediction, LLM comparisons, outlier detection, and vision-transformer interpretability.

Appendix H's claimed dedicated-DNS superiority cannot be verified because Table 14 contains no dedicated-model result.

M1.justification: The core architecture, frequency queries, projection, streaming modules and scaled log-spectral loss are retained. v3 adds limited task-specific adaptations, including removal of negligible-power high-frequency bins before URGENT processing and modified loss weights for dedicated training (Appendices F and A.3). It newly credits SpatialNet when motivating frequency projection and sharing. Older HiFi++, BBED, iSTFTNet and Wave-U-Net references disappear, while comparisons with specialized deterministic systems receive substantially more discussion.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the evidence behind the design: parameter-controlled architecture comparisons, direct discriminator tests, broader loss controls and sampling-rate sensitivity experiments address weaknesses in v1's component validation. These gains outweigh the loss of VoxCeleb uncertainty reporting and remaining reporting defects, notably the dedicated-DNS superiority claim unsupported by Table 14.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TF-Restormer research despite the changed title and format. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching.

before.justification: v1 reports original restoration, denoising, super-resolution, streaming and ablation results, including VoxCeleb evaluation in Appendix F.

The two-latent nudity variant already appears in v2. v3 describes applying existing score-based selection to unseen concepts without introducing a distinct algorithmic component.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites selected abstract, related-work, setup and results passages, updates author information and terminology, introduces dedicated Limitations and Impact Statement sections, and moves hyperparameter discussion earlier in the appendix. Most method exposition and existing analysis prose and ordering remain recognizable; the added scientific material does not constitute wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a conference layout with running headers and a single-column appendix, redraws Figure 2, reformats the main comparison table, and replaces the adversarial bar chart with Table 2. It combines v2 Figures 10–12 into Figure 9's panels, adds a style-erasure image grid and several tables, and relocates/resizes existing grids, heatmaps and multiplier plots.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SAEmnesia, with the same authors, core method and substantial shared experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated material.

The retained adapter-pretraining ablation changes from nine mixed benchmarks to eight GraphLand datasets, adding three GraphLand cases and removing four classic cases. The explicit with/without-LapPE comparisons disappear.

Its new generator-ablation Table 5 provides point scores without uncertainty values. No increase in independent repeated evaluation runs is stated.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn, and Figure 2 expands from four to eight panels with revised axes and a training-stage divider. improvement.justification: v1 supported its central graph-prior design largely through motivation, visual examples and an adapter-pretraining comparison. v2 adds generator comparisons using the same first-stage budget and quantitative synthetic/real graph analyses, substantially strengthening that evidence, alongside broader baseline comparisons and clearer reproducibility details. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GraphPFN and contain readable main text, figures, tables and Appendices A–D. All 16 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2 were inspected, and relocated material could be matched reliably.

E6.justification: Results change broadly under the revised pretraining. M1.justification: The architecture, supervised/MGM objectives, and graph structure generator remain essentially unchanged. Section 4.2 replaces optional Laplacian positional encodings in the attribute generator with node degree and PageRank, each included with probability 0.5. Appendix C also actually applies ECOC inference, which v2 only suggested as a possible extension.

P1.justification: v3 edits the abstract and method explanations, condenses three main experimental observations into two, and relocates the ensembling discussion to Appendix C. improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of previously untested design choices through MGM, adapter-architecture, and adapter-only finetuning controls, while adding evidence about runtime and applicability beyond 10 classes. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GraphPFN research work. Their complete text, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including the additional Appendix E in v3.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark results, component ablations, additional multiclass evaluations, runtime measurements, and comparisons with NodePFN.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link, Ashhad hyperparameters, SynthCity implementation provenance, and detailed metric-computation instructions in Appendix B.1. These specify synthetic sample counts, preprocessing, histogram construction and smoothing, scaling, and the Sinkhorn solver. It also adds dropout/weight-decay disclosures and privacy-training information while revising existing hyperparameters.

E1.justification: Both versions use AIDS, GBSG2, and METABRIC with the same populations and survival endpoints. The additions analyze retained data or change training and evaluation procedures; they introduce no new dataset, medical domain, or underlying prediction task.

E2.justification: v2 adds Ashhad to Tables 2–3, real-data-trained survival models as a reference in Table 3, and DP-GAN in the new private-training comparison. Some Ashhad entries are explicitly taken from its papers. The original five generative baselines remain, and comparative Kaplan-Meier plots also expand baseline participation.

E3.justification: Table 4 revises SurvDiff's epochs from 4000 to 1200, warm-up from 1500 to 150, maximum noise from 80 to 20, and learning rate from 0.002 to 0.001. v2 adds Shape and ETD metrics, ablation controls, parameter sweeps, and private evaluation at epsilon 8 and delta 10^-5. These are reported setting changes, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix J newly isolates duration-dependent weighting with a w=1 ablation and tests four decay-parameter values. Appendices C–E add event-time-conditioned covariate comparisons, marginal distributions, and separate censored/uncensored temporal analyses. The reduced-sample study is retained, while SurvDiff-only seed plots are replaced by comparative covariate/Kaplan-Meier panels.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations across ten seeds for their principal experiments. The new private-training and ablation tables follow that practice. No increased replication count, significance testing, or new uncertainty-estimation procedure is documented.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 substantially revise existing results: SurvDiff's AIDS C-index changes from 0.6826 to 0.7017, while its METABRIC Brier score changes from 0.1924 to 0.2120. Kaplan-Meier results also change, and Shape, ETD, privacy, and ablation results are added. These are revised results under changed reported settings, not controlled performance gains. The downsampling table is numerically retained.

M1.justification: The central joint diffusion model, survival head, and calibrated Cox-loss weighting remain. Table 4 changes the listed MLP depths from 2 to 3 and survival-MLP depth from 1 to 2. Appendix I adds an optional DP-SGD variant using per-sample gradient clipping and Gaussian noise.

P1.justification: v2 edits terminology and explanatory passages, organizes fidelity around four categories, promotes Results to a separate section, and expands and renames appendices. Most existing method and discussion prose remains close to v1, so the substantial scientific additions do not constitute wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: Experimental plots are extensively redrawn with revised colors, annotations, and panel arrangements. The main METABRIC t-SNE display moves to the appendix, while temporal distributions enter the main text. New marginal and temporal plots, comparative Kaplan-Meier panels, expanded Tables 2–3, and new ETD, privacy, and ablation tables substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Sections 1–2 and Table 1 newly acknowledge the Ashhad–Henao framework alongside SurvivalGAN and explain their staged generation relative to SurvDiff's end-to-end design. TabDDPM, SynthCity, and differential-privacy references are also added. Most previous research positioning remains; the swapped TabDiff citation suffix is merely bibliographic.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 8 corrects the Cox-loss denominator from exp(r_i) in v1 Equation 10 to exp(r_j) inside the risk-set sum. v2 also formally defines ETD and differential privacy and gives a clipped-gradient update. The existing diffusion mathematics is substantially retained, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evaluation of the central survival-generation claim through direct weighting ablations and event-time-conditioned fidelity evidence that v1 lacked. The additional Ashhad comparison, corrected Cox equation, and explicit metric-computation details also improve assessment and reproducibility. ETD's inconsistent equal-width/equal-mass bin descriptions and incomplete privacy-accounting details limit parts of the new material, but the evidence supporting evaluation of the core method is substantially stronger overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SurvDiff by the same authors. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on the same datasets, including new temporal-fidelity, private-training, and ablation results. Some explicitly attributed Ashhad results are borrowed, but extensive original results remain.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation-fidelity, downstream survival, Kaplan-Meier, and reduced-sample experiments on AIDS, GBSG2, and METABRIC.

results.title: SurvDiff: A Diffusion Model for Generating Synthetic Data in Survival Analysis

C1.justification: v2 drops automatic LLM-based constraint handling and its feasibility guarantee from the central contributions. It adds an explicit scalability claim up to 7,000 nodes and specifies 110 variants, including 99 unseen variants. The claim of being the first single neural solver covering over 100 variants remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations for ATSP degradation through symmetric-task bias, ReLD decoder weakness through hypernetwork optimization difficulty, and generalization through training-feature coverage. It interprets the new component and adapter experiments and adds dynamic VRPs as a future extension. The earlier LLM reliability and overfitting rationale is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds URS code-access information, the CPU specification, prize-generation details, and explicit documentation of URS-STL's 300-epoch schedule with decay at epoch 251. That schedule was unspecified in v1, so its disclosure does not establish a training change. Conversely, the LLM prompt, mask-generator code, and checker examples are removed.

E1.justification: v2 adds AOP, APCTSP, and ASPCTSP evaluations, increasing reported coverage from 107 to 110 variants. It also adds synthetic CVRPTW, CVRPB, and OCVRPTW scenarios with 1,000–5,000 nodes and Set-AGS benchmarks with 3,000–7,000 nodes, substantially extending the tested input conditions.

E2.justification: RouteFinder already appeared in v1's Set-X comparison, but v2 newly evaluates RF-TE and CaDA on shared tasks and retrains both for a 48-variant comparison (Appendix J.2). ELG joins the benchmark comparisons. Conversely, the AM comparison on SPCTSP disappears between v1 Table 10 and v2 Table 15.

E3.justification: New protocols include 16 instances per synthetic large-scale setting, constraint-matched baseline evaluations, equal 150-epoch training for URS and retrained comparators, and disabling augmentation across UDR-component ablations. Appendix D also changes the stated ACVRP oracle from OR-Tools to PyVRP. These do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond retaining the original ablations, v2 tests training-problem selection, attention efficiency, separate BIAS/WEIGHT contributions on unseen tasks, removal of every UDR component, and hypernetwork versus adapter decoders (Appendices G, J.1, and K.5–K.7). These substantially expand evidence about component necessity, efficiency, and generalization.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates and retain the same LKH3 one-run setting. No new training-seed information, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided. v2 Figure 4 replots existing ablation values without error bars.

E6.justification: Numerous unseen-task values and rankings change: URS's OCVRPBPTW gap changes from -3.47% to 10.05%, falling behind the retained neural comparators (v1 Table 10; v2 Table 15). The cause is unspecified. v2 adds extensive scalability, baseline, and ablation results, while retaining the 11 seen-task and Set-X results. Some original comparator entries disappear.

M1.justification: v2 removes the proposed LLM-driven mask-generation, validation, and reuse pipeline described in v1 Section 4 and Appendix G. Constraint masking remains, but its automated generation is no longer part of the presented method. The UDR, MBM, hypernetwork, and reinforcement-learning backbone remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution statement, and methodology narrative are substantially rewritten and reorganized. The standalone LLM section disappears, parameter generation receives a dedicated discussion, and the experimental and ablation narratives expand substantially. Appendices G and J are repurposed, and new subsections extend Appendix K.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, separates the pipeline and MBM diagrams, removes the LLM diagram, expands Table 1, and splits the seen-task table. The original summary ablation table becomes Figure 4. Numerous new experimental tables substantially change the presentation, while existing appendix tables are reformatted.

R1.justification: v2 removes Appendix A.3's positioning against LLM algorithm-generation approaches, including EoH, ReEvo, HSEvo, and AHD-MCTS. It expands comparisons of attention efficiency and supported problem scales and adds references supporting the broader evaluations. ICAM and RouteFinder publication updates concern the same previously cited works.

T1.justification: v2 Table 13 adds explicit asymptotic time and space complexity comparisons absent from v1. The final probability formula also replaces v1 Equation 9's general mask with a visited-node condition in Equation 10, despite retaining broader feasibility masking in prose. No new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: The matched and equally budgeted comparisons in Appendix J.2, component and adapter ablations in K.5–K.7, and scalability tests in Tables 5–6 address important gaps in v1's validation of generalization and design choices. Removing the LLM component reduces constraint-handling documentation, and unexplained score revisions remain a weakness. Nevertheless, the stronger experimental controls, diagnostic evidence, and reproducibility information provide a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same URS research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds scalability evaluations, controlled baseline comparisons, efficiency measurements, and further ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original routing experiments, zero-shot generalization results, benchmark evaluations, and component ablations in Section 5 and Appendices I–K.

results.title: URS: A Unified Neural Routing Solver for Cross-Problem Zero-Shot Generalization

C1.justification: The abstracts, introductions and conclusions retain the central claims: scalable simulation-based red-teaming, 300 cases spanning five risks, substantial search-agent vulnerability, and limited protection from common defenses. V4's additional experiments support existing claims about scalability and ongoing safety auditing.

C2.justification: V4 distinguishes unreliable search-result collections from intrinsically unreliable websites and explains the topical-relevance boundary in Appendices J.4–J.5. It adds interpretations of benign-condition failures, evaluator errors and generator dependence. It also describes helpfulness as perceived usefulness rather than factual accuracy, although the retained judging prompt still includes accuracy.

D1.justification: V4 supplies the new query-quality prompt, Claude API details and the forced-call implementation, and newly specifies greedy decoding for the original integrity-filtering agent. Public code/data access was already advertised in v1; v4 retains the GitHub address while removing the separate anonymous-access statement.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds a distinct query-quality assessment using HarmBench, WildChat, GAIA and SimpleQA Verified, extending represented data to malicious requests, real conversations and other information-seeking benchmarks. These datasets support query assessment rather than additional agent-safety benchmarking; the original five-risk coverage remains.

E2.justification: V4 Table 1 adds Claude-Haiku-4.5 and Claude-Sonnet-4.5 to both search-workflow and tool-calling comparisons. All previously evaluated main-table models remain, as do the Reminder and Filtering defense comparators.

E3.justification: New protocols include GPT-4.1 query-quality scoring on a 0–5 scale, forced execution of exactly three tool calls for injection-round comparisons, and evaluations on 27-case and 108-case difficulty tiers. Appendix I newly applies safety scoring to existing benign-condition responses, explicitly reusing them. The main experiment's search and decoding defaults are retained.

E4.justification: V4 adds query-representativeness and integrity checks, injection-round and persuasiveness ablations, open-source test-generation and difficulty-tier comparisons, a January 2026 timestamp experiment, and five paired safe/unsafe response examples. V1's existing configuration ablations, human-evaluator validation and GPT-5 reasoning analysis are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report three runs per test case and average their results. V4 introduces no new seed disclosure, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty-reporting practice. The 200-response human-agreement validation also retains the same counts and agreement rates.

E6.justification: All 35 retained main-table model/scaffold rows are numerically unchanged. V4 adds Claude results, including Sonnet's 4.6% tool-calling ASR, and recalculates aggregate averages; Claude runs are separately dated November 15. Substantial new results appear in Tables 4, 7, 8 and 10 and Figures 5 and 10, including the reported 0.81% average benign-condition ASR. These are additional findings, not same-setting improvements of retained models.

M1.justification: V4 adds experimental extensions: two-baseline tiered filtering for harder cases in Appendix E and explicitly persuasive website generation in Appendix F. The original three-stage generation, attainability/integrity filtering, checklist evaluation and single-website injection procedure remain intact.

P1.justification: V4 extensively rewrites the abstract and main narrative, moves detailed RAG comparisons and motivating-experiment setup into appendices, relocates dataset construction into experimental setup, and adds separate continuous-supervision and discussion sections. SafeSearch now consistently names the framework, with the benchmark described as its dataset.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns. V4 redraws framework diagrams, relocates the RAG comparison, combines the old reasoning-effort and risk-boundary illustrations, and adds multiple tables and response-example figures. Figure 8 also corrects the token-limit plot's horizontal-axis label, previously mislabeled as search-result count.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 and Appendix A substantially expand positioning against RAG, agentic RAG and knowledge-poisoning research, discussing differences in control, attacker capabilities and mitigation. V4 adds Crest-Search as closely related work and introduces references supporting the new dataset comparisons, while removing some earlier citations, including FaithEval and Safetywashing.

T1.justification: The mathematical description of queries, tool calls and mixing authentic results with one injected website is retained. Neither version presents theoretical propositions or proofs; v4's expanded conceptual distinctions and empirical scoring rubric do not introduce formal theory.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's reported vulnerabilities. Table 10 quantifies safety without injected content across the original agents, addressing an important attribution gap; the new timing, generator and difficulty experiments test whether findings depend on particular configurations. These additions improve confidence in the framework's validity and usefulness. The new helpfulness-description/prompt mismatch remains a limitation, but does not outweigh the stronger empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SafeSearch research. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support matching content across the substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V4 retains these original results and adds model evaluations, query-quality assessments, integrity controls, generation experiments and qualitative response comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original in-the-wild observations, evaluations across three search-agent scaffolds, defense experiments, configuration ablations and human validation of its evaluator.

results.title: SafeSearch: Automated Red-Teaming of LLM-Based Search Agents

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets and conclusion retain the same central claims: a widespread MCQ knowledge-prediction gap, a geometric account involving knowledge/prediction subspaces, and mitigation through KAPPA with some transfer beyond MCQs. The additional analyses principally strengthen support for these retained contributions.

C2.justification: v4 develops an abstract-feature explanation of KAPPA using separation from the unembedding space, explains how near-orthogonal subspaces can retain correlated representations, and discusses scale and distillation as possible causes. Appendix E.4 adds task-specific transfer-failure interpretations. Section 3 also softens v3's inference that underusing linear knowledge makes effective nonlinear knowledge use implausible.

D1.justification: v4 replaces the future code-release promise with a repository link and identifies the GSM8k-MCQ source. New appendices document centering, SVD rank tolerance, random-subspace construction, unembedding extraction and sampling/retraining recipes, substantially extending reproducibility information without establishing changes to the original training setup.

E1.justification: The benchmark datasets, subtasks and free-form evaluation tasks are retained. Distractor resampling and training subsets remain within existing coverage; Qwen3-32B extends model configurations. The GSM8k-MCQ source is newly identified, without evidence that the underlying dataset changed.

E2.justification: Base, CAA, DoLA and KP remain in the corresponding performance comparisons, and CAA/DoLA procedures are unchanged. New random-subspace controls support geometric diagnostics rather than introducing an evaluated competing intervention.

E3.justification: v4 adds principal-angle and CKA evaluation with random controls, cross-benchmark correlation protocols, Qwen3-32B and alpha=80 configurations, distractor-resampled testing, and retraining on 10–80% subsets. These substantially extend experimental design; the original splits, probe-training settings and main evaluation pipeline remain.

E4.justification: Beyond v3's logit visualization, hyperparameter sweep and transfer analyses, v4 adds quantitative subspace geometry, comparison with the unembedding space, distractor and training-size sensitivity, and correct-to-incorrect transfer analysis. Sections 4 and 6 and Appendices B/E substantially expand tests of mechanism, robustness and failure conditions.

E5.justification: v4 adds accuracy means and standard deviations across 10 distractor seeds, one-sided t-tests, three-seed training-subset averages, Spearman correlations with p-values, and random-control sampling details. These reporting practices were absent from v3 and concern the new analyses, not documented repetitions of all retained results.

E6.justification: v4 adds geometric, sensitivity, larger-model and transfer-loss results. Tables 2–3 revise Llama TruthfulQA KAPPA(3)/(6) accuracy from 73.5/65.5 to 65.6/73.5; Table 2 also revises Llama BBH-Algorithmic KAPPA(3) ACC/AGR from 49.2/81.9 to 49.5/82.9. New Table 13 reports Qwen3-32B accuracy of 84.0 with alpha=80 versus 79.5 for Base.

M1.justification: The two probes, minimal-perturbation intervention, alpha/beta alignment and token-wise application are retained. The corrected main update matches the solution already derived in v3 Appendix B.1. Centered subspaces are introduced for geometric analysis, without establishing a changed KAPPA intervention procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction and analysis narrative are substantially rewritten. Geometric analysis becomes a standalone section, and the appendices reorganize previously separate data, prompting, evaluation and probing material into a consolidated setup appendix, followed by geometry, derivation, baselines and results. Explanations and cross-references are extensively revised.

P2.justification: v4 adds dedicated geometry, correlation, training-size and gain/loss displays in Figures 8–14, plus Tables 13–15. Existing displays are relocated; Table 1 changes highlighting, and Figure 3 gains Pearson-correlation annotations and a revised caption. The original plotted data in Figures 1–7 are retained.

R1.justification: Related Work replaces some safety/toxicity/reasoning-steering examples with sentiment, personality and value-direction studies, including Tigges, Han and Jha. New references support CKA, logit-lens and feature-geometry discussions and identify the GSM8k-MCQ source. The central positioning connecting gap diagnosis with inference-time intervention remains.

T1.justification: v4 formally defines decision-relevant subspaces using mean-centered weights with rank at most k−1. It also corrects the main closed-form expression to use the unaugmented prediction-weight Gram matrix, resolving its inconsistency with v3's existing appendix derivation. The underlying optimization and Lagrange-multiplier proof are retained.

improvement.justification: v3's geometric explanation relied mainly on logit scatter plots. v4 substantially strengthens that central argument with centered-subspace measurements, random controls and cross-benchmark tests, while seeded sensitivity experiments and transfer-loss reporting improve assessment of robustness and limitations. The main update also becomes consistent with the existing derivation. Qwen's correlation remains nonsignificant and some mechanistic/distillation explanations remain inferential, but the added validation provides a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KAPPA study. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical evaluations and adds geometric measurements, larger-model experiments, sensitivity tests and transfer-loss analyses.

before.justification: v3 reports original probing, intervention, cross-dataset transfer and free-form generation results, including Tables 1–4 and appendix Tables 11–12.

results.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion recast the contribution as a shared-context principle instantiated by GRPO-MA. Claims of empirical necessity and strictly superior performance are narrowed to effectiveness, potential necessity within the stated estimator setting, and matching or slightly outperforming thought scaling. The claim of the first variance-based analysis is removed.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive qualifications about approximation error, residual correlations, breakpoint effectiveness, and validation at only the thought–answer boundary.
