It explains temperature changes as changing the estimation target, interprets weaker Pass@1 gains on difficult benchmarks through sparse rewards, and adds an interpretation distinguishing the roles of CoT and branching in manipulation.

D1.justification: Table 2 newly states N=10 for GSM8K/HumanEval, Table 8 reports Qwen3 seconds per training step, and Appendices G.6–G.7 document sampling temperatures and reward normalization for the new diagnostics. The existing hardware, software, prompts, and Appendix E hyperparameters are retained.

E1.justification: The evaluated datasets and tasks are retained. GSM8K and HumanEval already appear in v3 Appendix G.6 and Table 11; v4 redisplays their results in Table 2 and retains them in Table 14. New diagnostics reuse existing math, detection, and trajectory tasks.

E2.justification: Table 8 adds GRPO-T16A1 to the Qwen3-4B math comparison, previously limited to T4A1 and GRPO-MA-T4A4. Its code participation is unresolved: v4 prints a score but says that run was omitted. Other evaluated comparator sets remain unchanged; Appendix C.6's method mapping is not an additional evaluation.

E3.justification: v4 adds Pass@1 to AIME/LiveBench evaluation using the retained 100 generations, a Qwen3 T16A1 configuration, a temperature-0.1 trajectory control, and a fixed-prefix reward diagnostic. Appendix D.7 corrects the printed ANLS summation indexing. Existing splits and training hyperparameters are retained; these changes do not establish rerunning existing results.

E4.justification: New Appendices G.6–G.7 directly test whether rewards vary appreciably under a fixed thought and whether lowering sampling temperature explains branching's benefits. These targeted diagnostics supplement the retained answer-count ablation, covariance analysis, inconsistency analysis, case studies, and training curves.

E5.justification: Appendix G.6 newly specifies estimating within-thought variability from four completions and reporting mean variance and range. This concerns conditional reward variability, not uncertainty across training seeds. Data seed 42 and Appendix C.5's ten replications per sample remain unchanged; no confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Previously reported benchmark scores are retained. Table 2 adds AIME/LiveBench Pass@1: T4A4 scores 3.40/6.73 versus T4A1's 2.07/6.59. Table 8 adds Qwen3 T16A1 math accuracy of 17.90 and timings. Tables 12–13 add reward-variability measurements and temperature-0.1 trajectory results, including DFD 178.63. Redisplayed GSM8K/HumanEval values are unchanged.

M1.justification: The same thought/answer sampling, reward averaging, group normalization, clipped policy objectives, and KL penalty are retained in v3 Section 4.1 and v4 Section 3.4. The shared-context formulation and joint-expectation notation generalize and clarify the analysis without establishing an implemented algorithm change.

P1.justification: v4 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, theory narrative, and conclusion. It merges the separate preliminaries and method sections into Method and Analysis, placing the generic framework and analysis before the GRPO-MA instantiation. Terminology and appendix organization are revised, and conflict-of-interest, acknowledgement, and publication text are added.

P2.justification: Table 2 is expanded and reorganized, Table 8 gains a comparator row and timing column, and Tables 9, 12, and 13 are added. Tables 3–4 change their bolding conventions for near-ties. Existing Figures 1–18 retain their graphics, with relocation and limited caption edits.

R1.justification: v4 adds Oehlert (1992) and Appendix C.6's explicit mapping of TreePO, TreeRL, and TreeRPO into the shared-context framework, while positioning GRPO-MA more clearly as an explanatory instantiation. Most cited research is retained; the Chen reference consolidation and GTPO bibliographic update concern existing works.

T1.justification: v3 follows an approximate variance formula with limits stated for the variance itself. v4 Definition 3.1 and Section 3.3 formalize generic shared contexts, explicitly define conditional first-order estimation variance, add positivity, boundedness, and non-outlier assumptions, and restrict the variance-floor and monotonicity conclusions accordingly. Appendix C.4 also qualifies the answer-variance expression as a formal growing-dimension analogue rather than a rigorous fixed-dimension delta-method result.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially improves the reliability of the central theoretical argument by replacing v3's exact-sounding variance and necessity conclusions with explicitly conditional first-order results, stated regularity conditions, and clearer applicability limits. The reward-variance and temperature checks and Qwen3 thought-scaling comparison strengthen empirical support. These gains outweigh a localized new reporting inconsistency: Table 8 prints a T16A1 code score despite its caption saying that run was omitted.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GRPO-MA study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices A–H are readable and matchable despite restructuring and additions.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds a Qwen3 comparison, reward-variance measurements, and a temperature ablation.

before.justification: v3 reports original training and evaluation results across math, code, vision, and simulated manipulation, together with empirical diagnostics and ablations in the appendices.

results.title: Why Tree-Style Branching Matters for Thought Advantage Estimation in GRPO

C1.justification: The abstract and listed contributions retain the same central claims: a modular frozen-backbone adapter, PAI/CTC regularization, faithful attribute interventions, and identity preservation. The headline Pendulum and ADNI improvements are unchanged. The added experiments principally strengthen support for these retained claims.

C2.justification: New Appendices F and G discuss approximate inversion, information loss, the absence of formal identifiability guarantees, reliance on a supplied graph, and difficulties recovering graphs from observational data. V4 distinguishes empirical reversibility from theoretical identification. Conversely, it removes v1's specific warning that classifiers can misjudge unusual counterfactuals such as bearded female faces.

D1.justification: V4 extends Table 5 with CelebA-HQ configurations, expands the algorithm explanation, and documents SD3 conditioning/inference and graph initialization/threshold choices. Existing hardware and core training details remain. The promise to release experimental code upon acceptance is removed without replacement access information.

E1.justification: V4 adds CelebA-HQ with glasses, smiling, and mouth-opening interventions, additional conditioning attributes, and progressively combined interventions. It also evaluates causal-graph recovery on the three retained datasets. This expands both attribute coverage and task requirements beyond v1's counterfactual-generation evaluations.

E2.justification: The original benchmark comparator sets remain. V4 adds evaluated comparisons with VCI and DiffCounter on CelebA-HQ, alongside HVAE (Tables 4 and 14), and with SDCD, NOTEARS, and DAGMA for graph recovery (Figure 34). Several were only cited, or absent, in v1.

E3.justification: V4 introduces CelebA-HQ splits and training settings, including four additional conditioning attributes, plus SD3 evaluation. It adds reversal L1 and intervention-to-original LPIPS measurements, distinct from existing null-intervention reconstruction metrics. Graph discovery adds a shared 0.1 threshold. The original datasets' stated configurations largely remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V4 adds reversal-recovery analysis, a five-attribute compositional stress test, SD3 portability evaluation, and graph-recovery/convergence studies (Appendices E.4 and G). The original regularizer, guidance-scale, DDIM-step, and attention-guidance ablations remain. V1's classifier-failure case study and accompanying Figure 26 are removed.

E5.justification: V4 adds standard deviations to the CelebA results and explicitly reports three-seed means and standard deviations for its methods in Table 12. V1 supplied CelebA point estimates without a run count. ADNI uncertainty reporting remains. This establishes expanded reporting, not an explicitly documented increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: V4 adds CelebA-HQ, reversal, intervention-identity, SD3, and graph-recovery results. CelebA values also change: FID without attention guidance moves from 8.509 to 8.152, and with attention guidance from 5.386 to 5.213, now accompanied by uncertainty. These are revised statistical reports, not established same-setting performance gains. Pendulum, ADNI, and original sensitivity-table values are retained.

M1.justification: The original SCM, frozen SD1.5 adapter, PAI, and CTC remain. Appendix E.4 adds an SD3 adaptation using three text-embedding streams, flow-matching loss, and inversion-free FlowEdit inference. Appendix G adds an optional learnable adjacency matrix with an acyclicity penalty. These extend the actual training and inference procedures.

P1.justification: Much of the introduction and method prose remains closely matched. V4 removes the introductory T2I primer, expands the appendix algorithm explanation, and relocates detailed CelebA/ADNI results and discussion to Appendix E. End matter is reorganized, with limited wording and header changes.

P2.justification: V4 changes the main text and references to two columns, compresses main-result tables, and splits or redisplays full tables in the appendices. Several figures are rearranged, the main ADNI illustration is shortened, and substantial new reversal, compositional, SD3, and graph-learning displays are added. The old classifier-failure figure is removed.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds targeted discussion of Chao's diffusion causal mechanisms, Lyu's concept adapter, and Yeganeh's medical editing. Additional references support SD3, FlowEdit, identifiability, and causal discovery. The established positioning against VAE/GAN models, diffusion SCMs, and prompt-based editing remains largely intact.

T1.justification: The core SCM definitions and causal, PAI, and CTC equations remain substantively equivalent. The new identifiability discussion is qualitative and explicitly supplies no formal guarantee. The graph-learning extension describes an algorithmic penalty without adding a formal derivation, theorem, proof, or counterexample.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens validation through a CelebA-HQ comparison with DiffCounter, a second generative backbone, and direct reversal and identity-preservation measurements—important support missing from v1's single-backbone evaluation. CelebA uncertainty reporting and explicit identifiability qualifications further improve evidential quality. These gains outweigh removal of the classifier caveat and code-release commitment. Reporting still needs correction: for example, the claimed 79% CelebA FID reduction from 27.861 to 8.152 is approximately 71%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Causal-Adapter work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or reformatted in v4.

after.justification: V4 retains original empirical results and adds CelebA-HQ experiments, SD3 evaluations, compositional interventions, and causal-structure learning results.

before.justification: V1 reports original quantitative and qualitative counterfactual-generation results on Pendulum, CelebA, and ADNI, together with motivational experiments and ablations.

results.title: Causal-Adapter: Taming Text-to-Image Diffusion for Faithful Counterfactual Generation

C1.justification: Contribution 3 narrows 'outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines' to 'competitive performance' against representative application-specific baselines. The introduction also replaces broad absence-of-method assertions with qualified discussion of sampled-estimator bias. The central Safe KL approximation and convexity/smoothness claims remain.

C2.justification: The conclusion newly cautions that KL-specific structural properties may require separate analysis and explicitly identifies parameter tuning and limited task coverage as limitations. Appendix C connects objective values to downstream prediction while acknowledging that the baseline achieves higher overall accuracy under severe label noise.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds ACS data-source and split information, parameters for the new studies, and synthetic sample size and dimension. Tables 3 and 5 add time-per-epoch measurements. Existing architecture descriptions, hyperparameter grids and the code-access disclosure are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds ACS PUMS income prediction under California–Mississippi distribution shift, synthetic linear-regression data, and an 85%-label-noise MNIST scenario alongside the retained 25%-noise experiment. These substantially extend the represented populations and evaluation conditions.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparators remain LSOT, Genevay et al.'s kernel OT method, Levy et al.'s KL-DRO estimator and Wang et al.'s UOT-DRO approach. The added benchmark comparisons reuse the corresponding DRO baselines. Newly cited compositional optimization methods are not experimentally evaluated.

E3.justification: Existing experimental settings are retained, but Appendix C introduces substantial new protocols: asymmetric state splits, race-group RMSE/MAE, exact duality-gap evaluation through weighted least squares, and downstream classification metrics. Table 5 selects each metric's best value separately across gamma/lambda settings, including separately optimized hardest-class metrics.

E4.justification: v4 adds tests of robustness to population shift and severe label corruption, including whether lower DRO objectives translate into better overall and worst-group predictions. Appendix C.2 also adds an exact duality-gap analysis of optimization progress, supplementing the retained objective-value and parameter-sensitivity evidence.

E5.justification: New Figure 6 reports means over five seeds with minimum-to-maximum shading, introducing an uncertainty display different from the standard-deviation bands used in the retained convergence plots. Existing experiments retain their stated run counts and uncertainty reporting; no increase in their runs is established.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the original figures retain their results, while Tables 3–5 and Figure 6 add substantial findings. New ACS objectives include 109.3±0.4 for the baseline versus 106.0±0.9 at rho=10^-3. Under 85% noise, Table 5's best-over-settings results show proposed/baseline cross-entropy of 1.29±0.08/1.36±0.03 but accuracy of 0.34±0.02/0.41±0.04. These are newly reported comparisons, not improvements over v3 under identical settings.

M1.justification: Section 2.2 newly specifies a projected stochastic-subgradient procedure for the convex parametric case, including a bounded interval for alpha, a prescribed stepsize and iterate averaging. The Safe KL surrogate, application-specific estimators and experimental architectures remain unchanged; the shift in alpha notation is equivalent.

P1.justification: v4 makes targeted rewrites to the introduction, related-work discussion and conclusion, expands Section 2.2, and standardizes terminology and headings. It adds acknowledgements and Appendix C, moving the existing SoftPlus and LLM-disclosure appendices to D and E. The overall narrative structure remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v4 substantially expands the empirical displays with Tables 3–5 covering regression, worst-group performance, severe-noise objectives, classification and runtime, plus a logarithmic duality-gap plot in Figure 6. Figures 1–5 retain identical embedded graphics, and Tables 1–2 retain their structures; these original displays mainly undergo page reflow.

R1.justification: v4 adds substantive positioning against stochastic compositional optimization, discussing Qi et al. (2021, 2023), Wang and Yang (2022), and Yuan et al. (2022). It presents Safe KL as complementary to optimizers for the original objective, replacing v3's broader lack-of-universal-method framing. This materially revises the novelty context.

T1.justification: Proposition 2.4(iii) replaces the earlier linear error bound with a sharper logarithmic bound and extends its admissible rho range. Assumption 2.8, Theorem 2.9 and its Appendix A proof add a finite-iteration optimization guarantee. v4 also corrects the reversed approximation inequalities and the missing exponential in Corollary 2.5's proof.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses important gaps in v3 by adding an optimization guarantee under explicit assumptions, strengthening and correcting mathematical reasoning, and testing downstream robustness beyond objective minimization. The revised literature positioning and narrower claims improve reliability. The new evidence does not establish uniform superiority: Table 5 selects metrics across settings and reports lower overall accuracy and higher runtime for the proposed method. These qualifications limit the performance claims but do not outweigh the substantial gains in theoretical support and empirical assessment.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Safe KL/SoftPlus approximation work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable. The original appendices can be matched despite v4 inserting a new DRO appendix and renumbering later appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains those experiments and adds original distribution-shift, synthetic regression and severe-label-noise results in Appendix C, Tables 3–5 and Figure 6.

before.justification: v3 reports original continuous-OT and DRO experiments in Section 3, Tables 1–2 and Figures 2–3, plus kernel-based OT experiments in Appendix B.

results.title: Improved Stochastic Optimization of LogSumExp

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: dense rewards learned from passive-video temporal distances, strong sparse-reward RL performance on nine of ten Meta-World tasks within 200,000 interactions, superiority over comparison rewards, and transfer from human videos. Additional evidence does not redefine these headline claims.

C2.justification: V1 briefly acknowledges difficulty with back-and-forth motion; v2 explains it through visually identical observations with different remaining distances and discusses history-based disambiguation. V2 also adds interpretations involving goal-conditioned representation collapse, PROGRESSOR's structural limitations, and insufficient pre-contact feedback from environment rewards. These substantially expand mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents choosing alpha as ten times the maximum dense reward over the first 100 trajectories, the closest-demonstration rule for ILfO, and use of the first 100 ManiSkill demonstrations. These are documentation additions, not established changes to earlier experiments. The hyperparameter tables retain their values. V1's project-page link is omitted, without establishing that the resource itself became unavailable.

E1.justification: Appendix A.4.9 adds PushCube-v1 from ManiSkill3, extending evaluation to another simulator's dynamics and rendering through one manipulation task. The ten Meta-World tasks and three human-video tasks remain. The additional 100-robot-plus-20-human experiment reuses existing task and domain coverage.

E2.justification: V2 substantially expands the evaluated alternatives: Figure 15 adds TemporalOT and ORCA alongside OT and ADS, and Figure 19 compares against PROGRESSOR augmented with negative sampling. The original main baselines remain; GVL in the VOC comparison and BCO in the proxy-only experiment were already evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols compare pretrained versus scratch ViT-B, fixed alpha values of 0.1/0.5/1 versus adaptive weighting, K=10/20/30, and 100 robot demonstrations plus 20 human videos. V2 also explicitly assigns CLIP-pretrained ViT-B to all main progress-based baselines, whereas v1 discusses VIP's ViT retraining in the appendix. Both VIP backbones were already evaluated in v1; this does not establish new runs.

E4.justification: V2 adds representation PCA across demonstrations and successful/failed rollouts, reward-weight and discretization-bin sensitivity tests, a pretraining ablation, negative sampling for PROGRESSOR, and human-video augmentation with abundant robot demonstrations. These investigate previously untested robustness and mechanism questions. The existing component ablations, VIP-backbone analysis, and proxy-only experiment are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report RL curves as mean plus or minus standard deviation over eight seeds. V2's added experiments follow the same practice; no changed run counts, confidence-interval procedures, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results, including PROGRESSOR's improvement from negative sampling on window-close and drawer-open but not stick-push or basketball, and performance on ManiSkill3. Figure 4 replaces Rank2Reward's noisy basketball outputs with curves separating successful and failed rollouts. Main-comparison VIP curves also change alongside the revised backbone specification, so they do not establish a same-setting gain. Figure 3's VOC values and the headline 9/10-task claim remain.

M1.justification: Section 4.1, Equation 4 replaces exponential interval sampling, proportional to exp(-lambda*Delta), with reciprocal sampling proportional to 1/Delta. The signed temporal-distance target, two-hot objective, and frozen reward model remain. V2 also introduces a feature-difference variant specifically for representation analysis; the default model still concatenates features.

P1.justification: The six main sections and much of the prose remain. V2 locally rewrites the introduction, related work, and ablation explanations, corrects wording, adds impact and acknowledgment sections, and reorganizes the appendix around the additional proof and experiments. This is a limited narrative revision alongside the substantive additions.

P2.justification: V2 converts the main text from one column to two, redraws the overview, revises the framework display, and substantially resizes and relocates existing plots. It adds eight figures, including PCA and the new experimental comparisons, and updates captions, axes, and legends. Both hyperparameter tables are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to temporal cycle-consistency learning, Arrow of Time, TemporalOT, ORCA, and ManiSkill3. It refines progress-based positioning around goal conditioning, signed temporal distances, and VIP's objective, replacing some emphasis on online refinement. The broader related-work categories and most cited literature remain.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 replaces v1's normalized expert-trajectory potential argument with an explicit deterministic MDP, per-step penalty, optimal-value derivation, and exact time-to-go potential at gamma=1. It adds a visual-reconstruction assumption and an aliasing counterexample. New Appendix A.3 derives unboundedness for the stated formulation of VIP's objective.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for the retained claims through pretraining and parameter controls, additional OT comparisons, and a strengthened PROGRESSOR baseline. Section 4.3 makes theoretical assumptions and visual-aliasing failures explicit, while the alpha-selection disclosure improves reproducibility. The PCA uses a modified model, and the additional simulator covers only one task, limiting some interpretations. These limitations and the omitted project link do not outweigh the gains in empirical support and theoretical clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TimeRewarder and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Their retained content can be matched across the revised layout and numbering, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds representation analyses, controlled experiments, additional baseline comparisons, and a ManiSkill3 evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original Meta-World policy-learning results, progress-estimation evaluations, human-video transfer experiments, and ablations in the main text and appendices.

results.title: TimeRewarder: Learning Dense Reward from Passive Videos via Frame-wise Temporal Distance

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion redefine CodeChemist as an uncertainty-aware adaptive framework, making selective avoidance of costly or misleading transfer a central contribution absent from v1. The training-free functional-transfer claim remains. V2 also newly claims that its Lua score of 50.5 surpasses a reported leaderboard best of 43.0 (Figure 1).

C2.justification: V2 adds the spurious-consensus rationale for AST clustering, explanations of adaptive computation and oracle noise, and an interpretation linking failures to source-model problem-solving limits. New Section 6 explicitly limits applicability for language-specific non-functional properties, tasks difficult even in the source language, and repository-level generation beyond the single case study. V1 lacks these substantive qualifications.

D1.justification: V2 newly provides a code-access link, execution CPU specifications, clustering thresholds, and detailed cross-language input conversion and output normalization, including type tags, container handling, and numerical tolerance (Appendix A.2). These substantially improve implementation documentation beyond v1's hardware, sampling, and prompt details. The normalization disclosure alone does not establish that the underlying handling changed.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates Python, Lua, C++, and Java across the three retained benchmarks. V2 adds R and Julia on Ag-LiveCodeBench-X, Rust generation using C++ references on MultiPL-HumanEval, and a C# class-generation case on RepoClassBench Task 56 (Appendix B.5). These expand language coverage and introduce generation using repository context.

E2.justification: V2 adds Self-Debugging to the reported comparisons. MultiPL-MBPP and Ag-LiveCodeBench-X, compared only against Vanilla in v1, additionally receive Majority Voting, LLM Judge, and S* comparisons. Appendix B.4 also introduces evaluated CodeT and MBR-Exec comparisons on MultiPL-HumanEval; CodeT's earlier citation alone was not such an evaluation.

E3.justification: Timing comparisons change from Qwen-3B to Qwen-32B and add token usage. Oracle ablations replace Qwen-3B with Qwen-1.5B; new settings include additional sampling temperatures, candidate-count sweeps, Thinking Mode, and five-point code-style judging. The stated DeepSeek version changes from V3.1 to V3, without establishing whether experiments were rerun. Core benchmark sizes and the ten-candidate hedged-sampling budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V1 primarily ablates sampling strategy and reference-program count. V2 expands these analyses with direct oracle generation and alternative source languages, and adds adaptive-selection ablation, candidate/test-count sensitivity, consensus-rate analysis, conditional failure analysis, code-style assessment, and a repository-level case study (Tables 3–6 and 13; Figure 4; Appendices B–C). These test substantial new questions about selection, efficiency, reliability, and applicability.

E5.justification: Both versions report five differently seeded evaluations and p-values below 0.05 for selected models. V2 Appendix B.1 specifies full-evaluation repetitions and paired t-tests against the corresponding Vanilla baseline, whereas v1 Appendix A leaves the pairing and comparator unspecified. This refines statistical reporting without reporting an increase in runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive comparator, language, ablation, efficiency, style, and failure results. Table 1 replaces Qwen-1.5B C++/Java scores of 52.2/69.6 with 55.3/70.3 under the revised method. Figure 1 changes Qwen-14B's Ag-LiveCodeBench-X C++ Vanilla score from 31.6 to 30.6. Many other Ag-LiveCodeBench-X results are retained graphically, while MultiPL-MBPP results for Qwen-7B/14B, Llama-3B, and GPT-4o mini are omitted.

M1.justification: V1 always constructs high-resource test oracles. V2 first clusters target-language candidates by execution behavior and AST similarity, selects through in-language voting when uncertainty is low, and constructs cross-language oracles otherwise (Section 3.3; Algorithm 1). This adds a substantive routing and selection component while retaining hedged sampling and oracle-based scoring.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites and reorganizes the abstract, method narrative, experimental discussion, and conclusion. Method subsections are reordered, the algorithm moves to Appendix A.1, computational efficiency receives its own section, and v1 Appendices A–C are regrouped within Appendix B. The title and affiliation information also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout. The workflow diagram is redrawn for adaptive selection, Ag-LiveCodeBench-X results are also displayed as a new bar chart, and efficiency and sampling-budget plots are added. Benchmark tables are merged and expanded, new analysis tables appear, and retained prompt boxes are reflowed across two pages.

R1.justification: The related-work framework largely remains, but v2 adds GenX and Epicoder discussion and citations supporting new baselines, clustering, and repository evaluation. Section 2.1 also recharacterizes Bridge-C from an inference-based prompting approach in v1 to a framework generating alignment-training data. These are limited substantive changes within the retained research positioning.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.3 introduces execution and AST cluster counts and formally defines a binary uncertainty indicator through their threshold conditions. This is a new mathematical definition supporting adaptive selection. The existing softmax and pass-rate scoring formulas remain substantively unchanged, and neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important evidential and reproducibility gaps: it replaces Vanilla-only comparisons on two benchmarks with competing methods, tests the adaptive gate's accuracy and cost, documents cross-language execution handling, and states concrete failure boundaries. These substantially strengthen the paper. Reduced MBPP model reporting and unreconciled numerical prose remain weaknesses—for example, Section 4.2 retains the 51.7% C++ gain despite Table 1's revised 55.3 versus 34.4—but do not outweigh the improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CodeChemist research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including figures, tables, equations, and prompts, are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and reformatting.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark comparisons and additional adaptive-selection, efficiency, language-generalization, code-style, and failure-analysis results, including appendix experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original code-generation benchmark results, sampling and oracle-generation ablations, runtime measurements, and a CodeChemist–S* combination experiment.

results.title: CodeChemist: Test-Time Scaling for Low-Resource Code Generation via Functional Knowledge Transfer

C1.justification: The introduction newly claims this is the first study of Wasserstein noise robustness for measures on a fixed grid and explicitly distinguishes the problem from perturbing point-cloud locations. The central noise-scaling, robustness, and cryo-EM applicability claims otherwise remain.

C2.justification: v3 acknowledges similar W1 and W2 distance rankings under pure additive noise and explains W2's advantage through sensitivity to spatial shifts. Appendix A newly explains the unresolved grid-resolution gap between upper and lower bounds and why minimum-distance arguments miss spatial clustering of noise.

D1.justification: The embedded code link changes from the repository named Quantifying-the-noise-sensitivity-of-wasserstein to Quantifying-wasserstein-noise-sensitivity. A new Reproducibility paragraph specifies code for simulations and all figures. Both versions already advertise code; the PDFs establish changed access instructions, not newly verified availability.

E1.justification: DOTMark microscopy images, white-noise images, classic images, sparse synthetic images, and simulated E. coli Hsp90 projections remain covered. The new shift diagnostic analyzes translation and additive noise already represented in v2. The corrected DOTMark description in Section 4.2 agrees with v2 Figure 3's existing caption.

E2.justification: L2, W1, and W2 remain the core evaluated comparators, while W3 remains in the inter-image and sparse-image bound comparisons. The new shift experiment uses the existing core trio; removing theoretical-bound labels from legends does not remove comparators.

E3.justification: v3 Figure 8 introduces a controlled comparison between distances to spatially shifted images, using shifts of 3 and 8 pixels, and distances under increasing Gaussian noise. The original experiments retain their stated image sizes and procedures; their changed displays do not establish that evaluation settings or runs changed.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 adds a diagnostic testing when additive noise becomes indistinguishable from spatial displacement under each metric. Existing cross-image-class robustness analyses, cryo-EM case studies, and sparse-image explanations of decreasing distance are retained.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 2 newly reports 95% confidence intervals for L2, W1, and W2. Both versions already specify 100 independent trials for this experiment; no increase in runs is stated, and the interval-construction procedure is not explained.

E6.justification: v3 adds shift-versus-noise curves and reports approximately 3.5 times greater noise tolerance for W2 than W1 in that analysis. It replaces the noisy cryo-EM heatmaps, with a visibly more structured L2 pattern, and removes Figure 2's explicit fitted coefficients. These are reporting changes, not established performance gains under matched settings.

M1.justification: Both versions use the same positive/negative-part construction for signed Wasserstein discrepancies and the same zero-sum Gaussian noise model. The unbalanced-transport extension already appears in v2 Appendix B; the new bounds and experiments do not establish a changed computational method.

P1.justification: v3 selectively rewrites the abstract and signed-measure explanation, improves grammar, standardizes discrepancy terminology, and adds proof sketches and closing statements. The main sequence of Sections 1–5 and Appendices A–B remains intact, with much of the narrative retained.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column conference layout throughout and extensively reorganizes figure panels, captions, and legends. Image-class plots change from a horizontal strip to a 2-by-2 grid, heatmaps become clean/noisy rows, and Figure 2 displays confidence intervals and lower bounds. The shift experiment adds Figure 8; several other figures are relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: v3 adds Thorpe et al. (2017) on transportation distances for signal analysis and introduces explicit fixed-grid novelty positioning. It also presents unbalanced transport as an extension of the work rather than a largely separate robustness notion. Numerous publication-year and venue updates refer to retained works.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.5 and Appendix A add a general-p lower bound, C_p n^(2/p-1) sigma^(1/p), with a new proof. The rescaling theorem drops the nonzero-pixel condition and changes its remainder from O_p(sigma/n) to O_p(1/n). v3 also revises multiscale and Gaussian-variance derivations, tightens the inter-image bound's constant, corrects the squared-L2 expectation, and changes Appendix B's bound and proof to recognize zero total noise mass.

improvement.justification: For this theory-centered paper, the new lower bound in Theorem 3.5 and Appendix A substantially strengthens the central claim by establishing matching sigma^(1/p) dependence from below, beyond v2's upper bound and empirical support. Corrections to existing derivations further improve mathematical reliability. The grid-resolution gap remains, and v3's structured noisy-L2 heatmap conflicts with its retained random-pattern description, but these limitations do not outweigh the central theoretical gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work by the same authors. Their main texts, figures, equations, references, and Appendices A–B are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v3 retains original image-noise and cryo-EM simulation results and adds a spatial-shift-versus-noise experiment in Section 4.3 and Figure 8.

before.justification: v2 reports original DOTMark noise simulations, comparisons across image classes, and simulated cryo-EM experiments, including results averaged over 100 trials.

results.title: Quantifying the noise sensitivity of the Wasserstein metric for images

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion shift from presenting a particular equivariant scattering GNN with parameter-efficient performance to presenting vector diffusion wavelets as the basis of a broader GNN family. v2 explicitly claims effectiveness on wind and neural data and elevates the existing frame properties into the principal contribution statement.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations connecting vector diffusion to connection-Laplacian heat flow, wind masking to sensor failures, and whole-trial holdouts to generalization without neighborhood leakage. It also qualifies the wind training-time advantage with approximately 1.1 seconds of preprocessing and explicitly acknowledges the nonsignificant accuracy difference from MARBLE. v1’s empirical interpretation was largely confined to rotation sensitivity and parameter efficiency.

D1.justification: Appendices F–G disclose wind coordinate conversion, graph and model configurations, neural preprocessing, contrastive sampling, SVM settings, and optimization procedures. The disclosed code repository changes from esc-gnn to vdw-gnns, and CUDA 12.4 is specified. A new inconsistency remains: Appendix D says all runs use one GPU, while Appendix E.5 retains the four-GPU TFN exception; this does not establish an actual hardware change.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained synthetic ellipsoid tasks, v2 evaluates reconstruction of real-world wind measurements and representation learning from 24-channel macaque neural recordings across 44 experimental days. These introduce new domains, task requirements, and masked-sensor and unseen-trial scenarios.

E2.justification: The ellipsoid comparator set is unchanged after matching ESc-GNN to VDW-GNN. The new wind comparison evaluates DD-TNN alongside retained baseline families, and the neural experiment introduces evaluated comparisons with MARBLE, CEBRA, and LFADS (Tables 3–4).

E3.justification: The ellipsoid splits and training recipe are retained. New protocols include 2,000 wind measurements with observed/masked partitions, directed observed-to-masked graph connections, and random rotation testing. Neural evaluation introduces whole-trial holdouts, per-day cross-validation, three-dimensional embeddings, SVM probing, and neighbor-based test embedding estimation (Appendices F–G). These are new experiments, not revisions of an earlier neural or wind protocol.

E4.justification: v2 extends rotation robustness testing to wind reconstruction using randomly sampled rotations between 90 and 160 degrees (Section 4.2 and Table 3). The original ellipsoid non-equivariant ablation and rotation tests remain unchanged, making this a limited extension of the existing robustness analysis.

E5.justification: The existing ellipsoid mean-and-standard-deviation reporting across five folds is retained. v2 additionally specifies five wind repetitions with distinct sampling and rotation seeds, defines aggregation across daily neural cross-validation means, and adds two-sided paired Wilcoxon tests in Figure 5. These supplement the previous descriptive uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in ellipsoid Tables 1–2 are unchanged. New results include wind MSE of 2.7546 ± 0.3671 and rotated MSE of 3.2266 ± 0.5255, plus neural classification accuracy of 0.66 ± 0.14 versus MARBLE’s 0.65 ± 0.12, without a significant difference. New runtime and parameter results are added, while the ellipsoid inference-time entries from v1 Tables 3–4 are removed.

M1.justification: The original ellipsoid architecture is retained under the VDW-GNN name. However, Appendix F adds a vector-only wind model with neighbor-feature concatenation and residual prediction, while Appendix G adds a neural embedding model with supervised contrastive learning, hard-negative sampling, and neighbor-based inference for unseen nodes. These are substantive procedural adaptations.

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, renames ESc-GNN, and substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, and background. The standalone message-passing background is consolidated, a manifold-hypothesis subsection is introduced, and the architecture and complexity appendices are reorganized. The experiments are structured into three application subsections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. v2 adds a local-frame illustration, redraws and moves the architecture diagram into the main text, and adds wind/neural result tables and a daily-accuracy plot. The original equivariance illustrations remain as Figures 3–4. Ellipsoid runtime tables are reformatted without their inference-time columns.

R1.justification: The new manifold-hypothesis discussion substantially expands positioning within manifold learning and tangent-bundle neural networks, including Battiloro et al. and foundational diffusion-map work. Sections 4.3 and Appendix G further position the method relative to MARBLE, CEBRA, and LFADS. This extends the earlier emphasis on scattering and equivariant GNNs.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 adds an explicit optional manifold setting with intrinsic dimension d < D, tangent-bundle-valued features, and connection-Laplacian heat-flow notation. The main frame and equivariance theorems and their proofs are retained. Non-dyadic applicability already had a counterpart in v1 Appendix D, so its expanded discussion does not establish a new theoretical result.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1’s synthetic-only empirical support through documented wind and neural evaluations, relevant baselines, held-out-trial testing, and paired significance analysis (Sections 4.2–4.3 and Appendices F–G). These strengthen evidence of practical applicability while appropriately qualifying the MARBLE comparison. Removed inference timings, conflicting GPU statements, and differing supervision across neural baselines limit specific comparisons, but the overall evidential gain remains substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable and complete, including v1 Appendices A–E and v2 Appendices A–G. The retained vector diffusion construction, theorems, and ellipsoid experiments establish continuity despite the changed title and expanded scope.

after.justification: v2 retains the ellipsoid results and adds original wind reconstruction and neural representation experiments in Sections 4.2–4.3, Tables 3–4, and Appendices F–G.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original ellipsoid diameter and node-level vector prediction experiments in Tables 1–2, with runtime results in Appendix E.

results.title: VDW-GNNs: Vector diffusion wavelets for geometric graph neural networks

C1.justification: V2 makes low-cost training followed by frontier-model improvement a central contribution, adding explicit GPT-5 tax and Gemini software-agent efficiency claims to the abstract and conclusion. V1's parametric-memory framing is dropped. Its claim of transfer with no performance loss becomes a claim that useful gains survive transfer.

C2.justification: V1's explanation and mitigation discussion of over-advising—advisors solving problems that students copy—is removed. V2 instead develops interpretations involving harmful untrained advice, limited knowledge headroom, student-specific transfer losses and advantages over the preference oracle. It also reports that optional advisor queries fail because students rarely request help, and interprets limited math gains as knowledge saturation.

D1.justification: V2 adds SWE-specific hyperparameters, per-domain epoch tables, Tenacity data-selection instructions, interaction limits and scaled-personalization sampling details (Appendices A–D). SkyRL, the eight-H100 hardware disclosure and the code link are retained. Some specificity is lost: the math-correctness experiment no longer explicitly identifies v1's 1,000-example Omni-Math training set.

E1.justification: V2 adds SWE Agent Efficiency using SWE-smith issues from the Tenacity repository, introducing multi-turn software repair with interaction-efficiency requirements. The original review-personalization, math-solutions, translation, tax and math-correctness tasks remain, although their presentation changes.

E2.justification: V2 adds PAG and an in-context preference oracle to personalization, explicitly separates student-only and untrained-advisor controls, and adds GEPA to the MTOB and RuleArena comparisons. It also evaluates direct student RL on MTOB and an efficiency-prompt control for SWE. GEPA is explicitly not evaluated on SWE (Sections 4.1, 4.3 and 4.4.3).

E3.justification: V2 introduces SWE issue filtering, a 40-interaction cap, and resolve-rate/step-count evaluation. Appendix A replaces v1's generic 10-epoch setting with domain-specific budgets, including 20 for MTOB and 40 for RuleArena; weak-initialization training changes from 30 to 20 epochs. Frontier-student configurations, Llama advisors, the 3B/7B direct-RL comparison and 100-user scaling also add experimental settings. These are reported protocol changes, without establishing rerun history.

E4.justification: V2 adds analyses of advisor-family dependence, scaling personalization to 100 users, performance relative to direct RL, and SWE advice before versus after training. Cross-family transfer analysis expands beyond review length (Appendices D–E). The initialization analysis is revised, while v1's qualitative reasoning-trace analysis of over-advising is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% confidence intervals, but v2 supplies them for reasoning comparisons previously presented as point estimates in v1 Table 1. V2 also introduces explicit p-values for GPT-5 MTOB and SWE transfer results. Evaluation run counts, seeds and the construction of the intervals/tests remain unspecified.

E6.justification: The three personalization advisor rewards change from 0.932/1.000/0.946 in v1 Figure 3 to 0.941/0.996/0.948 in v2 Figure 5. Reasoning, transfer and retention scores also change, and substantial SWE, frontier, Llama, scalability and direct-RL results are added. For example, v2 Figure 4 reports Gemini 3 Pro steps decreasing from 31.7 to 26.3. Revised budgets and model configurations prevent treating all cross-version score changes as same-setting gains.

M1.justification: V2 adds an implemented multi-turn advising architecture that receives student actions and observations and supplies further advice, every five student actions in the SWE experiment. It also describes a tested advisor-as-tool-call variant (Section 3; Appendix B.2). V1's two-step and three-step pipelines and GRPO training remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The RQ-based evaluation narrative becomes a sequence covering specialized reasoning, frontier transfer, personalization and ablations. Related work and the appendices are reorganized, while retained review examples and prompts move to Appendices E.2 and F. The author list also changes.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. The framework diagram is redrawn, the introductory review example is replaced by a multi-turn training/transfer diagram, and the reasoning table becomes expanded plots. Initialization plots are merged, new ablation figures appear, and training settings are reorganized into hyperparameter and epoch tables.

R1.justification: Section 2 replaces the parameter-efficient-finetuning discussion with substantive comparisons to trained prompt generators: Black-Box Prompt Optimization, PRewrite, Directional Stimulus Prompting and Matryoshka Pilot. V2 distinguishes expert supervision, static versus instance-specific outputs and output constraints. It also adds literature supporting personalization baselines, agent tasks and curriculum filtering.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix C.1 introduces a mathematical definition of the SWE reward: zero for unresolved issues and 0.5 + 0.5(40 − steps)/40 for resolved issues. The existing review-length reward is unchanged and relocated to Appendix C.2. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens v1's limited controls and evidence for frontier applicability through separate student/untrained-advisor comparisons, PAG/oracle and direct-RL comparisons, and frontier/multi-turn evaluations. Scalability and advisor-family ablations, closer prior-work comparisons and expanded training details further improve support and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removed over-advising discussion and reporting errors, notably the abstract's claimed 24.6% Gemini 3 Pro step reduction versus Figure 4's 31.7-to-26.3 reduction, approximately 17%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Advisor Models. All 15 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable and support matching the methods, experiments, equations and displays despite substantial restructuring.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on the retained tasks and adds software-agent efficiency, broader frontier-model transfer, scalability and direct-RL comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original advisor-training experiments on personalization, translation, tax reasoning and mathematics, together with transfer and capability-retention evaluations.

results.title: How to Train Your Advisor: Steering Black-Box LLMs with Advisor Models

C1.justification: v3 drops the claims of being the first model-free risk-aware expressive-policy approach and the first objective-level OOD characterization. It emphasizes a simple modular framework and bounded-score CVaR stability while retaining the central risk-aware learning and empirical contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4 now explicitly conditions persistent leakage on maintained off-support density and distinguishes idealized KL control from diffusion/flow BC surrogates. Appendix A adds specific exclusions, including mean-variance, entropic and constrained-safety objectives. Appendix E.2 replaces broad early-training explanations with a qualification that fixed-checkpoint rankings need not reproduce Table 1.

D1.justification: Appendix F.3 adds ORAAC-Diffusion's mixing-coefficient sweep, while F.4 specifies state normalization, local-neighbor retrieval and leave-one-out calibration for the revised detectors. The abstract replaces the direct repository pointer with a project-site pointer advertising code and experimental results. Core architecture, optimization and hardware details remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 2-D risky bandit and the medium-expert/medium-replay variants of HalfCheetah, Hopper and Walker2d with stochastic hazards. The new ablation reuses existing tasks; the medium-expert safety plots already appeared in v2.

E2.justification: v3 adds ORAAC-Diffusion, identified as UDAC, to the six-task comparison in Table 1 and the OOD comparisons in Tables 2 and 6. v2 already evaluated it on the toy bandit. Other comparator sets are retained, including Table 3; FlowQL and FQL denote the same baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix F.4 replaces global action-space OOD detection with state-conditioned 1-NN using ten neighboring states, and joint state-action LOF/Mahalanobis detection. The Mahalanobis threshold changes from the 99th to the 95th percentile. Appendix E.2 also replaces the stated 1000-gradient-step evaluation with fixed-checkpoint evaluation using 1000-step rollouts; this documentation change does not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix E.3.1 and Table 4 isolate the roles of BC and CVaR by comparing full RADAC, BC-only and CVaR-only variants on two locomotion tasks, measuring returns and OOD rates. The detector-robustness analysis is substantially revised. Existing distortion, tail-sampling, toy-weight and risk-return analyses remain.

E5.justification: OOD reporting changes to mean plus standard deviation over three seeds. v2 used five seeds and standard errors for the main OOD table, and three seeds with standard errors for detector robustness. v3 removes the binomial standard-error calculation from Appendix F.4; other uncertainty-reporting practices largely remain.

E6.justification: RADAC's Hopper-medium-expert mean/CVaR changes from 130.74/-167.29 to 1277.74/800.64 in Table 1, and from -764.93/-1094.93 to 1513.27/967.21 in Table 3, reversing its ranking. v3 also adds comparator and ablation results and replaces OOD measurements. The Hopper revisions are unexplained, and OOD changes use different detectors, so these should not be interpreted automatically as same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 3, Algorithm 1 and Appendix D retain the BC-plus-CVaR objective, generative actor, double-IQN critic and diffusion/flow instantiations. Corrections to the BRAC exposition and clarification of native BC surrogates do not establish a change to RAMAC's procedure.

P1.justification: Paragraph rewrites clarify the abstract, introduction and method exposition; FlowQL is standardized as FQL, the method section is retitled, and an Impact Statement is added. Author/affiliation and citation presentation also change, while the main section sequence and appendix organization remain largely intact.

P2.justification: The main paper adopts a two-column conference layout, relocates and swaps the conceptual and pipeline figures, and splits v2 Figure 4 between v3 Figure 4 and appendix Figure 11. v3 adds the objective-ablation table, expands comparison tables and moves several retained plots to the appendix's end. These are substantial presentation changes, not new plot evidence.

R1.justification: v3 removes Tianyu Chen et al.'s 'Diffusion policies creating a trust region for offline reinforcement learning' and the associated contrast, and softens priority claims. Appendix C's positioning otherwise remains similar. UDAC and several other references receive publication/title updates rather than representing newly introduced works.

T1.justification: The brief OOD-mixture CVaR degradation bound is replaced by Proposition 4.3 and Corollary 4.4, bounding CVaR differences for bounded per-state utility scores through total variation and KL, with a new proof in Appendix B.3. Lemma 4.1 revises its density assumption to a measurable leakage region. Equation 1 also corrects the BC expectation to use dataset actions.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central behavior-regularization argument: state-conditioned OOD evaluation better matches the per-state theory, and the objective ablation plus diffusion-prior comparison address important control gaps. The proved CVaR stability bound and explicit theoretical qualifications improve mathematical precision. The unexplained Hopper score replacements remain a limitation, but the better-supported mechanism analysis provides a substantial overall quality gain independently of those higher scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAMAC work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A–F support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and reports additional objective-ablation and comparator results, alongside revised OOD measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original Toy Risky Bandit and Stochastic-D4RL experiments, OOD measurements and appendix ablations.

results.title: RAMAC: Multimodal Risk-Aware Offline Reinforcement Learning and the Role of Behavior Regularization

C1.justification: The principal claims about adaptive dual prediction, the annotated dataset, and transferable efficiency remain. The abstract and contribution list revise the headline accuracy improvement from 1.4% to 1.5% alongside a changed backbone set; this is a limited quantitative claim revision, not a demonstrated same-setting method improvement.

C2.justification: V1 attributes weaker MLVU comparisons to heuristics capturing domain-specific cues; v2 emphasizes insufficient candidate coverage and interprets segmentation as addressing it. Appendix F adds mechanism explanations for joint-training instability, teacher transfer, ranking drift, and frame preservation versus compression. V2 also replaces the specific discussion of internet-data biases with a generic impact statement.

D1.justification: V2 specifies the learnable query token, embedding sequence, and decoder's role, and documents implementation choices for segmentation and reproduced MovieChat. Core hardware, training times, hyperparameters, and JSON format remain. Some detail is lost: v2 omits the explicit KL-divergence identification of the classification loss and shortens the Stage II annotation prompt's guidelines.

E1.justification: V2 adds evaluation on the MovieChat-1K long-video QA corpus in Appendix F.7. The original six benchmarks, training corpora, and FrameOracle-41K collection remain, so coverage expands within the existing video-understanding domain.

E2.justification: Table 1 replaces GPT-4o with Qwen3-VL-8B and revises standalone comparators, adding Video-XL and Video-XL-2. Table 2 adds Qwen2.5-VL-7B comparisons with ViaRL and K-frames while removing LVNet, MoReVQA, and VSLS. Appendix F adds B-VLLM and reproduced MovieChat comparisons, alongside MovieChat+ and ReWind reference results.

E3.justification: V2 introduces substantial new evaluation designs: two annotators per instance across 4,000 samples, alternative supervision backbones, skipped and joint training stages, controls at fixed frame budgets, and ranking evaluation on 500 training videos. It also specifies token-budget and memory-compression comparison settings. The original Appendix A training budgets and hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses examine annotation correctness and sufficiency, filtering effects on question-type composition, curriculum shortcuts, joint-training instability, teacher dependence, uniform sampling at similar frame budgets, segmentation, ranking drift, and frame versus token or memory budgeting. V1's progressive training ablation is retained as Table 8, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V1 provides no comparable significance analysis. V2 introduces paired bootstrap resampling over questions with 10,000 iterations, percentile 95% confidence intervals, and a 0.05 significance criterion for Tables 1–2, marking nonsignificant changes in Table 1. These are new statistical reporting procedures, not evidence of additional training seeds.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive results, including 93.3% human-verified annotation accuracy and a 46.3% uniform-sampling control versus the retained 50.3% FrameOracle result in Table 12. Table 13 reports MLVU accuracy of 65.4% with segmented sampling versus 62.9% with the original candidate coverage. Table 1 replaces GPT-4o results with Qwen3-VL results; retained backbone scores and Table 3 efficiency values remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The dual-head selector and four-stage training procedure remain. Appendix F.4 adds segment-wise inference: apply the trained selector independently to two temporal segments and combine four selected frames from each. Expanded architecture descriptions do not establish a redesign of the original model.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method explanations, and results narrative. It moves the main-text training ablation into an expanded appendix, reorganizes dataset statistics, adds several appendix sections, and replaces the reproducibility and ethics statements with an impact statement.

P2.justification: V2 switches the main text to two columns, revises table organization and captions, and adds numerous analysis tables, question-type graphics, and dataset examples. V1's duration and frame-count histograms move into Figure 5; its qualitative Figures 5–6 remain as Figures 8–9. The changes substantially alter visual organization while preserving these earlier displays.

R1.justification: V2 acknowledges AdaFrame's earlier adaptive selection for video classification and adds MDP3 and ReFoCUS to the selection literature. Its new discussions of B-VLLM, MovieChat, MovieChat+, and ReWind substantially extend the positioning to token budgeting and memory compression, beyond v1's focus on frame selectors.

T1.justification: The RankNet loss, penalized frame-count target, and combined frame-count training objective remain mathematically equivalent. The bounded candidate notation clarifies an existing restriction. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs; the new analyses are empirical.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for dataset reliability and curriculum design through a 4,000-instance human audit, skipped/joint-training tests, controls at similar frame budgets, and bootstrap significance reporting. These address important evidential gaps in v1. The gains outweigh the loss of GPT-4o transfer evidence, although exact minimality remains unestablished by the human ±3-frame tolerance, and the token-budget comparison does not match computational budgets.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe FrameOracle and FrameOracle-41K. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including material relocated between versions.

after.justification: V2 retains original FrameOracle experiments and adds human annotation verification, further ablations, and additional benchmark comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original VideoQA accuracy, computational efficiency, training-stage ablations, and qualitative results for FrameOracle.

results.title: FrameOracle: Learning What to See and How Much to See in Videos

C1.justification: The central claims of tractable, unbiased AGRPO and improved inference tradeoffs remain. V2 recasts the contribution around multi-step denoising policy gradients rather than a faithful GRPO adaptation, and extends its headline efficacy claim to Sudoku with revised performance margins. Fourfold sampling acceleration was already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for GSM8K training outperforming MATH training, attributes baseline discrepancies to prompting and parsing, and argues that denser learning signals offset additional computation. Appendix G adds interpretations of robustness to generation artifacts and expands the retained entropy-collapse limitation with possible mitigations.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents hardware, training duration, reward construction, global batch size, clipping and KL settings, checkpoint selection, TRL usage, and inference/training sampling-mask consistency. Code release is planned, not established. Conversely, v1's learning rate, AdamW coefficients, and LoRA scaling/dropout details are omitted.

E1.justification: V2 adds training and evaluation on 4x4 Sudoku, extending coverage to grid-based constraint planning. Its MATH results also include GSM8K-to-MATH transfer and a MATH-trained comparison, replacing v1's reported OpenMathInstruct-2-trained model.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds LLaDA 1.5, wd1, and SPG, while removing the diffusion CoT SFT and UniGRPO comparisons. Diffu-GRPO and the autoregressive comparisons remain. The inference-frontier comparison also adds LLaDA 1.5 and drops diffu-GRPO.

E3.justification: V2 standardizes training at response length 384 and 128 sampling steps, changing v1's GSM8K and Countdown configurations. Training temperature changes to 0.6 and semi-autoregressive block length to 12, from 0.5/0.9 and 24/32 respectively. Table 1 now evaluates both 256- and 512-token outputs for every task; new ablation and timing experiments introduce additional controlled settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds measured ablations on Monte Carlo sample count, a joint ablation of low-discrepancy and entropy-based sampling, and computational-cost comparisons (Figures 3–4 and Table 2). These substantially extend v1's qualitative discussion of stability and compute tradeoffs. The appendix sample-response case is also replaced and analyzed.

E5.justification: V2 introduces shaded training-reward variability in Figures 3–4, described as within-run variance or standard deviation over 15-step rolling windows. V1 has no corresponding uncertainty reporting. Neither version reports independent-seed confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 1 substantially replaces and expands the results: v1 reports AGRPO accuracies of 87.3/40.8/40.0 on GSM8K/MATH/Countdown; v2 reports 88.1/42.0/82.4/95.2 at length 512 on GSM8K/MATH-500/Countdown/Sudoku. Changed training and evaluation conditions prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains. V2 also adds ablation and timing results; its claimed 1.4-point GSM8K margin does not match the listed 88.1 versus 84.5.

M1.justification: The core AGRPO objective and intermediate-state likelihood computation remain. V2 Section 4.2.2 adds entropy-weighted timestep sampling with an importance-weight correction, extending the existing Monte Carlo variance-reduction scheme without replacing the algorithm.

P1.justification: The title changes to Simple Policy Gradients for Reasoning with Diffusion Language Models. Extensive rewriting reorganizes the argument around MDPs and policy gradients, introduces a dedicated related-work section, and redistributes practical considerations and limitations across Appendices A–G.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main text and bibliography, redraws Figure 1, removes v1's pretraining schematic, and redesigns the inference plot and benchmark table. It adds ablation plots and timing/comparison tables, while substantially reformatting the appendix sample responses.

R1.justification: V2 replaces the focused diffu-GRPO/UniGRPO critique with substantially broader positioning in Section 6 and Appendix C. It adds substantive discussions of wd1, VRPO, DCoLT, SPG, and related policy-gradient research, distinguishing AGRPO through its multi-step formulation and timestep sampling.

T1.justification: V1 derives AGRPO by rewriting the GRPO sum as a timestep expectation. V2 substantially revises this reasoning through formal MDP and policy-gradient definitions and an explicit denoising-trajectory derivation. Appendix A adds the entropy-weighted estimator and Theorem A.1 proving its unbiasedness for the unclipped objective.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for AGRPO's stability and computational tradeoffs: Figures 3–4 and Appendix B test claims that v1 mostly discussed qualitatively. The explicit MDP derivation, estimator proof, and broader benchmark comparisons also improve the paper's foundation. These gains outweigh the loss of some optimizer details and the inconsistent GSM8K margin claim, although heterogeneous imported baseline results still limit comparative conclusions.

A1.justification: Despite the changed title and format, both PDFs present the same AGRPO research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original results on four reasoning tasks, additional ablations, training-time measurements, and sample responses.

before.justification: V1 reports original AGRPO training results on GSM8K, MATH, and Countdown, an inference-step experiment, and sample responses.

results.title: Simple Policy Gradients for Reasoning with Diffusion Language Models

C1.justification: The principal claims of effective reasoning post-training and fewer-step inference remain. Novelty is narrowed: v2 claims the first extension of denoising-MDP RL to dLLMs in Section 6, whereas v3 acknowledges other trajectory-based approaches and emphasizes scalable timestep estimation as its distinction.

C2.justification: v3 substantially qualifies the likelihood and alignment arguments. Remark 3.1 distinguishes stepwise likelihoods from any-order autoregressive likelihoods, while Appendix C explicitly acknowledges the random-training/confidence-decoding mismatch and explains its relationship to exogenous action positions. Section 5.4 also adds an interpretation of full-trajectory diminishing returns, and the new ablations support broader robustness interpretations.

D1.justification: v2 promises a future code release; v3 reports code availability and supplies a repository link in the abstract. It also specifies detached old-policy entropies and clarifies timing overhead. The relocated timing table changes its hardware description from '2xRTX6000 Ada' to '2xA6000 Ada' without changing timings; an actual hardware change or rerun is not established.

E1.justification: Both versions use GSM8K, MATH/MATH-500, Countdown, and 4x4 Sudoku, retaining GSM8K-Platinum evaluation. The added ablations vary training or decoding configurations within these tasks without adding datasets, populations, or task requirements.

E2.justification: The comparator sets in the benchmark, inference, and timing comparisons are retained. Table 1's 'LLaDA 1.5 (VRPO)' identifies the existing LLaDA 1.5 comparator. Newly discussed TraceRL and MDPO are not added to the reported empirical comparisons.

E3.justification: The evaluation design expands across several controlled settings. Appendix C adds random versus confidence-based decoding, Countdown training with n=192 and m=48 or 96, and rollout reuse with mu=1 or 4. Figure 3 replaces k=6 with k=8 and adds k=128. The principal benchmark protocol remains unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendix C tests dependence on decoding strategy, training denoising granularity, and off-policy rollout reuse. The extended Figure 3 additionally tests full-trajectory sampling, providing evidence about diminishing returns beyond k=32. These substantially broaden robustness and efficiency analysis; the existing variance-reduction ablation and sample-response analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Figures 3–4 retain the same 15-step rolling-window, within-run uncertainty displays. Neither version reports seed counts, repeated-run accuracy summaries, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Additional curves do not introduce a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Appendix C adds substantial results, including AGRPO random-decoding accuracies of 83.8% on GSM8K and 80.0% on Countdown, and Countdown accuracies of 63.3% versus 61.3% for mu=1 versus 4. Figure 3 adds k=8 and k=128 outcomes. AGRPO's Table 1 scores remain unchanged, but LLaDA 1.5's Countdown score at n=512 changes from 27.4 to 27.3, and the stated GSM8K margin is corrected from +1.4 to +3.6 percentage points.

M1.justification: Section 4.1 changes the stated KL estimator to sample from the old policy with a p/p_old importance correction. The core AGRPO procedure and variance-reduction components remain intact. Both versions use beta=0 in the main experiments, so this correction does not establish a change to those training runs.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries, methodological motivation, efficiency discussion, and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Policy-gradient background moves into Section 2, notation is standardized, and the appendices are reorganized around new cost analysis and ablations. These are substantial narrative changes beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: v3 adds three compact ablation tables, revises Figure 3's curves, legend, and timing-table structure, redraws and relabels Figure 1, and annotates Figure 2's speed/accuracy comparisons. Existing tables and Algorithm 1 are relocated. The overall visual format remains similar, and Figure 4 and the sample-response display are retained.

R1.justification: Section 6 now distinguishes ELBO-based and trajectory-based dLLM RL, adds TraceRL and MDPO, and positions AGRPO within the latter family through scalable estimation. This replaces the earlier first-extension positioning. Additional citations include Dream, simplified masked diffusion, and inverse distillation; publication updates to existing references are not new works.

T1.justification: New Proposition B.1 derives a quasiconvex training-cost approximation, C/sqrt(k)+D*sqrt(k), and its minimizer under explicit assumptions. Appendix A revises the estimator and proof to use rollout-specific entropy distributions from the detached old policy and explicitly conditions unbiasedness on fixed rollouts. These extend and refine the formal treatment beyond v2's estimator proof.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens support for AGRPO's central efficiency and robustness claims. Figure 3 adds the missing full-trajectory control: k=128 costs 158.1 seconds per step versus 72.4 at k=32, with only marginally faster convergence. Appendix C checks decoding dependence and rollout reuse, while revised mathematical qualifications and research positioning improve precision. These gains are substantive despite unchanged headline AGRPO accuracies; uncertainty across independent runs remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AGRPO study. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including material relocated between versions.

after.justification: v3 retains original AGRPO experiments and reports additional sampling-budget, decoding-strategy, denoising-step, and rollout-reuse results in Figure 3 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v2 reports original AGRPO results on four reasoning tasks, inference tradeoffs, training ablations, and timing measurements in Table 1 and Figures 2–4.

results.title: Simple Policy Gradients for Reasoning with Diffusion Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statement, and conclusion retain the same central claims: HP convergence under standard cost assumptions, optimal iteration rates, linear speed-up, and matching or sharper transient times. The sharper dimension dependence refines the detailed guarantees without redefining these headline contributions.

C2.justification: Section 4 and Appendix K, renamed L, substantially revise a central limitation. V3 calls polynomial dimension dependence unavoidable under its noise definition and suggests stronger assumptions for logarithmic dependence. V4 identifies the existing assumption with norm-sub-Gaussianity and leaves complete removal of dimension dependence open. Added discussions explain HP versus MSE failure guarantees and the advantages of last-iterate guarantees over averaging.

D1.justification: The implementation recipe retains the same sklearn generators and parameters, graph-weight construction, initialization, and simulation procedures. No code or data access information, hardware specifications, or runtime measurements are added.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic, strongly convex quadratic problems with Gaussian gradient noise and random communication networks. Added LLM motivation does not introduce an evaluated dataset or task.

E2.justification: Both empirical studies evaluate DSGD while varying thresholds and network sizes. No competing algorithm is added or removed; new citations concern theoretical positioning.

E3.justification: Appendix G in v3 describes the quadratic matrices as positive semidefinite; Appendix H in v4 corrects this to positive definite. This revises the reported setting, while the SPD generator, dimensions, networks, learning-rate schedule, and iteration budgets remain unchanged. It does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The existing investigations of exponential tail decay and linear speed-up are retained. No new ablation, robustness experiment, sensitivity test, or empirical case study appears.

E5.justification: The experiments retain 5,000 and 1,000 runs, respectively, and Monte Carlo sample counts of 3,000 and 600. The plotted shading is identical, with no new seed information, interval definitions, or statistical tests. Changes to theoretical concentration bounds belong to T1.

E6.justification: All six plot panels in Figures 1 and 2 are identical, and their accompanying findings are retained. These include the approximately 6,000-iteration tail-decay onset for threshold 0.0001 in Figure 1 and faster decay with larger networks in Figure 2.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains the same stochastic-gradient oracle and adapt-then-combine update. Revised step-size restrictions and the added averaged-iterate discussion concern theoretical guarantees for DSGD; no algorithmic component is replaced or introduced.

P1.justification: V4 adds Appendix B on MSE versus HP results, expands Section 3.3, rewrites the dimension-dependence discussion, and corrects several appendix theorem labels. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact; appendix renumbering largely follows the insertion.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 2 retain identical panels, axes, legends, and captions, and Algorithm 1 is unchanged. Reflow changes their placement relative to the surrounding text; Figure 2 now precedes the transient-time appendix instead of interrupting its opening discussion.

R1.justification: V4 adds references on accelerated and distributed clipping, smoothness, stochastic-approximation averaging, and LLM motivation, while removing the Vershynin reference. Appendix J also qualifies comparison with individual-regret guarantees for online games. The overall positioning around decentralized HP convergence and linear speed-up remains intact.

T1.justification: A new martingale concentration proposition and rewritten Lemma 2 proof substantially sharpen the average-noise bound. Theorems 1 and 2 replace leading sqrt(d) and d dependence with logarithmic dependence under the existing noise condition, with corresponding step-size and proof revisions. Appendix G also corrects the initial-error scaling, propagated into Appendix I's transient-time derivation, although the theorem restatement retains the old expression.
