Section 3.3 adds reasoning about slower step-size decay and Polyak-Ruppert averaging.

improvement.justification: The revised concentration argument substantially improves the central theory by replacing polynomial leading dimension factors with logarithmic dependence under the same noise assumption, resolving a limitation v3 incorrectly described as unavoidable. Correcting the initial-error scaling and clarifying noise definitions further strengthen the paper. Some inconsistencies remain: Appendix G's theorem restatement misses the initial-error correction, and the new averaging paragraph's step-size scaling conflicts with Theorem 1. These localized defects temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial theoretical improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DSGD convergence study. Their complete text, equations, figures, references, and appendices support comparison, including matching material across appendix renumbering.

after.justification: Appendix H retains these original simulations and their reported outcomes in Figures 1 and 2.

before.justification: Appendix G reports original quadratic-optimization simulations, with empirical mean-squared errors and tail probabilities in Figures 1 and 2.

results.title: High-Probability Convergence Guarantees of Decentralized SGD

C1.justification: The abstract and central claims about token-centric selection, efficiency, and gains of up to 9% remain substantially unchanged. The introduction and conclusion add applicability without separate target examples, while the contribution list drops v1's explicit claim to be the first method of its kind.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of target-size saturation, noisy-target stability, off-task generalization, and in-domain applicability. It qualifies v1's categorical length-agnostic interpretation and adds selection-specific bias and safety limitations. The earlier dedicated Limitations paragraph, including the explicit pretraining-curation caveat, is no longer present.

D1.justification: v2 documents cached nearest-fingerprint lookup, explicit IDF handling, and chat formatting. Appendix M supplies source-stratified reference construction, response-only training loss, evaluation fallback details, and Pythia-70M proxy hyperparameters. Section 5 adds timing conditions and warmup durations. The original shared LoRA recipe and hardware/software configuration are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds MMLU, BBH, multilingual TyDiQA, and TruthfulQA evaluations while retaining the original benchmarks. It also introduces MathInstruct as a training pool and evaluates broader math coverage through MATH, NumGLUE, SVAMP, Mathematics, and SimulEq, including selection without external target examples.

E2.justification: The evaluated selector roster remains unchanged. However, v2's new 7B-scorer transfer comparison includes full-data fine-tuning as a control (Table 3), absent from v1's transfer comparison. The original transfer comparator set remains intact in v2 Table 24; newly discussed methods such as QCS are not evaluated.

E3.justification: v2 introduces Llama-2-7B main experiments and transfer to Llama-2-13B, with benchmark-specific reference sets of 285, 81, and 9 examples for MMLU, BBH, and TyDiQA. The new MathInstruct experiments use 50% coresets and zero-shot program-of-thought/chain-of-thought fallback evaluation. Original commonsense and GSM8K protocols are retained alongside these additions.

E4.justification: The CommonsenseQA ablation table in v1 is replaced by expanded MMLU ablations covering pooling, IDF, fallback penalties, layers, and checkpoints. v2 also adds target-size and answer-corruption tests, evaluation outside the selection target task, qualitative fingerprint/fallback examples, and in-domain reference-size and scorer-recipe analyses (Appendices H–M).

E5.justification: Both versions report means over three seeds or runs with parenthetical standard deviations. Retained tables preserve their uncertainty values, and new experiments follow the same reporting practice. No increased run count, confidence-interval procedure, or significance-testing practice is introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial benchmark, transfer, robustness, and runtime results. Its new Table 1 reports a 48.56 macro-average for TRIM versus 48.27 for LESS; Table 5 reports selection times of 4.40 versus 35.76 hours. These are newly reported settings, not same-setting improvements over v1. Earlier Tables 1 and 3 survive unchanged as Tables 23 and 24, and GSM8K Table 2 retains its values.

M1.justification: The attention-saliency, fingerprint, cosine-scoring, fallback, and coverage-pooling pipeline is retained. Section 4.5 and Appendix M add a limited adaptation that constructs the reference set through source-stratified sampling from the candidate pool, enabling selection without external target examples.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the experimental narrative, moving the original Llama-3 suite into Appendix N and rewriting the introduction, setup, results discussion, and method explanations. Algorithm nuances become a separate appendix, and the dedicated Limitations section is replaced by an Impact Statement and distributed discussion.

P2.justification: The appendices switch from two-column to full-width presentation, with reorganized pseudocode and tables. Original budget curves are redrawn in Figure 5 with an added HellaSwag panel, source-composition displays are redistributed, and new benchmark, runtime, robustness, and qualitative-example tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: Section 2 and Appendix A add positioning against QCS and references concerning dynamic uncertainty, token-wise influence, and critical tokens. The explicit first-method novelty claim is withdrawn, and new datasets introduce additional citations. Most of the extended related-work discussion remains unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 explicitly defines IDF and its proposed weighting of Equation (9), whereas v1 only alludes to TF-IDF. The original numbered equations and computational-cost derivation otherwise remain, without new theorems or proofs. As written, positive class-constant IDF factors cancel under Equation (9)'s normalization, leaving the claimed frequency-suppression effect unsupported by that formula.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for central claims: Section 5 measures efficiency that v1 supported only asymptotically, while Appendices I–M directly test target sensitivity, off-task behavior, and selection without external targets. Broader evaluation accompanies preservation of the principal earlier results. The problematic IDF formulation and inconsistent default ablation values weaken clarity, but the controlled analyses and measured costs provide a substantial net improvement in the paper's empirical support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TRIM, with matching authors and core methodology. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison; earlier experiments can be matched to material retained in v2's Appendix N.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and reports additional benchmark evaluations, measured runtimes, robustness tests, and in-domain math selection experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning experiments, including commonsense and GSM8K results, cross-model transfer, budget comparisons, and hyperparameter ablations.

results.title: TRIM: Token-wise Attention-Derived Saliency for Data-Efficient Instruction Tuning

C1.justification: V2 frames the theoretical contribution as bin-scaling guidance under an idealized Markov approximation, qualifying v1's optimal-bin wording while retaining the detector and normality results. The reported reference-cost advantage also narrows from 5–5,000 times to 5–50 times in the main-results discussion.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations based on transition sparsity, marginal-versus-transition divergence, and possible pretraining-related false positives. It explicitly limits the Markov approximation and interprets theoretical variance as a conservative scale rather than precise finite-sample prediction. However, the new threshold discussion in Appendix E.2.13 reverses the score-sign interpretation given by Equation 2.

D1.justification: Appendix E.1 newly documents the 150-word input filter, 100–200-token generation, pairwise length matching, and model-family decoding defaults. New analyses provide attack prompts and threshold procedures, while v1's detailed R-Detect implementation discussion is removed. These disclosures do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: V2 adds DAIGT evaluation with more than 15 generators and Dolly human-response evaluation. DetectRL, already evaluated in v1, gains explicit mixed-domain, mixed-generator, cross-reference, and corrupted-input scenarios. RAID coverage from v1 Appendix A3.2.5 is removed; the original English, Chinese, and German coverage otherwise remains.

E2.justification: V2 adds Binoculars and FourierGPT and extends R-Detect to the main and per-dataset comparisons, expanding those comparator sets from 10 to 13 methods. V1 evaluated R-Detect only in a separate DetectRL/RAID comparison, which is removed rather than merely relocated.

E3.justification: New protocols include TPR at 1% and 5% FPR, F1 comparisons at fixed versus test-set-optimal thresholds, controlled decoding sweeps, larger proxy models, and white-box comparisons. Appendix B also adds Markov-order experiments controlling reference size and test length. The retained main experiments still specify 300 reference and 150 test samples per class.

E4.justification: V2 adds alternative-quantizer, unigram-versus-transition, GJS-versus-L1/L2, threshold, and decoding ablations. It substantially expands robustness testing and adds analyses of marginal versus transition signals and possible pretraining exposure. Existing bin-count, length, proxy-model, and T5-paraphrasing analyses remain.

E5.justification: Appendix E.2.3 adds targeted Shapiro-Wilk tests with p-values and empirical-versus-theoretical variance estimation. The existing three-random-test-set averaging and uncertainty reporting remain; additional result rows do not establish an increased run count.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive comparator, robustness, ablation, and statistical results while retaining SurpMark's matched main-table scores. XSum/Llama-3.2-3B baseline values are revised, including LogRank AUROC from 94.87 to 59.35 in v1 Table 6 versus v2 Table 15. The HC3 score histogram switches from OpenQA to psychology, and v1's aggregate DetectRL/RAID results disappear.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain proxy-model surprisals, shared k-means quantization, first-order transition matrices, the N/n mixing weight, and the thresholded GJS difference. Expanded methodological explanations and the new zero-threshold study do not establish a changed detector procedure.

P1.justification: The abstract, methodological explanation, and analysis narrative are substantially revised. Related work becomes a concise introduction subsection plus Appendix C; theoretical material is redistributed, experiments gain a new organization, and explicit limitations are introduced. These changes extend beyond simply inserting additional results.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, with figures and tables resized and rearranged. Main comparison tables gain baseline rows, numerous analytical tables are introduced, and the old R-Detect table is removed. V1 Figure 6 is separated into throughput and non-English figures in v2.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations and discussion for Binoculars, FourierGPT, Gray's approximation theory, Dolly, and pretraining-exposure research. RAID and Khandelwal's context-modeling reference disappear. The central positioning relative to global statistics, likelihood-free testing, and R-Detect remains.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 and Appendix B.2 add a formal relative-entropy-rate treatment of Markov approximation, deriving the incremental order gain through conditional mutual information. The original discretization bounds, N^(1/5) scaling, GJS/likelihood-ratio proposition, and normality proof remain; the normality theorem moves to Appendix D as Theorem D.14.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens support for practical use by explicitly testing reference-domain mismatch and corrupted inputs, important gaps in v1's evaluation. Component ablations, quantitative checks of Markov adequacy and normal approximation, and clearer generation details make the method's evidence and limitations more assessable. These gains outweigh the removed RAID comparison and localized inconsistencies, particularly the reversed score-sign explanation in Appendix E.2.13; the improvement does not depend on higher retained benchmark scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SurpMark. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds benchmark evaluations, ablations, distribution-shift tests, and statistical analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original detection experiments, sensitivity analyses, throughput measurements, and appendix evaluations of paraphrasing and R-Detect.

results.title: Black-Box Detection of LLM-Generated Text Using Generalized Jensen Shannon Divergence

C1.justification: The central OBD-based pruning and output-aware scoring contributions remain. v2 adds the claim that prior value-aware scores are isolated-value special cases and more explicitly identifies key sensitivity and key-value interactions as contributions beyond those methods.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the new value-aware comparisons as evidence for benefits beyond value norms. It adds limitations concerning decoding-centric reasoning, unevaluated agentic tasks, and small-context latency from unoptimized kernels. Earlier structural-bias, perturbation-window, and key/joint-combination discussions remain.

D1.justification: Reproduction guidance is substantially revised around a KVPress-based implementation. v2 specifies GQA aggregation, chat-template exclusions, AdaKV's safeguard, CriticalKV's budget allocation, and efficiency-benchmark hardware and procedures. Prefill budgets become 10–40%; LongBench's 32K truncation is removed. Appendix C changes H2O/SnapKV windows to 64 tokens and SnapKV pooling from max pooling with kernel 7 to average pooling with kernel 5. New timing protocols measure TTFT, decoding latency, and memory across batch sizes and context lengths.

E4.justification: v2 adds value-norm and two-stage scoring comparisons (Figure 4), plus complexity and empirical overhead analyses across context lengths and batch sizes (Appendix D.1). The oracle-recall/window analysis remains. Score-variant ablations shift toward RULER, while LongBench value/joint rows and the PG19 compression-sensitivity sweep are removed.

E5.justification: The new efficiency study explicitly identifies out-of-memory entries as linear extrapolations from measured data (Figure 6), introducing an estimation procedure absent from v1. Neither version reports independent-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: The result set is substantially replaced and expanded. For example, v2 Table 3 newly reports 50.55 for AdaKV and 65.49 with OBCache-K on query-agnostic RULER-4K at 30% KV. LongBench scores are replaced under revised settings, and value-aware comparison and efficiency results are added. Older PG19 compression curves and LongBench value/joint entries disappear. These are not same-setting performance gains from v1 to v2.

M1.justification: The OBD objective, three saliency formulas, accumulated decoding scores, and top-k eviction algorithms are retained. v2 renames the variants and documents GQA head aggregation for architectures already used in v1; this does not establish a changed underlying scoring or eviction procedure.

P1.justification: The introduction and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Existing methodological material is reorganized into standalone preliminaries and formal definitions, a theorem, and propositions. Appendices are reordered, limitations gain topic headings, and VALUE/KEY/JOINT terminology becomes V/K/V&K.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main text, rebuilds Figure 3 as a 12-panel evaluation grid, and restructures Table 1 around query-aware/agnostic settings. It adds value-aware comparison and efficiency figures plus a complexity table, and reorganizes the detailed appendix tables. The retained PG19 plot is reformatted and renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 substantially revises positioning by recognizing VATP and CriticalKV as prior value-aware approaches and distinguishing OBCache's OBD formulation and key-related terms from them. It also expands discussion of adaptive allocation, sparse attention, and query-agnostic compression, including AdaKV, PyramidKV, ShadowKV, and KVzip.

T1.justification: Appendix A.5 adds a groupwise perturbation objective and corresponding GQA score derivation. v2 also restores a missing factor of two in the key-Hessian expansion (v1 Equation 23; v2 Equation 22). Most existing derivations remain; their new theorem/proposition labels are presentation changes.

improvement.justification: The VATP/CriticalKV comparisons and revised positioning address an important gap in v1's novelty and effectiveness evidence. Broader RULER and query-agnostic evaluation, measured computational costs, and GQA analysis substantially strengthen validation and technical completeness. Some compression-sweep and variant results are lost, and run-to-run uncertainty remains unreported, but the overall gain in scientific support is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OBCache, and their main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison. Changed experimental settings limit direct performance comparisons but do not prevent comparison of the papers.

after.justification: v2 reports original RULER, LongBench, PG19, oracle-recall, and latency and memory results.

before.justification: v1 reports original NIAH retrieval, LongBench, PG19 perplexity, and oracle-token-recall results.

results.title: OBCache: Optimal Brain KV Cache Pruning for Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace headline improvements of 42.9%/55.8% with 54.3%/66.41%. The latter match 256-token Countdown accuracy-point gaps against d1 and LLaDA-Instruct, rather than the earlier approximately cross-length-average gaps. The central distribution-matching, weight-baseline, and reasoning-without-SFT contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning compatibility with SFT/DPO, generation parallelism explaining rollout-count timing, and sequence-level importance weighting contributing to stability. It also discusses late-training instability under heavy rollout reuse and interprets the new entropy measurements as supporting diversity preservation. The principal limitation to the LLaDA family and four elementary reasoning benchmarks remains.

D1.justification: Appendix C.2 newly specifies rollout temperatures of 0 for random-order sampling and 0.2 for Fast-dLLM, plus individual-weight-baseline assignments for the new DMPO-SFT and DMPO-LLaDA-1.5 variants. Added analyses document their hardware budgets and entropy-measurement procedure. Most existing implementation settings and code/data access information are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use GSM8K, MATH500, three-number Countdown, and 4-by-4 Sudoku. s1k already appears in v1's d1 training pipeline. The added initialization, sampler, and hyperparameter experiments do not introduce a new task, domain, or represented data population.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds cGRPO-LLaDA as an evaluated comparator across the four benchmarks. Coupled-GRPO was discussed but not included in v1's reported comparison. Dream-Instruct, LLaDA-Instruct, LLaDA-1.5, and d1-LLaDA remain.

E3.justification: The main zero-shot evaluation at 128, 256, and 512 tokens is retained. v2 adds SFT/DPO-checkpoint initialization arms, a compute-matched rollout-sampler comparison, and fixed-batch-size Countdown sweeps over N=4–32 and F=1–24 using six-hour and eight-hour budgets. It also specifies an entropy-evaluation protocol with N=16, F=8, and measurements every ten generations.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained but revised Sudoku weight-baseline study, v2 investigates compatibility with prior post-training, sampler efficiency, sensitivity to rollout count and buffer reuse, and rollout entropy (Table 1 and Figures 5, 7–9). These substantially expand the questions tested. v1's reward-dynamics analysis is retained as v2 Figure 6 rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Both versions already display shaded training curves without defining the bands or reporting repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2 extends this existing plotting practice but introduces no identifiable new uncertainty-estimation or statistical-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises reported DMPO-LLaDA Countdown accuracies from 64.84/75.78/79.69 to 67.19/80.86/82.81 at 128/256/512 tokens; its other nine scores and existing comparator rows remain unchanged. Three new model rows and additional efficiency, sensitivity, and entropy findings substantially expand the results. Section 4 newly reports comparable reward using 1.8 versus 5.78 PF-days; the revised Countdown scores should not be interpreted as isolated same-training-setting gains.

M1.justification: The WDCE/WDDO objectives, importance weights, three weight baselines, and core update algorithm remain unchanged. v2 adds Fast-dLLM with approximate KV caching and confidence-based sampling as an implemented rollout-generation option alongside random-order sampling (Section 4 and Appendix C.2), providing a limited procedural extension.

P1.justification: Existing prose receives local editing, headings and terminology are refined, and random-order autoregressive sampling gains the ROAR abbreviation. The reward-dynamics discussion moves to Appendix C.3, and appendix subsections are reorganized around new material. Most existing narrative and section organization remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 substantially changes typography and the width of the single-column layout. Figure 1 moves to the opening page and gains model series; Table 1 expands from five to eight model rows. Algorithm 1 and the original reward-dynamics figure move to the appendices, while four new figures display efficiency, hyperparameter, and entropy analyses. Existing plots are also reformatted.

R1.justification: v2 adds Campbell et al. (2024), Generative Flows on Discrete State-Spaces, and Ren et al. (2025a), How Discrete and Continuous Diffusion Meet, supporting the CTMC derivation. It makes the connection to already-cited DRAKES and MDNS more explicit. Most related-work positioning is retained; numerous venue updates concern the same cited works.

T1.justification: New Appendix B.1 introduces CTMC and path-measure definitions, Lemma B.1, and a stochastic-control derivation connecting WDCE to path-space KL matching. The earlier zero-temperature extension, variance-reduction argument, and WDDO proof are retained and renumbered. The new gamma(t)=1/t schedule, however, conflicts with the stated fully masked t=0 initialization and 1-t masking convention.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens empirical support for important advantages that v1 largely motivated prospectively: compute efficiency, effective rollout reuse, and diversity preservation receive direct tests in Figures 5 and 7–9. The added cGRPO comparison and post-trained initializations further improve evaluation. These address substantial validation gaps. The benefit is chiefly empirical: uncertainty bands remain unexplained, and the new stochastic-control appendix contains a time-schedule inconsistency, limiting the theoretical gain.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DMPO research work. All 22 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v2, including references and appendices, are readable. Text, equations, tables, figures, and relocated material support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds evaluated model variants, training-efficiency comparisons, hyperparameter ablations, and rollout-entropy results in Section 4 and Appendix C.3.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original DMPO fine-tuning results on four reasoning benchmarks, training reward curves, and a Sudoku weight-baseline ablation. Appendix C supplies experimental details and generated examples.

results.title: Enhancing Reasoning for Diffusion LLMs via Distribution Matching Policy Optimization

C1.justification: The central head-identification and 20–50% near-lossless cache-reduction claims remain. v2 adds an explicit end-to-end speedup contribution and knowledge-task applicability, while dropping v1's explicit contribution claim that reasoning heads are functionally distinct from retrieval heads.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning generation termination, response-length selection effects, and fixed-budget fairness. It acknowledges comparable reasoning/retrieval head sensitivity in Qwen-3 and specific error-pattern exceptions. Earlier explanations invoking noise from non-reasoning heads and more distributed Qwen-2.5 reasoning are removed.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the prompt template, top-p settings, exact Qwen-3 checkpoints, FSDP details, and per-model training costs. It also describes the efficiency measurement stack and updates the project-page link. Most original optimizer, hardware, and data-construction details remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds knowledge QA evaluations on MMLU-Pro Chemistry, Computer Science, Law, and Physics, substantially extending domain coverage beyond mathematical reasoning and Python programming. DeepScaleR training and the four original evaluation benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: H2O, R-KV, and DuoAttention remain the evaluated compression baselines, with full-cache and random-head controls retained where relevant. Appendix F compares budget settings of existing methods rather than introducing new comparison algorithms.

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen-3-4B model configurations, sampling of up to 500 instances per MMLU-Pro subset, latency/throughput sweeps, and batch-size comparisons at similar memory usage. It also introduces baseline-correct error analyses and fixed-versus-dynamic budget tests. The original main evaluation already used dynamic budgets.

E4.justification: New analyses examine response lengths on mutually correct samples, full-cache output-length distributions, and sensitivity to fixed versus dynamic budgets. Head-sensitivity and error-mode analyses are expanded and refined. The three original training-component ablations remain in Figure 8.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Results remain point estimates; the unchanged four GRPO samples per query concern training rather than evaluation uncertainty.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive Qwen-3 and MMLU-Pro results and reports 1.09–1.21× end-to-end speedups using doubled RLKV batch sizes at similar peak memory. Among matched results, Llama GSM8K at 0.4 sparsity changes from 88.4% to 86.8%, below R-KV's 88.3% and DuoAttention's 87.1% (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 4).

M1.justification: Both versions use frozen language models, mixed-attention gating, GRPO with L1 regularization, self-distillation sampling, adaptive penalty weighting, and top-k head selection for inference. The revised explanation introduces no new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, terminology shifts to reasoning-critical heads, and analyses move into a standalone Section 5. Future Work is rewritten, appendices are reorganized into A–F, an Impact Statements section is added, and the LLM-use declaration is removed.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, expands Figure 5 from eight to 24 panels, adds a compression schematic and efficiency/length/budget displays, and enlarges model coverage in tables and heatmaps. Error plots also receive revised legends, scales, and baseline bounds.

R1.justification: v2 adds sparse/gated-attention references and positioning, including Longformer, MoBA, Native Sparse Attention, and Gated Attention, plus Qwen3 and MMLU-Pro citations. The existing comparison with compression methods and RL-based efficiency research remains largely intact.

T1.justification: The substantive mixed-attention, GRPO, advantage, and adaptive-penalty equations remain equivalent. No formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs are introduced. The operational description of reasoning-critical heads clarifies the existing concept.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens generalization evidence through a third model and four knowledge domains, while Table 2 supplies actual runtime and memory measurements beyond v1's cache-budget comparisons. Additional analyses and reproduction details further strengthen the empirical case. These gains outweigh reporting defects, including Appendix E's inconsistent 200/3019 percentage and Figure 6's reversed panel descriptions. The speedups specifically concern larger batches at similar memory usage.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RLKV work and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. v1 Appendices A.1–A.4 match v2 Appendices A–D; the expanded material supports reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds a third model, MMLU-Pro evaluations, inference measurements, and additional analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original compression experiments on two reasoning models and four benchmarks, alongside head-masking, error-mode, and training-component analyses.

results.title: Which Heads Matter for Reasoning? RL-Guided KV Cache Compression

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction strengthen the headline claims from 20–50% to 20–60% near-lossless cache reduction and from at most 1.21× to 2.06× end-to-end speedup, specifying continuous batching at 60% reduction. These materially expand the claimed efficiency benefits, while the central RL-as-probe and reasoning-critical-head contributions remain.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations about long-context transfer, window size extending the near-lossless range, and concurrency explaining practical speedups. Appendix G expands the former future-work discussion into explicit limitations concerning static gating, dynamic-decision overhead, and degradation at sparsity ≥0.8. Appendix B also identifies unsupported SGLang caching features, substantially clarifying applicability and deployment boundaries.

D1.justification: v3 documents SGLang v0.5.2, its dual-pool implementation and caching restrictions, serving hardware, and the different engines used for Table 1's math/code and knowledge results. Figure 3 revises the reported Qwen-2.5 KV group size from 8 to 7 and removes detailed head/layer counts, without establishing a model replacement. Training hyperparameters, training costs, prompt instructions, and project access information remain.

E1.justification: v3 adds LongReason with 64K inputs and a 70K context, substantially extending evaluation to a long-input scenario beyond the existing reasoning and knowledge benchmarks. It evaluates Llama-3.1-8B-R1 and Qwen-3-4B-Thinking there; the original training data, benchmark coverage, and motivation studies remain.

E2.justification: KVZip is added as a comparator throughout Figure 5 and the three complete benchmark tables, and participates in the new LongReason comparison. H2O, R-KV, and DuoAttention remain in the corresponding original benchmark sweeps, making this a focused expansion of the comparator set.

E3.justification: The fixed-batch Transformers/FlashAttention-2 efficiency experiment in v2 Table 2 is replaced by SGLang continuous batching on one A100 40GB, with varying concurrency and sparsity, in v3 Table 3. New protocols include 400 of 794 LongReason samples at 70K context and three sink/local-window configurations. These are substantial evaluation changes, not directly comparable reruns of the old efficiency setting.

E4.justification: v3 adds a focused window-sensitivity ablation comparing 16+64, 32+128, and 64+256 tokens across sparsities, and explicitly examines transfer from 8K training rollouts to 70K evaluation. Existing training ablations, head-sensitivity tests, error analyses, and fixed-versus-dynamic-budget studies remain. The standalone single-layer latency/throughput analysis in v2 Figure 6 is removed.

E5.justification: Appendix B newly acknowledges SGLang nondeterminism and resulting run-to-run accuracy variation for both RLKV and full attention. This is a qualitative uncertainty disclosure; no run counts, seeds, quantified variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: All existing result rows in v2 Tables 4–6 are retained exactly in v3 Tables 6–8, alongside new KVZip rows. v3 adds LongReason, window-ablation, serving, and SGLang knowledge-summary results, while revising Table 1's selected operating points and omitting some older threshold-specific entries. Reported speedups change from 1.09–1.21× to 1.19–2.06× under different serving conditions, so this is replacement evidence rather than a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The mixed-attention gates, GRPO/L1 objective, training stabilization, and top-k head selection remain unchanged. Section 4.3 adds a serving adaptation previously described as future work: SGLang uses separate paged and circular-buffer KV pools, with freed memory reassigned to support more concurrent requests.

P1.justification: The revision tightens the method definition and qualitative-analysis prose, clarifies inference-time discretization, rewrites the conclusion, and moves expanded future-work material into Appendix G. It also adds acknowledgments and replaces the preprint notice with conference information. The main section sequence and overall narrative remain recognizable.

P2.justification: Table 1 changes from three baseline-comparison blocks into a compact RLKV-only benchmark-by-model summary with knowledge rows. The old efficiency figure and table are replaced by new serving, LongReason, and window-ablation displays. Figure 5 gains KVZip curves, Figure 7's horizontal-axis label is clarified, and retained appendix figures and expanded numerical tables are substantially rearranged.

R1.justification: v3 explicitly credits prior head-reallocation methods for gated mixed attention and adds KVZip and LongReason references. Appendix G substantially broadens positioning toward an on-policy approach applicable to pruning, sparse attention, token compression, multimodal tasks, and agentic reasoning, with numerous newly cited works. Publication-year and venue updates elsewhere are bibliographic edits rather than new research relationships.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 introduces a compressed-pool memory estimate, O(max_running_requests × W), and the theoretical speedup limit 1/((1−s)+sW/L), based on residual cache costs. The original method definitions and Equations 1–4 remain substantively unchanged; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens practical-efficiency and generalization evidence through continuous-batching measurements, 70K-context evaluation, KVZip comparisons, and window sensitivity, while preserving the original benchmark results and documenting deployment limitations. Important qualifications remain: Table 3's 2.06× speedup accompanies 73.8% accuracy versus 79.4% for full attention, and Table 2 shows KVZip beating RLKV on Qwen-3 at sparsity 0.2 despite the broad superiority statement. These qualifications limit the strongest claims but do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RLKV and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across renumbering, relocation, and revised displays, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds LongReason evaluation, continuous-batching measurements, and an inference-window ablation.

before.justification: v2 reports original benchmark accuracies, inference measurements, training ablations, head-sensitivity experiments, and error analyses in the main text and appendices.

results.title: Which Heads Matter for Reasoning? RL-Guided KV Cache Compression

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about implicit latent manifolds, denoising projections, geodesic interpolation/extrapolation and compatibility with different autoencoders and metrics. The more precise title and expanded introduction clarify this existing scope.

C2.justification: Appendix C adds substantive interpretations involving variational consistency, negative-curvature instability, off-manifold metric construction and codimension. It discusses projection-training overhead and competing methods' applicability restrictions. Figure 12 additionally interprets similar linear and geodesic shell paths as evidence of local flatness; earlier limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents a PyTorch L-BFGS implementation alongside SciPy BFGS, explicitly specifies noisy inputs as y_z=z+epsilon, and adds initialization and penalty guidance. Appendix C supplies comparator discretizations, half-circle network and data parameters, penalty limits, LAND hyperparameters, and training/computation times, substantially expanding technical reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v2 adds rotated-and-scaled letter-A images, a synthetic 3D point-cloud/VAE example, and noisy half-circle data (Figures 2, 16 and 17). The torus, SCAPE, CMU motion-capture, rotating-cow and Pose-NDF coverage is retained, so the expansion principally concerns additional synthetic scenarios.

E2.justification: Appendix C newly evaluates Stochman's parametric geodesic and exponential solvers, the RBF-based method of Arvanitidis et al. (2018), sigmoid uncertainty regularization from Arvanitidis et al. (2022), and LAND. LAND is also added to the retained cow-image comparison. These substantially extend v1's linear-interpolation and internal metric comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include 50-node torus paths versus eight-node splines with 50 metric evaluations and 2000 optimization iterations, plus half-circle tests using 6000 points and K=30. Motion-capture settings now specify decoder means and Leaky ReLU projection activations, differing from v1's sampled outputs and general ELU specification. These revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix C adds examinations of whether exponential shooting reproduces a minimizing torus path, stability with widely separated half-circle endpoints, and off-manifold failures or decoded artifacts in competing methods. The earlier torus noise, sampling-density and network-size sensitivity study remains unchanged as Figure 11.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The added timings and trajectories introduce no new statistical uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds numerical and qualitative comparison results. For example, C.1 reports torus energy/time of 4.7889/1.89 seconds for the proposed approach and 4.7892/2.48 seconds for Stochman under their respective discretizations. C.3–C.4 add runtime, nonconvergence and artifact findings. The motion-extrapolation example is also replaced; these are new or replaced results, not demonstrated v1-to-v2 performance gains.

M1.justification: The projection loss and variational geodesic algorithms are retained. However, Section 5.2 changes the specified decoder output used in geometric computations from a sampled decoding to the decoder distribution's mean, a limited revision to the reported inference procedure.

P1.justification: The title is refined, introduction and related-work passages are rewritten, and explanations of differentiation and initialization are expanded. Existing appendix material is regrouped into method and experiment details, followed by the new comparison appendix. Most existing main-text prose and its section sequence are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 2 and comparison Figures 15–18, and replaces the motion-extrapolation display while removing its latent-space panel. Figure 18 redisplays existing cow outputs beside new LAND results. Other figures are largely retained with revised numbering, placement or captions, producing a substantial expansion of the visual evidence.

R1.justification: Appendix C substantially expands positioning relative to parametric, graph-based, uncertainty-regularized and density-based approaches. New references include LAND, robust shortest-path methods, Stochman, Fermat distances and diffusion-based geodesics. Existing Arvanitidis references receive detailed methodological comparisons, and the discussion of Shao et al. is revised to emphasize nonzero latent-manifold codimension.

T1.justification: Section 3 corrects the convergence approximation condition from O(dist^-3) to O(dist^3). It also adds reasoning explaining why exponential-map optimization avoids second-order differentiation of the projection and decoder networks. The central variational definitions and convergence claims otherwise remain.

improvement.justification: v1's comparative validation relied chiefly on linear interpolation and internal metric variants. P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 5, appendix Figures A4–A8 and A13, Tables A11–A13, and prompt boxes. Tables A7–A9 gain columns, and Tables A9–A10 move onto separate pages. improvement.justification: v2 addresses important omissions in reproducibility and measurement validation: Appendix B supplies previously missing generation details, while Appendices A.1, A.4, and E.9 directly audit data preparation, human-profile matching, and reasoning labels. after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds model evaluations, language and prompt comparisons, contamination analyses, and manual validation studies.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, inference-time scaling experiments, and reasoning-trace and error analyses in Sections 4–5 and Appendices D–E.

results.title: LiveOIBench: Can Large Language Models Outperform Human Contestants in Informatics Olympiads?

M1.justification: The reported main reward changes from u+t above the threshold and u−t below it (v1 Equation 3) to u+|t−0.5| (v2 Equation 1). Retained numerical results do not establish that training was rerun.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, theoretical exposition, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Reward specification is integrated into the experiments section, and the appendices are reorganized around subgroup and judge analyses. The standalone ethics and LLM-usage statements are removed.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from one column to two, with revised typography and figure placement. v2 adds an algorithm display and several result tables, expands Table 2 with subgroup rows, and relabels/resizes retained plots. The unchanged filtered-response counts are transposed from v1 Table 5 into v2 Table 10.

R1.justification: Related work substantially expands positioning against classifier-guided generation, discussing PPLM, GeDi, DExperts, and diffusion guidance, with an explicit training-versus-decoding distinction. T1.justification: v1's calibrated-probability utility model and constant-helpfulness special case are replaced by general score-conditioned passing and rejection utilities. v2 adds an optimal-threshold global-minimum theorem and a proposition with a derivative proof establishing sufficient monotonicity conditions. This substantially revises the mathematical foundation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence by testing dependencies v1 left unexamined: prompt subgroups, alternative guards, and another judge reveal where aggregate safety–utility gains fail. A1.justification: Both complete, readable PDFs describe the same Boundary Guidance study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained experiments across the revised structure.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds long-context, alternative-classifier, prompt-subgroup, and alternative-judge evaluations.

results.title: Don't Walk the Line: Boundary Guidance for Filtered Generation

C1.justification: The central claims about separating editing from rendering and obtaining controllable representations across five domains remain. v2 adds explicit claims of robustness across inversion solvers and diffusion backbones in the abstract and conclusion, extending the original DDIM-focused account without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v2 develops a new interpretation of approximation errors, attributing small reconstruction differences to numerical noise and arguing that lifting, inversion, and VAE errors do not impede prediction. It also interprets kNN's advantage over MLP through neighborhood structure. Section 6 expands the earlier brief limitations into explanations of many-to-one ambiguity, long-range distortion, computational cost, and possible mitigations.

D1.justification: v2 adds solver parameters, MLP architecture and size, forecast histories, block and held-out sample counts, additional runtimes, and a fuller algorithmic pipeline. New solver experiments compare 8-step Rex-RK4 with 1000-step DDIM. The reported monkey S4 latent dimension changes from 12 to 16, and evaluation adds firing-rate correlation and RMSE dimensionality sweeps. These include new protocols and a revised configuration, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial checks of inversion error relative to VAE reconstruction, robustness across solvers and diffusion models, and decoder choice through kNN-versus-MLP ablation. Figure 5 adds generated-spike and firing-rate checks, while the dimensionality analysis gains RMSE curves. The earlier orthogonality analysis is retained as Appendix C.7.

E5.justification: Both versions report ± summaries and mean/std-style quantities without explicit random-seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. v2 continues the same reporting practice; additional result rows and changed uncertainty values do not establish a new statistical procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds forecasting and solver/decoder results and revises the dimensionality-sweep curves. Figure 5 replaces the monkey results: ConDA RMSE changes from 1.46 ± 0.45 to 0.67 ± 0.04 under the revised latent configuration, preventing a same-setting improvement comparison; firing-rate correlation r = 0.95 is newly reported. Table 1, the PCA/β-VAE comparison, classification scores, and CcGAN results retain their numerical values.

M1.justification: v2 adds ConDA implementations using Rex-RK4 inversion/sampling and IsoDiff latents alongside the original DDIM/cLDM pipeline. These extend the available inference procedures, while the contrastive objective, spline/TEX/KDE traversal, and core kNN lifting approach remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Appendix B reorganizes previously separate descriptions into two end-to-end algorithms and adds a DISFA running example; Appendix C is reordered, and an Impact Statement is introduced. This constitutes substantial narrative and structural revision.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 2 gains a Slerp row, the classification display is separated from Figure 3 into Table 3, Figure 5 gains multiple panels, and the dimensionality plots are redrawn with an RMSE row. New forecasting, solver, and decoder tables and a forecasting figure further expand the displays.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against NoiseCLR and DRCT, clarifies the relationship to diffusion/state-space models and LDNS, and introduces a discussion of reversible inversion literature including Rex-RK4, EDICT, BELM, and MALI. Some earlier sequential-diffusion and PIRD references disappear. These substantive changes go beyond publication metadata updates to retained citations.

It retains the CcGAN inversion loss and consolidates diffusion equations into algorithms. The central InfoNCE, spline, Taylor, and KDE mathematics remains equivalent, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central pipeline through explicit held-out forecasting, solver/VAE reconstruction controls, and a learned-decoder comparison (Tables 2 and 8–11), supported by clearer procedures and implementation details. These address important gaps in v1 concerning generalization and approximation errors. Claims that errors are negligible remain stronger than the controls establish, and some baseline mathematical detail is removed, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ConDA work and retain matching methods, datasets, and benchmark results. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds forecasting, inversion-solver, decoder, and neural-activity evaluations, including Tables 2 and 8–11 and the expanded Figure 5.

before.justification: v1 reports original generation, prediction, classification, and representation-analysis results across five domains, including the experiments in Tables 1–2, Figures 3–5, and Appendix C.

results.title: Contrastive Diffusion Alignment: Learning Structured Latents for Controllable Generation

C1.justification: The central theoretical contribution narrows from general SQ-dimension SGD hardness to finite-precision coordinate SGD on planted parity. Main empirical comparisons also expand to classical learners.

It adds interpretations of shifted-primality performance and tabular applicability. Fine-tuned models also enter the length-generalization and data-scaling comparisons in Figures 3–4, which previously compared the proposed method with training from scratch.

The selection-text revision does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method narrative and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. Related Work becomes a standalone section, experiments gain Setup/Methods Compared/Main Results subsections, and the appendices are reorganized into baseline details, condensed analyses and a separate finite-precision theory appendix. Title, terminology and author-list edits accompany this restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 substantially redesigns the presentation: expanded comparison matrices replace many plots and detailed tables, hyperparameter sweeps become a maxima table, reasoning traces are redrawn and consolidated, and the workflow diagram changes. Length/scaling figures gain comparator curves, and tabular results receive a new table. Replacing infinity-percent notation with 100-dagger preserves its stated meaning.

T1.justification: v1's general SQ-dimension bound T = Omega(d epsilon^2/B^(3/2)) is replaced by a planted-k-parity bound TB = Omega(sqrt(binomial(n,k))/2^b) under explicit b-bit coordinate-gradient access. v2 also adds a quantization-stability lemma, revised statistical-dimension derivations, and a proposal-mass-dependent validation generalization theorem with proof. The program-enumeration bound is retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central argument: v1 offered ERM-style assurances without a method-specific bound and compared mainly with neural learners; v2 adds a conditional proposal/validation theorem, explicit finite-precision restrictions on SGD hardness, and direct classical/TabPFN comparisons. Broader empirical evaluation and PBE positioning improve support and clarify novelty. Conflicting pattern labels, test-based tuning and unexplained ± values remain material weaknesses, but the theoretical and comparative gains outweigh them.

A1.justification: Despite changes to the title, authors and method name, both PDFs describe the same program-learning work. All 32 pages of v1 and 31 pages of v2, including figures, tables and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A retain original experiments and report additional algorithmic-task, baseline and tabular-benchmark results.

results.title: LLM Priors for ERM over Programs

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same central claims about computationally accessible program search, sample-efficient rule recovery, length generalization, and auditability. They emphasize dependence on capable proposers and active testing, discuss training/inference cost tradeoffs, and identify longer, more compositional, or prior-misaligned programs as potential failure conditions.

D1.justification: v3 adds five explicit prompt templates, model/tool configuration information, and runtime measurement details. However, it removes v2's code-availability sentence and repository hyperlink. Detailed settings for the newly added agents remain incompletely documented.

Tables 7–8 add prompt accuracies and runtime measurements; these are new results, not same-setting improvements over v2.

P1.justification: The abstract is condensed, the closing discussion is expanded into a numbered Section 6, and an Impact Statement and additional analysis subsections are inserted. Most existing prose and the overall section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from one column to two, substantially relocating and resizing figures and tables. after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and adds model/tool comparisons, prompt-sensitivity results, and runtime measurements.

before.justification: v2 reports original algorithmic and tabular classification experiments, length-generalization tests, data-scaling experiments, and hyperparameter analyses.

results.title: LLM Priors for ERM over Programs

These materially extend v1's collapse interpretations.

It prompts for specified structural complexity, avoids previous hypotheses and allocates queries proportionally to the ground-truth complexity distribution. P1.justification: V2 rewrites the title, abstract, introductory framing and conclusion, and substantially reorganizes existing material. P2.justification: The document switches from single-column to two-column layout, and v1's combined benchmark table becomes three larger task tables. V2 adds a biological-data figure and four substantive tables; the cost table loses a column whose values remain in prose.

results.title: HypoSpace: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Set-Valued Hypothesis Generation under Underdetermination and Sublinear Coverage Bounds

C1.justification: v4 removes the demonstrated beyond-medicine generality contribution and narrows performance claims to comparable-size open-source models or evaluated baselines. Its introduction instead foregrounds a contribution about learning case-conditioned clinical criteria rather than evaluator preferences or reusable templates. The central 7.0-to-27.5 medical performance claim remains.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive explanations of judge quality, rubric specificity, safety–verbosity trade-offs, filtering/SFT failure mechanisms and clinical oversight requirements. Appendix H.2 qualifies generalization as unseen prompts within a shared rubric framework, tempering v2's strong t-SNE-based contamination assurances. Appendix F.7 explicitly acknowledges inconclusive superiority over distilled SFT.

D1.justification: v4 supplies retrieval model identities and retrieval counts, detailed RL/SFT hyperparameters, software and server configurations, preprocessing limits and evaluation timing (Appendices A.3 and F). These largely document retained experiments. It also replaces the abstract's repository link with a project-page link and refers to released per-case scores and a harness; their availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

E1.justification: v4 removes v2 Section 4.5's InfoBench-Hard evaluation and associated WildChat training samples, eliminating the demonstrated non-medical instruction-following domain. The medical dialogue sources and HealthBench coverage remain; the expanded DoctorAgent-RL/MTMedDialog description clarifies retained data provenance.

E2.justification: v4 adds standalone Baichuan-M2-distilled SFT comparisons, no-retrieval and synthetic-seed alternatives, and training-judge variants (Tables 6, 9 and 16). It removes GPT-OSS-120B (high) as a Table 1 contestant and DeepSeek-R1/V3 judges from the calibration comparison formerly in v2 Table 3. The original rubric-generator comparator set is retained.

E3.justification: New designs include fixed-response judging on 200 training-pool cases, blinded physician review of 60 cases, matched 200-case HealthBench comparisons, and seed/judge experiments with specified 140/200-step budgets. Existing HealthBench decoding settings remain unchanged (v2 Table 6; v4 Table 15). Newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish that those experiments changed or were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained filtering, scaling, generator and SFT ablations, v4 adds training-judge sensitivity, physician validation, seed-source controls, within/across-case rubric redundancy, prompt-level contamination diagnostics, reward/entropy trajectories and stringent-filter failure analysis. Appendix G adds three scored clinical cases while retaining the original consultation example.

E5.justification: v2 provides point estimates and identifies single-seed scaling runs. v4 adds bootstrap confidence intervals for judge agreement, 1,000-resample paired confidence intervals and one-sided tests on 200 benchmark cases, and three grading trials reporting mean 27.4 and standard deviation 0.42. These additions concern evaluation uncertainty; single-seed scaling experiments remain explicitly identified.

E6.justification: The headline ORBIT scores of 27.5, 33.6 and 37.3 remain unchanged. v4 adds substantial findings, including 90.7% physician-rated rubric meaningfulness, seed-source scores of 17.89 versus 10.69, and a matched-subset ORBIT–base difference of 11.05. It removes InfoBench's 42.0-to-82.9 result and numerous nonduplicated theme/axis entries when compressing appendix tables.

M1.justification: The default retrieval, rubric rewards, GRPO, filtering and staged-restart procedure remains substantially unchanged. Appendix C.2 adds an optional synthetic seed-construction approach using multiple LLM generators, summarization and contrastive filtering. This is a limited procedural extension; the newly supplied pseudocode mainly documents the existing pipeline.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and extensive explanatory passages are rewritten, with the narrative refocused on medical validation. Limitations are integrated into the conclusion, and Appendix F is reorganized into dedicated data, baseline, training, stability, evaluation, statistics and ablation subsections. Separate failure-mode and extended-related-work sections further restructure the document.

P2.justification: v4 adds a motivation illustration, evaluator/physician panels, rubric-diversity and cost plots, training traces, heatmaps and contamination diagnostics. Several wide appendix result matrices become compact summary tables, alongside new configuration, statistical and case-study tables. Existing pipeline, radar, rollout-distribution and t-SNE figures are retained with relocation, caption editing or resizing.

R1.justification: New Appendix J substantially expands positioning against process rewards, rubric/checklist alignment and medical models, emphasizing final-response supervision, retrieved case specificity and multi-turn medical alignment. Citations also change, including adding RewardBench and Sharma et al.'s human–AI collaboration work and removing InfoBench. DoctorAgent-RL's updated title represents the same cited work.

T1.justification: Appendix H.2 introduces mathematical definitions for prompt/rubric nearest-neighbor similarities, thresholded and joint contamination rates, and within-set redundancy (Equations 6–10). These are limited analytical additions. The core optimization mathematics is substantially retained, and neither version supplies theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 offered sparse training/retrieval specifications and limited evidence for evaluator reliability and contamination control. v4 substantially improves auditability through detailed configurations, physician reference judgments, controlled seed/judge experiments, uncertainty estimates and prompt-level contamination diagnostics. Its explicit acknowledgment that the ORBIT–SFT confidence interval includes zero improves interpretive discipline. Removing InfoBench and detailed appendix breakdowns reduces breadth, but the gains address central reproducibility and validation weaknesses of the retained medical contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ORBIT framework and retain matched core experiments. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains original HealthBench experiments and adds judge comparisons, physician annotations, seed-source experiments and statistical analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original ORBIT training results on HealthBench and InfoBench, component ablations, distributional analyses and a consultation case study.

results.title: InfiMed-ORBIT: Aligning LLMs on Open-Ended Complex Tasks via Rubric-Based Incremental Training

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction now explicitly claim an automated LLM annotation capability. The main claims concerning compositional primitive geometry, cross-task transfer, and reasoning finetuning, along with the five-item contribution list, otherwise retain their scope.

C2.justification: v2 substantially extends mechanistic interpretation: Appendix F argues against simple token boosting, links interference to sequential algorithmic motifs, and qualifies the reconstruction argument with the comparison-vector exception. Appendices A.7 and G add interpretations connecting expressivity and layer choice to meaningful primitives. The main Discussion's task-coverage and linear-composition limitations remain largely unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 documents AIE calibration tasks, attention-head projection and averaging, and normalization choices in Appendix B.6; GPT-4o prompts and token-context sampling in Appendix C; and hardware and timing in B.7. It reports 5–10 minutes on four A40 GPUs for activation collection and 61 seconds for an example clustering run. The HTML inspection tool is promised for a project website, without establishing release.

E1.justification: TSP, 3-SAT, AIME, GraphNav, and the auxiliary graph-operation tasks are retained. New controls and sensitivity experiments reuse this coverage. The six AIE calibration tasks are newly specified in Appendix B.6, without establishing a change in the tasks previously used.

E2.justification: Appendices F.1 and F.3 add two substantive comparators absent from v1: injection immediately before unembedding as a bag-of-tokens control, and vectors reconstructed from their top-100 decoded tokens. These directly compare alternative explanations with the original primitive vectors; existing unsteered, few-shot, zero-shot, and shuffled-context comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include final-stream injection controls, per-primitive fixed-setting interference evaluation, annotation prompt comparisons, and sweeps over clustering layers, cluster counts, and response counts. Extraction is now reported using 200 responses, versus v1's stated 100. The missing-distance-computation score changes from 500 to 512. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices C.2, F.1–F.3, and G add tests of annotation robustness, lexical explanations of steering, interference between primitives, and sensitivity to clustering hyperparameters and sample size. These substantially extend validation beyond v1's existing injection-layer/magnitude experiments and nearest-neighbor strategy analyses, which are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies seed counts or repeated-run uncertainty procedures, and existing variability displays are retained. v2 adds correlation and clustering-agreement scores as robustness metrics, without introducing confidence intervals, significance tests, or new uncertainty-estimation practices.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 is numerically unchanged as v2 Table 2. Substantial new results appear in the annotation, control, interference, and robustness analyses. For example, Appendix F.3 reports +2458.5% comparison mentions for the reconstructed vector versus +1103.7% for the original, an acknowledged exception. Appendix G reports correlation above 0.98 between K=50 and K=100 dissimilarity matrices. These are added results, not demonstrated performance gains between versions.

M1.justification: v2 adds GPT-4o cluster annotation, algorithmic-versus-linguistic grouping, and expressivity-based ranking to the manually interpreted pipeline in v1 (Section 4.2; Appendices A.7 and C). This substantially extends primitive identification, while retaining the core clustering, vector extraction, and steering procedures.

P1.justification: The main six-section narrative remains, with localized tightening of methods/results prose, terminology standardization, and repaired appendix references. Existing appendices are reordered, an Impact Statement is added, and the short LLM Usage Disclosure is removed. Much of the increased length documents new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: Figure 1 gains an annotation stage; existing main figures are rearranged and receive clearer axes and labels. v2 adds a definitions table, extensive annotation and control tables, and robustness Figures 11–13. Retained appendix figures are relocated and resized. One new presentation defect remains: Figure 11's caption describes a panel c that is not displayed.

R1.justification: v2 adds Hawasly et al., Petukhova et al., and Kopf et al. to motivate latent-space clustering, Han et al. for elbow selection, and Gallegos et al. for the Impact Statement. The broader positioning relative to interpretability and function-vector research remains stable.

T1.justification: v2 introduces a formal expressivity definition and complexity analysis, and corrects the normalization of the mean g from 1/n to 1/m in Section 4.2. Core steering and transfer mathematics remain. The new expressivity definition is internally inconsistent: Equation (5) uses radius divided by unique-token count, whereas the prose specifies the reciprocal.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central mechanistic evidence by testing lexical alternatives, examining interference under fixed settings, and checking clustering robustness—important gaps in v1's validation. Detailed extraction and annotation instructions also improve reproducibility, while the reconstruction exception appropriately qualifies the interpretation. The contradictory expressivity formula and missing Figure 11 panel weaken particular additions, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in testing and documenting the core framework.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework, models, and principal experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across reorganization and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds automated annotation results, intervention controls, interference analyses, and clustering robustness experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original activation analyses, primitive-vector interventions, composition and transfer experiments, and nearest-neighbor strategy analyses, including in its appendices.

results.title: AlgoTrace: Algorithmic Primitives and Compositional Geometry of Reasoning in Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add claims about open-ended captioning benefits, and the abstract expands the identified design factors to include data volume and model choice. The central claims about verifiable SSL rewards, reasoning improvements, and cross-domain applicability remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of data scaling, architectural generality, corruption resilience, and proximity to oracle-reward performance. Appendix J supplements the diminishing-returns discussion with harder-task evidence, while Appendix K attributes entropy and response-length behavior to KL regularization and perception-focused tasks. The earlier task-alignment and negative-transfer qualifications remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds code and model-hosting identifiers, DINOv2-based negative construction details, and parameters for new evaluations. Original GRPO and hardware disclosures remain largely unchanged. The abstract announces released resources, but the reproducibility statement still promises code release upon acceptance, leaving release status internally inconsistent.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluations on V*, RealWorldQA, BLINK, MME-RealWorld-Lite, and CapArena image captioning, plus corrupted-image MMBench scenarios. These substantially broaden visual conditions and task requirements beyond the retained visual and graph benchmarks.

E2.justification: Appendix G introduces a VLM-R1-style Golden-3B baseline trained with downstream answer rewards and compared against SSL4RL on MMBench and SEED-Bench. CapArena additionally uses GPT-4o, CogVLM-19B, and MiniCPM-8B captions as comparators. v1 primarily compared SSL4RL variants with their base models.

E3.justification: Added studies introduce a 60/40 training/test split for the Golden-3B comparison, Gemma3-4B training with batch size 256, approximately 4,000/18,000/118,000-sample training regimes, and weak/strong corruption protocols. Captioning introduces GPT-4o judging, pairwise scores, and min-max normalization. These are additional protocols; the original Qwen GRPO settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained difficulty, model-size, combination, attention, and reward-curve analyses, v2 adds data-volume scaling, base-model choice, corruption robustness, harder-task experiments, and captioning case studies. It also extends documented difficulty analyses to ImageNet and adds entropy and response-length training diagnostics.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed studies, confidence intervals, or formal significance tests. The new entropy plots describe model behavior during training rather than uncertainty in experimental estimates.

E6.justification: Corresponding MMBench tables revise Jigsaw averages from 79.11 to 77.82 for 3B and from 86.27 to 87.73 for 7B. The 3B 3x3 Jigsaw result changes from 80.38 to 75.12, reversing its tabulated difficulty trend. Numerous new evaluation and ablation results are added, although Figures 4 and 5 retain outdated Jigsaw values.

M1.justification: Appendix J adds two exploratory SSL tasks: identifying a masked patch and selecting a positive view among DINOv2-mined hard negatives. These extend the available reward tasks while retaining the original four visual tasks, graph tasks, and GRPO framework.

P1.justification: Much of the introduction, framework, conclusion, and retained appendix prose remains unchanged. v2 reorders ImageNet evaluation and ablations, moves benchmark and graph details into appendices, and revises headings and transitions around the expanded experiments. This is localized restructuring rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial table and figure displays for captioning, oracle comparisons, robustness, scaling, Gemma, harder tasks, and training diagnostics. It splits the graph-results table and relocates SEED-Bench results. Figure 3 is reduced to one attention example; the other example remains available in the appendix.

R1.justification: Section 2 newly credits Jigsaw-R1 as a direct predecessor and positions SSL4RL as generalizing that approach across tasks and domains. Appendix J also acknowledges concurrent Spatial-SSRL. This materially refines novelty positioning beyond v1's discussion of general SSL and self-reward literature, alongside additional method and benchmark citations.

T1.justification: Section 3 retains the corruption-based formulation, reward definitions, and regularized GRPO objective in Equation 1. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs, and the added task descriptions and empirical interpretations introduce no substantive mathematical development.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for generality: the Golden-3B comparison addresses v1's lack of a trained RL comparator, while Gemma, corruption, and harder-task studies test previously unexamined boundaries. Explicitly acknowledging Jigsaw-R1 also improves novelty attribution. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, particularly stale Jigsaw plots and insufficiently explained CapArena score aggregation, although those issues still limit confidence in parts of the expanded evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SSL4RL, with matching authors, framework, and substantial shared experimental content. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds captioning, further visual benchmarks, supervised-RL comparisons, robustness tests, and additional ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on MMBench, SEED-Bench, ImageNet, and graph benchmarks, alongside task-difficulty, model-size, and reward-combination experiments.

results.title: SSL4RL: Revisiting Self-supervised Learning as Intrinsic Reward for Visual-Language Reasoning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about jointly capturing utility and diversity, avoiding external resources, and improving accuracy and training efficiency. The additional evidence does not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: Section 3.1 adopts correlation wording, and Appendix E newly acknowledges difficulty rigorously proving the nuclear norm's relationship with loss reduction or effective rank. Appendix B.2 adds projection-specific explanations, while B.7 qualifies the offline comparison because throughput is not directly comparable.

D1.justification: Section 4.1 newly specifies default buffer size M=1024 and projection dimensions d1=128, d2=8. Appendix B adds limited implementation and comparison details, including K-means class prototypes and FisherSFT's matched training conditions. The original hyperparameter tables and code-access information are retained.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained benchmarks, v2 adds MATH training and evaluation for longer mathematical reasoning, plus evaluations on MATH500 and AMC23 after GSM8K training (Appendices B.4–B.5). These introduce substantial coverage of longer reasoning and explicit distribution-shift scenarios.

E2.justification: Appendix B.7 adds FisherSFT as an evaluated offline comparator across the four original benchmarks, using matched selection fractions. The original Regular, Random, MaxLoss, MaxGrad, RHO-Loss, and GREATS comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds evaluations with batch size 16, full-parameter fine-tuning, Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, 2048-token MATH sequences, and cross-dataset testing. These supplement the retained main protocols. B.4's blanket statement that previous sequence lengths were 512 conflicts with ScienceQA's retained 256-token setting in Table 18.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the original component ablations and parameter sweeps. Tables 7–9 test buffer policies, distance aggregation, and projection constructions; Figures 3 and 9 add norm/rank and Frobenius-norm/utility diagnostics. Further experiments examine robustness across training regimes, longer reasoning, and distribution shifts.

E5.justification: Both versions state four repetitions with different random seeds and report ± values. The additional correlation plots retain the existing Spearman-correlation and p-value reporting approach; no new uncertainty-estimation procedure or increase in repetitions is stated.

E6.justification: Tables 3–4 retain their original values, but Tables 7–15 add substantial results. For example, Table 13 reports MATH accuracy of 46.27% for UDS versus 45.66% for GREATS; Table 14 reports MATH500 accuracy of 42.56% versus 42.27%. Figure 2's correlation trace also changes while retaining its positive trend. Added configurations do not establish same-setting gains over v1.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains nuclear-norm scoring, bilinear SRFT projection, FIFO memory, average-distance scoring, and top-K selection. Appendix B.2 evaluates alternative components as ablations without changing the proposed default procedure.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section ordering are retained. Changes comprise localized heading and notation edits, brief setup and related-work expansions, and new Appendix B.2–B.7 subsections, without extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual evidence with two additional correlation plots and nine new experimental tables. Figure 2 is placed alongside the new Figure 3, and existing tables and figures are redistributed. The original schematic, diversity illustration, selection-budget plot, and sensitivity plots are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of offline selection methods from Sachdeva et al., Axiotis et al., and Deb et al., plus references supporting the added mathematical benchmarks. The overall online-versus-offline positioning remains stable. FlyLoRA's venue update refers to the same cited work.

T1.justification: Lemma 3.1, Theorem 3.2, and the mathematical derivations in Appendix C remain unchanged apart from equivalent notation. The added projection discussion and empirical correlations do not introduce new formal derivations or proofs.
