improvement.justification: v2 addresses substantial validation gaps in v1 by testing specific design alternatives, full fine-tuning, longer reasoning, distribution shifts, and an offline comparator. These experiments strengthen evidence for UDS's design and applicability; explicit defaults and the added theoretical limitation improve assessability. New experiment settings remain briefly documented and include a sequence-length inconsistency, but the added controlled and robustness evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UDS research and contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–F. Retained material can be matched despite additions, relocation, and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds design ablations, alternative training configurations, mathematical-reasoning and distribution-shift evaluations, and an offline-method comparison.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix B report original fine-tuning accuracy, Pass@1, throughput, component ablations, and parameter-sensitivity results.

results.title: Utility-Diversity Aware Online Batch Selection for LLM Supervised Fine-tuning

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: evaluating continual learning from simulated user feedback across diverse tasks and finding existing memory systems insufficiently effective and efficient. The additional experiments support these retained claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: v3 newly interprets human ratings as feedback indistinguishability, noise sensitivity in terms of data quality versus coverage, and backbone controls as evidence that system design drives performance differences. It adds explanations involving irrelevant retrieved memories and a qualification about dataset imbalance in MemoryBench-Full. These substantially extend the interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v3 adds access information for MemoryBench-Full and Mistral-generated feedback, revises code/data pointers, explicitly states that Mem0g was not used, and clarifies that timing includes indexing and retrieval. Hardware, generation parameters, retrieval limits, and LoRA training settings were already documented in v1.

E1.justification: The eleven source datasets, three domains, two languages, and four task formats remain. Coverage expands to human assessment of feedback and Legal-domain scenarios with altered user selectivity and noisy satisfaction signals. JRE-L/SciTechNews denotes retained coverage; MemoryBench-Full is introduced but explicitly not evaluated.

E2.justification: The eight LLMsys comparators and the action-feedback SFT baseline are retained. The new human study in A.2.5 adds professionally written human feedback as a comparator for simulated feedback. Adding MemBench to Table 1 is research positioning, not an evaluated system baseline.

E3.justification: A.1 changes the stated evaluation judge outside WritingBench from GPT-4o-mini to DeepSeek-V3. The reported LiSo Locomo sample count changes from 25 to 250 in v1 Table 6 versus v3 Table 9, without establishing an actual rerun. New protocols include a 200-task human comparison, two noise sweeps, and Mistral system/simulator controls on the Legal domain.

E4.justification: v1 already contains feedback ablations, learning trajectories, and timing analyses, which v3 largely retains. v3 substantially extends validation through human feedback assessment, selectivity and Gaussian-noise robustness tests, system/simulator backbone comparisons, and a Legal-domain case study examining retrieved memories and erroneous responses.

E5.justification: v3 Tables 13–14 introduce systematic mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting for the detailed off-policy results, whereas v1 reports point estimates. These deviations are across test examples. Table 7 additionally reports Fleiss' kappa for human judgments; neither addition establishes repeated experimental runs or run-based confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Aggregate and raw Qwen3-8B/32B results are extensively revised. For example, Open-domain Vanilla/BM25-M normalized scores change from 0.5259/0.5990 in v1 Table 7 to 0.6523/0.5720 in v3 Table 10. Changed evaluation settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting gains. Human win rates, noise responses, backbone comparisons, and case-study outcomes are also newly reported.

M1.justification: The Task Provider, User Simulator, and Performance Monitor framework, feedback prompts, and action-probability rules are retained. Expanded baseline descriptions, alternative backbones, and robustness experiments do not establish a change to the proposed default procedure.

P1.justification: Most prose, section ordering, and prompt templates remain. v3 expands explanations of memory categories, baseline architectures, evaluation scope, and timing; adds appendix subsections for new analyses; standardizes JRE-L/SciTechNews naming; and edits author/header information.

P2.justification: v3 adds a memory-taxonomy illustration, dataset classification and human-assessment tables, two tables displaying standard deviations, three noise-analysis figures, and backbone-comparison and case-study tables. Existing displays are redistributed, and framework labels and the benchmark-comparison table are revised. This substantially expands the visual presentation beyond renumbering or numerical updates.

R1.justification: v3 adds MemBench by Tan et al. (2025) to the benchmark comparison and cites LLM-Evolve by You et al. (2024), distinguishing task-local conversational feedback from persistent feedback logs. These are limited additions to otherwise retained research positioning.

T1.justification: The continual-learning formulation in Section 2.1 and the logistic, binary, and copy-action probability rules in A.2.3 are unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced; Gaussian perturbations specify an experimental condition.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the benchmark's central simulated-feedback component. Compared with v1's automated feedback-effect checks, A.2.5 adds direct human quality comparisons, while A.3.9–A.3.10 test feedback noise and backbone dependence; Tables 13–14 also expose variation across test examples. Low rater agreement and Legal-only robustness controls limit the strongest claims about human indistinguishability and backbone independence, but the complementary validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MemoryBench study. The main text and complete appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, datasets, equations, tables, and figures can be matched despite additions and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains original system evaluations and additionally reports human feedback assessments, noise experiments, alternative-backbone comparisons, and a retrieval case study.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, feedback comparisons, on-policy and stepwise experiments, and measurements of memory and inference time.

results.title: MemoryBench: A Benchmark for Memory and Continual Learning in LLM Systems

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution statement replace 'the first inference-time defense framework' with 'an effective inference-time defense framework.' The central methodological contribution and claims about reducing harmful responses while preserving utility remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations of the architectural modality gap, nonlinear decomposition failure, data-limited RRS performance, attack transfer, judge bias, and sample-level selectivity. B.11 additionally interprets reported ASR as an upper bound and safety gains as underestimated, although its confusion matrix does not establish strictly one-sided errors or those general conclusions.

D1.justification: v2 announces code and constructed-dataset release and supplies an access location absent from v1. It also adds architecture details, an explicit formula for the existing projection ablation, clarification of shared calibration data, defense runtimes, and attack construction parameters. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to the original method.

E1.justification: The original audio benchmarks and text-only evaluation are retained. Appendices B.7 and B.12 add Jailbreak-AudioBench accent, volume-emphasis, and laugh-emotion conditions, explicit PGD/Gaussian perturbations, and spoken PAIR/GCG attacks involving semantic rephrasing and adversarial suffixes. These substantially broaden evaluated input conditions.

E2.justification: v2 expands comparison beyond the original adapted prompt and steering defenses by evaluating the audio-specific fine-tuning defense RRS in Table 11. Table 10 also adds SVD and kernel-PCA alternatives against PCA. The original AdaShield, FSD, MDSteer-h2s, and MDSteer-c2r comparators remain.

E3.justification: The original main-table settings remain, including 100 calibration pairs, alpha=0.1, and k=10. New protocols evaluate four additional LALMs, train RRS with 100 samples, conduct a blinded stratified human study of 500 responses, and test 50 samples per PAIR/GCG attack. CKA and per-sample alignment measurements are also introduced.

E4.justification: Beyond retained component, prompt, and hyperparameter ablations, v2 adds decomposition alternatives, speech and attack robustness tests, quantitative representation comparisons, human-judge error analysis, and individual-sample selectivity analysis (B.5 and B.7–B.13). These investigate substantial additional questions about mechanism and reliability.

E5.justification: v1 does not report repeated-run counts or uncertainty estimates. v2 identifies default seed 42 and adds a five-seed study with individual results, means, and variances. It also reports human–judge agreement and Cohen's kappa, plus standard deviations, Welch's t-test, and Cohen's d for sample-level alignment.

E6.justification: Tables 1–9 and the existing plotted results are retained, while Tables 10–18 add substantial new outcomes. For example, Table 13 reports MiDashengLM Figstep ASR of 12.80% versus 0.00% and BRR of 57.20% versus 53.20%, comparing No Defense with SARSteer. Table 17 adds Kimi-Audio PAIR ASR of 58.0% versus 10.0%.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain text-derived refusal steering, PCA removal of the safe subspace, and layerwise inference-time activation updates. The new ablation formula and architecture description provide documentation; the alternative decompositions are experiments rather than replacements for SARSteer.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained, with localized editing and expanded explanations. The contents list becomes a descriptive appendix guide, Section 5.5 supplies an appendix pointer, and an Impact Statements paragraph is added. The additional scientific sections do not constitute wholesale rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 converts the main text and references to a two-column ICML layout and substantially rearranges and resizes figures and tables. Figure 3 gains an explicit PCA block and expanded caption, and Tables 10–18 are added. The new layout also retains a repeated template heading, 'Submission and Formatting Instructions for ICML 2026.'

R1.justification: v2 acknowledges RRS and ALMGuard as existing audio-safety approaches and narrows its novelty positioning. It adds references supporting the new attacks, models, and PCA discussion, and removes the Qwen-audio 2023 citation. The broader related-work organization and LLM/LVLM positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4's local-linearization derivation is unchanged. New Appendix B.13 mathematically defines a per-sample activation-alignment proxy and argues that it indicates the refusal-logit effect. This is a limited addition to the mathematical reasoning, although the connection to the gradient-dependent logit change is not established.

improvement.justification: Five-seed results and a blinded human check of the safety judge address important stability and evaluation-reliability gaps in v1. Additional models and attack conditions substantially strengthen evidence about generalization, while release information improves reproducibility. New interpretations remain problematic: B.11 does not establish ASR upper bounds, and B.13 does not validate activation alignment as a logit-effect proxy. These weaknesses limit the added claims, but the stronger empirical validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SARSteer research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and expanded supplementary material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds experiments on additional models, speech variations, attacks, statistical stability, and human evaluation of the safety judge.

before.justification: v1 reports original safety and utility evaluations, component and hyperparameter ablations, and experiments on base and text-only models.

results.title: SARSteer: Safeguarding Large Audio Language Models via Safe-Ablated Refusal Steering

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central contribution and reliability claims. The conclusion now qualifies them with classification undercoverage and slow convergence, explicitly presenting TabMGP as a procedure that requires diagnostic checks.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantial applicability guidance concerning non-stabilizing finite rollouts, low-diversity datasets and ill-conditioned loss problems, and residual instability in skin and wine. It also removes v2's inference that skewed or multimodal densities demonstrate greater expressiveness. These changes materially qualify the interpretation of empirical reliability.

D1.justification: The code-release instructions change from anonymous hosting to a named GitHub repository. Appendix G documents the MLP architectures, activations, and binary-response threshold used for the new data generators. Existing TabPFN checkpoints, temperature, ensembles, hardware, and reported timings remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix G adds Concrete and Phoneme semi-synthetic scenarios combining real covariates with fitted nonlinear MLP response mechanisms. This extends the represented data-generating conditions within the existing regression and classification tasks; the original 30 setups remain.

E2.justification: New Tables 6–7 substantially broaden the comparisons with Bayes under a diffuse N(0, 10²) prior and a TabPFN-initialized copula method adapted from Nagler and Rügamer. The original Hessian-prior Bayes and standard Copula are retained. Neither copula variant is evaluated on the multinomial setups.

E3.justification: The original experimental settings remain unchanged. Supplementary protocols add empirical-covariate resampling with MLP-generated responses, longer convergence runs, and sensitivity tests varying T=N−n from 100 to 1000 while holding observed sample size fixed. These additions do not establish reruns of the retained main tables.

E4.justification: Appendices F and I substantially expand convergence validation: Figure 7 extends slow-converging rollouts, Figure 8 tests sensitivity to the observed dataset, and Figure 9 measures coverage and credible-set size across rollout lengths. These analyses expose unstable trajectories and residual sensitivity beyond v2's single-dataset diagnostics.

E5.justification: Figure 8 newly reports convergence diagnostics over 20 independent observed datasets per setup, extending the single observed realization used in the retained diagnostics. The main coverage experiments still use 100 repetitions; confidence intervals and significance tests are not newly introduced.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 and the original marginal-result tables retain their numerical results. Substantial new results appear in Tables 5–7 and Figures 7–9: semi-synthetic TabMGP coverage is 0.86 for Concrete and 0.98 for Phoneme, alternative baselines receive extensive result entries, and longer/repeated rollouts reveal both stabilization and failure cases.

M1.justification: Both versions use Bayesian-bootstrap covariates, sequential TabPFN response sampling, and loss minimization over completed rollouts. v3 corrects Algorithm 1's conditioning indices and explicitly initializes each rollout, matching the growing-context procedure already described in v2's Figure 1 and text.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and narrative are retained, with sentence-level editing and clearer explanations of baselines and rollout length. New appendices are inserted before the retained density and marginal-coverage material, the appendix contents list is removed, and author and conference text is reformatted.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from one-column to two-column layout, relocating Figure 1 and compressing the main tables. Figure 6 is reorganized into regression and classification panels. Three new tables and three new figures are added, while existing density and marginal-coverage displays are retained and relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: Section 4 sharpens the distinction between Nagler and Rügamer's conditional inference and TabMGP's unconditional loss-defined functionals, and adds criticism of copula bandwidth tuning. The cited-work inventory is retained; updated Fong–Yiu and Cui–Walker references correspond to existing works.

T1.justification: The posterior definitions, martingale and a.c.i.d. conditions, Bayesian-recovery argument, predictive-training derivation, and credible-set formulas are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical correction is supplied; the added convergence discussion is interpretive.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens scrutiny of the paper's central reliability claim. Longer and repeated-dataset diagnostics address v2's limited convergence checks, while alternative-prior and TabPFN-initialized copula comparisons address important baseline gaps. Reporting the resulting failures and applicability limits improves interpretation rather than merely adding favorable evidence. Finite-horizon diagnostics still do not establish a convergence guarantee.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TabMGP research. All 36 pages of each version, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support comparison. Retained material can be matched across reformatting and appendix renumbering.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds semi-synthetic evaluations, alternative-baseline results, and further convergence and sensitivity experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original coverage experiments across 11 synthetic and 19 real-data setups, alongside convergence diagnostics, posterior-density plots, and marginal-interval results.

results.title: TabMGP: Martingale Posterior with TabPFN

C1.justification: V1's Ant-centered claim of 73% improvement expands into claims of outperforming prior methods across five tasks, 18–35% gains over compute-matched zero-shot generation and reward transfer to four default morphologies. Judge-driven Pareto coverage becomes an explicit contribution. The central novelty claim about multi-agent robot co-design is retained.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations involving transferable reward shaping, super-additive co-design interactions, morphology-dominated Swimmer gains and targeted responses to judge feedback. It qualifies judges' usefulness when stability metrics are uninformative and expands limitations to simulator artifacts, sim-to-real transfer and scaling costs. These substantially extend v1's brief discussion of constrained edits, computation and prompt sensitivity.

D1.justification: Appendices A–F add Ant design prompts, shared control/judge prompts, reward interfaces and expressions, XML parameterization, task-specific RL hyperparameters, baseline implementation details and hardware/time/token/cost accounting. V1 provides only broad implementation descriptions. V2 also promises code and configuration release upon publication; the PDFs do not establish an actual release.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only Ant. V2 retains Ant and adds HalfCheetah, Hopper, Swimmer and Walker2D, substantially broadening the locomotion dynamics and morphologies tested. Both versions use Brax; the MuJoCo terminology does not establish a simulator replacement.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's original-Ant and thesis/synthesis comparisons, v2 evaluates Eureka, RoboMoRe and Bayesian optimization against D2C. Eureka and RoboMoRe were previously cited but not experimentally compared. V2 also adds zero-shot, single-agent and single/no-judge comparison conditions.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a search-then-retraining evaluation design, increases trained candidates from up to eight to sixteen per round and switches the reported backbone from GPT-5 to GPT-5.2. It describes S as cumulative 2D distance from the origin, replacing v1's forward-distance description, and adds normalized reporting and new ablation protocols. These differences prevent direct same-setting score comparisons.

E4.justification: V1 mainly examines thesis/synthesis performance over rounds. V2 adds morphology/reward cross-over experiments, controlled debate and judge ablations, Pareto coverage, reward-code similarity, critique-action associations, a debate transcript, evaluation-metric validation and LLM-backbone sensitivity (Sections 3.2–3.4 and Appendices D, G–I).

E5.justification: V1 reports 95% confidence intervals across reward candidates. V2 reports independent search-seed and final-policy variation, mean±standard deviation and per-seed scores, alongside Welch tests, Hedges' g, FDR correction and association tests. V1 does not disclose a comparable independent-seed count, so this is not evidence of a simple increase in identical repeated runs.

E6.justification: V1 Table I reports Ant scores of 3715.42 for the original robot and 6421.67 for D2C. V2 Table 1 reports 14886±459 and 47084±1469 under its revised setup, not a directly comparable performance gain. Numerous results are added, including reward transfer improving four tasks and the Swimmer exception: D2C morphology with Default reward scores 9379, above full D2C's 8639.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes substantially: v1 generates rewards before synthesis and trains both thesis and synthesis designs; v2 critiques untrained theses, generates rewards after synthesis and trains four synthesized morphologies per round. V2 also restricts pluralistic judging to the round winner instead of each evaluated candidate.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, agent responsibilities are reorganized and explained more explicitly, and the experiments become separate setup, main-results, dynamics and ablation subsections. Limitations and conclusion are separated, and a structured appendix with a contents page is introduced. The title and document style also change.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview, replaces the original Ant performance display with broader benchmark and multi-panel trajectory plots, and separates morphology illustrations into a cross-method/task grid. New heatmaps, hypervolume plots, statistical tables and transcript illustrations substantially change the visual presentation, alongside a redesigned main-text layout and single-column appendices.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning through quality-diversity research, specification gaming, self-debugging and optimization references. Section 4 and Appendix J articulate distinctions from RoboMoRe, MAP-Elites and other design/reward systems more explicitly than v1, including a new comparison matrix. This exceeds bibliographic or citation-style editing.

T1.justification: The co-design optimization in Equations (1)–(2) is substantively retained. V2 adds limited mathematical definitions: the cumulative distance-from-origin score and the difference-in-differences interaction term used to characterize co-design synergy. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 directly addresses v1's weak support for advantages over single-agent pipelines through controlled component comparisons, evaluated prior methods and independent training repeats. Its prompts and technical appendices substantially improve reproducibility. Important reporting problems remain: Figure 3 does not consistently support the stated 18–35% gaps, Appendix H's run accounting conflicts with the main budget, and the conclusion says 'without retraining' although Table 1 specifies retraining. These weaken precise claims, but the added controls and implementation evidence provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Debate2Create by the same authors. All pages, equations, tables and figures were readable and inspected, including v2's Appendices A–J; v1 contains no appendix.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on five locomotion tasks, component ablations, reward-transfer results and additional analyses in Appendices G–I.

before.justification: V1 reports original Brax Ant simulation results, including thesis-versus-synthesis performance in Figure 2 and the discovered design's score in Table I.

results.title: Debate2Create: Robot Co-design via Multi-Agent LLM Debate

C1.justification: v2 drops the repeated claim of being the first unified speech-and-audio SSL framework and makes complementary teacher distillation, domain fusion and token-mixing robustness central contributions. The broad unified-representation and SUPERB leadership claims remain, but the claimed contribution set changes substantially.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting secondary-source preservation to robustness, Dasheng's speech weaknesses to its MAE objective, and backbone choice to efficiency and fine-tuning performance. Appendix G newly argues that feature matching imposes teacher-performance limits and risks semantically inappropriate cross-domain averages. These are interpretations rather than proved guarantees. Existing data-imbalance and voice-conversion limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 discloses NVIDIA A800 80GB hardware, GPU counts and approximate GPU hours in Table 9, plus token-mixing sampling and SNR details. Conversely, it omits v1's quantiser-training disclosures of 100 LibriSpeech hours and 50 balanced-AudioSet hours. Both versions still promise future code and model release.

E1.justification: The named main training corpora and evaluation tasks are retained, including SUPERB, HEAR and low-resource LibriSpeech tests. However, the new USAD-aligned experiment in Appendix G provides training totals and excluded corpora without listing the included corpora. Whether this introduces different training populations cannot be established from the PDFs.

E2.justification: v2 adds USAD Base/Large to ASR and audio-tagging fine-tuning comparisons and introduces Dasheng 1.2B in SUPERB, where ATST-Frame disappears. HuBERT Large and Dasheng-Base fine-tuning comparisons are removed. New denoising, Transformer and k-means controls further expand the comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 introduces token mixing on 10% of training samples with sampled SNRs between -5 and 5. New experimental protocols include 300k-update architecture/target comparisons, a 2000-cluster k-means control using masked-only loss, teacher-layer sweeps and a 95.3k-hour USAD-aligned training configuration. Existing benchmark metrics and principal fine-tuning splits remain.

E4.justification: New studies test token mixing against denoising, teacher-layer selection, Zipformer versus Transformer, MVQ versus k-means targets, dual-domain loss weighting and the influence of teacher choice in comparison with USAD. Existing teacher-model, codebook-count, masked-loss and UMAP analyses remain. The original dual-domain strategy study moves into Section 5.4.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, experimental seeds, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests. Results remain point estimates; stochastic augmentation is not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Numerous new control results and revised benchmark values appear. With revised pre-training, SPEARs Large reports diarisation error changing from 3.20 to 2.30 and separation SI-SDRi from 11.20 to 11.67 (v1 Table 13; v2 Table 14). Its dual-domain Large concatenated HEAR average changes from 81.78 to 82.46 in the main tables; v2 Table 16 retains 81.8 despite individual scores supporting approximately 82.46.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.3 introduces power-weighted stochastic token mixing, changing supervision for mixed waveforms to incorporate both sources' targets. MVQ, Zipformer and the main asymmetric objective remain. The revised asymmetry description also resolves v1's appendix/main-text contradiction rather than demonstrating a reversal of the underlying method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related work are extensively rewritten. v2 adds a main-text ablation section, reorganises the appendices, changes Ethics Statement to Impact Statement, and removes standalone Reproducibility Statement and LLM Usage sections. Terminology and section titles are also revised.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from one-column to two-column layout. v2 adds a token-mixing diagram and multiple experimental tables, resizes existing displays, restructures HEAR tables by training-data scale, and changes the selected SUPERB columns. The original loss-sensitivity and UMAP plots are retained and relocated.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially repositioned around EncodecMAE, MT2KD and USAD, with expanded distinctions between discrete prediction and feature matching. A new discussion compares SPEAR with SALMONN, Audio Flamingo 3 and Qwen-omni. Earlier discussions and citations concerning MERT, SSAST and general model-compression distillation are removed.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions of stochastic token selection, temporal offset and the signal-power mixing coefficient in Equations 4–5. Existing MVQ reconstruction, quantiser-training and masked-prediction mathematics remain equivalent. No new theorem or proof establishes the asserted teacher-performance bound.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central design choices through architecture and same-teacher-layer target comparisons, teacher-matched USAD evaluation, and a direct token-mixing ablation. These address attribution gaps in v1's largely cross-model comparisons. Corrected asymmetric-loss documentation and compute disclosures also help assessment. Imperfect controls, unproved feature-matching claims, stale HEAR appendix averages and omitted quantiser-training details remain drawbacks, but the targeted experimental evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both complete, readable 25-page PDFs describe SPEAR. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison despite substantial rewriting and some internal reporting inconsistencies.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds token-mixing, architecture, quantisation-target, teacher-layer and USAD comparison experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original SPEAR fine-tuning, SUPERB and HEAR results, together with teacher-selection, loss-weighting, codebook and representation analyses.

results.title: SPEAR: A Unified SSL Framework for Learning Speech and Audio Representations

C1.justification: The claimed evaluation contributions shift from event-level consistency and content clarity toward hierarchical scene alignment, character identity tracking and multiscale dynamics. Agreement with human judgments becomes an explicit main contribution. The abstract emphasizes strong background consistency versus weak character consistency, and v1's claim to the first systematic benchmark is omitted.

C2.justification: v1 interprets internal correlations as evidence that static-quality bias and metric entanglement are limited. v2 instead discusses shared semantic dependencies and associations between perceptual quality and other scores. It adds explanations for using complete frames in background evaluation, attributes weak complexity associations to restricted variance, and acknowledges a visual-style exception with a hypothesis about auditor-text hallucinations.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands prompt templates, verification instructions, baseline-adaptation details and human-annotation documentation. It newly specifies generation defaults of 16 fps and 480p with exceptions. Conversely, v1 Section 7's release URL and statement that draft prompt data are available disappear; this removes access information without establishing that the resources themselves were withdrawn.

E1.justification: The long-video task and eighteen themes remain, but v2 substantially revises the evaluated input requirements: descriptive prompts enriched with evaluation information become stories with identifiable characters and fixed appearance constraints across scenes (Section 3.2; Appendix D.2). The auxiliary complexity comparison adds AniMaker/TinyStories prompts, while v1's Text-to-Image-2M aesthetic-calibration corpus is no longer used.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains all nine original generators and adds StoryAdapter, SANA-Video, LongLive and LongSANA. StoryAdapter is evaluated through a Wan2.2 image-to-video adaptation. v2 also introduces explicit comparisons against QA-based and direct-scoring HERD alternatives and a character-removal background-consistency variant (Table 3 and Figure 4).

E3.justification: The evaluated prompt count changes from 240 to 234, with substantially revised metric scales, sampling and aggregation. Generated event-level comparator prompts are replaced by verified scene splits that reconstruct the original prompt verbatim; complexity scoring changes from DeepSeek-V3.1 to V3.2. New protocols include human evaluation of a random 5% of generated videos and dynamic-quality calibration on 100 disjoint annotated videos.

E4.justification: v2 adds human-alignment validation, background-masking ablation and comparisons of HERD implementations. Theme and prompt-complexity analyses are retained but revised in Appendix C; the specific event-alignment/temporal-consistency entanglement analysis from v1 Section 4.4 disappears. Appendix E replaces three pairwise examples with five cases displaying all thirteen methods.

E5.justification: v2 newly discloses generation seed 0 and three-annotator mean opinion scoring. The repeated randomized MLLM judgments described for v1's content-clarity metric disappear with that metric. These are limited changes in randomness and estimation reporting; neither version provides confidence intervals or multi-seed uncertainty for benchmark performance.

E6.justification: The main and supplementary result sets are extensively replaced and expanded. VGoT leads v1 Table 2 with an overall score of 72.17, whereas LongLive leads v2 Table 2 with 70.56 under the revised prompts and metrics; these are not comparable-setting performance changes. New results include human-alignment coefficients, such as HERD SRCC 0.5844, component comparisons, dynamic-quality scores and new qualitative cases.

M1.justification: The evaluation procedure is substantially redesigned. DeQA-based perceptual scoring replaces aesthetic/technical scoring; direct MLLM scoring and hierarchical scene-gated VQA replace description similarity and Hungarian event matching. SAM3 tracking with MLLM verification replaces event-based character-consistency extraction. HERD changes from seven-dimensional polarity-aware QA to six-dimensional auditor/evaluator scoring. Standalone content clarity disappears, while multiscale dynamic quality and streaming implementations are introduced.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and central methodological exposition are extensively rewritten. Benchmark construction and evaluation become separate main sections, experiments are reorganized, and theme/complexity analyses move into restructured appendices. The new LoCoT2V-Eval terminology accompanies substantial narrative restructuring rather than an isolated renaming.

P2.justification: The main text switches from one to two columns, the overview is redrawn, and new evaluation-pipeline and human-validation displays are added. Table 2 gains input-format groups and different metric columns. Several radar/violin displays are replaced by bars or heatmaps, and qualitative comparisons expand into full-method grids with prompts presented separately.

R1.justification: The methodological positioning broadens substantially: v2 explicitly draws on DPG-Bench/FIFA for fine-grained alignment, DEVIL for multiscale dynamics and recent image-quality assessment work for perceptual scoring. StoryBench, AniMaker and newer generation methods enter the discussion. References supporting the former design, including FingER and Hungarian matching, disappear; these changes go beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v1's event-matching inversion penalty, transition-abruptness formulation and intra-/inter-event consistency definitions are removed. v2 introduces formal scene gates, character/facet aggregation and scene-normalized FGA equations, together with perceptual and multiscale dynamic-score definitions (Section 4; Appendix B.3). These substantially change mathematical metric definitions, although neither version presents theoretical guarantees.

improvement.justification: v1 asserts evaluation reliability without validating scores against human judgments. v2 addresses this important deficiency through a three-annotator study, component comparisons and disjoint calibration data (Table 3, Figure 4 and Appendix B), while acknowledging the HERD visual-style exception. Verified prompt splitting also strengthens experimental control. Although release information and some earlier analyses are lost, the new validation substantially strengthens the evidence supporting the paper's central contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LoCoT2V-Bench project. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and rendered figures, support reliable comparison despite substantial methodological and organizational revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of thirteen methods, human-annotation results, evaluation-method comparisons and updated supplementary analyses and examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of nine video-generation methods, prompt-complexity measurements, correlation analyses and qualitative examples in the main text and appendices.

results.title: LoCoT2V-Bench: Benchmarking Long-Form and Complex Text-to-Video Generation

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the central claims: unsupervised model selection and misspecification testing from one measurement through Bayesian cross-validation and data fission, with broad sampler compatibility and computational efficiency. The added theory and experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: E.3 newly explains CLIP's poor discrimination through semantic similarity and DreamSim's increased detection power and false positives through style sensitivity. E.5 explicitly limits robustness when the posterior sampler collapses, including 15 DiffPIR steps at blur 2. These add substantive applicability boundaries beyond the earlier blur, alpha, and MRI-embedding caveats.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds pseudocode, parallel-sampling guidance, and a runtime configuration specifying K=10, N=20, L=1 and 210 samples on a 16 GB V100. E.3 specifies CLIP patch-32 features, the penultimate visual hidden state, and L2 normalization. These are substantial documentation additions; code/data access links remain unchanged. The new batch-size disclosure is incomplete.

E1.justification: Appendix B adds an evaluated galaxy-image denoising task, extending coverage to an astronomical domain and another restoration task. The earlier Gaussian simulations, natural-image deblurring datasets, Poisson-noise experiment, and brain/knee MRI coverage are retained.

E2.justification: ProxNest, previously only discussed and cited, becomes a directly evaluated model-selection comparator in Appendix B/Table 5. This adds comparison with computed Bayesian evidence beyond the residual-based alternatives. The Bayesian and empirical-Bayesian residual comparators in Table 1 remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 adds MAP/posterior-mean PSNR validation for galaxy priors, four-prior deblurring comparisons with PSNR/LPIPS and 40-sample posterior means, and controlled embedding and diffusion-step sweeps. Section 4.1 also changes the stated Gaussian noise variance from 1 to 0.05; this establishes a reported setting revision, not that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The existing alpha and convergence analyses are supplemented by exact-versus-approximate Bayes-factor studies (Figures 15–16), LPIPS/DINOv2/CLIP/DreamSim ablations (E.3), and OOD-detection sensitivity to DiffPIR discretization (E.5/Figure 24). These substantially expand testing of embedding dependence and failure under degraded posterior sampling.

E5.justification: The 95th-percentile reference thresholds, nominal 5% significance level, and Type I error/power reporting remain. v3 adds no repeated-run uncertainty estimates, seed studies, confidence intervals, or changed uncertainty-reporting procedure; its additional rejection rates reuse the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: v3 adds runtime measurements, galaxy evidence/PSNR rankings, four-prior comparison scores, embedding rejection rates, and sampler-degradation curves. The Gaussian finite-K reference curve is replaced by an analytical limit. Table 2 changes FFHQ Type I error at blur 5 from 6.7% to 0%, while v2's claim of 100% DINOv2 accuracy on brain images is removed. Kernel-selection, main MRI, and Poisson table values are retained.

M1.justification: The data-fission procedure, likelihood- and posterior-based scores, and Monte Carlo estimators remain substantively unchanged. Algorithm 1 documents the existing procedure; testing additional priors and embeddings instantiates the existing framework rather than introducing a new method component.

P1.justification: Most retained prose closely matches v2. v3 makes local wording, title, affiliation, and citation-style edits; adds Section 4.4 as an appendix roadmap and an Impact Statement; and expands the appendix headings. The main narrative and conclusion are largely unchanged.

P2.justification: v3 adds a framework schematic, Bayes-factor and sampler-degradation plots, a blurred-input gallery, and runtime/prior/embedding tables. Figure 3 redraws the reference curve as an analytical limit, and Figure 7 adds likelihood-score threshold lines. The conference formatting and figure/table placement also change substantially, while most earlier visual material is retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for DreamSim, BLIP-2, and Pereyra et al.'s stabilized MCMC method. The background clarifies Shoushtari et al.'s requirement for multiple measurements with collectively spanning forward operators. The broader research positioning remains stable; most other bibliography changes concern style or metadata.

T1.justification: v3 adds Proposition 1, explicit regularity assumptions and a limit proof in C.3, plus analytical Bayes-factor and split-averaged log-score derivations in Equations 20–27. Equations 18–19 correct the normalization from (2π)^m to (2π)^(m/2). The new proof nevertheless uses c_alpha in Equation 29 where the m-dimensional Jacobian requires c_alpha^m.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important validation gaps by checking agreement with Bayesian evidence (Table 5), testing embedding and sampler failure modes (E.3/E.5), and quantifying computational cost (Table 4). Expanded derivations, corrected Gaussian normalization, and implementation guidance further strengthen the paper. These gains outweigh localized new defects, including the Jacobian factor in C.3 and missing batch-size value in A.2.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, framework, and retained experiments. All 20 pages of v2 and 26 pages of v3, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures sufficient for comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds galaxy-denoising comparisons, runtime measurements, broader prior comparisons, embedding ablations, and sampler-degradation experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original Gaussian simulations, blur-kernel selection experiments, natural-image OOD detection under Gaussian and Poisson noise, and MRI reconstruction/model-selection results.

results.title: Bayesian model selection and misspecification testing in imaging inverse problems only from noisy and partial measurements

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central contributions: unified vision–motion codes, heterogeneous-data exploitation, a model-agnostic three-stage framework, and strong performance across six robot embodiments and over 120 tasks. Additional evidence does not redefine these main claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of codebook saturation, comparable shared/separate codebooks under alignment, human-video benefits, and action-semantic clustering across embodiments. It also explicitly identifies XR-1's precision failures on tiny screws, adding a concrete applicability limitation absent from v1's discussion.

D1.justification: v2 identifies XR-D's relationship to RoboMIND 2.0, specifies the motion-decoder conditioning used, and documents feature extraction and similarity aggregation for the new retrieval analyses. Existing architecture tables, hyperparameters, hardware, training costs, inference speeds, and project access information are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds CALVIN D-to-D evaluation, extending coverage to simulated, language-conditioned manipulation using CALVIN's 34-task repertoire. The original real-world embodiments and tasks remain. Identifying XR-D as a RoboMIND 2.0 subset does not establish a change to its represented training data.

E2.justification: The new CALVIN comparison in Table 17 introduces evaluated comparators OpenVLA, Qwen-π0, and Qwen-GR00T, alongside RDT-1B, π0, and π0.5. This adds a distinct comparison suite; comparator membership in the retained real-world and ACT/DP adaptation experiments is unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 introduces CALVIN testing on 1,000 five-instruction sequences and new retrieval and controlled-ablation protocols. It also changes Stage-2 from absent to downstream-task training for Exps. 2 and 4–9 in v1 Table 4/v2 Table 3. This is a substantive reported-setting revision, without establishing that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds codebook-size, embedding-dimension, modality-only, shared-versus-separate-codebook, and Ego4D ablations. Appendices G–I add nearest-neighbor retrieval, t-SNE analyses, and baseline/XR-1 failure cases. The earlier cross-embodiment transfer analysis is retained as Table 16, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Appendix G.2 and Table 18 newly summarize normalized nearest-neighbor similarity distributions using modes and averages, extending descriptive statistical reporting beyond success-rate averages. Neither version reports repeated-training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: New results include motion-only, vision-only, and unified-code success rates of 35.0%, 50.0%, and 66.7% in Table 14; Ego4D ablation results of 32.5% versus 38.3% in Table 15; and CALVIN scores of 4.256 for XR-1 versus 3.885 for π0.5 in Table 17. Retrieval statistics and failure findings are also added. Matched original real-world scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 revises the stated motion-decoder inputs: v1 specifies language and observations alongside the motion code, whereas v2 permits optional conditions and explicitly uses proprioceptive states in its implementation. The dual-branch UVMC architecture and three-stage framework otherwise remain stable.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, methodology, and experimental narrative undergo substantial condensation and rewriting. Ablations precede generalization, appendices are reorganized into A–J, and an Additional Analyses section is added. The LLM-writing disclosure is removed and an Impact Statement appears.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column layout to two columns. Figure 2 is redrawn with explicit conditioning and token labels, the ablation table's stage columns are restructured, and existing displays are relocated. New CALVIN, retrieval, t-SNE, and failure-case figures accompany four additional tables.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to CALVIN and RoboMIND 2.0 and connects XR-D to the latter. It removes the Weblab xArm reference by Matsushima et al., replacing the corresponding dataset citations with Oh et al. The broader positioning against action-only and video-only representation learning remains.

T1.justification: Appendix G.2 introduces a formal construction of the cross-task retrieval statistic: a pairwise motion–vision similarity matrix, column-wise maxima, and a normalized nearest-neighbor vector. Existing training mathematics is mostly compacted or renotated; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct vision-only/motion-only and human-video controls despite their importance to its central motivation. v2 addresses these gaps in Appendix D and adds representation evidence, simulation benchmarking, and explicit XR-1 failure cases, substantially strengthening validation and clarity about limitations. These benefits are tempered by absent uncertainty estimates and inconsistent Stage-2 labels attached to identical results in v2 Tables 3 and 15.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same XR-1 research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting and added analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those original empirical results and adds CALVIN simulation results, additional ablations, representation analyses, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original real-world robot evaluations, few-shot adaptation, environmental generalization tests, and ablation results.

results.title: XR-1: Towards Versatile Vision-Language-Action Models via Learning Unified Vision-Motion Representations

C1.justification: The introduction explicitly adds greater ranking stability across subsets and related domains, and makes transfer to unseen families and newer model populations a principal contribution. This expands the claimed validation scope, although the abstract, conclusion and headline efficiency claims remain essentially unchanged.

C2.justification: V3 adds targeted qualifications: the lower asymptote may reflect priors, prompting, decoding, memorization or heuristics rather than literal guessing, and 3PL is not universally superior to 2PL. Appendix C.3 also interprets sparse residual dependence as potentially arising from shared templates or topics.

D1.justification: V3 documents construction details for the new transfer cohorts, including Mixtral exclusion, the 2024-05-01 release cutoff and exclusion of 844 models lacking release dates. Existing calibration and implementation disclosures remain, and removing '.git' from the repository URL does not establish changed resource access.

E1.justification: The five main benchmarks and all 57 MMLU subjects are retained. Section 4.6 adds ARC generalization scenarios targeting a completely withheld Mixtral family and later-release models, extending evaluation beyond the original random-split setting.

E2.justification: V3 newly evaluates a 2PL alternative against default 3PL ATLAS in Table 12. The original comparator membership—Random100, TinyBenchmarks, MetaBench-Primary and MetaBench-Secondary—remains unchanged; Table 13 varies the reference estimator rather than adding an external baseline.

E3.justification: V3 adds disjoint split-half ranking comparisons, related-benchmark consistency tests, ARC family and temporal holdouts, Q3 diagnostics, and parameterization/reference-estimator controls. Section 4.6 specifies calibration/test cohorts of 3,296/321 and 2,998/322 models. These substantially expand evaluation design while retaining the original main settings.

E4.justification: New analyses test ranking reproducibility and cross-benchmark consistency (Section 4.5), family and temporal robustness (Section 4.6), local independence (Appendix C.3), and sensitivity to 3PL versus 2PL and WLE versus EAP references (Appendices G.3–G.4). These address several previously untested validity questions.

E5.justification: Section 4.5 and Table 4 newly report averaging split-half correlations over ten random partitions. This concerns a new analysis, not increased repetitions of the original experiments. Existing MAE standard errors across models remain unchanged, without added confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: All original table values, including the complete MMLU results, are retained. Five new tables report stability, transfer, Q3 and sensitivity findings: Table 4 reports WinoGrande correlations of 0.943 for raw-accuracy rankings versus 0.981 for ability rankings; Table 5 adds temporal ARC ability MAE of 0.126 at the 0.1 stopping threshold. These are new evaluations, not same-setting improvements over v2.

M1.justification: The proposed ATLAS pipeline and Algorithm 1 retain 3PL calibration, common-person linking, top-five randomesque selection, EAP updates and precision-based stopping. The new 2PL and alternative-reference experiments test sensitivity without revising the default method.

P1.justification: V3 rewrites the contribution paragraph and parameter explanations, condenses part of the discussion, swaps the two existing item-informativeness/performance-extremes subsections, and adds analysis subsections. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column preprint to a two-column conference layout. Displays are resized and relocated, Figures 2 and 3 exchange numbering and order, and five new tables are added. Existing appendix tables and figures are retained and reflowed.

R1.justification: V3 adds Habba et al. (2026), Rodriguez et al. (2021), and Q3-related sources by Yen, Christensen and colleagues, and Marais; it removes Zhuang et al. (2023). Positioning relative to TinyBenchmarks, MetaBench and Fluid Benchmarking remains largely unchanged.

T1.justification: The IRT, Fisher-information and EAP equations, calibration-complexity argument, metric definitions and p-IRT derivation are retained. Revised parameter explanations clarify the existing 3PL formula; the new diagnostics and sensitivity tests do not introduce formal theoretical results.

improvement.justification: V2 inferred better measurement largely from reconstruction accuracy, rank reordering and examples. V3 directly tests ranking stability and transfer (Tables 4–5), checks local independence (Table 8), and examines parameterization and reference-estimator sensitivity (Tables 12–13). These address central validation gaps and add useful qualifications about 3PL, substantially strengthening the paper. Transfer evidence remains limited to ARC and one held-out family.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ATLAS research. Text extraction and visual inspection cover all 23 pages of v2 and 24 pages of v3, including equations, figures, tables and appendices, with no material reading gaps.

after.justification: V3 retains those empirical results and adds ranking-stability, distribution-shift, local-dependence and estimator-sensitivity results.

before.justification: V2 reports original ATLAS evaluations against static baselines, psychometric and ranking analyses, and experiments across 57 MMLU subjects in Appendix G.

results.title: Adaptive Testing for LLM Evaluation: A Psychometric Alternative to Static Benchmarks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the same claims about RoS improvement, coordinated mirror-descent value dominance, conditional optimality, and non-i.i.d. extensions. Theorem 4.2's revised optimality wording expresses the existing claim.

C2.justification: The interpretations of coalition gains and unequal individual benefits under heterogeneity remain unchanged, as do the iPinYou limitations and future-work boundaries. The substantive revisions concern proof reasoning and formal assumptions rather than a separate reinterpretation of the findings.

D1.justification: Implementation and reproducibility disclosures are retained, including initialization, mirror map, learning rate, dataset split, normalization, and resampling procedure. No new code, hardware, or data-access information is supplied.

E1.justification: Section 6 and Appendix D retain the same symmetric and asymmetric synthetic scenarios and simulations using the iPinYou Season 2 test data. No dataset, task, or evaluated environment is added or removed.

E2.justification: Every reported experiment retains the same comparison between Independent bidding (Algorithm 1) and Coordinated bidding (Algorithm 2), using the same mirror-descent auto-bidder.

E3.justification: The experimental settings are unchanged, including Table 1's coalition sizes and horizons, entropy mirror map, learning rate, data normalization and sampling, and utility/value metrics.

E4.justification: Both versions contain the same comparisons under bidder heterogeneity and the same per-bidder learning trajectories. Appendix D retains its existing supplementary plots without adding ablations, robustness tests, or case studies.

E5.justification: Both versions report 100 independent simulations, 95% confidence intervals using 1.96 times the standard error, and the same interval-omission threshold in Table 1. Revised mathematical probability bounds belong to the theoretical analysis.

E6.justification: All eight rows of Table 1 are identical, including uncertainty values. The eight plotted panels comprising Figures 1–5 also match exactly, and the empirical findings are retained.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the same independent bidding, highest-value-bidder coordination, and mirror-descent updates. V3 introduces clipped utilities and a virtual bidder for the proof only; these do not modify the bidding procedure.

P1.justification: Section 4's proof sketch and Appendix B's exposition are substantially rewritten and reorganized. The formerly separate boundary-case subsection is integrated into a unified proof with named lemmas and revised stages. Smaller edits include an affiliation update and an introduced unresolved algorithm reference in Theorem 5.2.

P2.justification: The figures and table retain their contents and structures. Figures 1–2 shift relative to the surrounding discussion, Figure 2's caption changes slightly, and revised proof displays alter page layout. There is no substantive visual redesign.

R1.justification: Section 1.1 and all 32 references are unchanged. The positioning relative to utility-maximizing coordination and previous auto-bidding research is retained.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 replaces v2's independent-multiplier lower-bound argument with new virtual-bidder domination, clipped-utility bounds, deterministic sublinear RoS violation, and a dual-envelope argument (v3 Lemmas B.5–B.10). The existing interior and boundary analyses are consolidated and refined. Lemma B.1 explicitly adds a strictly positive outside-bid density assumption and establishes existence of the reference multiplier.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the central Theorem 4.1 proof: its clipped-utility and dual-envelope argument avoids v2 Claim B.2's unsupported assumption that independent bidders' utilities are bounded by B, although internal second-price payments can exceed B. The positive-density premise newly stated in Lemma B.1 remains unreconciled with the broader main-text guarantee, and a broken algorithm reference is introduced. These limitations temper, but do not outweigh, the important theoretical repair.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, On the Coordination of Value-Maximizing Bidders. Text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D are readable and support a complete comparison.

after.justification: V3 retains these original simulation results in Section 6, Table 1, and Figures 1–5, including Appendix D.

before.justification: V2 reports original simulations using synthetic valuations and iPinYou-derived data, with outcomes in Table 1 and Figures 1–5, including Appendix D.

results.title: On the Coordination of Value-Maximizing Bidders

C1.justification: The central claims about novel bias formation, greater stratification in stronger models, and the effectiveness of explicit diversity incentives remain. v4 adds a concluding claim that models only begin unlearning after exceedingly unlikely outcome sequences (Discussion, Appendix J), extending the paper's message about resistance to correction.

C2.justification: v4 develops a more specific mechanism account: outcome feedback principally drives stochasticity, semantic framing shapes allocation patterns, and accumulated context alone does not explain stratification. It also interprets forced-failure responses through anchoring while acknowledging that first deviation does not guarantee unlearning. The diversity-versus-success limitation already present in v2 Appendix G is retained in v4 Appendix K.

D1.justification: v4 adds a code-repository link on the title page and exact templates for the abstract bandit and compressed-summary experiments (Appendices A.2–A.3), including summary construction and omission of groups with no hires. It also documents baseline coefficients and continuation handling. Existing prompting and hyperparameter information is largely retained.

E1.justification: v4 adds an abstract bandit scenario without social or occupational semantics and feedback-altered scenarios, including forced-failure continuations. These extend the simulated decision conditions within the existing allocation task family. Hiring, refugee resettlement, conscription, and real-demographic scenarios are retained.

E2.justification: v4 adds evaluated Thompson-sampling and UCB1 baselines, substantially broadening comparison beyond humans and random assignment (Section 4.1, Appendix E). Primary model comparisons also add GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash. The matched p=0.1 human reference displayed in v2 Figure 5 is absent from the replacement v4 Table 2.

E3.justification: The original 40-round, 30-run primary design remains, but v4 adds substantial control protocols: compressed histories, temperature zero, five fixed job trajectories with ten trials each, and removal of outcome feedback and bonus wording. Its new continuation experiment imposes ten failed rounds per job quadrant and measures first deviation, recording 11 when none occurs. The abstract task additionally evaluates allocation entropy.

E4.justification: v4 adds analyses testing context accumulation, semantic framing, sampling variance, job-order variance, feedback dependence, and resistance to renewed exploration (Sections 5.1–5.2, Appendices G and J). Appendix E also examines UCB1 exploration-coefficient sensitivity. Existing ReAct, unequal-success-rate, real-demographic, and diversity-tradeoff analyses are retained under different appendix labels.

E5.justification: v2 already reports repeated runs and 95% confidence intervals. v4 newly states that significance testing accounts for a Benjamini-Hochberg correction at alpha=0.05 and adds uncertainty entries for GASI controls. The primary run count remains 30; the new correction disclosure does not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial results for newer models, bandit baselines, and mechanistic controls. Examples include GASI values of 0.63, 0.61, and 0.61 for GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Gemini 3 Flash, and Thompson-sampling SI=0.61 (Table 1, Appendix E). Matched allocation matrices and many older results remain unchanged. v4 Table 2 reports random-assignment SI=0.291, whereas v2 reports 0.25 and v4's main results and Table 3 retain 0.25; this discrepancy is unexplained.

M1.justification: v4 introduces a tested context-summary inference variant: demographic-job counts and empirical success rates replace the full dialogue history (Section 5.1, Appendix A.3). This extends the intervention procedures; the core hiring paradigm and diversity-bonus mechanism remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The overall six-section narrative remains, with copyediting and focused revisions to the introduction and discussion. Model settings move from Section 4.1 to 3.3, several appendices are reordered, acknowledgments are added, and the Ethics Statement becomes an Impact Statement with essentially the same content.

P2.justification: v4 adopts a two-column conference layout and extensively revises displays. Figure 3 gains BGD alongside SI, v2 Figure 5 becomes v4 Table 2, and v2 Figure 6's two feature-ablation panels merge into v4 Figure 5 with corrected feature labels. Table 1 expands and new control tables appear. Existing appendix allocation matrices are reflowed without changing their numerical contents.

R1.justification: The distinction between pretrained stereotypes and emergent interaction-driven biases remains the central positioning. v4 adds connections and citations concerning statistical discrimination, classical bandit policies, anchoring, and long-context failures. It removes the standalone HELM leaderboard and Sutton–Barto references; publication and author-name updates elsewhere concern retained works.

T1.justification: Appendix J adds brief probabilistic reasoning linking consecutive failures to probabilities of 10^-1 through 10^-5 and arguing that the required failure sequence bounds natural unlearning likelihood. The metric definitions and Appendix B's SI–mutual-information lemma and proof are unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 supported emergence mainly through stochastic assignments and initial-association tests. v4 substantially strengthens the central mechanism analysis with classical bandit comparisons and targeted controls for sampling, job order, feedback, context length, and semantic framing. Added prompts and a code link improve reproducibility information. Some conclusions remain overstated—the forced-failure probe measures first deviation, not completed unlearning—and Table 2 introduces an inconsistent random baseline, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial improvement in supporting evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work with the same title, authors, and central experiments. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding equations, tables, figures, and allocation matrices can be matched despite substantial reformatting.

after.justification: v4 retains original LLM experiments and adds newer-model evaluations, bandit comparisons, controlled ablations, and forced-failure continuation results.

before.justification: v2 reports original LLM hiring simulations, intervention experiments, and supplementary analyses in Sections 4–5 and the appendices. The separately attributed human baseline is not the sole empirical evidence.

results.title: Large Language Models Develop Novel Social Biases Through Adaptive Exploration

C1.justification: v3 makes RVPO and interactive visual optimization central contributions and claims broader applicability to executable generation with black-box feedback. It extends the headline state-of-the-art claim to UI editing. v1 instead emphasizes the first unified open-source UI model and full foundational training recipe; those explicit first-of-kind claims are removed.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations of training-stage benefits, explicit reasoning, evaluator reliability, reward hacking, and computational efficiency. It acknowledges individual polishing regressions and attributes diminishing returns to approaching a capability ceiling, while restricting editing to localized, well-specified changes. These qualifications and explanations go beyond v1's predominantly positive aggregate interpretations.

D1.justification: v3 discloses verifier data construction and fine-tuning settings, including 8,500 filtered triplets and 200 training iterations, plus deduplication, benchmark separation, and data-filtering procedures. It adds research-only, non-commercial licensing and raw-data withholding disclosures. Some v1 details disappear, including the SFT teacher identifier, task-specific construction instructions, and the additional billion language-code tokens.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluation on the 69-task UIEdit-Bench and WebCode2M-Long, substantially extending systematic testing of instruction-guided editing and long webpages. Editing already appeared in v1 training and demonstrations, so it is not an entirely new capability. The original drafting and polishing benchmarks remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct, and Claude-4-5-Sonnet-thinking. Appendix G adds comparisons with WebSight VLM-7B, Design2Code-18B, UICopilot, DCGen, and ScreenCoder. Conversely, the comparator-only reward baseline in v1 Table 3a disappears from the corresponding v3 comparison.

E3.justification: v3 introduces human pairwise and 0–5 rating protocols, component-level and DINOv3 metrics, controlled Think/Answer comparisons, and latency/token-cost evaluation. These are substantial additions to the evaluation design. The original o4-mini drafting evaluator, threshold of 80, Gemini-2.5-Pro polishing evaluator, and main training budgets are retained.

E4.justification: v3 adds training-stage and Think/Answer ablations, human–verifier validation, evaluator sensitivity, absolute-positioning reward-hacking analysis, polishing oscillation analysis, and efficiency measurements. The real-data ablation is retained. Removing the intermediate comparator-only condition reduces evidence isolating the incremental benefit of round-robin ranking.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without repeated-run uncertainty. v3 explicitly repeats generation and judging five times and reports means and standard deviations in Table 10. Appendix F adds annotator variability, error bars, correlations, effect sizes, and agreement statistics. Table 14 also introduces ± values, without clearly defining their statistical meaning.

E6.justification: The retained Table 1 rows and test-time scaling values are unchanged. v3 adds extensive results, including UI editing overall scores of 4.87 for RL versus 4.60 for SFT, human preferences, additional metrics and baselines, repeated-run outcomes, and diagnostics. The comparator-only polishing results of 93.0/78.0 in v1 Table 3a are removed; the additions do not establish improved performance over v1 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The model, three-stage training, GRPO, and round-robin comparator already exist in v1; naming these RVPO does not establish a new method. However, v3 Algorithm 1 changes tie screening and specifies tournament rewards, while Appendix A retains absolute drafting rewards and replaces continuous polishing rewards with binary improvement. These conflicting descriptions prevent reliably determining the implemented reward change.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around visual optimization, with UI-to-code generation renamed UI drafting. Related work moves after experiments, training becomes a separate section, and the appendix is reorganized into sections A–H. This substantially changes the narrative and document structure.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout and replaces Figure 1's qualitative comparison panel with workflow and RVPO diagrams. Reward and real-data ablation tables become bar charts, and numerous tables and human-evaluation plots are added. The six appendix demonstration images are identical assets, resized and relocated rather than new cases.

R1.justification: The benchmark, dataset, and UI-system literature remains largely intact. v3 adds ScreenAI and evaluator-related work including RLAIF, ImageReward, HPS v2, and Omni-Reward, while removing some citations such as Radford's CLIP reference and Step-3. Novelty emphasis shifts toward RVPO, but the related-work discussion receives a limited expansion rather than a wholesale replacement.

T1.justification: v3 introduces a formal feedback map, black-box visual-discrepancy minimization, stochastic preference definitions, and a rank-based surrogate objective, alongside explicit training and GRPO equations. v1 contains reward pseudocode and simpler scoring definitions but lacks this formal optimization framework. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v1 relies mainly on VLM-judged point estimates without direct validation of evaluator reliability. v3's human studies, repeated full-pipeline evaluations, and cross-evaluator checks substantially strengthen the evidence supporting its central empirical claims; additional ablations and verifier-training details improve explanation and reproducibility. Inconsistent reward definitions and overstated claims of evaluator impartiality remain important weaknesses, but the validation gains outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UI2CodeN, with matching core experiments and demonstration images despite substantial rewriting. Their main text, appendices, equations, tables, and figures support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds human evaluations, repeated-run measurements, additional comparisons, and diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results, iterative polishing experiments, reward and training-data ablations, and qualitative demonstrations.

results.title: UI2Code^N: UI-to-Code Generation as Interactive Visual Optimization

C1.justification: The architectural feasibility contribution remains, but v3 makes systematic inference benchmarking and superiority over autoregressive baselines central contributions. Its abstract and conclusion identify cache-reusing Mamba block diffusion as the uniquely linear-scaling, highest-throughput strategy. v1 treated block diffusion as future work and centered its claims on backbone replacement and hybridization.

C2.justification: v3 explains declining full-sequence throughput when denoising steps grow with length, extending v1's fixed-step saturation account, and identifies cache reuse as crucial for beating AR inference. It more explicitly acknowledges small-scale generalization weaknesses. Appendix B adds substantive limitations concerning fixed acceptance factors, batch-one timing, and the absence of training optimized for cached block decoding.

D1.justification: v3 Appendix A/Table 6 newly discloses optimizer settings, learning-rate bounds and schedule, global batch size 512, weight decay, EMA, antithetic sampling, clipping, and additional Mamba implementation settings. These fill substantial reproducibility gaps. The earlier model-configuration table and conditioning equations are mostly relocated; the new disclosures do not establish changed training settings.

E1.justification: MMLU, evaluated in v1 Appendix A/Table 5, is absent from v3. DCLM training, seven held-out perplexity datasets, and the other five downstream tasks remain. Throughput scenarios expand to block-cached generation up to approximately 262K tokens, versus the earlier 65K maximum.

E2.justification: v1's efficiency comparison uses DiffuTran and Mamba variants. v3 Figure 2 adds evaluated DiffuTran + Fast-dLLM and hybrid + Fast-dLLM configurations, Transformer and Mamba autoregressive baselines, and comparisons among block-cached Transformer and Mamba models. These substantially broaden the actual comparator set.

E3.justification: v1 fixes 128 denoising steps; v3 uses K=L/p with p=8 or 16 and explicitly measures generated tokens divided by total decoding time. New protocols include 32-token blocks and longer generation ranges. Timing evaluation narrows from 0.5B/1.3B to the largest scale, warm-ups decrease from five to three, and Table 1 adds average perplexity across datasets.

E4.justification: v3 removes the with/without-MLP comparisons reported throughout v1. It adds comparisons of cache recomputation versus reuse and two denoising-step factors. Figure 3 introduces fitted quadratic, linear, and constant latency components at 1K and 65K tokens to investigate the source of scaling differences.

E5.justification: Reported timing averages change from 20 decoding runs in v1 Section 4.1 to five in v3. v3 also introduces constrained estimation of latency coefficients. Neither version reports confidence intervals, timing dispersion, training-seed variability, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Retained quality-table values exactly match v1's +MLP rows; v3 removes results without MLP layers and MMLU results, and adds average perplexities. Efficiency results are substantially replaced: Figure 2a reports 8.2×/4.3× gains at K=L/8, and Figure 2c reports 2.3×/1.9× over block-cached DiffuTran. These differ in conditions from v1's 4.4×/2.6× comparisons and do not establish same-setting performance improvements.

M1.justification: The retained backbones correspond to v1's +MLP variants, with the same diffusion objective. However, v3 Section 4.3 adds block-autoregressive inference that retains caches across blocks, propagates forward Mamba states across blocks, and restricts reverse scanning to the current block. v1 left block-diffusion integration to future work; this adaptation changes the inference procedure.

P1.justification: Beyond model renaming and authorship updates, v3 substantially rewrites the introduction, contributions, and conclusion; places modeling quality before throughput; and moves detailed architectural mathematics into Appendix A. The earlier downstream appendix is replaced by configuration and limitations sections, with new takeaway summaries throughout the experimental narrative.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from one to two columns. Figure 2 is redesigned around decoding strategies and logarithmic throughput axes, replacing the earlier scale-specific throughput/latency panels. Figure 3 and complexity/hyperparameter tables are added. Quality tables remove variant rows, add an average column, and change placement; the configuration table moves to the appendix.
