R1.justification: Most related work remains. v3 adds Caduceus, data-efficiency, and foundational attention references, explicitly acknowledges prior SSM diffusion for biological sequences, and credits related bidirectional backbones. Several reasoning-model and benchmark references disappear. These changes refine the literature coverage and text-specific novelty boundary without fundamentally replacing the research positioning.

T1.justification: The diffusion and backbone equations are largely retained or relocated. Beyond v1's brief backbone-complexity discussion, v3 Table 3 and Section 4.3 develop FLOP, memory-traffic, arithmetic-intensity, and throughput expressions covering AR and cached diffusion variants. Substituting K=L/p yields O(1/L²) versus O(1/L) throughput scaling for full-sequence Transformer and Mamba diffusion. This is a substantial analytical extension, without new theorem proofs.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central efficiency argument through explicit total-decoding measurements, length-scaled steps, Fast-dLLM and AR controls, and analysis separating cache reuse from recomputation. Appendix A also fills major reproducibility gaps. These gains outweigh the removed MLP/MMLU evaluations and fewer timing repeats. Important qualifications remain: quality under the fastest cached decoding is unvalidated, and Section 4.3 incorrectly associates the 8.2×/4.3× ratios with K=L/16, whereas Figure 2 assigns them to K=L/8.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, renamed from DiffuApriel to DiffuMamba. All 15 pages of each version, including figures, tables, equations, references, and appendices, support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original language-model evaluation results and reports expanded inference benchmarks and fitted latency analyses in Figures 2–3.

before.justification: v1 reports original training and zero-shot evaluation results, throughput and latency measurements, and additional downstream results including MMLU in Appendix A.

results.title: DiffuMamba: High-Throughput Diffusion LMs with Mamba Backbone

C1.justification: The three headline contributions remain prediction from batch/context size, a repetition frequency–reliability frontier, and the joint roles of dependency, categories, and marginal distribution. Model-size independence becomes explicit in v2's abstract but was already claimed in v1 Appendix D. The additional validation does not itself redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive discussion of task-dependent emergence, tokenization effects, model-scale limits, and differences between attention, logit contribution, and output accuracy. Crucially, Appendix J.3 acknowledges that constrained sampling violates the intended independence condition and leaves low-PS/high-LA behavior unexplained. These qualifications materially complicate v1's interpretation that local dependency is necessary for induction-head formation.

D1.justification: New Appendix A/Table 2 documents architectural dimensions and training details including learning rate 5e-4, weight decay 0.1, 1% warmup, and cosine scheduling. v2 also specifies Pythia sizes and configurations and supplies a code-access URL absent from v1. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond the earlier model and checkpoint descriptions.

E1.justification: Both versions use English CC100, its bigram-based semi-natural data, and the same nine synthetic Markov configurations. The added measurements evaluate the existing repeated-token copying behavior. Larger sample counts and model configurations change experimental settings rather than dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 5 introduces an explicit comparison between the proposed batch/context regression and a full regression additionally containing model size, evaluated on identical held-out folds. v1 has no corresponding full-versus-reduced comparison. Newly cited methods such as OLMo are not evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The reported natural-data schedule changes from a 100M-token sample repeated for ten epochs to a 1B-token sample used for one epoch, retaining the 1B-token budget. v2 adds GPT2-125M and GPT2-350M training configurations, logit attribution and associative-recall metrics, and five-fold regression validation using 28 training and seven test models per fold. The schedule revision alone does not establish which retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 Section 4 and Appendix J systematically test whether findings from prefix matching persist under logit attribution, recall accuracy, and target-token rank across all three experiments. These analyses reveal metric-dependent exceptions to the dependency finding. The full-versus-reduced regressions also newly test whether model size contributes to emergence prediction.

E5.justification: v1 reports correlation significance and simulated random-attention thresholds but lacks regression-coefficient uncertainty. v2 Tables 3–4 add standard errors, t-tests, p-values, and 95% confidence intervals across four emergence metrics, enabling explicit tests of model-size effects. Neither version reports uncertainty across repeated language-model training seeds.

E6.justification: The expanded PS regression changes batch/context coefficient estimates from -0.51/-0.56 to -0.3689/-0.6155. New Table 5 reports held-out results, including reduced-model PS R-squared values of 0.7653–0.9284. Figures 9–15 add extensive LA/AR results, including strong copying-related outcomes under high-repetition -D conditions despite low PS. The frontier result for Zipf[+D+C] matches v1 Table 1; v2 corrects v1's conflicting prose label.

M1.justification: The emergence predictor changes from T/sqrt(BC) in v1 Appendix D to T/(B^0.37 C^0.62) in v2 Section 5, after testing and dropping a model-size predictor. This refines the existing regression approach; the constrained sampling algorithm and intended matrix-optimization procedure remain intact.

P1.justification: v2 extensively reorganizes the narrative with separate related-work, metric-selection, discussion, and limitations sections. It moves the predictive-law development, category-similarity explanation, and synthetic-distribution summary from appendices into the main text, restructures the appendices, and revises the title and introductory framing.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main layout, adds metric-development plots and regression tables, and colors the emergence scatterplot by model size. v1's binary Table 1 becomes a graded PS heatmap, while its distribution-statistics Table 3 moves into the main text. The old TWU-normalization Figure 5 is removed, and extensive alternative-metric displays are added.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands research positioning through a dedicated related-work section and new discussion. It distinguishes natural-language pretraining from Zucchet et al.'s sparse-attention task and Park et al.'s Markov-mixture setting, incorporates additional mechanistic and architectural work, and connects the study to broader behavioral and vision phase transitions.

T1.justification: v2's main emergence equation restores inverse scaling consistent with v1 Appendix D, whereas v1 Equation 1 incorrectly printed multiplication. Appendix H also corrects the duplicated within-category loss to an across-category expression in Equation 21. Most mathematical definitions, the sampling algorithm, and the stationary-distribution entropy derivation are retained; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 relies on PS-centered validation and an in-sample emergence-law fit with limited training documentation. v2 substantially strengthens this foundation through larger-model experiments, held-out regression validation, coefficient uncertainty, and complementary behavioral measurements. Appendix J also exposes an important sampling confound and metric-dependent limitation that v1 overlooks. Remaining inconsistencies, including the normalization constant T and Table 5's R-squared caption, limit precision, but the gains in validation, transparency, and reproducibility constitute a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same induction-head study, with matching authors and three core experiments. The complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, and figures are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds larger-model evaluations, alternative behavioral measurements, regression statistics, and cross-validation results.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model training experiments using natural, semi-natural, and synthetic data, including induction-head measurements and emergence-point regression.

results.title: Predicting the Emergence of Induction Heads in Language Model Pretraining

C1.justification: The central emergence-time and repetition claims remain. V3 adds an introduction/conclusion claim connecting emergence timing non-monotonically to final validation loss and training efficiency. It narrows categoriality/distribution claims to modulation near the decision boundary and qualifies the conclusion about individual properties by the PS metric.

C2.justification: V3 adds critical-batch-size and retrieval-difficulty explanations, explicitly suggesting that the predictive law may describe only a pre-saturation regime while acknowledging uncertainty about large-context reversals. Appendix G questions the naturalness of uniform token-level repetition constraints, and Appendix L qualifies its corpus comparisons as proxies. Appendix C also corrects the earlier reversed interpretation of negative regression coefficients.

D1.justification: The code-access pointer changes from predict-ih-review to predict-ih. Appendix L documents tokenizer vocabulary sizes and an analysis sample exceeding 10M tokens. Core training hyperparameters remain in Table 2; the 64-token synthetic training context was already disclosed in v2 Appendix E.

All four corpora are analyzed with three tokenizers. This is additional data-analysis coverage; induction-head training experiments are not replicated across these combinations.

E2.justification: The full and model-size-free emergence regressions remain compared in Table 5. No external baseline method is added or removed. The additional tokenizers are settings for corpus analysis, rather than competing methods evaluated against a proposed tokenizer.

E3.justification: V3 adds final-loss evaluation with identical 64-token validation chunks and a batch-128 context sweep extending to 4096. The semi-natural grid grows from 50 to 60 configurations through reliability 0.2, and repetitive-chunk proportions extend to 80–100%. Displayed PS and AR normalizers also change; the PDFs do not establish whether retained scores were recomputed.

E4.justification: V3 adds quantitative onset/slope analyses in Figure 2, seed robustness in Section 6.2, emergence-versus-validation-loss analysis in Section 9, and corpus/tokenizer sensitivity analysis in Appendix L. These address additional questions about repeatability, training outcomes, and generalization. V2's alternative-metric analyses are retained in Appendix K.

E5.justification: V2 already reports regression uncertainty and five-fold cross-validation. V3 explicitly trains two additional seeds for six configurations, reporting three-seed confidence intervals and standard deviations in Figure 4 and Table 6. It also adds onset/slope correlation tests and sequence-level standard-deviation reporting for the corpus analysis.

E6.justification: New results include reliability-0.2 heatmap cells, a boundary-fit MSE of 0.019, three-seed estimates, and corpus/tokenizer statistics in Table 8. Section 9 newly reports validation loss decreasing until batch size 64 and then increasing with context fixed at 1024. The original regression and cross-validation values in Tables 3–5 remain unchanged.

M1.justification: V3 Section 7.3 adds a sigmoid predictor of prefix-matching score from log frequency and log reliability, with an explicit decision boundary. This supplements the retained emergence-time law; the language-model architectures and substantive constrained-generation procedure remain the same.

P1.justification: The predictive-law exposition is condensed and separated from Experiment 1 into a dedicated Predictability and Robustness section. Results and discussion are substantially rewritten around shifting, slanting, and training dynamics, alongside widespread terminology and grammar editing. Appendix headings are reorganized while their existing technical material is retained.

P2.justification: Figure 2 gains onset/slope panels, and the repetition heatmap becomes an expanded observed-versus-predicted display. V3 adds seed, validation-loss, and corpus/tokenizer figures and tables. Regression tables gain significance coloring and are relocated. Figure 11 explicitly redisplays Figure 7 rather than contributing another experiment.

R1.justification: V3 adds critical-batch-size references by McCandlish and Merrill, plus references for the additional corpora and tokenizers, and removes Oh and Schuler (2023). Its comparison with Zucchet et al. shifts toward competing context-size effects. The broader positioning within induction-head and in-context-learning research remains intact.

T1.justification: Equations (1), (3), and (4) change normalization from 1/(|x|-1) to 1/|x|. Appendix H corrects the stated KL expression from a ratio of logarithms to the logarithm of a probability ratio. Section 7.3 also derives an explicit fitted boundary. Existing entropy derivations remain, without new theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens support for its predictions: v2's single-seed timing results gain direct repeatability checks for six configurations, and its visually characterized repetition boundary gains an explicit quantitative fit. Controlled validation-loss analysis and candid discussion of possible saturation limits improve practical interpretation, while formula corrections improve mathematical correctness. Corpus generalization remains a proxy analysis and causal explanations remain tentative, but these limits are acknowledged and the overall gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: V3 retains those original results and adds training-seed replications, predictive modeling, validation-loss analyses, and corpus/tokenizer data analyses.

before.justification: V2 reports original language-model pretraining experiments, synthetic-data experiments, emergence-point regressions, and supplementary analyses using several induction-head metrics.

results.title: Predicting the Emergence of Induction Heads in Language Model Pretraining

E3.justification: V3 adds Falcon-7B evaluation, starting-layer sweeps under both precisions and update variants, and Hellinger, rank, Top-1 and parameter-norm measurements in Appendix C. Appendix C.2 and C.4–C.5 substantially expand the analysis of numerical failures and update choices.

E6.justification: Figures 3–5 contain revised Gemma traces and token matches; Section 4.2 changes reported Stable bfloat16 agreement from 98% to 100%. Appendix C adds Falcon matching results, bfloat16 degradation when updating only the final layer, and scaling/norm findings. The algorithm revision and changed image-generation history preclude treating these as controlled same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 now propagates the actual patched block output instead of the recorded target activation, allowing subsequent patches to compensate for numerical errors. Appendix B's footnote and C.5 also introduce a variant that updates Wdown and rescales m. The core rank-1 construction and existing Stable RMSNorm inversion remain.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Local revisions clarify the MLP function and scaling notation, correct theorem/lemma references and replace the misleading 'poem' description with 'forecast'. Dedicated limitations, future-work and disclosure passages are added.

P2.justification: The main text switches to a two-column conference layout with running headers and substantial reflow. Existing figures and Table 1 are resized or relocated, axes and legends are revised, and Figures 6–13 add extensive multi-panel experimental displays.

R1.justification: V3 adds Almazrouei et al. (2023) for Falcon and Innocenti and Achour (2025), including a substantive comparison concerning bias-free architectures, normalization and multilayer proofs. It also elaborates the connection to Mazzawi et al.'s thought patches while retaining the existing research positioning.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds an impossibility theorem for fixed post-RMSNorm scaling, while Appendix E derives trace-loss gradient-step representations of the updates. V3 also introduces explicit nonzero-input/activation qualifications and per-layer conditions in its definitions and theorems. The original controllability lemmas and RMSNorm inversion derivation are largely retained under new numbering.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens support for the general architectural claim through Falcon validation and ablations that examine numerical failure and patch placement. Explicit assumptions, Appendix D and Section 6.1 also clarify the framework's boundaries, while Algorithm 1 addresses propagation of numerical errors. These gains outweigh limited reporting weaknesses, including removed hardware labels and Appendix C.2's inconsistency between its rank-correlation definition and interpreting near-zero plotted values as agreement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, and their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable. V2's Appendices A–B correspond to v3's retained material; v3 additionally includes Appendices C–E.

after.justification: V3 retains original Gemma experiments and reports additional Falcon-7B results, layer-depth ablations and scaling-variant comparisons in Appendix C.

before.justification: Section 4 and Figures 3–5 report original Gemma 3 experiments comparing contextual and patched generation, including token agreement, logit differences and total variation distance for text and image contexts.

results.title: Equivalence of Context and Parameter Updates in Modern Transformer Blocks

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the claim of a shared expected descent direction with the more precise claim that both strategies target the same weighted objective, and explicitly describe weights as prescribed and fixed. The three principal contributions concerning weighted-space analysis, penalty factors, and topology design remain.

C2.justification: Remark 6.6 explicitly limits the comparison to standard single-loop GT and disclaims universal minimax or lower-bound conclusions; Section 9 adds directed-graph and optimality limitations. The topology interpretation also changes substantially: v2's spectral-gap maximization claim becomes a narrower minimum-edge-coefficient guarantee requiring an additional edge condition.

D1.justification: v4 supplies the new weight vectors and tailored-graph degree sequences, clarifies that weights remain fixed across seeds and topology comparisons, and explains the additional scalar communication required by weighted mixing. Conversely, it removes the explicit least-squares step size α=0.12 supplied in v2, reducing reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate synthetic isotropic least-squares optimization and CIFAR-10 classification using the same topology families. Added network sizes, weight vectors, and partition imbalance vary configurations within this retained data and task coverage.

E2.justification: The empirical comparisons remain Strategy I versus Strategy II. The larger-network experiments extend these same comparators; newly cited algorithms are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v4 expands least-squares settings from 16 to 16/32/64 nodes and CIFAR-10 to 32 nodes, introduces more imbalanced weight vectors, and adds distance-to-optimum evaluation. The new CIFAR-10 curves cover 2,000 iterations versus 2,500 for retained settings. Appendix F.3 also revises A_i=ζ_i I to A_i=√ζ_i I while retaining the gradient formula; this establishes a specification correction, not evidence that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix F.4 and Figure 6 add a focused diagnostic testing whether both strategies approach the same optimum and comparing their residual errors. Larger-network experiments also extend robustness evidence under stronger weight imbalance, although network size and imbalance change together.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging ten seeds for least-squares and six for CIFAR-10, with the same composite noise-seed rule. No confidence intervals, significance tests, or new uncertainty-reporting practice are introduced.

E6.justification: The original 16-node plots and spectral-gap entries are retained. v4 adds larger-network convergence and classification results, distance-to-optimum curves, and spectral-gap entries: for example, the tailored 32-node graph reports 0.343 for W versus 0.040 for W_ds. These are additional results under new configurations, not improvements over v2 under unchanged settings.

M1.justification: The weighted GT updates and mixing-matrix construction remain unchanged. Algorithm 6 makes a limited pseudocode correction: initial degree deficits become max{0, d_i−deg(i)} instead of d_i−deg(i), retaining the same positive-deficit edge-selection and stopping rules.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain. v4 revises aggregate-dynamics and interpretation passages, adds motivation and consensus exposition in the appendices, and introduces explicit limitations and acknowledgments. Existing appendix material is largely retained under shifted lettering.

P2.justification: The separate CIFAR-10 figures become a full-width Figure 3 combining retained panels with a new 32-node row. v4 also adds larger-network least-squares, distance-to-optimum, and 32-node classification figures, and restructures Table 1 into network-size blocks. Existing adjacency diagrams and 16-node appendix plots are retained.

R1.justification: Related work adds bilevel optimization and Markovian sampling references, including Kong et al. (2025) and Sun et al. (2023), while new motivation cites additional weighted-learning literature. Fan (1949) is removed. The main positioning relative to diffusion, exact diffusion, and directed-network optimization remains.

T1.justification: Theorem 7.2 replaces the incorrect unnormalized quadratic form with a weighted Dirichlet form, and v4 adds ε≥1/2 for the spectral-gap reformulation. Corollary 7.3 and its proof are substantially replaced by a centered Rayleigh-quotient comparison and a different sufficient edge condition. Theorem 7.1 replaces fixed η=0.1 with a derived constant, while Appendix C corrects missing factors and summation terms in the convergence proof.

improvement.justification: v4 repairs an important deficiency in the central topology argument: the transformed Laplacian and its quadratic form are corrected, and the comparison accounts for the different orthogonality constraints in Theorem 7.2 and Corollary 7.3. Clearer applicability limits and additional convergence diagnostics further strengthen the paper. These substantive gains outweigh the limited reproducibility regression from omitting the least-squares step size.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same weighted decentralized gradient-tracking study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching material moved between appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds larger-network experiments and distance-to-optimum measurements in Section 8 and Appendix F.

before.justification: v2 reports original noisy least-squares experiments and ResNet-18 training on CIFAR-10, including convergence curves, test accuracies, and computed spectral gaps in Section 8 and Appendix E.

results.title: Row-Stochastic Matrices Can Provably Outperform Doubly Stochastic Matrices in Decentralized Learning

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction recast the problem around separate attention and capability gaps and introduce the proved approximation bound as a principal contribution. V1's abstract claim that sparse training improves extrapolation by mitigating attention sinks is removed in favor of broader long-context capability claims. Claims about strong benchmark performance and flexible inference budgets remain.

C2.justification: V1 attributes long-context failure to attention sinks; v2 Appendix L explicitly distinguishes the observed anomaly from sinks and instead explains it through RoPE frequency aliasing and token locality. Section 7.4 adds qualifications concerning SSA's retrieval beyond its alignment-training range, MoBA's longer-distance retrieval, and FullAttn's recovery after continued training. Appendix E newly acknowledges the kernel's lack of KV caching.

D1.justification: V2 adds an SSA code-access link, detailed RoPE settings, benchmark sample counts, decoding instructions, PG19 sampling information, and measured training and inference costs. Existing architecture and gating details largely move into Appendix C without changing. The newly disclosed evaluation details substantially improve reproducibility documentation without establishing that every corresponding setting changed.

E1.justification: V2 adds DCLM data for continued pretraining and efficiency testing at 64K and 128K contexts. SmolLM pretraining and the existing commonsense, WikiText, PG19, RULER NIAH, and LongBench evaluation coverage are retained. The expansion primarily extends the existing language-modeling scope.

E2.justification: The headline comparators remain FullAttn, MoBA, and NSA. Comparator membership changes in the NSA-component analysis: v1 Figure 5 includes selection-plus-window, window-only, and selection-only/MoBA controls that are absent from v2 Table A8's comparison with SSA. V2's NSA-nowindow corresponds to the earlier compression-plus-selection variant, rather than introducing an entirely new baseline.

E3.justification: Long-context evaluation is substantially redesigned around factor-4 RoPE scaling and an additional 10B tokens of continued training at 32K. ARC-Challenge changes from a stated 25-shot setting to 5-shot. NSA's window is reported as 128 tokens for both receptive fields, replacing v1's description of an additional half-receptive-field window. Figure 1 also replaces the 300M-model preliminary experiment with 1B-model results.

E4.justification: The core receptive-field, routing-ratio, alignment-direction, and alpha ablations are retained across v2 Tables 2 and A14. V2 adds L2 alignment, NSA-to-full-attention replacement tests, and RoPE/local-distance diagnostics, and revises the NSA window analysis. It removes the gated-attention comparison, fixed-budget block-configuration comparison, and long-context stream/alignment controls, substantially changing the supplementary evidence.

E5.justification: V1 does not state a repeated-evaluation or uncertainty-reporting procedure. V2 introduces five-seed commonsense averages with plus/minus quantities, lists the seeds, identifies LongBench and NIAH as single-run evaluations, and averages inference timing over 30 runs. These are evaluation repeats, not evidence of five independently trained models; the meaning of the plus/minus statistic is not explicitly defined.

E6.justification: Numerous results change, including SSA's full-inference WikiText perplexity from 15.19 to 15.28 in Table 1. Long-context tables are replaced and expanded under RoPE scaling and continued training; Figure 4 also changes the reported unscaled SSA trend from stability through 32K to divergence beyond the training window. Timing, NSA-conversion, and L2 results are added, while the core 300M ablation values remain. Changed protocols prevent interpreting the revision as uniform same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 corrects alignment-loss accumulation: v1 overwrites the accumulated loss inside the layer loop, whereas v2 adds each layer's contribution. This is a limited correction to the stated algorithm; both versions otherwise specify the same equal-probability full/sparse routing and bidirectional SmoothL1 alignment. It does not establish that the training implementation changed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method motivation, and results discussion are extensively rewritten around the two-gap framework. V1's background/observations structure becomes separate preliminary, theoretical-framework, and SSA sections. Appendices are substantially reorganized, Algorithm 1 moves out of the main text, and the alpha ablation moves into supplementary material.

P2.justification: Table 1 incorporates uncertainty displays, the long-context table is redesigned into parallel RoPE and continued-training comparisons, and the ablation table is reshaped and split. Figures 1 and 3 are redrawn and relabeled, Figure 4 is substantially redesigned, and the earlier appendix attention plots are replaced by RoPE, QK-product, and positional-distance displays alongside new tables.

R1.justification: V2 adds references for the efficient-attention survey, FlashAttention-2, DCLM, and WikiText, while removing the Vaswani, CoDI, and DoPE references. The related-work taxonomy and positioning relative to MoBA, NSA, InfLLM-v2, and DSA remain largely intact. Numerous publication and bibliographic updates concern the same cited works.

T1.justification: V2 adds Propositions 4.1 and 4.2, a formal capability/attention-gap decomposition, and Theorem 1 bounding attention-output error by dropped attention mass, with proofs in Appendices A and B. These go substantially beyond v1's formulas and empirical motivation. The sparse-attention complexity expression also changes from O((ks)^2) to O(Nks); the attention-sparsity definition itself is retained.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's support and reproducibility through a proved attention-approximation bound, repeated evaluation, measured costs, and explicit RoPE/continued-training controls. These substantially strengthen assessment of the central claims despite the loss of useful gating and block-configuration ablations. Some overstatement remains: Table A2 claims less than 18% training overhead, although continued training takes 176 versus 136 GPU-hours for SSA and MoBA at receptive field 256.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SSA research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports additional continued-training experiments, efficiency measurements, and diagnostic analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original model-training experiments, commonsense benchmark scores, perplexity, long-context retrieval results, and ablations.

results.title: SSA: Sparse Sparse Attention by Aligning Full and Sparse Attention Outputs in Feature Space

C1.justification: Both versions retain the central claim of training-free collaboration combining latent reasoning with lossless working-memory transfer, together with the same expressiveness, complexity, and headline performance claims. The additional backbone evaluations strengthen support for the existing generality claim.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive interpretations concerning the joint contribution of reasoning and communication, shorter final-answer decoding, generalization across model families, and debugging text as a faithful probe capable of locating errors. The existing heterogeneous-agent qualification merely moves from Appendix C.3 to G.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate GSM8K, AIME24/25, GPQA-Diamond, MedQA, ARC-E/ARC-C, MBPP+, and HumanEval+. The new backbone evaluations, ablations, and debugging cases reuse this existing task and dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v3 Table 7 adds two evaluated comparison variants: Latent Reasoning + Text Communication and Text Reasoning + Latent Communication. The original Single, Sequential TextMAS, and Hierarchical TextMAS comparator sets remain intact.

Alignment visualization adds Qwen3-14B; the existing Qwen3-8B analysis moves to Figure 11. The earlier depth analysis and beehive case study are retained.

E5.justification: v3 introduces a descriptive correctness-association analysis, reporting conditional proportions with explicit denominators for 80 correct and 20 incorrect final answers in Table 8. Three-independent-run averaging remains unchanged, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are added.

E6.justification: The original Qwen benchmark entries are unchanged after matching the renumbered tables. v3 adds Llama results and numerical findings on final-agent tokens, diversity, hybrid variants, and debugging. For example, Table 4 reports sequential ARC-E accuracy of 91.2% for LatentMAS versus 89.6% for TextMAS on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; this is a newly evaluated configuration, not a performance gain over v1.

M1.justification: v3 Appendix A.2 revises the alignment computation by multiplying the ridge solution by 1/beta, absent from v1 Appendix A.1. Appendix F also introduces optional parallel text probes for debugging. The core latent-generation and KV-memory-transfer architecture remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The established exposition is largely retained, with local rewrites, shorter section titles, separate efficiency and in-depth-analysis sections, and relocation of related work and discussion. Appendix A reverses the order of justification and derivation, and prompt headers rename Judger to Solver.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main-text layout and substantially rearranges displays, including moving the hierarchical benchmark table into the appendix. It adds Tables 4–8, reorganizes alignment plots, redisplays existing performance summaries, and removes Figure 8's accompanying numerical table while retaining its plot.

R1.justification: Section 6 and Appendix H add focused discussion of latent model collaboration and visual latent reasoning, including new citations such as Latent Visual Reasoning, Monet, and SWE-agent. Embodied-MAS surveys and Transformer Copilot are removed. The central positioning as training-free unification of latent reasoning and communication remains.

T1.justification: Appendix A replaces the token-index distribution model with bounded semantic combinations and an output-scale parameter beta. Theorem A.1 removes the distinct-row and nonsingular-alignment assumptions, changes the Wasserstein bound, and supplies a revised proof and alignment derivation. The main expressiveness, information-preservation, and complexity theorems remain substantively unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central mechanism through component ablations, non-Qwen evaluations, and direct accounting of final-agent token savings—questions not directly tested in v1. Quantitative diversity analysis and the generalized alignment argument further improve assessability. These gains are tempered by revised budget descriptions accompanying unchanged original scores and by debugging correlations that do not establish causal faithfulness, but the overall evidential improvement remains substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LatentMAS. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and the equations, tables, figures, and relocated material can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds Llama evaluations, component ablations, representation-diversity measurements, and debugging analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark accuracy, token usage, inference timing, alignment and latent-depth ablations, and a GSM8K case study.

results.title: Latent Collaboration in Multi-Agent Systems

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion add two central contributions: identifying regimes where calibrated LLM evaluation has lower variance than fully human evaluation, and establishing robustness advantages over other estimators under calibration/test distribution shift. The original bias-correction, uncertainty and adaptive-allocation claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 explains the variance advantage over human evaluation and why label shift undermines competing estimators. It explicitly qualifies robustness through stable conditional judge behavior, discusses length/style dependence and multiclass estimation difficulties, and softens v1's assertion that calibration-label composition is fully controllable to something sampling strategies can sometimes influence.

D1.justification: v2 documents the Arena judge identity and response-pair construction, and Appendix D supplies the distribution-shift data-generation settings. The repository information and printed Python implementation are retained. Arena judge prompts and per-model sample counts are not supplied.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only synthetic binary-judgment simulations. v2 adds real human-preference data from Chatbot Arena, estimating win rates for six target models, and a distinct scenario where calibration and test label distributions differ while judge behavior remains fixed.

E2.justification: Beyond the retained naive-estimator and equal-allocation comparisons, v2 evaluates calibration-only, difference and conditional-calibration estimators against the proposed estimator in Figure 5. Table 1 identifies their formulas; the difference estimator is attributed to Angelopoulos et al. (2023a).

E3.justification: v2 adds an Arena protocol using GPT-4.1-mini, human-preference labels and random 90%/10% test/calibration splits. Its shift experiment fixes test accuracy at 0.5 and varies calibration accuracy from 0.25 to 0.75, with n=1000 and m=200. The n=200 simulation branch is removed. Both calibration budgets, 200 and 500, already existed in v1 and remain in v2.

E4.justification: Section 7 and Figure 5 add a substantive robustness analysis testing how calibration/test label shift affects competing estimators' bias. Conversely, v1's small-test-set sensitivity results in Appendix C.1–C.2 disappear. Analyses varying judge reliability and calibration budget remain.

E5.justification: v2 adds reporting over 100 random Arena splits, including averaged bias, interval coverage and interval length. The existing 10,000-replication Monte Carlo practice and 95% confidence-interval construction are retained; no increase in the retained simulations' replication count is stated.

E6.justification: v2 adds label-shift bias results and reduced Arena bias across all six targets. Table 2 reports 95%–99% coverage and average interval lengths of 0.178–0.267. Retained simulation plots also show different estimates and interval lengths under matching captions, while n=200 results disappear. The Figure 3 budget example changes from approximately 200 samples per class to 200 total despite retaining the same curves.

M1.justification: The estimator, confidence-interval formula and adaptive allocation rule are retained. Algorithm 1 corrects its final assignment from 'm1 ← m − m0' to 'm0 = m − m1', fixing the written budget-completion step. The printed estimator and confidence-interval code is unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, problem setup and method/theory exposition undergo extensive rewriting, including contribution bullets and a more explicitly structured problem statement. Related work precedes the setup, empirical validation is divided into simulations and Arena evaluation, and Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix A. The appendix organization is substantially revised.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from one column to two columns, with redesigned figures, legends, captions and equation placement. v2 adds the human-variance diagram, distribution-shift plot, Arena bias chart and two tables. Eight small-test-set simulation figures are removed, and retained plots and the code listing are reformatted and redistributed.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated Related Work section and substantially develops positioning against prediction-powered inference and calibration-based estimation. New citations include PPI++, cross-prediction-powered inference, Kloos et al., Meertens et al. and Miller. Section 7 makes distributional assumptions a central distinction from prior approaches.

T1.justification: v2 adds Proposition 6.1 and its proof characterizing when calibrated LLM evaluation has lower variance than human-only evaluation. Section 7 formalizes label shift, confusion-matrix invariance and competing estimators' assumptions; Appendix B.3 adds an estimator-equivalence derivation. The earlier bias and allocation propositions remain, with the bias proposition reparameterized using total calibration budget.

improvement.justification: v1 supports the framework through stylized simulations. v2 substantially strengthens practical validation and method selection through Arena results, explicit estimator comparisons under label shift, and a proved variance comparison with human evaluation. These gains outweigh the removed n=200 simulations and the new Figure 3 budget-example error: the retained formula gives an interval length around 0.13 at 200 total samples, above the claimed 0.1 target. Missing Arena prompts and sample counts still limit reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and retain the same central estimation framework. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and visual inspection resolves extraction issues in equations, figures and tables.

after.justification: v2 reports Monte Carlo results, a distribution-shift simulation, and original Chatbot Arena evaluations using GPT-4.1-mini judgments in Sections 7–8 and Appendices D–E.

before.justification: v1 reports original Monte Carlo results on estimation bias, confidence-interval coverage and calibration allocation in Section 5 and Appendix C.

results.title: How to Correctly Report LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluations

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the central bias-correction, uncertainty, allocation and conditional robustness claims. The introduction makes a limited addition to the contribution list by explicitly promising empirical positioning of contemporary judges within the variance regimes.

C2.justification: V4 adds substantive discussion of human disagreement, task-dependent variance advantages and ranking deterioration caused by limited calibration. Appendix B discusses rare-category estimation difficulties. Appendix A expands the earlier nuisance-factor discussion, adds complementarity with judge debiasing and adaptation, and removes the conformal-prediction future direction. These changes substantially clarify applicability and failure conditions.

D1.justification: Added appendices document response-pair selection and positive-class encoding for judge positioning, multicategory calibration construction, and ground-truth ranking construction and split settings. The binary Python listing and stated repository access are retained, moving from Appendix C to Appendix F.

E1.justification: V4 adds AlpacaEval data for GPT-4 win-rate analysis and a synthetic six-category review-score distribution-estimation task. The review categories label simulated outcomes, not actual reviews. Existing Chatbot Arena coverage and binary simulation configurations are retained.

E2.justification: The distribution-shift comparison retains the naive, calibration-only, difference/PPI and conditional-calibration comparators. Added experiments continue comparing raw judgments with corrected estimates. Additional LLM judges supply alternative judge configurations, rather than new correction baselines.

E3.justification: V4 introduces seven-judge Chatbot Arena positioning and four-judge AlpacaEval protocols, plus a six-category simulation with 1,000 test and 200 calibration items. Appendix K adds Kendall's tau, exact-ranking recovery and a GPT-4.1 condition using a 60%/40% test/calibration split. The original binary simulations and 90%/10% Chatbot Arena protocol are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses locate measured judge characteristics within theoretical variance regimes and examine whether judgment bias distorts model rankings. Appendix K also tests calibration-budget sensitivity through the additional 40% calibration condition. Original allocation analyses, distribution-shift experiments and the appendix binary simulation grid are retained.

E5.justification: New Table 3 reports means and standard errors over 10 multicategory Monte Carlo repetitions. Existing confidence-interval reporting, 10,000 binary simulation replications and 100 random Chatbot Arena splits remain unchanged; the new repetition count does not indicate fewer runs for retained experiments.

E6.justification: Original Table 1 values and matched plots are retained. V4 adds category-count estimates, judge characteristics, additional bias results and ranking outcomes. Table 4 reports raw/corrected exact-ranking recovery of 0%/37% for Gemini-3-Flash, 86%/46% for GPT-4.1 with 10% calibration, and 61%/75% with 40% calibration. These are newly reported comparisons under distinct conditions, not improvements over v3 scores. Figure 20 displays five target models despite adjacent prose referring to six.

M1.justification: Appendix B develops v3's prospective multinomial extension into an explicit, tested k-category estimator using an estimated confusion-matrix inverse. This extends the procedure's inputs and outputs, while the binary estimator, confidence-interval construction and adaptive allocation algorithm remain unchanged.

P1.justification: V4 edits introductory prose, adjusts the ordering within Section 6, moves future work into Appendix A and reorganizes the appendices. Author affiliations and publication information also change. Most existing exposition and the main section sequence remain intact, so the added scientific material does not amount to wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: V4 adds judge-positioning Figures 6 and 11, asymmetric-regime Figure 9, the three-panel bias Figure 20, and Tables 3 and 4. Figure 1 gains sensitivity/specificity labels, while existing displays are resized, relocated or renumbered. This substantially expands the visual presentation; retained plots are not new results merely because they moved.

R1.justification: V4 adds the Li et al. (2023) AlpacaEval reference and discusses complementarity with judge-level debiasing and adaptation. Positioning relative to Rogan–Gladen correction, PPI and conditional calibration remains substantially unchanged. Other bibliography revisions mainly concern formatting and metadata.

T1.justification: Proposition 6.1 and its appendix proof expand the variance comparison from equal sensitivity and specificity to asymmetric q0 and q1, deriving a generalized condition and admissible accuracy interval. Appendix B additionally formalizes multicategory labels, confusion-matrix estimation and the nonsingularity requirement. The original binary estimator and confidence-interval derivations remain.

improvement.justification: V3's variance theorem covered symmetric judge errors and lacked empirical positioning of real judges. V4 generalizes that theorem and connects it to measured judge characteristics on two benchmarks. The ranking experiments expose calibration-induced losses as well as benefits, and expanded limitations make the guarantees more useful and better qualified. These are substantial improvements in theoretical applicability and evidential support, despite minor inconsistencies such as Appendix K's six-model prose accompanying five-model bias plots.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. All 18 pages of v3 and 22 pages of v4, including their appendices, provide readable text, equations, tables and figures sufficient for reliable comparison.

after.justification: V4 retains those results and adds multicategory simulations, empirical judge-positioning analyses, AlpacaEval results and ranking-recovery experiments.

before.justification: V3 reports original Monte Carlo simulations, Chatbot Arena analyses and distribution-shift experiments in Sections 7–8 and the appendices.

results.title: How to Correctly Report LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluations

C1.justification: V2 extends the claimed contributions from closed-form transforms with preliminary RTN evidence to GPTQ integration and efficient GPU implementation. Its abstract and introduction claim quantified W4A4 advantages and up to 6.6-fold per-layer throughput. The abstract and conclusion also qualify the earlier blanket optimality wording to near-optimality.

C2.justification: V2 Appendix A.2 explains why equalizing coordinate marginals can leave multivariate outliers intact. Section 6 adds explanations involving NVFP4's group size and top-element preservation, and qualifies NVFP4 accuracy gains as often within run-to-run variability. The earlier interpretation of MXFP4 as exhibiting mixed FP/INT behavior remains.

D1.justification: V2 adds detailed GPTQ pseudocode, CUTLASS kernel design, transform storage layout, tiling and hardware information, plus a source-code link. Appendix B newly discloses emulated BF16/FP16 quantization, disabled Qwen thinking mode and the Llama MMLU-CoT reporting convention. These disclosures do not establish that those existing evaluation settings changed.

E1.justification: V2 adds C4 evaluation following FineWeb calibration (Appendix B, Table 3). The existing FineWeb-Edu layer-loss evaluation and LM Evaluation Harness/Platinum task coverage are retained. Additional model sizes expand configurations rather than dataset or domain coverage.

E2.justification: V1's end-to-end comparisons primarily use identity and Hadamard transforms with RTN. V2 Table 2 adds reported comparisons with SmoothQuant, QuaRot, SpinQuant, GPTQ-I and GPTQ-H/MR-GPTQ. GPTQ comparators also enter retained Platinum experiments, while Figure 2 introduces GPU comparisons against QuTLASS Hadamard-plus-quantization and bare FP4 kernels.

E3.justification: V2 introduces GPTQ evaluation, Qwen3-32B accuracy experiments, C4 KL-divergence measurement and BF16-normalized GPU throughput tests. The latter specify RTX 5090, batch size 1024, group size 32 and multiple layer shapes, including Llama-3.1-70B. The original layer-loss protocol remains 32 calibration samples of length 2048.

E4.justification: The original WUS-removal and layer-loss ablation is retained. V2 Section 5 and Figure 2 add an overhead analysis comparing bare FP4 GEMM, Hadamard-plus-quantization and WUSH-plus-quantization, examining the runtime cost of using distinct adaptive transforms across blocks.

E5.justification: Appendix B newly states that results are aggregated over multiple random seeds, including the C4 results. V1 already reports ten-run random-rotation averages and Platinum standard deviations. V2 does not establish increased run counts or introduce significance tests, and exact seed counts remain unspecified.

E6.justification: V2 adds GPTQ, C4, Qwen3-32B and GPU results and revises existing entries. Qwen3-8B MXFP4 RTN-WUSH average accuracy changes from 75.45 in v1 Table 2 to 74.91 in v2 Table 4. Llama-3.1-8B MXFP4 RTN-WUSH remains 73.21 while RTN-H changes from 71.47 to 70.45. These are reported-result revisions; complete cross-version protocol equivalence is not documented. Table 1 changes only scaling and rounding.

M1.justification: The closed-form WUSH construction is retained, but v2 Algorithm 1 adds GPTQ integration with interleaved transform construction and intra-block/inter-block error propagation, alongside an RTN fallback. This implements a substantive procedure that v1 explicitly left as future work.

P1.justification: V2 separates Related Work and Methodology from the introduction, moves the algorithm before the theory, and relocates extensive derivations into Appendix A. It substantially rewrites the abstract and explanatory narrative, introduces dedicated GPU coverage and reorganizes the experimental presentation.

P2.justification: V2 adds geometric and approximation illustrations, GPU speedup plots and a KL-divergence table. Accuracy tables are restructured, while existing Platinum heatmaps and boxplots are enlarged, arranged vertically and largely moved to Appendix B. Table 1 changes its displayed scale to 10^-3.

R1.justification: V2 positions MR-GPTQ as the state-of-the-art comparison target, discusses its QuTLASS kernels and connects the integration to Chen et al.'s GPTQ formulation. The underlying cited works are retained; changes such as FlatQuant's publication update are bibliographic rather than new research coverage.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix A.1 adds a decomposition-invariance lemma and proof, and Appendix A.3 supplies derivations for previously asserted special cases. The central optimality theorem, quantization-noise models and Gaussian/Laplacian bounds are retained; much of the expanded appendix relocates existing mathematics.

improvement.justification: V1 left GPTQ integration and efficient kernels as open problems; v2 supplies an algorithm, implementation details and measured evidence addressing both. Broader baseline comparisons and reproducibility disclosures substantially strengthen practical validation. A material caveat is that the headline 6.6-fold speedup corresponds to bare FP4 in Figure 2; WUSH including transformation and quantization peaks near 5.8-fold. This overstatement and incomplete seed details temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WUSH research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization.

after.justification: Sections 5–6 and Appendix B report original quantization losses, model accuracy, C4 KL-divergence results and GPU measurements.

before.justification: Section 3 reports original quantization losses and Llama/Qwen benchmark accuracy in Tables 1–2 and Figures 1–4.

C1.justification: The central benchmark contribution and warning about insecure agent-generated code remain. However, v2's claim that mitigation fails to increase correct-and-secure solutions is qualified in v3 to acknowledge modest increases with functional costs. The headline insecurity claim is also moderated from over 80% to over 70%.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly identifies implementation-coupled tests as a threat to evaluating alternative secure solutions. It replaces v2's explanation of self-selection's inferiority with a hypothesis that contextual risk understanding makes it competitive with oracle guidance, and adds explanations involving domain knowledge and cross-file coordination. The general limitations in Appendix E remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds curation-stage yields, repository/CWE mappings, and the expert-review rubric and cross-checking procedure. It newly specifies removal of .git history and identifies o3 as the log-parser model; these disclosures do not establish when those implementation choices changed. Most existing prompts, Docker instructions, and project-access links are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate repository-level, security-sensitive Python feature requests drawn from ReposVul and MoreFixes across ten application domains. v3 documents screening the existing 200 tasks down to 186 and correcting CWE annotations. The changed sample counts, domain categorization, and 77-to-79 CWE count do not establish additional task or language coverage.

E2.justification: Gemini 3 Pro already appears in v2 Table 5, so merging its results into v3 Table 3 does not add an overall comparator. However, v3 includes it in the conditional-security and CWE-category comparisons in Section 4.2 and Figure 4, where v2's corresponding analyses compare only three models. The frameworks and mitigation comparators are retained.

E3.justification: v3 evaluates 186 retained tasks with revised security tests and corrected CWE annotations. Conditional model-security comparisons expand from three models using OpenHands to four models with results averaged across frameworks. CWE grouping and domain stratification also change, and the transition matrix switches from generic-to-oracle to generic-to-self-selection. The pass@1 metrics and 200-step limit remain.

E4.justification: v3 adds an expert audit quantifying security-test implementation coupling (Appendix B.5) and a four-model analysis relating performance to the number of edited files (Appendix A, Table 9). It revises the CWE, domain, and mitigation analyses and removes the Wagtail step-count anecdote. The four detailed vulnerability case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without adding repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests for agent performance. The new expert review does not introduce uncertainty estimates or inter-rater agreement statistics.

E6.justification: Results are extensively replaced under revised benchmark conditions. SWE-Agent with Claude 4 Sonnet changes from 61.0/10.5 FuncPass/SecPass in v2 to 57.0/11.8 in v3. Mitigation SecPass changes from generic/self-selection/oracle scores of 10.5/9.5/10.5 to 11.8/14.5/15.1. The leading conditional-security framework changes from OpenHands to SWE-Agent under revised aggregation. These are not isolated same-setting performance gains; v3 also adds audit and task-complexity results.

M1.justification: The benchmark-construction method gains a substantive human quality-control stage. Beyond v2's execution-based validation, v3 adds expert review, manual revision of implementation-coupled security tests, and a second cross-check determining final task inclusion (Section 3.2; Appendix B.5). The feature-masking procedure and mitigation strategies remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The introduction and benchmark motivation are substantially rewritten, related work is reorganized, and mitigation explanations are revised. The appendices now begin with expanded dataset statistics, followed by reorganized curation documentation. These are substantial narrative and structural edits beyond changes in scientific content or pagination.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column report to a two-column conference layout. Pipeline diagrams are redrawn, the CWE Venn diagrams become grouped bars, and the domain chart gains separate project/task encodings. Gemini results are consolidated, new appendix tables appear, and the verification and Django illustrations move into the appendices.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning through vibe-coding studies, HumanEval/MBPP and newer SWE-bench-related work, plus a new discussion of vulnerability detection, exploitation, and repair. Devign, PrimeVul, CVE-Bench, PatchEval, and SEC-Bench help articulate the distinction between preventing vulnerabilities during feature implementation and addressing existing vulnerabilities.

T1.justification: Section 5 changes the definition of the auxiliary incorrect-solution ratio: v2 conditions on the union of securely solved tasks across all settings, whereas v3 conditions on tasks securely solved by other strategies. This changes its denominator. The main benchmark mathematics remains, and neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2's execution checks could accept security tests tied to one reference implementation. v3's expert audit, manual revisions, and cross-checking directly address this important measurement-validity problem (Section 3.2; Appendix B.5). Corrected CWE annotations and the new complexity analysis further strengthen the evidence. These gains outweigh retaining 14 fewer tasks, although the revised scores cannot establish performance changes under fixed conditions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SUSVIBES and contain readable main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Their revised task sets and evaluation settings permit a reliable content comparison, although updated scores are not uniformly comparable under identical conditions.

after.justification: v3 reports agent evaluations on 186 tasks, mitigation experiments, and additional original analyses of task complexity and expert assessments of security-test quality.

before.justification: v2 reports original coding-agent evaluations, security-prompting experiments, and vulnerability case studies. Tables 3 and 5 together evaluate three frameworks with four models.

results.title: Is Vibe Coding Safe? Benchmarking Vulnerability of Agent-Generated Code in Real-World Tasks

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion expand from improved inference-time tool use to experience-driven policy learning through RL. v2 adds claims of improved long-horizon exploration and generalization to unseen tasks and tools without domain-specific experience collection, together with quantified inference and out-of-distribution RL improvement claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of RL exploration versus experience reuse, domain-dependent skip rates, possible SFT overfitting, candidate-count noise, and summarization speed–accuracy tradeoffs. Appendix F identifies weaker adherence to external guidance as a limitation of stronger reasoning models. v1 discusses smaller-model benefits but lacks these RL interpretations and the specific adherence limitation.

D1.justification: Appendices C–E supply previously missing retrieval details, including all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings and cosine similarity, exact summarization prompts, invocation and context-handling rules, and initial-memory collection procedures. They also document RL hyperparameters, hardware and timing. These substantially improve reproducibility; newly disclosed inference details do not establish that retained experiments were changed or rerun.

E1.justification: The four benchmark families and ACEBench's online-memory scenario are retained. v2 additionally reports RL transfer experiments, but Section 5.1 describes τ-Bench as Telecom for evaluation and Retail for training, without clearly matching these subsets to the result tables. The PDFs do not reliably establish whether additional domain/task data are introduced or only the learning and evaluation design changes.

E2.justification: v2 introduces a substantial RL comparison against standard GRPO, SFT on successful H-EPM trajectories, and AgentEvolver (Table 3). The original inference comparators—base models, ReasoningBank, ToolNet and retrieval—and the GNN4Plan ablation are retained.

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen3-4B/8B inference configurations, evaluates the method directly with GPT-5.1, and introduces GRPO training on 500 tasks for one epoch, with batch size 8 and eight rollouts per task. New controlled protocols vary candidate counts, summarization strategies and RL guidance. The original benchmark metrics and approximately 800/200 ToolSandbox split remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The original component, efficiency and graph-traversal ablations are retained. v2 adds candidate-count and weight-parameter sensitivity, a 30-trajectory entropy analysis, implicit versus explicit summarization, RL skip-rate comparisons, half versus all guided rollouts, and masking versus discarding guidance (Tables 3–5 and 7–10). Figure 4 also adds a detailed trajectory case study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports evaluation seeds, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals or significance tests. v2's training rollout counts and entropy-analysis sample size describe data collection; they do not introduce statistical uncertainty reporting for the performance estimates.

E6.justification: The retained GPT-4 inference scores, ACEBench results and original ablation values are unchanged. Substantial new entries include Qwen evaluations, GPT-5.1 with H-EPM, RL comparisons and supplementary analyses. For example, v2 Table 2 newly reports GPT-5.1 with H-EPM at 0.921 on τ²-Bench alongside the retained 0.842 base score. v1's GPT-5.1 ACEBench scores, 0.433 end-to-end and 0.674 process accuracy, are removed.

M1.justification: The renamed method retains the graph-based adaptive inference design. v2 substantially extends it to memory-guided GRPO training, including probabilistic skipping of procedural suggestions, memory updates during training, and masking or discarding added guidance during policy optimization (Section 4.3; Appendix C.5).

P1.justification: v2 retitles the paper, renames the method, and substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, formulation and methodology around hybrid memory and learning. Related work and experiments are reorganized, with graph-related discussions and ACEBench moved to appendices. This is extensive narrative restructuring beyond the added scientific content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns, with resized and relocated displays. v1 Figures 2 and 3 become v2 Figures 1 and 2, while v1 Figure 1 moves to Appendix B as Figure 3. Tables 1 and 4 expand, the GPT-5.1 comparison is restructured, and new RL/analysis tables and trajectory Figure 4 substantially extend the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v1 positions its method as avoiding SFT/RL training costs; v2 positions it as improving experience reuse and exploration within RL. It introduces a substantive contrast with AgentEvolver and adds GRPO/DeepSeekMath and HybridFlow references. RLFactory and Hou et al. are dropped, while the existing tool-graph and graph-memory discussions are retained in Appendix A.

T1.justification: Section 4.2 revises the stated weight definition from successful tool-pair invocations to successful trajectories containing the transition, explicitly indexing the reciprocal-length sum by trajectory. Section 3 also replaces set-union history updates with ordered histories. These are limited formal revisions; no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v2 resolves v1's deferred GPT-5.1 method evaluation through a same-backbone comparison, supplies critical missing implementation details, and adds controls that test retrieval and RL design choices. These changes substantially strengthen reproducibility and evidential support beyond merely expanding scope. Unclear benchmark-domain mappings and incorrect appendix cross-references limit precision, and statistical uncertainty remains unreported, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same state-annotated tool-graph research, renamed from SIT-Graph to H-EPM and extended in v2. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout. v1 ends with references and has no appendices; v2's Appendices A–F are available and included in the comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds model evaluations, reinforcement-learning comparisons, sensitivity experiments, entropy measurements and computational-cost results.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, online-memory experiments on ACEBench, and component and retrieval ablations in Tables 1–4.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the central contribution from attention-map and moment convergence to horizon-dependent recovery of full-network logits, predictions, and classification accuracy. The refined geometric horizon also becomes a more explicit organizing claim.

C2.justification: v3 explains slowdown through alignment between attention directions and high-variance token directions. It corrects the earlier suggestion that the original text experiments tested non-i.i.d. sampling, distinguishing dependent source text from structured subsampling. It also adds heavy-tail failure discussion and interprets downstream results as diminishing returns from additional keys.

D1.justification: v3 replaces the supplementary-code statement with an explicit repository link and supplies details for the new experiments, including mean pooling, fine-tuning duration, and window/hybrid construction. The existing BigBird reference-token, subsample-size, and repetition details are relocated to Appendix A rather than removed.

E1.justification: v3 adds an 11-category arxiv-classification task and synthetic tokens uniformly distributed on a unit sphere in dimension 50. These substantially extend coverage beyond v2's Gaussian simulations and Wikipedia/CC-News attention-statistics experiments, which are retained.

E2.justification: Population or full-context attention remains the reference for finite-token approximation, with this comparison extended to classification. BERT supplies an additional validation architecture, and window/hybrid sampling supplies robustness conditions; no competing baseline algorithm is introduced or removed.

E3.justification: v3 adds BERT evaluation, local-window sampling with 50 random keys, and half-local/half-random sampling. Classification introduces three-epoch fine-tuning, 2400 test documents, 64–4096 sampled keys, and prediction-level metrics. Horizon diagnostics use the revised definition. The original reference-token and subsample-size settings remain in Appendix A.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether slowdown persists beyond Gaussian tokens, BigBird's sparse architecture, and i.i.d. key sampling (Figures 8–11). Figure 2 additionally stratifies downstream behavior by horizon. These directly investigate robustness and applicability questions that v2's experiments did not establish.

E5.justification: v3 reports five Monte Carlo repetitions and ±3σ bands for classification, and 500–1000 subsamples with ±3 standard-error bands for BERT. The original 500-repetition budget is retained. Some uncertainty labeling is removed: v2 Figure 5 explicitly identifies 95% confidence intervals, whereas corresponding v3 Figure 7 does not.

E6.justification: New classification results report 86.4% dense accuracy and 84.5% at 1101 sampled keys, alongside new BERT, sphere, and windowed-sampling results. Existing BigBird plots also change: the mean horizon-rate correlation becomes -0.64 from -0.68 under the revised horizon definition. Figure 6's exact exponents are inconsistent between legend and caption, although both report sub-parametric convergence.

M1.justification: The underlying single-head and multi-head attention operators remain unchanged. Absorbing the attention scaling into the query/key matrices clarifies notation. The new architectures and sampling patterns are experimental settings, while the revised horizon changes the analysis rather than the proposed computational method.

P1.justification: The main section sequence remains intact. v3 tightens explanatory passages and proof sketches, moves experimental appendix material ahead of the theoretical tools, and relocates implementation details. Affiliations, correspondence information, publication text, and acknowledgements are also updated.

P2.justification: v3 adds substantial multipanel classification, BERT, and structured-sampling figures. Existing horizon plots are redrawn with revised axes and legends, and BigBird covariance displays are combined with BERT panels in Figure 9. The expanded experimental figures move from the final appendix to Appendix A.

R1.justification: The reference list is unchanged. Section 2 removes the distinction that this work studies moments whereas Boursier and Boyer study L2 error, consistent with v3's added MSE result. Other research positioning remains substantially stable.

T1.justification: v3 replaces Ψ = ||Σ||₂||Σ^(1/2)A||₂² with H² = ||Σ^(1/2)AΣ^(1/2)||₂² in the moment-rate bounds, supported by ellipsoidal truncation and optimization over an invertible matrix. It adds general-set convergence, MSE and layer-composition corollaries, a heavy-tail counterexample argument, and polynomial-radius bounds under additional assumptions in Appendix E. The uniform-denominator proof is substantially revised, but its new sample-size threshold is not reconciled with Theorem 4.2.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens practical validation: v2 measured attention moments, while v3 directly tests downstream predictions and accuracy and checks architectural and sampling robustness. The geometric refinement and clearer treatment of the i.i.d. assumption also improve explanatory value. These gains outweigh remaining inconsistencies, including Figure 6's conflicting exponents and the unreconciled theorem/proof sample-size thresholds, which limit confidence in precise quantitative claims.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Token Sample Complexity of Attention by the same authors. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v3 retains original convergence experiments and adds uniform-sphere simulations, BERT experiments, structured-sampling tests, and downstream classification results.

before.justification: v2 reports original Monte Carlo experiments on Gaussian tokens and attention-output convergence experiments using BigBird on Wikipedia and CC-News, including appendix results.

results.title: Token Sample Complexity of Attention

C1.justification: Alongside the retained framework, stability, and pruning contributions, v4 elevates training-set-only model and recipe selection across four deployment scenarios to a main contribution. Its conclusion also adds a two-phase TPV–test-loss relationship, substantially extending and qualifying v2's broad empirical correlation claim.

C2.justification: v4 explains that low TPV can accompany underfitting and higher test loss, restricting useful positive correlation primarily to low-training-loss regimes. It adds weaker cross-architecture reliability and optimizer-dependent applicability limitations in Appendix I. It also explains why sharpness and label-noise sensitivity can respond differently to Jacobian spectral changes.

D1.justification: Appendices D.3.4, G.3, and I provide substantial new reproducibility information: noise calibration, regularization grids, architecture specifications, BERT tokenization, optimizer schedules, checkpoint evaluation, and Pets head replacement and fine-tuning instructions. The code-repository link is unchanged; the addition is primarily technical documentation.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained synthetic, CIFAR, and ImageNet coverage, v4 evaluates AG News topic classification and TREC question classification with 20% label corruption, and transfer learning on Oxford-IIIT Pets with 10% corruption. It also adds CIFAR-100 training trajectories under 30% corrupted labels.

E2.justification: The new training-recipe comparison evaluates Jacobian sharpness, Tr(Heff), against training-set label-noise TPV as predictors of test-set sensitivity (Figure 11; Appendix I.4). The pruning comparator set remains Jacobian, L1, BatchNorm scale, FPGM, WHC, Taylor, and Random.

E3.justification: The retained ImageNet experiment's reported protocol changes from 10 SGD epochs at learning rate 10^-6 with fixed sigma = 0.01 to five AdamW epochs at 10^-8 with adaptive noise scaling. New experiments introduce regularization grids, checkpoint-based TPV evaluation, and a two-phase Pets fine-tuning protocol. These are substantive experimental-design changes.

E4.justification: v4 adds single-regularizer sensitivity sweeps examining underfitting and overfitting, plus TPV trajectories through image-classifier training and BERT fine-tuning (Section 5.3; Appendix G.3). These investigate when the TPV–test-loss relationship holds or reverses, beyond v2's retained width, sample-size, and perturbation-size analyses.

E5.justification: v4 newly specifies ImageNet sampling seed 0 and repetition details for added trajectory experiments, including three perturbation runs per BERT checkpoint. Appendix I.4 introduces qualitative Spearman-correlation reporting for recipe rankings. Retained experiments keep their repetition counts; no new confidence-interval or significance-testing framework is introduced.

E6.justification: New results include U-shaped TPV–test-loss relationships for label smoothing and dropout, training-trajectory patterns, Pets model-selection outcomes, and opposing sharpness versus TPV rankings in Figure 11. ImageNet TPV values also change under the revised protocol, rather than demonstrating a same-setting gain. Original pruning and width/stability findings are retained.

M1.justification: Appendix D.3.4 adds adaptive perturbation scaling, sigma = c times sigma_0, where c is the reference model's mean absolute output. This modifies noise generation in the existing perturb-and-retrain estimator. The central trace framework and JBR scoring procedure remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, empirical narrative, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Related work moves earlier, empirical verification and applications become separate sections, and the full JBR derivation and pruning discussion move into a dedicated appendix. This substantially reorganizes the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v4 adds regularization, trajectory, and model-selection figures and redraws the ImageNet plot. Original pruning displays are consolidated in Appendix H as Figures 21–24, retaining both MAC and pruned-filter-percentage views. Existing stability figures are also relocated or resized, producing substantial visual reorganization beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v4 adds connections to information-bottleneck analyses and epoch-wise double descent, citing Tishby and Zaslavsky, Shwartz-Ziv and Tishby, and Nakkiran et al., alongside new dataset and regularization references. Several NTK and spectral-bias references are removed. The central local-versus-global positioning remains, and pruning-related work is retained in Appendix H.2.

T1.justification: The stability theorem now assumes isotropic covariance and replaces the NTK coefficient 2 with (n_train+n_test)/p. Appendix A replaces the spectral-to-operator-norm inference with a trace-based proof. SGD and quantization statements change zero-loss assumptions to small nonzero residuals, and v4 removes the finite-sample assertion X-transpose-X/n = I when n is smaller than the input dimension.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses an important proof gap in v2's Appendix A through an explicit isotropy restriction and trace-based argument. Its new regularization analyses reveal when low TPV indicates underfitting, materially improving interpretation of the proposed generalization signal, while detailed protocols improve reproducibility. The narrower theorem still does not establish every broader model-selection claim, and cross-architecture rankings remain imperfect, but the gains in rigor and applicability boundaries are substantial.
