A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TPV framework and JBR pruning method. Their text, equations, figures, references, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v4.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical experiments and adds regularization, training-trajectory, and model-selection results, including BERT text-classification and Oxford-IIIT Pets experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original synthetic, CIFAR-10/100, and ImageNet experiments on TPV stability, label-noise sensitivity, and pruning, including supplementary results in Appendix F.

results.title: TPV: Parameter Perturbations Through the Lens of Test Prediction Variance

C1.justification: The central contributions remain an expert-grounded taxonomy, fixed rubrics, task-specific guidance, and report-wide information verification. v3 updates the claimed rubric resource from 130 to 101 items. Its conclusion also drops v1's explicit assertion that systems lag behind human experts, focusing instead on shortcomings in request fulfillment and analytical soundness.

C2.justification: v1 characterizes granular rubrics as worsening evaluator reliability and dense extraction with small batches as essential. v3 interprets granular rubrics as producing a slight reliability recovery, finds that greater extraction density need not improve coverage, and favors batch 20 for efficiency. Appendix F additionally identifies severe verification-label imbalance and interprets the new adversarial tests. The original limitations paragraph remains unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds substantial reproducibility information: actual model/service configurations, evaluator identities and costs, human rating instructions, taskwise correlation and tie handling, metric normalization, and detailed prompt templates. It also adds a DEER repository link. These fill gaps in v1, whose promised baseline-configuration appendix instead contains benchmark comparisons; newly disclosed details alone do not establish procedural changes.

E1.justification: Both versions retain coverage of 50 HLE-derived report tasks across 13 domains. v3 adds an adversarial verification scenario using human-reviewed claims with negated meanings or altered numerical values (Appendix F.3, Table 16). The larger query-log sample does not itself establish broader report-task coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparison replaces Claude Opus 4.1 with 4.5, replaces Gemini Pro with Flash for the fast setting, and removes Gemini think+search. Claim extraction compares GPT-5 and GPT-5-mini instead of GPT-4.1 and GPT-5-mini. v3 also compares OpenAI embedding retrieval against BM25. These revise comparator sets across several experiments; the sliding-window comparators remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported query-log sample changes from 5,045 to 5,842, and Figure 3(b) changes from two sampled tasks per domain to all tasks. Rubric and diversity metrics change, verification ablations switch to GPT-5-mini, and new experiments vary retrieval, reasoning effort, and context size. Human correlation now averages per-judge metrics, whereas v1 describes correlating averaged judge scores with human scores.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands verification analysis with a batch-size, reasoning-effort, retrieval-method, and Top-K study on original and adversarial claims (Table 16). It removes v1's class-specific classification diagnostics (Table 15). The backtracking-versus-sliding-window analysis on 131 claims is retained unchanged as v3 Table 15.

E5.justification: v3 Table 2 adds standard deviations across five evaluator models to human-correlation results previously reported as point estimates. Figure 3(b) also adds ± variability annotations, without clearly defining them. These are additions to uncertainty reporting, not evidence of additional repeated runs.

E6.justification: The main score table is extensively revised: Qwen3-235B fast's mean changes from 6.67 to 5.11 under revised scoring, so this is not a same-setting performance decline. The granular-rubric Pearson correlation changes from 0.53 to 0.62 and Krippendorff's alpha from 0.17 to 0.33; expert-guidance values remain 0.75 and 0.55. v3 adds adversarial results and removes v1's per-class classification results.

M1.justification: The hybrid architecture and semantic backtracking remain, but the reported rubric changes from 40 elements/130 items to 46 criteria/101 items. Diversity scoring changes from CV to normalized HHI, the selected retrieval configuration changes from BM25 to OpenAI embeddings, and verification distinguishes access errors from unsupported claims. The direct-quotation/Fair Use component described in v1 Appendix G.3 is no longer described in v3.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, related-work section, information-verification exposition, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. Evaluation dimensions receive consistent new terminology, and residual DREX naming is corrected. The appendices are reorganized, with taxonomy foundations consolidated and dedicated baseline, human-evaluation, and prompt sections added.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn to show concrete rubric scoring and claim–source relationships. The taxonomy table moves to the appendix, rubric examples expand from one dimension to five, and new guidance, prompt displays, and an ablation table are added. Heatmaps gain revised labels and variability annotations, and the document adopts a different page format with extensively rearranged floats.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds RigorousBench and concurrent-work positioning, and revises capability comparisons, including recognizing implicit verification in ReportBench and DeepScholar-Bench more fully than v1. Section 2 removes the dedicated claim-verification survey, including InFact, MAPLE, ALiiCE, and CiteEval, while adding Prometheus, Prometheus 2, and MT-Bench judging references. This materially changes the literature coverage and comparative positioning.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix F.4 replaces the CV-based diversity definition with normalized HHI and its score transformation, and explicitly defines count-to-score normalization. The backtracking and hierarchical averaging equations remain equivalent apart from notation. No new theoretical guarantee or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves reproducibility and the ability to assess its validation: Appendices F–I supply scoring rules, model configurations, human-evaluation calculations, and prompts that v1 largely omitted. Adversarial tests address the original verification set's severe class imbalance, while uncertainty reporting and revised ablation interpretations improve evidential clarity. Removing per-class diagnostics and leaving the rubric revision insufficiently explained are drawbacks, but the documentation and validation gains outweigh them.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DEER. Their main texts, appendices, figures, tables, and equations are readable and support reliable matching despite the changed title, terminology, and organization.

after.justification: v3 reports original benchmark and human-agreement results, revised module evaluations, and additional adversarial verification experiments in Appendix F.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, human–LLM agreement measurements, and claim-extraction and verification experiments in Section 6 and Appendices F–G.

results.title: DEER: A Benchmark for Evaluating Deep Research Agents on Expert Report Generation

C1.justification: v2 makes identifying and overcoming spectral bias a central contribution, elevates gradient starvation and memory scaling in its contribution statements, and extends performance claims to physical robots. It removes v1's abstract emphasis on fixed dispersive-loss temperatures and improved few-shot generalization. The central directional-alignment and single-step-efficiency claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 newly interprets spectral filtering as inadequate fine-motion guidance and discusses memory scaling as a barrier to larger networks. Appendix E.1 attributes longer-horizon JVP degradation to compounding open-loop errors and interprets DDE's relative performance as greater long-horizon stability. The earlier DDE accuracy–memory tradeoff remains and receives substantially expanded discussion.

D1.justification: Appendices C–D add synthetic target-generation and evaluation procedures, direct output-vector optimization details, and physical-robot training and testing settings, summarized in Table 4. v2 also newly states that code and robot demonstration material accompany supplementary material; their actual availability cannot be established from the supplied PDFs.

E1.justification: The original 37 simulation tasks remain. v2 adds physical Place Bottle, Clean Table and Slip Ring tasks, plus synthetic multi-frequency regression and 2D velocity-optimization scenarios. Although Section 5.1 initially mentions four real-world tasks, Table 2, Figure 6 and Appendix D consistently document three.

E2.justification: The main simulation comparator set is retained. However, the convergence comparison changes: v1 Figure 4 includes SimpleDP3 and separate MP/MP+dis curves, whereas v2 Figure 5 includes DP3 and MP1 alongside FlowPolicy and OMP. The new physical-robot comparison reuses DP3, FlowPolicy and MP1.

E3.justification: New physical-robot protocols use 50 demonstrations per task, 20 trials with randomized object placement, and prediction/execution horizons of 16/8. Appendix E introduces horizon configurations 4/3, 8/4 and 16/8. The simulation description also replaces v1's four-state-history wording with a two-step observation history and specifies execution horizon 3; this reported revision does not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled spectral-bias and directional-starvation experiments in Figure 2, JVP-versus-DDE memory measurements across tasks and horizons in Table 3, and action-chunk sensitivity in Appendix E.1. The original tabulated loss and DDE ablations remain, merged into Table 1, while the convergence analysis is revised.

E5.justification: Reported simulation seeds change from 0, 1, 2 to 0, 10, 20. Both versions retain three runs and mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting, so no increase in repeated runs is established. The new real-world results report aggregate success rates without uncertainty estimates or repeated-training information.

E6.justification: Main simulation means remain unchanged, but aggregate standard deviations change: OMP 1.7 to 1.6, the dispersive-loss ablation 2.0 to 2.2, and the joint-loss ablation 2.5 to 2.6. Training curves are replaced. New physical-task rates are 80/75/70% for OMP versus 70/65/55% for MP1. Additional synthetic, memory and horizon results include long-horizon DDE outperforming JVP, 78.2% versus 76.6%. These additions do not establish improved retained simulation means.

M1.justification: The cosine alignment loss, weighted reconstruction/dispersive/alignment objective, DDE approximation and single-step inference remain unchanged. Lcos becomes LDA, while OMP-JVP and OMP-DDE explicitly name the original full method and DDE variant already evaluated in v1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related-work subsections reverse order, the method is reorganized around three theoretical barriers and two solution components, and experiments receive setup/performance subsections. An impact statement and Appendices A–E substantially extend the document's narrative structure.

P2.justification: v2 merges the original results and ablation tables, adds real-world, memory, hyperparameter and horizon tables, introduces synthetic-analysis plots and robot photographs, expands the environment montage, and redraws convergence curves with revised legends and step ranges. Figure 1 and the trajectory schematic are retained, with the latter renumbered.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A substantially expand coverage of equivariant policies, one-step models, reinforcement learning, foundation models and world models, including OneDP, OpenVLA and Octo. DDE is newly connected to finite-difference research by Karakida et al. and motivated by Wang et al.'s Transition Models. Retained works' venue/year updates are bibliographic changes.

T1.justification: Beyond v1's cosine-law and angular-gradient derivation, v2 adds a spectral-decay theorem and proof under a stationarity assumption, radial/tangential gradient analysis with a directional stiffness ratio, and a derivation of JVP activation-memory doubling. These substantial formal additions appear in Section 4.2 and Appendix B.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses two important weaknesses of v1: simulation-only validation and unmeasured DDE memory-saving claims. Physical-robot comparisons with documented trial protocols, direct memory measurements and horizon sensitivity materially strengthen practical support. These gains outweigh reporting shortcomings, including missing real-world uncertainty and the Appendix E.1 claim of 82.3% medium-horizon JVP performance despite Table 5 reporting 80.7%. The stronger spectral-bias claims remain less directly supported because Figure 2 does not evaluate OMP's claimed correction.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OMP research, with matching objectives and retained simulation benchmarks. Text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v2 includes Appendices A–E, which were also inspected.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation results and adds physical-robot evaluations, synthetic experiments, memory measurements and action-horizon sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original OMP success rates, component ablations and training curves on three Adroit and 34 Meta-World tasks.

results.title: OMP: One-step Meanflow Policy with Directional Alignment

C1.justification: The principal claims about training-free personalization of frozen VLAs and superiority over prompting baselines remain. The introduction newly claims that the visual highlight and matched instruction rewrite must work together, with neither component alone reliably closing the control gap, sharpening the claimed contribution beyond the earlier effectiveness claim.

C2.justification: Appendix E adds interpretations concerning language–vision alignment, reference consensus, reference-count saturation, and the saliency–occlusion tradeoff. Expanded Appendix D.2 explains why reference voting cannot enforce cross-camera identity and discusses risks of erroneous joint associations. Appendix F qualifies the multi-user demonstration as reference-based ownership binding rather than visual ownership inference. These substantially expand mechanism and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies reference cropping, normalized final-layer DINOv2 CLS features, voting tie-breaking, missing-detection/mask fallbacks, and default opacity 0.5. It expands rewriting and sequential-execution instructions, adds a project-page link, and identifies a commit for the referenced π0 implementation. These improve implementation specificity without establishing changes to the core perception procedure.

E1.justification: The main simulation benchmarks and generic training tasks remain. The real-world suite replaces the marker task with a pouch task, confirmed by descriptions and images. Appendix F adds a limited shared-scene scenario requiring sequential manipulation of two users' objects, a dog figurine and an ornament.

E2.justification: The main Generic VLA, Soft Prompt, and Short/Long Hard Prompt comparator families remain. New Appendix E adds controlled comparison variants against full VAP: Mask-only, Rewrite-only, averaging instead of voting, and bounding-box prompting.

E3.justification: Table 4 changes stated VLABench episodes per task/run from 25 to 50, although Table 9 retains 125×10 total episodes. Appendix A changes the reported real-world action horizon from 4 to 32 and hard-prompt generation from GPT-4o with one reference view to GPT-5.1 with all views. New ablations introduce reference-count, opacity, and component controls; Appendix F adds a 20-trial two-step protocol and metrics. These reporting revisions do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V1 includes token-embedding, attention, and failure analyses but lacks the component ablations added in Appendix E. Tables 10–13 test highlight/rewrite coupling, voting versus averaging, reference counts, and prompt geometry/opacity. V2 also revises attention examples and adds real-world success and failure rollouts, substantially expanding diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Figure 5 newly includes error bars identified as standard deviations across four tasks. Tables 3–4 explicitly identify their reported values as means; both versions already state ten runs. The added variability reporting concerns differences across tasks and does not establish additional seeds, confidence intervals, or increased repeated-run counts.

E6.justification: Table 2 changes VAP's bottle visual-matching CMR/SR from 73.2/60.6 to 83.2/75.0 and variant-aggregation SR from 58.2 to 62.5. Figure 5 replaces marker results with pouch results and changes mean pick-and-place SR from 56.2 to 58.8; revised tasks/settings prevent treating this as a matched performance gain. Tables 10–14 add substantial ablation and sequential-task results, including 65.0% two-step success.

M1.justification: The core grounding, tracking, highlighting, and instruction-rewriting pipeline remains. Appendix F adds sequential execution of compound requests: decompose into sub-goals, manipulate one target, clear its mask, and re-ground the next target after the scene changes. The cross-view association proposal in Appendix D.2 remains future work.

P1.justification: Large portions of the introduction, related work, method overview, benchmark descriptions, results, and conclusion are rewritten and condensed. V2 adds an instruction-rewriting subsection and separate ablation and practical-usage appendices, while moving the existing discussion from Appendix E to G. The extensive editing goes beyond inserting new scientific content.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 10–14, real-world rollout Figures 18–20, and the sequential demonstration in Figure 24. Existing failure figures are renumbered, with real-world examples added to two of them. Attention Figures 9–12 are revised, and Figure 5 gains error bars and updated task imagery. Main-text tables and figures also move within the condensed layout.

R1.justification: Section 2 removes the Octo and GR00T N1.5 citations while retaining the broad positioning against foundation-model personalization and visual prompting. Appendix A.3 adds a connection to identifier conventions in DreamBooth and Yo’LLaVA. Most other reference changes update metadata or convert existing footnotes into bibliography entries.

T1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds mathematical definitions for shared cross-view assignments, including an unobserved-target option, and a MAP-style objective combining reference evidence, cross-view consistency, and visibility priors. It also defines alternative association scores and geometric penalties. This is a localized formalization of future work; the existing grounding equations remain and no proofs or guarantees are added.

improvement.justification: V1 demonstrates effectiveness but does not isolate the contributions of VAP's components. V2's Tables 10–13 address this important validation gap through controlled comparisons and sensitivity tests, substantially strengthening support for the design. Additional implementation details and applicability analysis also help. Reporting remains imperfect: Table 9's VLABench episode count conflicts with revised Table 4, and its unchanged 31.9% real-world failure rate conflicts with Figure 5's updated scores, which imply about 30.6%. These issues temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial validation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VAP research work. All pages, including figures, tables, equations, and appendices, support comparison; retained content can be matched across rewriting and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds component ablations in Tables 10–13 and a real-world sequential manipulation experiment in Table 14.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation and physical-robot experiments in Tables 2–4 and Figure 5, plus embedding, attention, and failure analyses.

results.title: Bring My Cup! Personalizing Vision-Language-Action Models with Visual Attentive Prompting

C1.justification: V2 drops the explicit complex-domain reflection contribution and expands the claimed scope to approximate and partially observed symmetries. ModelNet10 evidence and superiority over LieGAN for discrete groups become central contributions. The distribution-learning formulation and last-minute-convergence contribution remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds an explanation based on cancellation of inconsistent targets from nonsymmetry transformations and an interpretation of partial symmetries through conditional distributions. It replaces the Ico failure narrative with recovery using power scheduling, discusses masking robustness and prior sensitivity, and reframes limitations around small point clouds, limited object counts and scalability.

D1.justification: V2 Appendices B–C substantially expand v1's sparse training documentation with dataset construction, network widths, time embeddings, Transformer configuration, optimizers, learning rates and weight decay. They also specify prior construction and rejection rules, an RTX 4090, batch size 512, and per-epoch times of approximately 18 seconds for LieFlow versus 50 for LieGAN.

E1.justification: V2 adds rotated ModelNet10, partially observed C4, masked point clouds and tilted-axis SO(2) cases. It removes the complex-domain D4 reflection task, the dataset of four synthetic shapes, and the Gaussian-distributed SO(2) rotation case from v1 Appendices C.4–C.5. Icosahedral symmetry was already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: LieGAN remains the only baseline family, but its evaluated variants are narrowed within retained comparisons. Table 1 drops the two-generator variant; Table 2 drops the one- and six-generator variants and retains the earlier three-generator results. No new baseline family is introduced.

E3.justification: Reported synthetic architecture settings change, and the GL(2) coefficient range changes from uniform [-π/2, π/2] in v1 Appendix B to [-π, π] in v2 Appendix C, with determinant rejection added. New protocols include selecting 100 ModelNet10 objects with 128 points each, masking points, sweeping skewness and comparing training time. These descriptions do not establish that all retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a skewness ablation with training curves, a comparison of GL(2) prior constructions, and tests of missing C4 orientations and masked ModelNet10 observations. The nonuniform SO(2) case study is removed. The existing SO(2)-to-C4 posterior and velocity analysis is retained in Appendix D, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The retained posterior-entropy plots describe flow behavior rather than uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: New results include 0.428 for the matrix-composition GL(2)-to-C4 prior, 0.118 for synthetic Ico with power scheduling, and ModelNet10 masking errors of 0.156, 0.186 and 0.212. V1's Ico failure is replaced by reported recovery under revised settings. Several inherited scores remain identical, including Tet/Oct/z-axis SO(2) values 0.0885/0.0962/0.0429. Reflection and removed appendix-study results disappear.

M1.justification: The flow-matching loss, exponential interpolation and transformation-composition procedure remain. V2 adds matrix-composition prior sampling and a Transformer predictor for ModelNet10, and changes the reported synthetic predictors from three-layer GELU MLPs to five-layer ReLU MLPs. Section 4.3 interprets partial symmetries using the existing procedure.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method exposition and conclusion, swaps related work and preliminaries, and reorganizes the experiments. The lengthy convergence analysis moves to Appendix D, while dataset, training, scheduling and additional-result material receive separate appendices. The title and author information also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns, and Figure 1 is redrawn. V2 regroups 2D histograms, expands 3D visualization panels, splits Table 2 into synthetic and ModelNet10 subtables, and adds masking and skewness tables and curves. Existing diagnostic plots move to Appendix D; reflection and removed case-study displays disappear.

R1.justification: V2 adds Wu et al. (2015) for ModelNet10 and removes the GELU reference and the Huang and Mangoubi diffusion references. Related work now positions LieGAN alongside Allingham et al. as closest and explains that LieGAN can discover discrete groups with suitably chosen priors. Most cited research is retained.

T1.justification: New Section 4.3 defines input-dependent symmetry subsets Hx satisfying q(hx)=q(x), and formalizes conditional transformation distributions and their marginalization. The target-field derivation in Appendix A and the posterior-computation derivation and algorithm are retained. No new theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important weaknesses in v1's evaluation and reproducibility through tests on 100 rotated ModelNet10 objects, controlled masking experiments, a quantitative skewness ablation and substantially fuller training details. These provide stronger support beyond hand-built synthetic objects and better justification for the schedule choice. Removing reflection and nonuniform-rotation studies and narrowing LieGAN variants loses useful evidence, but the gains are substantial overall. Repeated-run uncertainty remains unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LieFlow and retain matching core algorithms, equations and analyses. The complete main texts, appendices, figures and tables support reliable comparison despite retitling and substantial reorganization.

after.justification: V2 reports original synthetic and ModelNet10 experiments, including partial symmetries, masked observations, timing comparisons and a time-schedule ablation.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic symmetry-discovery experiments, Wasserstein-1 comparisons with LieGAN, and appendix experiments on multiple objects and nonuniform rotations.

results.title: Discovering Symmetry Groups with Flow Matching

C1.justification: The central distribution-learning formulation and last-minute convergence contribution remain. v3 broadens empirical claims to MI-Motion, additional baselines, and noisy approximate symmetries. Its conclusion also replaces v2's suggestion of improved downstream sample efficiency and generalization with future evaluation of downstream utility.

C2.justification: Beyond v2's scale and prior-parameterization limitations, v3 explains failures of global support assumptions, stabilizer ambiguities, logarithm branch and cut-locus issues, and the absence of an explicit algebraic group description. The Impact Statement now discusses incorrect inferred invariances and downstream bias. Partial-symmetry discussion emphasizes input-specific subsets rather than the earlier marginal closure demonstration.

D1.justification: The training appendix is retained as v2 Appendix C becomes v3 Appendix D, preserving architectures, optimizers, hardware, and timing details. v3 newly specifies evaluation ground distances, LieGAN's uniform coefficient prior, additional baseline configurations, and MI-Motion sampling of 500,000 skeletons with 20 joints. These are limited documentation additions.

E1.justification: v3 adds MI-Motion human skeletons whose approximate symmetry comes from the observed data distribution. It also adds labeled joint-distribution tasks, rectangles with nontrivial C2 stabilizers, and rotationally perturbed observations combined with masking. The original arrow, tetrahedron, and rotated ModelNet10 coverage remains.

E2.justification: v2 evaluates LieGAN as its sole comparison method, including its one- and four-generator variants. v3 adds SGM and Augerino to the retained ModelNet10 comparison in Table 2 while preserving LieGAN, substantially broadening the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: v3 introduces relative improvement over random sampling alongside Wasserstein-1 distance. Added evaluation protocols include orbit-based labels for Augerino, conditional partial-symmetry evaluation, and a 3 × 3 combination of masking ratios and rotational-noise magnitudes. The newly specified ground distances and LieGAN coefficient prior do not establish changes from v2's unspecified experimental choices.

E4.justification: Masking-only robustness expands to rotational and combined noise tests. New analyses examine finite stabilizers, input-specific partial symmetries, and functional symmetries (Figures 18–21 and 28). Figure 21's labels conflict with Section 5.3, limiting that analysis. Existing convergence and skewness studies remain, although the explicit ModelNet10 no-power quantitative comparison is removed while its visualization remains.

E5.justification: v2 reports point estimates without seed counts or uncertainty. v3 first reports averages and standard deviations over three random seeds across the quantitative tables, including appendix results. This substantially changes uncertainty reporting but does not establish an increase from a known earlier run count. No significance tests are added.

E6.justification: Many numerical estimates are replaced. For example, ModelNet10 LieFlow Wasserstein-1 values change from 0.113 to 0.149 ± 0.013 for Tet and from 0.156 to 0.129 ± 0.005 for Ico. New baseline, relative-improvement, motion, conditional-symmetry, and noise results are reported; the ModelNet10 no-power value 0.717 is removed. These are revised reported results, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The core loss, Algorithms 1–3, and power time schedule remain unchanged. Section 5.3 adds a limited adaptation for functional symmetry discovery: concatenating one-hot labels with spatial coordinates and learning joint spatial and label transformations under SO(2) × SO(2) on four-dimensional point clouds.

P1.justification: v3 shortens the partial-symmetry explanation, reorders contribution bullets, rewrites the conclusion and Impact Statement, and updates affiliation and publication information. The overall section sequence and much of the method and appendix prose remain intact; the added scientific sections do not constitute a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: Tables gain uncertainty and relative-improvement displays; the original combined Table 2 is split between v3 Table 2 and appendix Table 5, and Table 3 becomes a grid. Motion, rectangle, conditional, functional, and noise plots substantially expand the visual evidence. Reporting defects include Table 3's reversed row/column caption and an ablation axis changed from epochs to steps while its caption still says epochs.

R1.justification: v3 adds He et al. (2021), Li et al. (2024), Hu et al. (2025), and the MI-Motion reference by Peng et al. (2023), and explicitly contrasts Augerino's supervision requirements with LieFlow. Most research positioning remains unchanged; publication and bibliographic updates to existing references are not additional works.

T1.justification: v3 adds Proposition 4.1 and Appendix B's assumptions, Theorem B.4, and proof that sampled transformation supports are contained in H under ideal convergence and structural conditions. This does not prove equality with H. Appendix A also refines identifiability through trivial infinitesimal stabilizers and explains finite versus continuous stabilizers; the existing flow and posterior derivations remain.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation beyond v2's imposed-symmetry datasets, LieGAN-only comparisons, and unreported variability through MI-Motion, SGM/Augerino comparisons, and three-seed uncertainty. The conditional support theorem and explicit failure assumptions also clarify applicability. The theorem establishes containment rather than complete recovery, and inconsistent functional-task labels and table/axis captions weaken particular additions. These limitations do not outweigh the stronger empirical foundation and clearer boundaries.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LieFlow research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds MI-Motion experiments, further baseline comparisons, rotational-noise tests, and rectangle and functional-symmetry experiments.

before.justification: v2 reports original symmetry-discovery experiments on synthetic point clouds and rotated ModelNet10, including quantitative comparisons, masking tests, and time-schedule analyses.

results.title: Discovering Symmetry Groups with Flow Matching

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions expand from two bounds and TRM to include the Adaptive bound, length-neutral masking, and empirical training stability. The introduction additionally conditions the guarantee on global divergence verification, although the headline claim of first non-vacuous monotonic-improvement guarantees remains.

C2.justification: v2 distinguishes a length-independent threshold from length-dependent rejection probability and discusses potential bias against long reasoning responses. Remark 6.2 separates the full and masked surrogates and introduces an acceptance-rate heuristic for their relationship. The experiments also motivate complementary roles for max filtering of outliers and average filtering of accumulated drift.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the experimental model, backend pairing, GRPO group size 16, training/rollout batch sizes 32, learning rate 1e-6, sampling settings, and thresholds. Appendix D adds implementation pseudocode, a SER code snippet, and a suggested threshold range of 0.03–0.10. Sampled max-filter guidance changes from absolute log-ratio to the squared-log k2 score; hardware and maximum response length remain unspecified.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates no datasets or tasks. v2 trains on deduplicated DAPO-MATH-17k and evaluates mathematical reasoning on AIME25 under inference/training backend mismatch. Code generation, tool use, and MoE routing remain motivational examples rather than evaluated coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds an evaluated PPO-clipping comparator against TRM in Figure 2, using clipping limits [0.8, 1.28]. Figure 1 separately compares Token IS with PPO clipping. v1 discusses PPO analytically but contains no evaluated comparison methods.

E3.justification: v2 introduces a Qwen3-8B-Base Zero-RL/GRPO protocol with vLLM rollouts and FSDP training. It adds avg@32 evaluation with top-p 0.95 and temperature 1.0, a defined Log Absolute PPL Gap metric, and experiments with specified masking thresholds. These are new protocols, not revisions of existing v1 experiments.

E4.justification: Figures 2–3 introduce empirical tests of max versus average filtering and whether combining them maintains stability under relaxed thresholds. v1 has no corresponding sensitivity or component studies. Figure 3's 0.002 curve is labeled TRM-Max in the legend but TRM-Avg in the text, leaving that curve's identity uncertain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v2's avg@32 specifies evaluation sampling rather than reporting run-to-run uncertainty.

E6.justification: New Figures 1–3 report training stability and AIME25 outcomes for Token IS, PPO, and TRM variants; there are no corresponding v1 empirical scores. Table 1 retains the small-divergence values 1677, 35.0, and 8.2 while adding other bound comparisons. Appendix A.2 introduces a numerical error: for training probability 0.001 and rollout probability 0.9, v2 reports the ratio as approximately 900 rather than v1's approximately 0.001.

M1.justification: The original exact-KL TRM objective and batch normalization remain. Appendix D adds LN-TRM, which masks using position-weighted, length-normalized ratio deviations, and SER, which uses unweighted mean absolute ratio deviations. Algorithms 2–3 therefore introduce substantively different sequence-acceptance procedures.

P1.justification: Retained introduction, background, theory, and method passages are extensively rewritten and expanded. Proofs from v1 Appendices B–C move into the main text, the estimator discussion moves from Appendix D to B, and discussion and conclusion are combined. The author and affiliation header is also revised.

P2.justification: v2 adds three experimental figures with two panels each, two algorithm displays, and length-bias tables. Table 1 is redesigned around divergence regimes and capped versus uncapped bounds, while the PPO analysis receives revised headings and a caption as Table 2. v1's dilemma and estimator-value tables are removed.

R1.justification: A new Related Work section expands positioning around trust-region theory, distributed RL, and exposure bias. v2 adds reasoning, GRPO, and DAPO references and acknowledges Qi et al. (2026) for independently noting the linear special case. Dao (2022) and Kearns–Singh (2002) are removed; renamed bibliographic entries such as DeepSeek-V2 represent retained works.

T1.justification: v2 adds capped forms of the Pinsker-Marginal and Mixed bounds, the per-position Adaptive bound, and its importance-ratio/tower-property proof in Appendix C. Theorem 6.1 replaces v1's masked-surrogate improvement condition with a full-surrogate condition requiring globally bounded KL. Appendix D adds formal length-bias analysis and guarantees for the new masking variants.

improvement.justification: v2 adds direct experimental support for previously untested stability claims and replaces v1's accepted-sample-based guarantee with an explicitly conditional theorem requiring global KL control. The Adaptive-bound proof and length-bias analysis substantially improve theoretical detail and applicability qualifications. These gains outweigh localized problems, including Figure 3's labeling conflict and Appendix A.2's reversed ratio. However, the narrow evaluation without reported uncertainty and the acceptance-rate heuristics do not establish the global monotonic-improvement guarantee empirically.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TRM research work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, including equations, tables, algorithms, and v2's experimental figures; restructuring does not prevent reliable comparison.

after.justification: Section 7 and Figures 1–3 report original mathematical-reasoning training experiments, including AIME25 scores and training–rollout divergence measurements.

before.justification: v1 contains theoretical bounds, proofs, and numerical illustrations of formulas, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

results.title: Trust Region Masking for Long-Horizon LLM Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: v2 presents three tighter bounds and their minimum. v5 expands the central contribution to a KL/TV bound family and claims the tightest known guarantee across all divergence regimes. This broadens both the scope and comparative strength of the theoretical contribution, while retaining the central TRM and long-horizon motivation.

C2.justification: v2 Remark 6.2 uses high acceptance to justify approximate equality of masked and full surrogates. v5 Remark 4.3 explicitly rejects this inference and separates global-precondition validity from finite-sample robustness. Appendix G further explains that its reward-form value guarantee does not generally certify Algorithm 1's advantage-form stop-gradient update, and identifies the exponential cost of its precondition-free sample-ratio bound.

D1.justification: Implementation documentation becomes slightly less explicit: v2 separately specifies training and rollout batch sizes of 32, whereas v5 says only 'batch size 32'. Detailed LN-TRM/SER listings are condensed. Stored-logit computation, k2/k3 recommendations, total-batch normalization, and SER code and threshold range remain available.

E1.justification: Both versions train on deduplicated DAPO-MATH-17k and evaluate mathematical reasoning on AIME25 using Qwen3-8B-Base. No additional dataset, task, domain or experimentally tested mismatch scenario is introduced.

E2.justification: Figures 1–3 retain their respective comparisons: Token IS versus PPO clipping; PPO versus TRM-Max and TRM-Avg; and loose individual criteria versus their combination. Figure 3 corrects the 0.002 legend from TRM-Max to TRM-Avg, matching v2's accompanying prose rather than introducing another comparator.

E3.justification: Table 1 changes the illustrative bound-evaluation settings from small/large KL divergence with cap comparisons to KL-only versus KL+TV information, specifying token TV 0.005 and sequence TV 0.05. The neural experiments retain the stated model, GRPO settings, learning rate, clipping and masking thresholds, evaluation sampling and avg@32 metric.

E4.justification: The numerical analysis shifts from the cap and divergence-regime comparisons in v2 Table 1 and Appendix C.5 toward KL/TV complementarity and their crossover. The numerical length-acceptance grid is removed, while its analytical length-bias argument remains. The empirical max/average/combined-criterion ablation retains its question and overall conclusion.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The avg@32 evaluation convention remains unchanged; the theoretical discussion of rejection probability does not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Figures 1 and 2 are identical. Figure 3 replaces the combined-criterion curves: at the shared step 600, its plotted AIME25 score changes from approximately 0.212 to 0.239 under the retained stated settings, and reporting extends from about step 670 to 760. Table 1 adds TV-based numerical bounds, including 24.7 and 4.1, and removes large-divergence entries. Its old minimum labeled 'Adaptive' corresponds to the later 'Unified B*', not the standalone Adaptive row.

M1.justification: The core TRM algorithm and SER procedure remain. Section 4.3 adds optional maximum-TV masking, and Appendix F changes LN-TRM's position weights to take the minimum over coupling and Pinsker bounds. LN-TRM and SER already existed in v2; they are not newly introduced methods.

P1.justification: The paper is extensively rewritten and reorganized. Related work is integrated into the introduction, background explanations are compressed, token-level failure analysis joins the TRM section, and most main-text proofs move into reorganized appendices. The experiments, conclusion and length-neutral discussion are substantially condensed beyond changes required by the new scientific content.

P2.justification: Table 1 is substantially redesigned around bound routes and KL-only/KL+TV columns. The PPO clipping table, numerical length-acceptance grid and separate LN-TRM/SER algorithm panels disappear. Figures 1–2 are relocated with revised captions; Figure 3 is redrawn with changed axes and a corrected legend. The length-bias comparison table is retained and renumbered.

R1.justification: The main positioning against classical trust-region methods and implementation mismatch remains. Several citations disappear, notably Qi et al. (2026) and its explicit attribution of an independently noted linear bound, and Yu et al. (2025), the cited source of the clipping settings. The revised Fang Liu reference retains the same arXiv identifier and represents an updated work rather than a new citation.

T1.justification: v5 substantially extends the retained KL theory with TV-based Pinsker-Marginal and Mixed bounds, a capped Coupling bound, and TV/hybrid Adaptive bounds with new derivations. Remark 2.1 corrects the constant relating the surrogate forms and specifies the baseline needed for value-level guarantees. New Appendix G derives an accepted/rejected-region guarantee with a support assumption, rejection penalty and distinct sample-ratio regime. Several foundational proofs are relocated rather than newly added.

improvement.justification: v5 substantially improves the theoretical accuracy and scope of the paper. Remark 4.3 corrects v2's consequential claim that high acceptance makes masked and full objectives approximately interchangeable, while Remark 2.1 fixes the value-level surrogate normalization. The expanded bounds and Appendix G provide explicit derivations and clearer conditions. The new guarantee still does not establish monotonicity of Algorithm 1's general update, and its sample-ratio case has exponential cost; v5 now states these limits. These gains outweigh the modest loss of implementation and citation detail.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Trust Region Masking work. All pages, including appendices, are readable, and the equations, tables, figures and reorganized sections support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v5 Section 5 retains original training and evaluation results in Figures 1–3, including revised results for the combined masking criterion.

before.justification: v2 Section 7 reports original Qwen3-8B-Base training experiments on DAPO-MATH-17k, with AIME25 scores and training–rollout mismatch curves in Figures 1–3.

results.title: Trust Region Masking for Long-Horizon LLM Reinforcement Learning

C1.justification: The core learnable-tokenization contribution persists, but the headline performance claim expands to five benchmarks covering long-range and variant-effect tasks. The introduction's contributions now explicitly include preserving functional motifs as single chunks, stability under structural variants and improved long-context computational efficiency.

C2.justification: v4 interprets component ablations as evidence of necessity, multispecies gains as benefits from data diversity, and computation savings as compression offsetting routing overhead. Biological interpretation expands to motif preservation and SINE-age gradients, while the robustness explanation extends beyond small variants. These substantially broaden v3's functional-region granularity and indel-stability explanations.

D1.justification: Appendices B–C substantially expand documentation of repeat weighting, retention targets, ratio-loss weight, precision, GPU/step budget and benchmark-specific heads and inference. v4 also resolves the Transformer-depth inconsistency and clarifies vocabulary padding. Conversely, v3's per-task selected hyperparameter tables and explicit fine-tuning GPU and reverse-complement augmentation disclosures are removed.

E1.justification: v3 already evaluates NT, revised NT and Genomic Benchmarks. v4 adds BEND's seven tasks and DNALongBench's five tasks, extending coverage to gene finding, epigenomic profiling, variant effects and long-range prediction. It also adds multispecies pretraining ablations and GIAB structural-variant scenarios.

E2.justification: Existing benchmark comparator sets are retained. v4 adds matched 6-mer/BPE controls and single-nucleotide computation comparisons, plus CNN and Caduceus-PH linear-probing comparisons in Figure 2. The biological tokenization comparison changes from DNABERT-2 BPE to GROVER BPE. These changes substantially broaden direct comparison of tokenization alternatives.

E3.justification: Reported pretraining changes from approximately 35B processed bases with Adam/cosine decay to approximately 52B with AdamW/WSD. Fine-tuning search grids expand, and the NT epoch limit increases from 15 to 20. New protocols include controlled 50M-parameter, 2B-token ablations and frozen-backbone, windowed long-input evaluation. These are documented setting changes; retained scores do not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v4 adds component-removal and multispecies ablations, computation-versus-length analysis, motif-fragmentation tests and structural-variant robustness. The H3C13–15 gene-track case studies are removed. The existing chromosome analysis is substantially revised to examine annotation-specific chunk maxima and SINE-age groups across chr1–22 and chrX.

E5.justification: Revised-NT captions change mean plus/minus standard error to mean plus/minus standard deviation (v3 Tables 3 and 6; v4 Tables 2 and 10). Three seeds and the full table's numerical uncertainty values are retained. The PDFs neither explain the relabeling nor establish additional runs.

E6.justification: Substantial results are added for the new benchmarks and analyses. For example, v4 Table 5 reports overall MCC 0.390 versus 0.332 without mask protection; Figure 4 reports 1.22 versus 2.47 chunks per motif for DNAChunker and BPE. Existing full NT, Genomic and revised-NT tables retain their numbers. The revised-NT summary MCC is corrected from 0.657 to 0.660, and the original NT win count from 10 to 13.

M1.justification: v4 introduces an inference adaptation for long inputs: overlapping windows, scatter/gather reaggregation and reference/alternate-allele features (Appendix C.4). The core segmenter, mask protection, residual gating and losses remain unchanged. The main-text correction from 8 to 30 Transformer blocks agrees with v3 Appendix A rather than establishing an architecture enlargement.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, experimental narrative and conclusion undergo substantial paragraph-level rewriting. Revised-NT evaluation moves from ablations into downstream tasks, and the appendices are reordered and extensively restructured. Method exposition remains largely stable; correspondence, publication-header, acknowledgment and conflict-disclosure text also changes.

P2.justification: The architecture diagram is redrawn, and Figure 1c replaces chromosome distributions with motif-fragmentation summaries. v4 adds long-benchmark, computation and motif charts plus BEND and ablation tables. Gene-track plots disappear, chromosome scatterplots become median/p95 bar panels, and the revised-NT summary separates enhancer and promoter rows.

R1.justification: v4 adds benchmark, annotation and background references and sharpens the contrast between autoregressive and masked DNA models, while retaining the central positioning around learnable tokenization. The DNAGPT citation changes from Yang et al.'s text-detection work to Zhang et al.'s genomic model. Publication updates to H-Net, PatchDNA and Evo2 represent the same works.

T1.justification: Appendix D newly defines the region-level statistic m_A as the maximum length of chunks whose centers fall inside an annotated region, underpinning the revised biological analysis. Existing routing, dechunking, loss and mutation-similarity equations are unchanged. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v3 supports its architectural choices mainly through benchmark performance and observational tokenization analyses. v4 adds controlled component comparisons, quantitative motif and computation analyses, and broader evaluation with documented long-input handling, substantially strengthening attribution and applicability evidence. Expanded implementation details and corrected summaries also help assessment. Removed per-task hyperparameters and unexplained changes to training settings and uncertainty labels remain reporting weaknesses, but the added controlled evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs present DNAChunker with the same authors and core framework. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds BEND and DNALongBench evaluations, controlled ablations, computation measurements, motif analyses and structural-variant experiments.

before.justification: v3 reports original downstream benchmark results, biological tokenization analyses and ClinVar mutation experiments, including additional results in Appendix B.

results.title: DNACHUNKER: Learnable Tokenization for DNA Language Models

C1.justification: The three central contributions—multimodal latent reasoning, temporal latent prediction, and fast–slow coordination—remain. The abstract and introduction broaden the empirical claims from six Franka tasks to ten real-world tasks across tabletop, mobile, and dexterous settings, claiming respective improvements of 13, 14, and 14 percentage points. The simulation advantage remains claimed in the introduction.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the added experiments as evidence of applicability to larger action spaces and more complex embodiments. Appendix E newly attributes failures to height/position errors, collisions, and missing visual feedback. The horizon discussion now explains choosing four steps because further extension provides no improvement, replacing the earlier emphasis on reasoning latency tradeoffs.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds platform, camera, control-vector, and MLP adaptation specifications for AgileX and TienKung. v3 also discloses the 3.3B total model size, fixed modality-ablation settings, and separate expert inference speeds. Its architecture description now agrees with the 384×384 experimental inputs already stated in v1. The explicit Tashan tactile-sensor description disappears, without establishing hardware removal, and the project-page address changes without establishing a new code release.

E1.justification: v3 adds two AgileX mobile tasks, arranging dishes and sorting spoons, and two TienKung dexterous-hand tasks, opening a drawer and placing a button. These introduce coordinated base–arm control and articulated-hand manipulation. The ten RLBench tasks, six Franka tasks, long-horizon test, and Appendix A pretraining dataset mixture are retained.

E2.justification: The six RLBench comparators and three Franka comparators remain unchanged. New mobile and dexterous comparisons reuse π0.5 and CoT-VLA. SpatialVLA is omitted only from these added tasks, with poor depth estimation given as the reason; it is not removed from any matched earlier comparison.

E3.justification: The reported SFT schedule changes from 40 reasoning epochs followed by 300 action epochs to 300 joint epochs, and the backbone size description changes from 1B to 1.5B. Real-world evaluation now specifies three repetitions of 15 rollouts at different tabletop positions. New platforms introduce three-view mobile and single-view dexterous protocols. These document revised settings without establishing that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 Figure 5 extends the existing temporal-horizon sweep with five- and six-step conditions. Appendix E adds three qualitative failure cases involving incomplete wiping, plate collisions, and missed drawer grasps. The other component ablations and long-horizon analysis are retained; the full attention heatmap comparison is relocated to Appendix D rather than newly added.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports three repetitions of real-world evaluations and aggregate uncertainty values: LaST0 72% ±3, SpatialVLA 41% ±2, π0.5 59% ±4, and CoT-VLA 50% ±2. The statistic represented by these real-world ± values is not explicitly defined. Simulation retains three seeded evaluations and variance reporting. Newly disclosed repetition counts do not establish an actual increase in runs.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds four task columns, with LaST0 success rates of 0.67, 0.27, 0.87, and 0.60. Retained tables revise LaST0 Water Plants from 0.65 to 0.60, CoT-VLA egg placement from 0.53 to 0.33 and its mean from 0.53 to 0.50, and SpatialVLA's Franka mean from 0.39 to 0.41. Figure 5 adds five-/six-step results of 80%/79%. Changed training and evaluation descriptions prevent interpreting revised entries as same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: v1 Section III-E trains the reasoning expert first, then freezes it while training the action expert; v3 Section 3.5 instead jointly optimizes both experts. Appendix B also introduces 20-dimensional mobile and 26-dimensional dexterous action interfaces with input/output MLP adaptation. The underlying multimodal latent CoT and shared-attention architecture remain.

P1.justification: v3 extensively condenses and edits the abstract, related work, methods, results discussion, and conclusion. CoT preliminaries, KV-cache explanation, and detailed execution discussion move into appendices, while hardware and task descriptions are reorganized by embodiment. It also replaces numbered citations with author–year citations, updates authorship, removes the future-work paragraph, and adds an Impact Statement.

P2.justification: v3 changes the document template and appendix layout, redraws Figure 1 with embodiment examples, and removes Figure 2's training-stage panel. Table 2 gains grouped embodiment columns; the temporal-ablation plot gains bars. Setup figures are merged and relocated, execution montages are expanded, and new hardware and failure figures appear. The original complete attention grid is retained in the appendix.

R1.justification: v3 removes the reinforcement-learning post-training discussion and associated citations, including GRAPE, ConRFT, and SimpleVLA-RL, alongside some background references. It adds Latent Implicit Visual Reasoning and references for the two new robot platforms. The central positioning relative to explicit CoT, LCDrive, and ThinkAct remains.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds mathematical definitions of the 20-dimensional mobile and 26-dimensional dexterous action vectors. The original policy factorization, interleaved latent sequence, and cosine loss remain unchanged; the factorization moves to Appendix F.1. No new theorem, proof, or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's embodiment evidence is confined to Franka configurations. v3 substantially strengthens applicability evidence through coordinated mobile manipulation and dexterous-hand experiments, accompanied by concrete control specifications and baseline comparisons. Newly reported real-world uncertainty, extended horizon analysis, and explicit failure cases improve transparency and expose practical limitations absent from v1. These gains are substantial, although each new platform has only two tasks and the revised joint-training recipe is not directly compared with staged training.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LaST0 research. All 16 pages of v1 and 18 pages of v3, including figures, tables, equations, and appendices, support comparison. Visual inspection resolved extraction artifacts, and relocated material was matched across versions.

after.justification: v3 retains original simulation and Franka results and reports additional mobile and dexterous manipulation experiments, extended ablations, and failure cases.

before.justification: v1 reports original RLBench experiments, component ablations, six real-world Franka tasks, and a repeated-execution long-horizon evaluation in Tables I–II and Figure 4.

results.title: LaST$_{0}$: Latent Spatio-Temporal Chain-of-Thought for Robotic Vision-Language-Action Model

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion add a second central claim: convergence for preconditioning exponents beyond the original sum of 1/2, without decoupled weight decay. The original classical-exponent guarantee and its conditional comparison with optimal SGD convergence remain.

C2.justification: Section 3 explains why rates for different ω cannot be directly ordered. Remark 1 adds a spectral-norm-constrained optimization conjecture and explains the difficulty of extending weight decay across the generalized family. The broader non-Euclidean interpretation in v2 Appendix A is removed; existing practical-setting caveats remain.

D1.justification: The documented toy initialization, noise-matrix entries, and weight-decay sweep are revised. GPT-2 architecture, training recipe, logging procedure, eight-H200 hardware disclosure, and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same stochastic quadratic toy task and GPT-2 pretraining on OpenWebText. The revised toy constants are settings within this retained coverage.

E2.justification: Both explicitly omit optimizer comparisons in their own experiments (v2 Appendix E.1; v4 Section 5.1). Comparisons involving AdamW, Muon, SOAP, and Splus remain attributed to prior work; no evaluated comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: For Figure 1, X1−X* changes from [[−1,−2],[2,1]] to [[−1,−3],[3,1]], the noise matrix A changes from all ones to all tens, and λ=10^-5 is added to the sweep. The objective, iteration budget, other optimizer settings, and GPT-2 training/logging protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The existing weight-decay sensitivity experiment is revised through changed initialization and noise, an additional λ value, and replacement curves. The gradient-norm-ratio and preconditioner spectral-floor analyses in Figures 2–3 are retained unchanged.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The stochastic-gradient-noise estimation procedure used for Figure 3 is also unchanged.

E6.justification: Figure 1's curves change: v2 lists nonconvergence for λ=10^-1, 10^-2, and 10^-3; v4 additionally lists 10^-4 and reports a new 10^-5 trajectory. These results use revised settings, so they do not establish a same-setting performance change. Figures 2–3 and their findings are unchanged.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 broadens its exponent constraint from 1/p + 1/q = 1 to 1/p + 1/q = 2−ω, with 0<ω≤2. This expands the allowable updates, including the momentum-SGD endpoint, while retaining the same momentum, preconditioner recursions, and weight-decay update.

P1.justification: V4 substantially reorganizes the narrative: discussion paragraphs become numbered subsections, matrix lemmas and full proofs are integrated into Section 4, and Appendix E becomes Section 5 before the conclusion. The separate proof sketch, Appendix A, acknowledgements, and impact statement disappear, and the opening and conclusion are rewritten around two contributions.

P2.justification: The two-column main text and references become single-column, extensively changing equation and algorithm layout. Figure 1 is enlarged and redrawn with revised ticks and an additional legend entry. Figures 2–3 retain their graphical content but move from the appendix into the main document.

R1.justification: V4 adds references concerning Clarifying Shampoo, K-FAC, Muon with Newton-Schulz, and AdamW implicit bias, while removing the citation cluster accompanying Appendix A. The retained Gratton–Toint comparison now specifies its noise assumption and α-dependent rates. The main positioning against earlier Shampoo convergence analyses remains.

T1.justification: V4 adds Theorem 2 and its Section 4.5 proof, establishing an O(K^-ω/4) convergence bound for the powered singular-value measure under λ=0. It generalizes supporting inequalities and adds Lemma 8 proving finiteness of the required expectations. The original theorem is largely retained, while v2 Appendix A's steepest-descent variational derivations are removed.

improvement.justification: Theorem 2 and its full proof substantially extend the paper's central theoretical applicability beyond the original exponent constraint, with unrestricted constant β for the zero-weight-decay case. Lemma 8 strengthens proof rigor by establishing required finite expectations, and the extension's limitations are explicit. These gains outweigh the loss of the peripheral steepest-descent discussion, while the original empirical support is retained.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AdamW-style Shampoo research. All 23 pages of v2 and 30 pages of v4 are readable, including v2's appendices and their retained, relocated material in v4.

after.justification: Section 2.6 and Figure 1 report revised toy simulations. Section 5 retains the original GPT-2/OpenWebText results in Figures 2–3.

before.justification: Figure 1 reports original stochastic quadratic simulations. Appendix E reports GPT-2 pretraining diagnostics on OpenWebText in Figures 2–3.

results.title: Convergence Rate Analysis of the AdamW-Style Shampoo: Unifying One-Sided and Two-Sided Preconditioning

C1.justification: V3 qualifies generalization as transfer within the studied urban-flow distribution and softens direct 3D extensibility to an extension requiring future validation. Its contribution statements also include stochastic diffusion comparisons and withheld-sensor tests, while retaining the central GenDA contribution and headline performance claims.

C2.justification: V3 explicitly discusses the single-neighborhood, steady-2D validation boundary and the absence of hard PDE, mass-conservation, and boundary-condition enforcement. It adds deployment validation and calibration requirements, interprets the hierarchy ablation, and revises excessive-guidance failure from overfitting sparse or noisy measurements to over-correction especially at higher sensor densities.

D1.justification: V3 adds an implementation repository link and Appendix B.4 describing baseline observation encoding, POD-3DVar's covariance-weighted reconstruction, and MultiMesh-VP conditioning. The existing GenDA hyperparameters, hardware, training budget, and preprocessing details are retained. The PDFs establish the added access information, not the repository's operational availability.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same Bristol dataset, six altitude slices, 360 wind directions per slice, and random, cloud, and trajectory sensing configurations. The new withheld-sensor and probabilistic evaluations reuse this coverage and change evaluation procedures rather than the represented domain or reconstruction task.

E2.justification: V3 adds POD-3DVar and the directly conditioned stochastic diffusion baseline MultiMesh-VP to Table 1 and Figure 5, substantially broadening the comparison methods. Figure 10 also adds LCSVD and these two methods to the component-wise comparison, which in v2 contains only MGN, MS-MGN, and GenDA.

E3.justification: Section 3.3 introduces evaluation restricted to withheld sensor nodes; Appendix C.2 specifies providing 25% of a fixed network's measurements and withholding 75%. V3 also introduces ensemble CRPS, marginal-distribution Wasserstein evaluation, and the single-mesh control. The existing altitude split and GenDA training and sampling settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v2's guidance, density, and sensing-strategy analyses, v3 directly tests the multiscale hierarchy through SM-GenDA in Appendix C.3. It also adds withheld-measurement diagnostics, ensemble and distribution analyses, and a density-specific guidance sweep showing instability with strong guidance at higher observation counts.

E5.justification: V2 reports variation in reconstruction metrics across cases and sensor placements. V3 additionally defines and reports finite-ensemble CRPS to assess predictive distributions, and Table 3 specifies aggregation over 60 evaluations. These are new statistical reporting practices; the PDFs do not establish increased independent training runs or specify the numerical ensemble size.

E6.justification: The existing scores in Tables 1 and 2 are retained, but v3 adds substantial baseline, withheld-sensor, guidance, probabilistic, and ablation results in Tables 1, 3, and 5–8. Figure 10 also changes GenDA's component RRMSE values from 0.123/0.278 to 0.124/0.283 for the same stated 253-degree, 1662-observation example. These are reported value revisions, not evidence of an overall method improvement or decline.

M1.justification: GenDA retains its two-level graph architecture, EDM training objective, sensor-dropout conditioning, and classifier-free guidance sampling. The single-mesh variant is introduced as an ablation; explanations of known wind direction and possible off-mesh observations do not establish changes to the implemented method.

P1.justification: The main narrative sequence and most method and training prose remain intact. V3 makes localized rewrites to the introduction, comparisons, and conclusions, adds an Impact Statement and new experimental subsections, renumbers retained Appendix C material, and updates author and affiliation text.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column preprint layout to a two-column conference layout. V3 adds five tables, expands Table 1, and redraws Figures 5 and 10 with additional comparator rows and adjusted color scales. Other figure images are retained with placement or sizing changes.

R1.justification: V3 adds Song et al. (2021) and Vermeulen and Heemink (2006) to position the new diffusion and variational assimilation comparisons. The broader related-work narrative is retained; the Amorós-Trepat citation's publication update refers to the same work.

T1.justification: Appendix C.2 introduces the finite-ensemble CRPS definition in Equation 22 for the new probabilistic evaluation. The posterior, guidance, graph-network, training, and original metric equations remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V3 addresses important gaps in v2's empirical support through a stochastic comparator, a direct multiscale ablation, withheld-sensor evaluation, and ensemble scoring (Tables 1, 3, 6, and 8). Its explicit applicability and physical-consistency limitations also better align claims with demonstrated evidence. Ensemble size and baseline hyperparameters remain incompletely documented, but the stronger validation and more restrained claims provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GenDA and the same Bristol urban-flow study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–C support reliable comparison despite additions and substantial reformatting in v3.

after.justification: V3 retains those empirical results and adds baseline comparisons, withheld-sensor evaluation, probabilistic scores, and a multiscale architecture ablation.

before.justification: V2 reports original reconstruction experiments on CFD-derived urban flows, including baseline comparisons, sensor-placement tests, and guidance and observation-density analyses.

results.title: GenDA: Generative Data Assimilation on Complex Urban Areas via Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance

C1.justification: V4 retains the central entropy-degradation observation and JustGRPO contribution, while narrowing categorical statements about arbitrary order to qualified findings for general mathematics and coding tasks. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion also shift from broad superiority language toward effective or competitive performance.

C2.justification: The central entropy-degradation interpretation remains. V4 adds a missing-context explanation for random-order failures, interprets general-capability retention, and frames bidirectional refinement as an expectation and future direction. It also acknowledges heterogeneous baseline settings and stronger HumanEval baselines, while removing v3's inference that length robustness rules against fixed-length memorization.

D1.justification: V4 newly specifies full-parameter tuning and one-token decoding for the retained JustGRPO results, and clarifies baseline settings and result provenance. It explains recording entropy during rollout for the existing fast variant and adds the rationale for uniformly using 125 training steps. The original hyperparameter values, hardware, data preparation, and project-page access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix E adds actual evaluations on MMLU, MMLU-Pro, HellaSwag, and ARC-C, substantially extending coverage from mathematics and coding to broader knowledge and commonsense capabilities. The original four reasoning benchmarks and training datasets are retained.

E2.justification: Appendix D adds fully random decoding and JustGRPO-Random as evaluated comparators. Table 1 also incorporates LLaDOU and LLaDA-1.5 into its highlighted comparison, whereas v3 explicitly excluded their displayed reference rows. The other diffusion-RL comparator identities remain unchanged, including those reproduced under aligned settings.

E3.justification: V4 adds baseline reproductions aligned on full-parameter fine-tuning, one token per decoding step, and generation length 256 (Table 2), addressing settings differences in the retained system-level comparison. It also introduces the fixed-permutation RL control and extends the HumanEval temperature evaluation from Pass@128 to Pass@256. Clarifications of existing JustGRPO settings do not establish changes to its original experiments.

E4.justification: New Appendix D tests whether random decoding avoids the confidence-based sampler's limitations and whether a fixed random training order can match left-to-right RL. It supplies sampling results, a training ablation, and a malformed-output case study. These substantively extend the alternative explanations tested. The block-size and efficiency analyses already existed in v3; the temperature analysis is extended.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The Pass@k estimator is unchanged; extending its plotted range does not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1's numerical results remain unchanged, but Tables 2 and 4–6 add substantial results. Examples include aligned GSM8K scores of 83.8/84.7/86.9 for d1/ESPO/SPG versus JustGRPO's 89.1, and 82.2 for JustGRPO-Random versus 89.1 for AR training. General-capability scores and Pass@256 temperature results are also added. Reproduced baseline scores use different settings from v3's quoted results.

M1.justification: The core JustGRPO formulation, architecture, rewards, and parallel inference remain unchanged. V4 adds the JustGRPO-Random ablation variant, using a single fixed random permutation during RL. JustGRPO-Fast corresponds to v3's existing Ours-Fast top-25%-entropy variant; its relocation and clearer explanation do not establish another method change.

P1.justification: V4 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, result discussion, and conclusion, alongside the title and explanatory passages. It promotes the block-size analysis from Appendix B.3 into Section 3.1 and training efficiency from Appendix D into Section 5.3, reorganizes the appendices, and adds impact and acknowledgement sections.

P2.justification: V4 adds Tables 2 and 4–6 and revises Table 1's caption, row presentation, highlighting, and footnotes. It redraws the block-size analysis against block size, extends temperature-plot axes, and relocates the efficiency figure with renamed legends. Several other figures move or receive expanded captions while retaining their underlying graphics.

R1.justification: V4 adds the connection to sequence-order information through Varshney and Goyal, and cites ParallelBench and corrective diffusion models when discussing future bidirectional refinement.
