Appendix D.1 changes 'one-sided' to 'two-sided', although its directional alternative remains inconsistent. Existing five-fold/five-seed reporting and baseline confidence-interval procedures are retained; additional result rows do not establish increased runs.

E6.justification: Existing Table 3 entries and Figure 3 results are retained. Added results include Optimal Checklists' mean AUROC of 0.62 versus AgentScore's 0.71, rule-pool FasterRisk/MIP/greedy means of 0.69/0.65/0.53, privacy-attack outcomes, and missingness results favoring AgentScore on CF but Optimal Checklists on ICU mortality. Table 14's full-data scores differ from Figure 3; they are newly reported results, not demonstrated same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: The reported procedure changes missing-input handling to permit imputation before a rule defaults to false (Appendices B/D.1), and Appendix F changes final threshold fitting from Dval to Dcon. The rule grammar, agent roles, checklist structure, and prompts remain unchanged. These are limited procedural revisions, with implementation certainty limited by inconsistent split descriptions.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled 'Automatic Construction of Clinical Scoring Systems with LLM Agents'. Contributions, related work, method explanations, baseline discussion, and conclusion receive focused rewrites; acknowledgments and appendix subsections are added. The overall section sequence and much of the existing narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is enlarged across both columns and its caption expanded; all eight figures retain their artwork. v2 adds a main-text algorithm summary and Appendix Tables 11, 13, and 14, extends several comparison tables, and relocates four PLR rows. The overall visual style remains stable.

R1.justification: v2 newly recognizes Zhang et al.'s Optimal Checklists as an existing unit-weighted checklist learner and revises the central comparison toward fixed-feature selection versus automatic derived-rule construction throughout the introduction, related work, and Tables 2/7. Appendix C.2 also adds positioning relative to FunSearch, OPRO, and LLM-SR. This substantially revises research positioning beyond bibliographic edits.

T1.justification: The mathematical rule families, score definitions, constrained objectives, Jaccard definition, and complexity arguments in Section 2 and Appendices E.1/F remain substantively unchanged. No new theorem, proof, or mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: The direct Optimal Checklists comparison and shared-rule-pool controls address important gaps in v1's prior-work comparison and attribution of performance gains. Together with corrected research positioning, these substantially strengthen the paper's scientific case. Privacy and missingness audits add useful bounded evidence. Conflicting hyperparameter/split descriptions and unexplained differences between external-validation result sets still limit reproducibility, but the central comparison and attribution gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AgentScore work despite the changed title. Their main texts, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–G are readable and support reliable matching.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds rule-pool comparisons, a membership-inference audit, and missing-measurement experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original clinical prediction experiments, external validation, ablations, and a study with 18 clinicians in Section 5 and Appendix E.

results.title: Automatic Construction of Clinical Scoring Systems with LLM Agents

C1.justification: The abstract changes the maximum parameter-saving claim from 15-fold to 33-fold, already reported for SST-2 in v2's body, and explicitly acknowledges Deep Ensembles' likelihood advantages. The conclusion replaces a consistent calibration–OOD tradeoff with a task-dependent claim. The central low-rank variational and theoretical contributions remain.

C2.justification: Sections 4.6 and H.1 replace a uniform OOD-superiority interpretation with task-specific tradeoffs. v3 withdraws the description of 0.790 coverage as near 95%, distinguishes interval-calibration AUC from ECE and point accuracy from calibration, and corrects MNIST/Fashion-MNIST ranking interpretations. It also explains moderate runtime scaling and explicitly qualifies the supplementary ensemble and recovered rank-sweep evidence.

D1.justification: Appendices G.5.4 and H.5–H.6 add substantial reproducibility information: profiling hardware and memory-measurement API, warmup and measurement budgets, optimizer distinctions, ensemble sampling, and SWAG training phases, ranks, seeds, and posterior-sample counts. Existing documentation clarifies parameter accounting and experiment-specific Monte Carlo counts. MNIST's stated scaling range is corrected while retaining division by 126, rather than documenting a new preprocessing operation.

E1.justification: Dataset and task coverage is retained: MIMIC-III with newborn OOD, Beijing forecasting with Guangzhou OOD, SST-2 with AG News OOD, MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and toy-regression extrapolation. The added comparisons and profiling use existing coverage.

E2.justification: SWAG changes from an acknowledged missing comparison in v2 to an evaluated posterior baseline across all three main benchmarks in Section 4.5 and Appendix H.6. This substantially extends the comparison to another scalable posterior approach. The original six-method benchmark comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v3 introduces controlled profiling with 10 warmup and 50 measured steps, a seven-configuration rank sweep, ensemble prediction aggregation, and dataset-specific SWAG training protocols. Existing reported settings also change: Beijing validation/test sizes become 6,260 rather than 7,553, and the toy uncertainty analysis changes its stated percentile range and in-domain window. These corrections do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendices H.4.1–H.4.2 add controlled efficiency analysis and rank sensitivity of memory, training, and inference costs. Appendix H.5 tests whether low-rank ensembling mitigates calibration deficiencies, previously only hypothesized. Existing predictive rank ablations, initialization comparisons, calibration-bin checks, and OOD analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Table 2 first displays standard deviations for the existing four-run Beijing results, previously shown as means alone. Figure 6 changes its seed count from five to four, and Appendix G.1 narrows the general repeated-run statement to main-text experiments. New profiling and ensemble studies explicitly disclose single-run limitations; no increase in runs for retained results is established.

E6.justification: New results include controlled profiling and rank-sweep measurements, the ensemble's 0.731 OOD AUROC and 0.415 NLL in Table 17, and SWAG outcomes in Tables 18–20. Existing values also change: low-rank Beijing MAE at 100% retention changes from 10.55 to 10.63 between v2 Table 11 and v3 Table 12, while Table 3 changes Rank-1 AUPR-In from 0.272 to 0.271. Most original benchmark scores remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The factorized posterior, ELBO, optimization, and architecture-specific implementations in Section 2 are unchanged. Appendix H.5 adds an implemented five-member low-rank Bayesian ensemble that aggregates 20 posterior draws per member; v2 discussed low-rank ensembles only as potential future work.

P1.justification: v3 makes focused rewrites in the abstract, results discussion, conclusion, and appendix interpretations, expands the running title, and introduces subsections for the added material. The overall narrative sequence, methods organization, and Appendix A–I structure remain intact.

P2.justification: The tabular presentation expands substantially with profiling, rank-sweep, ensemble, and SWAG tables. Main-text Table 4 redisplays a subset of Appendix Table 13. Table 2 gains standard-deviation formatting, and several captions and placements change. Figures 1–20 retain their underlying plots; their relocation is not new experimental evidence.

R1.justification: The introduction and new Appendix A.6 substantially broaden positioning against reduced-rank regression, probabilistic/Bayesian matrix factorization, deterministic compression, and function-space or post-training uncertainty methods. New Watanabe references distinguish measure-theoretic singularity from singular learning theory. SWAG also receives a citation and substantive empirical positioning.

T1.justification: Theorem 3.4 receives a direct null-support proof of singularity. Theorem 3.7 corrects its tail-error term from the sum of squared singular values to its square root, matching the retained appendix proof. Appendix C.5 restricts the 1-Lipschitz MAE statement to scalar outputs and corrects MSE smoothness from two to one. The broader theoretical framework and generalization proofs remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the central efficiency and uncertainty arguments. SWAG evaluations address an explicitly acknowledged comparison gap, while matched profiling separates modest epoch-time gains from larger parameter and memory savings. Mathematical corrections and task-specific interpretations repair misleading statements in v2. The additions remain limited by single-run profiling and ensemble evidence, differing SST-2 reference values, and unchanged percentage improvements accompanying corrected MAEs in Table 12. These issues constrain confidence but do not outweigh the substantial gains in supporting evidence and accuracy of interpretation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same low-rank Bayesian neural-network study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–I are readable and support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds SWAG evaluations, controlled computational profiling, and a low-rank ensemble study.

before.justification: v2 reports original MIMIC-III, Beijing forecasting, and SST-2 experiments, plus MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and toy-regression results in Appendix I.

results.title: Singular Bayesian Neural Networks

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: the large unified EEmoDB dataset, a two-stage emotion-assessment framework, and strong in-domain and cross-domain performance. New experiments support these existing claims without redefining their scope.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands interpretation of dataset reliability and training effectiveness. It distinguishes discrete and continuous validation roles, discusses ambiguity from plausible distractors, and adds explanations involving catastrophic forgetting, emergent reasoning consistency, prompt robustness and reward weighting. Appendix F.5 newly discusses training-data confounding and attributes the controlled comparison’s advantage to the multi-stage framework.

D1.justification: Table 10 newly discloses comparative SFT settings, including full fine-tuning’s learning rate, global batch size, weight decay and warmup ratio; this does not establish changes to existing experiments. The abstract replaces the anonymous code link with GitHub access described as covering both dataset and code, and the Ethics Statement specifies CC BY-NC 4.0 licensing.

E1.justification: The seven source datasets and evaluation coverage remain unchanged: EEmo-Bench, Artphoto, ArtEmis, UNIAA Sentiment and AesBench AesE. Additional audits and controls use retained data and tasks; semantically equivalent prompts preserve task requirements.

E2.justification: V2 additionally evaluates Emotion-Qwen after SFT on EEmoDB against EEmo-Logic in Table 14. This introduces an adapted comparator trained on the proposed dataset, while the original comparator sets in Tables 1–3 remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix C.2 revises discrete VAD validation from 180 samples and three experts to 1,800 samples and five experts. V2 adds continuous validation using 600 samples, six annotators and a nine-point SAM scale, plus a 400-instance QA evaluation by three annotators. New experiments also introduce shared-data fine-tuning controls, paraphrased prompts and textual/semantic reasoning-consistency checks.

E4.justification: Beyond v1’s stage/task ablations, v2 tests full fine-tuning followed by GRPO, expands annotation-quality validation, and adds reasoning–answer consistency and prompt-variation analyses. Tables 15–17 newly ablate format-reward weight, the squared ranking margin, regression reward and emotion-similarity reward parameters.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 first reports Krippendorff’s alpha for discrete and continuous VAD annotations, adding inter-annotator reliability estimation to v1’s agreement reporting. The existing repeated cross-validation and five-round LLM judging remain unchanged; model-seed variability and confidence intervals are not newly reported.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their results, but v2 adds substantial validation, training-loss, consistency, prompt-control, baseline and reward-ablation results. Appendix C.2 replaces VAD agreement rates of 83.33%, 83.33% and 80% with 94.00%, 93.83% and 91.17% under the enlarged study, so these are not matched-protocol gains. Table 4 changes the final model’s Artphoto F1 from 40.31% to 38.68%, matching the retained Table 3 value.

M1.justification: The proposed Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone, LoRA SFT followed by GRPO, and ranking, hybrid-regression and emotion-similarity rewards remain unchanged. V2 evaluates alternatives through ablations without replacing the proposed method.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized wording and formatting edits, adds equal-contribution and conference information, acknowledgements and an Ethics Statement, and expands several appendix subsections. The main narrative and section order remain largely intact; retained prompt sections are principally renumbered.

P2.justification: V2 adds a substantial appendix table suite, Tables 10–17, displaying settings, training losses, consistency checks, prompt sensitivity, the adapted baseline and reward ablations. Table 4 gains another experimental row. Existing Figures 1–13 are retained, with caption and placement adjustments rather than replacement.

R1.justification: V2 replaces the Ekman 1982 chapter with the distinct 1992 article, An argument for basic emotions, and briefly connects reasoning consistency to DeepSeek-R1 in Appendix F.4. The broader related-work positioning remains stable; other bibliographic updates concern retained works.

T1.justification: Equations 1–13, the CES-to-VAD mapping assumptions, training objectives and reward definitions are retained. The added explanations and empirical reward comparisons introduce no new formal results, derivations or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses central evidential gaps in v1: expanded human validation tests continuous synthetic scores and generated QA, while the shared-data baseline and reward ablations strengthen support for the framework’s contribution beyond aggregate benchmark performance. These additions substantially improve rigor. Some interpretations remain overstated: reasoning–answer consistency does not establish reasoning correctness, and one adapted baseline does not fully isolate architectural effects.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EEmoDB and EEmo-Logic. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across inserted sections and pagination changes.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and reports additional human validation, controlled comparisons, robustness tests and reward ablations.

before.justification: V1 reports original benchmark evaluations, training ablations and human validation of generated VAD labels in Section 5 and Appendices C and F.

results.title: EEmo-Logic: A Unified Dataset and Multi-Stage Framework for Comprehensive Image-Evoked Emotion Assessment

C1.justification: The central contributions concerning component design, alignment, and stabilization are retained. The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and conclusion extend the empirical claims from NLP to NLP and computer vision, including a new claim of state-of-the-art image-classification performance.

C2.justification: Appendix F newly attributes most performance gains to component design, with stabilization providing an additional benefit. Section 4.4 interprets the fixed-configuration results as evidence of practical transferability, and Section 5 explicitly identifies nonlinear theoretical analysis as an outstanding limitation.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds targeted-layer descriptions and hyperparameter rows for Qwen and CLIP, while retaining the earlier configurations and code-access information. Documentation remains incomplete for the added 70B experiments, and v2 no longer supplies the explicit one-epoch count stated in v1.

E1.justification: The GLUE, MetaMathQA/GSM8k, and Code-FeedBack/HumanEval coverage is retained. v2 adds image classification on Stanford Cars, DTD, EuroSAT, GTSRB, RESISC45, SUN397, and SVHN, substantially extending evaluation beyond language to visual domains.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the original NLP tables is unchanged. The new image-classification comparison in Table 13 includes LoRA-Pro and zero-shot CLIP, neither previously reported as an evaluated comparator; LoRA-Pro was already cited in v1.

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen-3-0.6B, Qwen-3-8B, and LLaMA-3-70B settings, a CLIP image-classification protocol using prompt-based classifiers and test accuracy, and a controlled evaluation fixing the component configuration across models. Section 4 also replaces the explicit single-epoch statement with equal but unspecified epoch counts; this does not establish an actual budget change or rerun.

E4.justification: The original component sweeps, initialization tests, and gradient analysis remain. Section 4.4 adds fixed-configuration robustness testing, while Appendix F adds a component-design-versus-scaling ablation, Qwen and CLIP sensitivity analyses, and fixed-budget design tests on LLaMA-3-70B and CLIP.

E5.justification: Both versions state that results use means and standard deviations over three random seeds, with no stated increase in runs. However, the added CLIP appendix results in Tables 18–20 and 23–24 and LLaMA-3-70B results in Tables 21–22 omit standard deviations, making uncertainty reporting less complete for these analyses.

E6.justification: Tables 2–11 and the computational-cost results are retained unchanged. Newly reported results include Qwen GSM8k scores of 65.83 and 86.56, CLIP average accuracy of 90.08 versus LoRA-One's 89.57, and scaling-only and design-only ablation scores of 49.43 and 55.62. Some new appendix averages are internally inconsistent: the first vision row in Tables 18 and 19 reports 89.69, although its seven listed scores average approximately 87.26.

M1.justification: The summed Kronecker update, component-design principles, initialization, scaling rule, and efficient computation remain unchanged in Sections 3 and 4. The new default-configuration experiment evaluates an existing configuration rather than introducing a new method component.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized grammar and terminology corrections, clarifies alignment notation, fixes the NLG results cross-reference from Table 9 to Table 10, and updates publication and acknowledgment text. It adds experimental subsections and Appendix F while preserving the existing narrative organization.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the table presentation with new benchmark, robustness, and ablation tables and an enlarged hyperparameter table. Figure 1's unchanged curves are enlarged and rearranged from side-by-side panels above Table 9 to vertically stacked panels below it; the computational-cost table is relocated and renumbered without changing its results.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for the vision datasets, CLIP, Qwen3, and Zhang and Pilanci's LoRA work, and explicitly connects its linear setting to earlier LoRA theory. The related-work discussion and positioning against KronA and MoKA otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, assumptions, alignment theorems, stabilization theorem, and proofs in Appendices B–E retain their substance. v2 adds explanatory notation around Equation 11 and corrects prose typos, without introducing or revising formal results.

improvement.justification: The new vision evaluation and fixed-configuration test substantially strengthen evidence for applicability beyond v1's NLP experiments. Table 17 also directly tests whether gains arise from component design or stabilization, addressing an important attribution gap. These validation gains outweigh localized shortcomings: inconsistent averages in Tables 18–19, missing uncertainty for some appendix results, and less explicit training-budget documentation weaken parts of the added evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CDKA research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching v1's Appendices A–E to v2 and identifying the added Appendix F.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds Qwen evaluations, image-classification results, fixed-configuration robustness tests, and appendix ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original CDKA benchmark results, component and initialization experiments, gradient trajectories, and computational-cost measurements. These are distinguished from baseline results attributed to prior work.

results.title: Diving into Kronecker Adapters: Component Design Matters

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same novelty, detail-preservation, mixed-precision, and W4A6/W4A4 performance claims. The stated 5.8× model-size and 6.14× operation reductions are unchanged.

C2.justification: Sections 4.4–4.6 add explanations of runtime bottlenecks, a cautious perceptual-regularization hypothesis for DreamClear, calibration-domain stability, and weight-versus-activation sources of artifacts. New limitations identify difficult thin, repetitive, and high-contrast textures and qualify deployment claims because native arbitrary-precision kernels are unsupported. The earlier general warning about no-reference IQA metrics is retained.

D1.justification: v4 substantially expands deployment documentation: parallel execution of SVD-G with the quantized branch, a Triton implementation of SVD-L avoiding dense reconstruction, and mapping mixed-precision schedules to standard low-bit computations. It also supplies profiling hardware and batch size and local-study sampling details. These are newly documented details, not established changes to the earlier implementation; the code/model release promise remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Section 4.5 adds DIV2K calibration data and calibration-transfer scenarios using DrealSR and DIV2K instead of RealSR. The four existing evaluation datasets and super-resolution task remain unchanged; DreamClear adds a backbone rather than a dataset or task.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in the retained benchmark comparisons and ablations is unchanged. The new runtime comparisons reuse FP and SVDQuant, while the local artifact study reuses existing component variants; no new competing quantization method is introduced.

E3.justification: v4 adds several evaluation protocols: W4A4 profiling with batch size 16 on a reported RTX-4090 48GB GPU, DreamClear configurations, alternative 32-image calibration sets, and targeted 64×64 regions from 32 randomly selected RealSR images. The local study introduces ROI-PSNR, Edge MAE, and Color MAE. These are new experiments; the original benchmark settings are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component and rank ablations, v4 tests sensitivity to calibration domain and quantifies local fidelity, edge, and color artifacts across component combinations in Tables 8–9. DreamClear generalization and the component runtime breakdown further expand analysis of applicability and deployment bottlenecks.

E5.justification: The new tables continue point-estimate reporting without adding repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Existing variance plots are unchanged; the newly specified image counts describe evaluation samples, not repeated runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their values, while Tables 5–9 add substantial results on efficiency, DreamClear, calibration robustness, and artifacts. Table 6 reports FP/Q-DiT4SR latency of 3099.30/686.50 ms, or 4.51× speedup. Table 9 reports baseline/full-method ROI-PSNR of 19.6684/20.9590. These are newly reported evaluations, not improvements to the retained benchmark scores.

M1.justification: H-SVD, VaSMP, VaTMP, and their quantization and scheduling procedures remain unchanged. The new execution details document implementation, and Section 4.5 explicitly applies the same framework to DreamClear without backbone-specific modification.

P1.justification: The document adds Sections 4.4–4.6, acknowledgments, and an impact statement, and replaces the preprint notice with conference publication text. These are localized structural additions; the existing introduction, method exposition, results discussion, and conclusion receive little rewriting.

P2.justification: Five new tables substantially expand the quantitative presentation, separately displaying practical efficiency, runtime components, DreamClear results, calibration robustness, and local artifacts. Figures 1–9 and Tables 1–4 are retained, while the inserted displays reflow the closing sections and references.

R1.justification: v4 adds references for NTIRE 2017/DIV2K, Pixelated Butterfly, Scatterbrain, and Monarch, and explains implementation connections to Nunchaku and structured matrices. The IMPQ-to-CoopQ update concerns the same cited arXiv identifier, 2509.15455, rather than a newly introduced work. Overall novelty positioning remains stable.

T1.justification: Equations 1–23, Gaussian and high-rate assumptions, hierarchical decomposition, distortion reasoning, and bit-allocation mathematics are unchanged. The added empirical metrics and implementation discussion introduce no new formal definitions, proofs, or derivations.

improvement.justification: v3 supports deployment chiefly through parameter and operation counts. v4 adds measured memory and latency, including the modest efficiency penalty relative to SVDQuant, and strengthens generality and detail-preservation evidence through Tables 7–9. These additions address important validation gaps, while explicit artifact and kernel-support limitations improve transparency. Exact precision mapping and statistical uncertainty remain insufficiently documented, but the overall evidential improvement is substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Q-DiT4SR and support reliable comparison of the text, equations, tables, and figures. All 11 pages of v3 and 12 pages of v4 were inspected; neither supplied PDF contains a separate appendix.

after.justification: v4 retains these original results and adds runtime measurements, DreamClear evaluation, calibration robustness tests, and local artifact analysis in Tables 5–9.

before.justification: v3 reports original super-resolution evaluations on four datasets, quantitative ablations in Tables 2–4, and visual and activation analyses.

results.title: Q-DiT4SR: Exploration of Detail-Preserving Diffusion Transformer  Quantization for Real-World Image Super-Resolution

C1.justification: The abstract now explicitly claims introducing a benchmark for long-sequence MCIT, developed as TriGap in Section 5.1. This adds an independent benchmark contribution to v1's method contribution; the two-drift diagnosis, three method components and general performance claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of hyperparameter sensitivity, subtraction versus ratio scoring, anisotropic scaling versus projection, structured expert specialization, isolated router-induced forgetting and transferable capabilities. Appendix L also links routing stability to sparse inference. The original limitations concerning ambiguous task boundaries and varying formats remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a Prism code pointer and infrastructure reference, selected hyperparameters, selection using 20% of UCIT training data, per-task TriGap sample counts, and randomized top-64 decomposition/storage details. It also explicitly identifies the retained CoIN baseline scores as adopted from original publications.

E1.justification: Beyond CoIN, v2 evaluates UCIT, the new ten-task TriGap benchmark and cross-benchmark transfer to MMMU. Coverage expands to captioning, medical and chemical questions, documents/charts, traffic scenes, aerial disaster imagery and additional reasoning tasks.

E2.justification: The seven CoIN comparators are retained. New comparisons actually evaluate Zero-shot, FT-LoRA, Replay-LoRA and CL-MoE on TriGap/UCIT; Table 9 additionally evaluates GPM-style hard-projection and VPT-CPG-style constant-scaling substitutions.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 changes the reported setup from LoRA in all linear layers with a projector learning rate to FFN-only LoRA training. This does not establish that retained experiments were rerun. New protocols include UCIT-based hyperparameter selection, alternative CoIN task orders, fixed-expert/representation controls and quantitative forgetting evaluation.

E4.justification: Appendices F–L add hyperparameter sensitivity, task-order robustness, scaling/freezing design comparisons, freezing-related routing entropy, controlled router-drift causality, quantitative forgetting, MMMU generalization and compression/efficiency analyses. These substantially extend the retained component ablations and diagnostic plots.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed or repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations or significance tests. The additional results continue to use point estimates.

E6.justification: The original CoIN comparison and component-ablation values remain unchanged, including SAME's 66.82 average. v2 adds TriGap and UCIT averages of 46.53 and 67.12, MMMU results of 36.35 for SAME versus 34.83 for MoELoRA, and numerous analysis results. M1.justification: The spectral-aware routing, curvature-aware scaling and adaptive freezing procedures remain unchanged, as do Algorithms 1–2. The revised experimental setup and newly disclosed decomposition implementation do not establish a change to the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most introduction, method and conclusion prose and the main section sequence remain intact. Rewriting is concentrated in benchmark discussion and mathematical appendices. Pseudocode moves from Appendix E to A, other appendices are reorganized, and affiliations, publication information and acknowledgments are updated.

P2.justification: v2 adds benchmark tables, an extensive appendix table suite and a full-page TriGap example figure. Figure 2 gains boxed visual groupings, while retained tables and plots are relocated. The original layer-wise utilization plot is preserved as Figure 10 rather than newly added.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through TriGap's claimed gaps relative to CoIN/UCIT and explicit distinctions from GPM-style projection and VPT-CPG-style scaling. It adds dataset, infrastructure and methodological references and expands comparator descriptions; the orthogonal-subspace-learning and SmoLoRA references are removed.

T1.justification: The main projection argument and Riemannian update remain. However, v2 Appendix D introduces a Neural Feature Matrix–AGOP proportionality with exponent 1/2 and replaces the detailed Jacobian derivation. Appendix C removes explicit LoRA-factor approximation qualifications and changes approximate constraint saturation to equality.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond CoIN through additional domains, controlled drift experiments, robustness tests and design comparisons. Previously missing hyperparameters and code-access information also improve reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized regressions: Table 12 has inconsistent forgetting signs and a MoELoRA average incompatible with its listed values, while the theoretical appendices make LoRA-factor approximation qualifications less explicit.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SAME and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables and appendices. The complete 17-page v1 and 25-page v2 support reliable comparison despite appendix reorganization.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds TriGap, UCIT, robustness, design-choice and out-of-distribution evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original CoIN evaluations, component ablations, router/expert-drift diagnostics, efficiency measurements and qualitative analyses.

results.title: SAME: Stabilized Mixture-of-Experts for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: human-reasoning-based VLM editing, topology-guided embeddings, state-of-the-art editing, and improved generalization with locality and efficiency. Added experiments support these existing claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v4 adds explicit limitations concerning codebook search costs and inaccurate or incomplete human reasoning. It interprets replacement-noise degradation as loss of relevant facts, distinguishes answer and reasoning contributions, and interprets source-stable hyperparameters as evidence of largely data-agnostic selection. These extend the retained retrieval-based explanation.

D1.justification: The future-release promise becomes a statement that code and data are available through a repository link. v4 also documents source-specific layer indices and weights, combined-dataset ablations, and filtering counts of 389 A-OKVQA and 74 FVQA images. Repository availability is reported by the PDF, not independently verified.

E1.justification: FVQA and A-OKVQA remain the editing benchmarks. v4 adds Flickr30k images for embedding-selection validation in Appendix A.3 and introduces editing scenarios with injected or replaced irrelevant reasoning, extending source and input-condition coverage.

E2.justification: IKE-COT newly participates in both Table 1 comparisons and sequential-editing Figure 12; v1 reports the other COT variants but no IKE-COT results. The five base editors remain. New Table 3 also introduces ground-truth answer and reasoning prompting controls.

These substantially extend the evaluation design. The original four VLMs, editing metrics, and sequential evaluation every 200 edits on 50 sampled edits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v4 adds tests of noisy feedback, the separate contributions of answer and reasoning entries, sensitivity to embedding-selection data, automatic patch quality, and alternative layer-selection criteria (Tables 2–5 and 7). These substantially broaden mechanism and robustness checks. Existing embedding, retrieval-parameter, and key-merging ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 4 replaces separate VLM trajectories with averages across VLMs and shaded bands, changing variability reporting for sequential editing. The bands are not statistically defined. The existing B=10 Monte Carlo sampling and bias mean/standard-deviation reporting remain unchanged; no additional seeds or repeated-run counts are documented.

E6.justification: Table 1 substantially revises IKE scores while preserving every other existing result row. For A-OKVQA with LLaVA-1.5-7B, IKE accuracy changes from 0.27 to 0.97 and image generality from 0.34 to 0.95 under unchanged reported settings; the cause is unstated. IKE-COT and the new robustness, component, selection, and patch-quality studies add substantial results.

M1.justification: The codebook, visual patchification, key merging, dual embedding, and retrieval procedures remain unchanged. The explicit yes/no patch filter, descriptive scoring prompt, and 90%/10% merging thresholds added to the main explanation already appear in v1 Appendix C.

P1.justification: v4 makes localized language corrections, expands motivation and method explanations, adds subsections, and numbers and reorders the ablation discussion. Most existing prose and the overall narrative structure remain. Publication and correspondence information also change.

P2.justification: The empirical presentation expands with new robustness and component tables in the main text and selection and patch-quality tables in the appendices. Table 1 gains IKE-COT rows, Figure 4 is redrawn using averages and bands, and Figure 12 adds IKE-COT series. Retained figures are resized or relocated; v1 Table 2 becomes v4 Table 6.

R1.justification: v4 adds Plummer et al. (2015) for Flickr30k. results.title: ReasonEdit: Editing Vision--Language Models using Human Reasoning

D1.justification: v2 documents the structured-teacher construction, MNIST architecture and optimizer settings, OLMo model/script identifiers, and the Pythia learning-rate schedule. It removes v1's paragraph specifying FP16 loading, automatic device placement, and caching. The existing code-access link remains unchanged.

OLMo is evaluated on the retained FineWeb dataset, so its addition alone does not expand dataset coverage.

The new fitting comparison uses identical Pythia points, independently fitted offsets, and R-squared to quantify collapse quality.

It also addresses possible bias in the original time-variable comparison through independent refitting (Figure 29). Existing optimizer, initialization, weight-decay, and residual-model analyses are retained.

No new repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval, or significance-testing procedure is documented. The added R-squared values assess fit quality.

E6.justification: New results include approximately one-third scaling across structured-data conditions, a MNIST training-loss exponent of 0.35, and OLMo exponents of 0.35 ± 0.01, 0.30 ± 0.01, and 0.36 ± 0.02 for 1B, 7B, and 13B. P1.justification: The overall section structure and most existing prose are retained. Changes include targeted wording revisions, a reorganized transition from toy models to LLMs, new appendix subsections and explanatory notes, expanded acknowledgements, and an impact statement.

P2.justification: Figure 6 is rebuilt as a four-panel display incorporating v1's appendix Figure 26, with changed vertical scaling in the logit panel. New Figures 23, 26, 29, and 30 display structured-data, MNIST, fitting-comparison, and OLMo results. Most other figures are retained and relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for MNIST, OLMo, and Liu et al.'s residual-model work, plus a paragraph interpreting earlier reported scaling exponents. The established positioning against data-structure explanations remains intact; the publication update to an existing reference is bibliographic.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 replaces an asserted analytic expansion with an energy-gap derivation, explicit continuity and positive-density assumptions, and discussion of degeneracy and alternative universality classes. Gradient outer-product expressions are corrected. However, new Equation 80 contains an indexing error: its i-indexed sum uses eta_t rather than eta_i.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central justification: Appendix A.3 derives previously asserted low-temperature behavior under explicit assumptions, while Figure 29 addresses the potentially unfair comparison by independently fitting both time parameterizations. Structured-data, MNIST, and OLMo results broaden validation. These gains outweigh local notation and documentation regressions, although the LLM gap-density condition and rotation explanation remain unverified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and retained equations, results, and relocated figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds structured-data experiments, MNIST training results, OLMo evaluations, and a comparative fitting analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original toy-model training experiments, numerical calculations, and evaluations of Pythia checkpoints on FineWeb.

results.title: Universal One-third Time Scaling in Learning Peaked Distributions

Additional experiments support these existing contributions without redefining them.

C2.justification: V3 adds explanations connecting recent-context encoding to tracking changing dynamics and the biased prior to efficient one-step generation. It also interprets Hopper’s weaker separation and proposes probe accuracy as a dataset-diversity diagnostic. These substantially expand applicability and mechanism discussions, while the original stationary-dynamics limitations paragraph remains.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redesigned from two setting-specific panels into grouped Seen/Unseen/OOD bars. Tables 1 and 2 expand, four new tables present supplementary evidence, and the Meta-DT table moves to the appendix. This substantially expands the empirical displays, while most other figures are retained.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, diffusion derivations, and Appendix A toy-case reasoning are retained. Separating diffusion index k from environment time t, standardizing action-space notation, and clarifying covariance do not introduce substantive mathematical changes.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DADP and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E. Matching retained and relocated material supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V2 reports original MuJoCo and Adroit evaluations, representation and utilization ablations, and guidance-scale and context-source experiments.

results.title: DADP: Domain Adaptive Diffusion Policy

D1.justification: Both disclose Julia BigFloat with 1000-bit precision, 1000 iterations in under 10 seconds on a laptop, and code in supplementary material. No implementation-resource or access information changes.

E1.justification: Both evaluate quadratic minimization over the Euclidean ball with the same optimizer-location and initialization scenarios. The generalized ball and ellipsoid results are theoretical extensions, not added evaluations.

E2.justification: The comparisons between random and constructed initializations remain unchanged. Newly cited work is not evaluated as a baseline; Table 1's added short-step designation concerns a cited theoretical guarantee.

E3.justification: Both retain exact-line-search simulations, the 10^-4 accuracy threshold, the 10,000-point grid at r0=1, and the same stable-phase stopping rule. No revised experimental protocol is reported.

E4.justification: Initialization sensitivity, grid-resolution effects, bisection behavior, and perturbation observations are retained. New Figure 6 visualizes the stable-trajectory geometry already analyzed in v1 Sections 3.1 and 4.

E5.justification: The multiple-initialization reporting is unchanged. Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Matched convergence curves and grid-search results are unchanged, including v1 Figure 6 versus v2 Figure 7 and v1 Figure 8 versus v2 Figure 9. The added phase-space visualization illustrates previously reported findings.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1, the FW updates and stepsize rules, and the grid/bisection/backward reconstruction procedures are retained. Corrected recurrence indexing and parity notation do not establish a changed computational method.

P1.justification: Targeted prose edits clarify coordinates, jump reasoning, bisection parity, and proof steps; affiliations and the preprint date also change. The overall section order and Appendix A–C organization are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 6 showing the existing stable trajectory and its bounds. Retained figures and Table 1 are relocated, subsequent figures are renumbered, and text reflows without a broader visual redesign.

R1.justification: v2 adds Grimmer and Liu (2026), contrasting algorithm coverage, dimensional restrictions, and set smoothness, and cites Goncharov and Ivanov (2017) for geometric definitions. It also adds short steps to its account of Garber and Hazan (2015), including Table 1.

T1.justification: v2 revises the set-curvature definitions, replaces Proposition 5's sufficient jump bound with a necessary condition, adds Lemma 8 on forward dynamics, and corrects feasibility and inversion arguments. Appendix C replaces informal estimates with explicit bounds and establishes r0>=1/18 independently of the horizon. Theorem 6 adds Omega(mu D^2/t^2) scaling; the ellipsoid corollary changes from an infinite-horizon statement to horizon-dependent initializations with exact line search.

improvement.justification: Appendix C supplies the horizon-independent r0>=1/18 bound missing from v1's central lower-bound argument and replaces informal Taylor estimates with explicit bounds over the stated domain. These changes substantially strengthen the mathematical support for the main result. Restricting the ellipsoid corollary to finite horizons and exact line search also removes an overbroad formulation while preserving the headline contribution.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Frank-Wolfe lower-bound work. Their main text, equations, figures, table, and complete Appendices A–C are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original numerical simulations and search results, alongside its theoretical analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original numerical simulations, including convergence trajectories, an initialization landscape, and grid/bisection search results in Section 3 and Appendix B.3.

results.title: Lower Bounds for Frank-Wolfe on Strongly Convex Sets

C1.justification: The novelty claim, two central contributions, and 84.5 VBench claim remain. The abstract and introduction broaden the deployment contribution from 2.3x acceleration on RTX 5090 to approximately 2–3x across diverse GPUs, with updated throughput claims.

The limitations replace the unresolved Hopper-adaptation concern with A100 tuning caveats and newly acknowledge residual artifacts; the restriction to 1.3B models remains.

Appendix H adds staged deployment and memory analyses across hardware and durations.

Publication-header, correspondence, and method-label edits are limited rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds long-video examples and two qualitative ablation figures, plus tables for long-video scores, configurations, new baselines, device efficiency, and memory. The deployment chart is redrawn with an additional kernel-optimization stage. Existing benchmark displays are retained, and v1 Figure 7 becomes v2 Figure 10 rather than a new result.

R1.justification: v2 adds related-work citations such as Mixture of Contexts and Pack and Force Your Memory, references supporting the new evaluations and deployment, and discussion positioning sparse attention against caching and token reduction. It removes the Brooks world-simulator reference. The main taxonomy and novelty positioning remain; publication updates are not new works.

The Markov-chain, KL, and Pinsker derivation is retained from v1 Appendix B in v2 Appendix C; its notation corrections do not constitute a new proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, three introductory contributions, and substantive conclusion retain the claims about unitary approximation limits, relaxed graph/mesh convolutions, and strong diffusive-PDE performance. Appendix B.2 proposes gradient stability as another explanation for unitary-network benefits, and C.6/C.8 interpret the new local-smoothness and component results.

Appendix C.8 adds direct tests of unitary layers, zero padding, activation, and readout architecture, while C.6 reports a new local-smoothness analysis, substantially extending the diagnostic evidence.

Added results extend these reporting practices without changing retained replication counts or introducing new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark, multiscale-smoothness, and weather table values are unchanged. Further ablation results, truncation curves, and local-smoothness findings substantially expand the reported outcomes.

Sections 5.2-5.3 rename encoder-decoder components as compositional smoothness-breaking components; the additional truncation-selection explanation elaborates an existing suggestion.

P1.justification: The revision consistently renames the encoder-decoder terminology and appendix dataset headings, adds an appendix contents list, and expands the conclusion into a Discussion section. Sample initializations move to C.9. Most existing prose and the main narrative sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds a ten-panel truncation figure and the substantial baseline/ablation table block in Tables 5-10. It redraws Figure 2 with revised terminology and dimension labels, groups Table 2 columns by architecture type, and relocates initialization tables. Existing empirical plots and qualitative images are retained.

results.title: DECO: Decoupled Multimodal Diffusion Transformer for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation with a Plugin Tactile Adapter

E4.justification: v4 adds UniVTAC comparisons with and without tactile input, taskwise timeout/slippage diagnostics, and action-stride/budget sensitivity tests. E5.justification: Appendix C.3 newly specifies identical evaluation seeds for the UniVTAC comparison. Existing Wilson 95% confidence intervals remain unchanged. The simulation additions provide no training-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results are unchanged. New results include DECO averages of 94.2% on LIBERO, 85.3% on RoboTwin, and 56.4%/58.0% on DexJoCo rand-obj/rand-full; both DECO and DECO.p average 82.1% on UniVTAC. Tables 21–26 and accompanying diagnostics add substantial new findings, not same-setting improvements over v3.

M1.justification: Appendix C.2 adds a T5 language encoder to DECO for language-conditioned RoboTwin evaluation, a limited architectural and input adaptation. The original multimodal pathways, flow-matching objective, two-stage training, and tactile adapter remain unchanged.

P1.justification: v4 appends Appendix C with four benchmark subsections and short diagnostic discussions. Reference venue abbreviations, citation suffixes, and the version stamp also change. The main narrative and Appendices A–B undergo no substantive rewriting or reorganization.

P2.justification: Tables 21–26 substantially expand the tabular presentation with benchmark comparisons, an eight-task failure breakdown, and separate DexJoCo randomization displays, including explanatory footnotes. Existing Figures 1–8 and Tables 1–20 retain their content and layout; references reflow and appendix pagination shifts.

R1.justification: New references support the simulation benchmarks and comparators, including LIBERO, UniVTAC, DexJoCo, OpenVLA-OFT, and newer VLA/tactile policies. Appendix C adds limited positioning concerning model size and pretraining requirements; Section 2 and the original novelty framing remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The problem formulation, flow-matching loss and inference update, conditioning equations, and tactile-embedding formulation in Section 3 are unchanged. Appendix C adds no formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs.

improvement.justification: v3's empirical evidence was confined to the authors' real-robot dataset. Appendix C substantially strengthens assessment beyond that setting through external benchmarks and environmental variation. The UniVTAC null tactile result and stride/failure diagnostics also clarify applicability limits. Heterogeneous comparator training and missing simulation uncertainty estimates limit ranking claims, but the disclosed qualifications and more diagnostic evidence provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DECO and DECO-50. All 21 pages of v3 and 25 pages of v4, including their appendices, support comparison. The existing material is retained; v4 principally adds Appendix C.

after.justification: v4 retains those original experiments and adds DECO simulation results on four benchmarks in Appendix C. These qualify independently of the externally sourced comparator scores.

before.justification: v3 reports original real-robot evaluations, tactile-adapter ablations, distribution-shift tests, and encoder comparisons in Section 4 and Appendix B.

results.title: DECO: Decoupled Multimodal Diffusion Transformer for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation with a Plugin Tactile Adapter

C1.justification: The main applicability claim narrows from seasonal and non-seasonal diseases to seasonal epidemics, although the new Impact Statement retains the broader assertion. The abstract replaces the earlier 15–35% RMSE reduction and 1–3-week peak-timing improvement with a 27–70% reduction against the strongest baseline and best peak-detection accuracy across five datasets.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies parameter interpretation: recovery rate is described as the model's preferred decomposition of effective reproduction dynamics rather than a direct recovery-rate estimate. It adds double-peak smoothing as a single-strain SIRS limitation, dependence on preprocessing choices, and an explanation for the two-component advantage on varying-parameter SIRS. V1's more general uncertainty and spatial limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds frequency-based mode grouping, delay-offset alignment, and seasonal-period fallbacks to Algorithm 1. Appendices F/H disclose split grids and dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning, but not selected hyperparameter values or training budgets. The stated implementation location changes from an anonymous 4open.science repository to a named GitHub repository.

E1.justification: V2 removes the COVID-like illness symptoms dataset and its results throughout the paper and appendices, eliminating the only real-world non-seasonal disease benchmark. The four synthetic settings and ILI data from ten HHS regions remain.

E2.justification: The peak-error comparison expands from v1 Figure 10 to v2 Figures 10/A4 and Tables A3/A4 by adding LSTM, EINN-SEIRm, NeuralODE, and KAN-ODEs. These methods already participated in v1 forecasting comparisons. TimeKAN and TimeMixer++ remain evaluated in v2 figures despite being omitted from its new numerical tables.

E3.justification: Training-only decomposition replaces full-series preprocessing, substantially changing forecast information availability. The illustrated SIR peak comparison changes from split 0.2 in v1 Figure 10 to 0.1 in v2 Figure A4. V2 also revises the stated metric specification and describes aggregation across multiple splits, although its relationship to the figures showing individual splits remains unclear; this does not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 removes CLS-specific architecture, component-count, decomposition-method, and time-delay ablation evidence from v1 Figure 14, retaining these questions on five settings in Figure A9. Appendix F explicitly discusses split-placement robustness, without providing separate scores for each split. Regional and physics-mismatch analyses remain.

E5.justification: V1 states that results are averaged over multiple seeds but provides no corresponding standard deviations. V2 introduces mean-and-standard-deviation tables, benchmark and ablation error bars, peak-error uncertainty, and parameter-trajectory bands. Neither version specifies seed counts, so an increase in repetitions is not established.

E6.justification: Benchmark values, peak errors, inferred trajectories, and ablation rankings change extensively. ILI EpiNode RMSE changes from approximately 0.006 in v1 Figure 9f to 0.0093 in v2 Table 1, while the strongest plotted baseline changes from LSTM to TimeMixer++; these are not established same-protocol comparisons. For varying-parameter SIRS, three components cease to be best: v2 Figure A9b reports approximately 0.009 for two components versus 0.019 for three. Wavelet also replaces VMD as the best decomposition there.

M1.justification: V1 Algorithm 1 decomposes the full infection series into forecasting controls. V2 restricts VMD to training observations and introduces forecast-window controls using linear trend extrapolation, seasonal repetition, and the training residual mean. This changes the forecasting procedure and its access to future information; the latent ODEs, SIRS dynamics, and observation loss remain.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative, moving regional analyses, ablation results, and the baseline-capability comparison into appendices. Results and conclusion passages are rewritten, new appendix sections explain splits and tuning, and acknowledgements and an Impact Statement are added.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column main-text layout, redraws the framework diagram, and adds numerical benchmark, split, and peak-error tables. Benchmark and peak plots are redistributed between main text and appendices, while ablation displays gain numerical labels and uncertainty bars. Numerous retained figures are resized or relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds forecasting references supporting channel extrapolation, including Harvey, Cleveland and colleagues, Bloomfield, Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, and Zeng and colleagues. Additional epidemic-modeling references support the new multi-strain and identifiability discussion. The central positioning relative to neural ODEs and mechanistic hybrids remains.

T1.justification: V2 Equations 9–11 introduce mathematical definitions for trend extrapolation, periodic seasonal extension, and residual continuation beyond the observation window. The existing VMD/ADMM and SIRS mathematics remain substantially unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 Algorithm 1 replaces full-series controls with training-only decomposition and explicit forecast extensions, addressing future-information leakage in v1's procedure as written. This substantial correction, broader uncertainty reporting, and the recovery-rate identifiability caveat strengthen validity and interpretation. Removing CLS narrows validation, and v2 misattributes KAN-ODEs/EARTH scores to TimeKAN/TimeMixer++ in Section 4.5.1 while leaving split aggregation ambiguous. These reporting weaknesses limit confidence in the advertised gains but do not outweigh the procedural and interpretive improvements.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same EpiNode study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

after.justification: V2 reports original forecasting, peak-error, parameter-recovery, regional, and ablation results, including revised numerical comparisons.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic and surveillance-data forecasting experiments, failure-mode demonstrations, parameter-recovery results, and ablations.

results.title: How (Not) to Hybridize Neural and Mechanistic Models for Epidemiological Forecasting

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same central claims: expressive context-to-LoRA generation in one pass, reduced adaptation costs, strong task performance, and scaling potential. The added experiments and recurrent extension do not redefine those headline contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretation and applicability discussion through explanations of the architecture ablations, insufficient training as a possible cause of SHINE-R's gap to In-Context, and missing reasoning-oriented training as an explanation for GSM8K performance. It also introduces interpretations linking context quality and length to adaptation success.

D1.justification: v2 supplies additional details such as linear-control depths and hidden size 8192, the supplementary conversation-generation/testing recipe, and joint multitask training. The code pointer changes from Yewei-Liu/SHINE to MuLabPKU/SHINE. Existing hardware, optimizer, base hyperparameters, and Appendix B data-processing instructions remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds LongBench long-context QA and summarization, including MultiFieldQA-English, Qasper, and QMSum. Appendix E.5 adds joint training and evaluation on DailyDialog, GSM8K, Persona-Chat, and SAMSum, extending coverage to conversational generation, mathematical reasoning, personalization, and summarization.

E2.justification: Appendix E.3 adds DoRA and IA3 as evaluated MS MARCO MQA comparators alongside the existing LoRA SFT approach. This expands the supplementary fine-tuning comparison; the original Naive, In-Context, Generative Adapter, and test-time-training comparison sets remain.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce SHINE-R training on contexts up to 18K tokens, joint multitask fine-tuning after MQA training, and SFT sweeps over 3/5/10 conversations and 5/10/20 epochs. Architecture studies add parameter-matched controls and further configurations. Table 11 explicitly applies SQuAD-style F1 to all four new tasks; original SHINE settings remain.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds linear-projection, final-layer-memory, and attention-design ablations; SFT budget sensitivity; context-quality/length analyses; and additional layer/rank scaling curves. These substantially expand tests of architectural choices and performance dependencies. The original coupled-attention 'Bitter Lesson' analysis is retained as E.1.

E5.justification: Figures 15–16 newly report fitted relationships and r coefficients between context characteristics and F1. The existing mean, median, and P10/P90 reporting in Figure 5 is retained. No additional seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests are documented.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–4 remain numerically unchanged, while v2 adds LongBench and multitask scores, SFT accuracy/runtime grids, and diagnostic curves. For example, the new 10-conversation/20-epoch settings yield 58.50 F1 for LoRA and 56.52 for DoRA. Table 11 reports GSM8K F1 of 25.27 for SHINE versus 44.48 for In-Context. These are additional results under newly reported settings.

M1.justification: Section 5.5 introduces SHINE-R, a recurrent extension that processes context chunks sequentially. It generates separate adapters for updating the encoding of later chunks and for final inference, concatenating the saved adapters. This substantially extends the procedure beyond the retained SHINE architecture and objectives.

P1.justification: Most existing scientific prose and the overall narrative remain. Changes include localized grammar and notation corrections, front-matter updates, expanded related-work organization, new experimental subsections, and appendix reorganization: old Appendix D becomes E.1, while old Appendix E becomes D.

P2.justification: v2 adds the SHINE-R diagram, five analysis figures, the LongBench table, three SFT-grid tables, and the multitask table. These substantially expand the visual presentation. All original figure graphics are retained, with some relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands research positioning through new discussions of test-time training, other architectures, and additional applications, with many added citations. Appendix C.7 adds a conceptual comparison with Drag-and-Drop LLMs. The Anonymous-to-Charakorn update for Doc-to-LoRA refers to the same existing work.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, objectives, and Appendix B/C complexity derivations are retained. Section 3.4 corrects R to the already-defined output dimension O in parameter slicing, a notation repair. SHINE-R is described procedurally without a new formal derivation or proof.

improvement.justification: Appendix E.2–E.3 substantially strengthens v1's limited empirical controls for architectural and efficiency claims through parameter-matched ablations and broader SFT method/budget comparisons, including settings where SFT wins on F1. Long-context and multitask evaluations also expose applicability limits. Sparse SHINE-R training details and a text-quality interpretation stronger than the near-zero correlations temper the gains, but the central validation is materially stronger.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SHINE. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable and matchable, including material moved or renumbered in v2.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds long-context, multitask, architecture-ablation, and fine-tuning comparison results in Section 5.5 and Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction/completion, QA, architecture-ablation, and scaling results, including Figure 5 and Tables 1–4.

results.title: SHINE: A Scalable In-Context Hypernetwork for Mapping Context to LoRA in a Single Pass

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the dedicated consistency-checking-circuit claim with narrower causal involvement of a latent set. Detection versus sustained resistance becomes a central contribution, generalization beyond SAE directions is newly claimed, and the fine-tuning conclusion is explicitly restricted to one training recipe.

C2.justification: V1 interprets ESR and prompting effects as evidence of internal monitoring circuits. V2 allows restarts to be text-conditioned and considers richer corrective context alongside internal mechanisms as explanations for sustained recovery. It adds substantive limitations concerning steering paradigms, implicit-recovery measurement, heterogeneous latent functions and the generality of its fine-tuning findings.

D1.justification: V2 documents the holistic judge's full prompt, Wikipedia-vector construction and prefix preparation, and explicitly states that fine-tuning used no active steering. It discloses that detailed matched-steering counts were not preserved. Existing implementation details, LoRA hyperparameters and code-access information remain unchanged.

E1.justification: V2 extends the retained recovery task with 20 disjoint prompts spanning biology, history, economics, physics and literature. It also evaluates Wikipedia-derived perturbations and prefilled response scenarios (Appendices A.3.5–A.3.8), providing targeted additional coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds Wikipedia-derived residual-stream vectors as an evaluated comparison with SAE steering, plus clean-prefix and matched steered/no-prefill comparators in Sections 3.6–3.7. The original five-model and matched random-latent comparisons remain.

E3.justification: New protocols include discovery-disjoint evaluation, four off-topic prefill lengths, 447 matched-prefix episodes scored by a separate continuation-only judge, and blind human validation of 40 responses. Appendix A.2.2 also corrects the reference judge from Sonnet to Haiku, aligning it with the main text without establishing that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds tests of text-conditioned restarts, resistance beyond generic on-topic context, positive- versus negative-effect latent subsets on held-out prompts, and generalization beyond SAE vectors. Appendix A.2.3 additionally analyzes the holistic judge's false positives. The boost sweep, random-latent control and temporal activation analyses already existed in v1.

E5.justification: The Wikipedia-vector experiment introduces Wilson confidence intervals and a two-proportion test (Appendix A.3.6). Existing confidence-interval reporting and the three independent random-ablation sets are retained; an increase in repeated-run counts is not reported.

E6.justification: Original results, including the 3.8% Llama-3.3-70B ESR rate, remain unchanged. New results include 3.6% ESR with Wikipedia vectors, 7.0–13.5% restart rates under unsteered prefilling, and continuation scores of 8.7, 30.4 and 54.5 in Table 6. Table 4 adds held-out ESR rates of 5.0% without ablation versus 3.3%, 2.9% and 3.8%; its combined-ablation row does not support the blanket 30–45% reduction claim. Human validation also reveals holistic-judge overscoring.

M1.justification: The core SAE steering, threshold calibration, contrastive latent selection, ablation, meta-prompting and masked LoRA training procedures remain unchanged. The 26 'off-topic detectors' are renamed 'self-correction-associated latents'; the new vector and prefix procedures are evaluation controls.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list and discussion are extensively rewritten around detection and sustained resistance. Terminology changes throughout, metric explanations are consolidated, and new Sections 3.6–3.7 move the existing sequential-activation discussion to Section 3.8.

P2.justification: All 21 original figures are retained. V2 adds a matched-prefix bar chart, a judge-versus-human scatterplot, a metrics table and three control-results tables. Existing displays are repositioned and renumbered, with revised captions, while the overall visual design remains stable.

R1.justification: Section 4 adds a focused comparison with reasoning-model 'aha moments', citing Guo, Yang and Zhou and colleagues. New citations to Huang, Gur-Arieh and Ameisen and colleagues support caution about SAE feature descriptions. These additions refine the existing positioning within self-correction and interpretability research.

T1.justification: The steering and ablation equations and threshold definition in Appendices A.1.3–A.1.4 are unchanged. The new metrics table consolidates existing definitions and their standard relationship; no new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves the match between claims and evidence by retreating from v1's dedicated-monitoring-circuit interpretation and directly testing text-conditioning alternatives. Held-out evaluation and disclosure of the failed holistic judge address additional validity concerns. Missing matched-steering counts and Table 4's inconsistent reduction claim remain weaknesses, but the stronger controls and more defensible interpretation provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ESR study. All main-text and appendix pages are readable, and the corresponding experiments, equations, tables and figures can be matched reliably.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds prefix controls, held-out-prompt evaluation, Wikipedia-derived steering and human validation of an exploratory judge.

before.justification: V1 reports original steering, meta-prompting, latent-ablation and fine-tuning experiments, including supplementary controls and activation analyses.

results.title: Endogenous Resistance to Activation Steering in Language Models

C1.justification: The main latent-reasoning contribution and performance claims remain. However, v5 corrects the headline 10.84× inference-speed claim to a reasoning-step reduction, separately reports 5.96× wall-clock speedup, and narrows the conclusion to the paper's chemistry-specific empirical scope.

C2.justification: Beyond v3's interpretability limitation, v5 discusses task-dependent regressions, source overlap, reused RL prompts, reward-design sensitivity, and GRPO instability. It interprets joint-training weakness as an optimization issue, treats counterfactual alignment as optional, and explicitly limits the efficiency theory's explanatory scope.

D1.justification: v5 documents Coconut-Chem's training sequence, states that component ablations are trained from scratch, and discloses GRPO task sampling and prompt reuse. Appendix K supplies hardware, software, precision, sharding, warm-up, and timing details. The front matter also adds model-weight access information alongside code availability.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same approximately 14k-example training snapshot and evaluate the same chemical tasks from ChemCoTBench, Mol-Instructions, ChEBI-20, and ChemLLMBench. The added scale and training analyses reuse existing coverage; no new dataset, domain, or distinct input scenario is introduced.

E2.justification: Appendix M adds evaluated comparisons with Qwen-3-8B (SFT+GRPO), Stage 1+4, and Stage 1+2+3, alongside joint Stage-4 and three-epoch GRPO variants. These substantially expand the training controls beyond v3's retained text-only, staged chemical, and Coconut-Chem comparators.

E3.justification: v5 adds matched 4B and 14B evaluations, joint-versus-frozen Stage-4 controls, a three-epoch GRPO variant, and model-side wall-clock evaluation with a specified timing protocol. These introduce substantial experimental settings beyond the retained 8B setup; they do not establish changes to the original benchmark settings.

E4.justification: Appendices L–P add reward and format diagnostics, training-duration and joint-optimization analyses, topology-sensitive component ablations, a counterfactual-alignment ablation, and an overlap audit. The budget-performance curves already present in v3 Figure 11 are incorporated into v5 Figure 6, rather than constituting a new analysis.

E5.justification: The existing sign-test reporting is retained. v5 additionally reports evaluation across 50 seeds, 2026–2075, with means and standard deviations in Table 19, and adds ±1 standard-error reporting to Figure 5. The seed information concerns repeated evaluation; independent retraining is not stated.

E6.justification: The original benchmark and component-ablation table values are retained, including the 59.88% ChemCoTBench win rate. New results include 52.42% and 51.80% aggregate ChemCoTBench win rates at 4B and 14B, respectively, and wall-clock ratios ranging from 10.1× for reactions to 0.9× for description. Numerous training-variant, diagnostic, overlap, and variability results are also added.

M1.justification: The molecular encoder, adapter, ChemUpdater, latent projector, recurrent reasoning loop, and four-stage training procedure remain unchanged. ChemAdapter is renamed Chemical Adapter. Newly evaluated training variants and component removals are ablations, rather than replacements for the proposed method.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites revise the abstract, introduction, conclusion, and terminology, including continuity–discretization gap becoming modality mismatch. Results discussion is partly reordered, author information moves to the front, and an Impact Statement is added. Most existing method and appendix exposition is retained.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column Haven layout to two columns, with widespread resizing and relocation of displays. v5 merges the existing budget figures, adds uncertainty shading, introduces Tables 4 and 11–23, and reorganizes appendix tables. This substantially changes the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v5 adds MMSciBench and Proteo-R1 citations and removes CellForge, ChemDFM-R, and the RDKit software reference. Most other reference changes update publication metadata for retained works. The positioning relative to chemical LLMs and existing latent-reasoning approaches remains broadly unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A retains the mathematical definitions, assumptions, Theorem A.9, and its proof; the training-loss equations also remain unchanged. The new statement that the efficiency analysis is interpretive qualifies its interpretation without revising the formal mathematics.

improvement.justification: v5 resolves an important evidential weakness by measuring wall-clock latency and separating it from reasoning-step savings, including reporting the description slowdown. Additional training controls, scale comparisons, uncertainty reporting, and overlap diagnostics substantially strengthen empirical scrutiny, while expanded limitations better constrain the conclusions. Efficiency-mean aggregation remains insufficiently explained in Table 16, but the overall gains in validation and claim accuracy are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LatentChem. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and additional validation material in v5.

after.justification: v5 retains those original empirical results and adds model-scale comparisons, timing measurements, training variants, diagnostics, and repeated evaluations.

before.justification: v3 reports original LatentChem benchmark results, component ablations, latent-budget experiments, noise interventions, and representation analyses.

results.title: LatentChem: From Textual CoT to Latent Thinking in Chemical Reasoning

C1.justification: The central PC–BP scaling contribution remains, but v3 adds a quantitative relative-error claim and makes its limiting conditions explicit. The abstract and summary narrow the nonlinear claim from convergence to BP to high gradient alignment, better matching the reported measurements.

C2.justification: Section 3.2 and Appendix A.8.2 newly explain how PC's lazy regime can depart from BP as the output-scaling constant approaches zero. Section 6.2 replaces the suggested factor-L training speedup with a narrower statement about sequential weight-update cost. The main inference-cost, linearity, and short-training limitations remain.

D1.justification: The transformer appendix now explicitly documents token-index inputs, next-token targets, block functions, projection and MLP dimensions, sequence averaging, and omission of the causal mask from notation.
