E1.justification: Both versions use the same Gaussian-input binary toy task, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet, and character-level Tiny Shakespeare. No dataset, task, or distinct evaluation scenario is added or removed.

E2.justification: BP remains the comparator in the corresponding main-text and appendix experiments. The standard-versus-mean-field parameterisation comparisons are also retained; no evaluated comparison method is added or removed.

E3.justification: The reported transformer loss normalization changes: v2 Eq. 126 encloses cross-entropy within the 1/(2TP) energy factor, whereas v3 Eq. 154 uses a separate 1/P term with sequence-averaged cross-entropy. Other documented budgets, model sizes, metrics, and inference settings remain unchanged. This is a reported normalization revision, without evidence of reruns.

E4.justification: The same width/depth sweeps, feature-learning-parameter sensitivity analyses, standard-parameterisation controls, residual-versus-plain-network comparisons, and Tanh/ReLU experiments remain. The revised discussion of learning regimes introduces no new experimental analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-seed averaging for the gradient-alignment heatmaps, representative runs for Figure 4, and consistency across seeds where error bars are omitted. No repeated-run count or uncertainty-reporting practice changes.

E6.justification: Corresponding experimental figures retain the same plotted data, curves, and comparisons, including all appendix results. No empirical result entries are added, removed, or numerically revised; the nonlinear findings receive more cautious interpretation.

M1.justification: The stated transformer computation changes: v2 Eq. 128 includes 1/sqrt(d_i) factors on query, key, and value projections, whereas v3 Eq. 156 omits them while retaining standard-Gaussian initialization. The core PC procedure remains unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether this specification revision reflects an implementation change or a documentation correction.

P1.justification: The abstract and portions of the introduction, convergence discussion, and limitations are rewritten, with terminology such as 'BP-like' and 'heuristic' refined. A dedicated gradient-convergence appendix section is inserted, while the main narrative and section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 updates captions and theorem-box layouts and redistributes retained appendix figures across pages. All numbered figures and tables remain; the experimental plots are reused rather than replaced with new displays.

R1.justification: v3 adds Yang et al. (2021), Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer, and uses it for the corresponding attribution. It also describes the relationship to Ishikawa et al.'s SGD parameterisation more cautiously. The overall related-work coverage and positioning remain similar.

T1.justification: v3 substantially revises Appendices A.4–A.5, including changing PC-specific width corrections from Theta(N^-1/2) to O(N^-1). Desideratum 5 now requires a Theta(1/L) contribution per residual block, and Theorem 2 explicitly assumes L/N tends to zero. New Appendix A.6 derives layerwise and complete-gradient relative-error bounds of O(1/N) for fixed-depth MLPs and O(L/N) for residual networks, with non-vanishing-gradient conditions.

improvement.justification: v2 largely motivated gradient convergence through objective convergence and less accurate derivative scaling. v3's revised derivations and new Appendix A.6 directly address this central justification gap with relative-gradient bounds and explicit conditions. Together with more restrained nonlinear and speedup interpretations, this substantially strengthens the paper's theoretical support. The unexplained connection between revised transformer formulas and retained experiments leaves a limited reproducibility ambiguity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains these original experiments and their results, including nonlinear CNN and transformer experiments and the appendix analyses.

before.justification: v2 reports original neural-network training experiments, including PC–BP gradient comparisons, width/depth sweeps, and learning-regime analyses in Figures 1–4 and the appendix.

results.title: On the Infinite Width and Depth Limits of Predictive Coding Networks

C1.justification: The abstract, empirical contribution bullet, and conclusion broaden the claimed validation from controlled graph reasoning to graph tasks plus standard mathematical reasoning benchmarks. The central finite-sample, feedback/saturation, and curriculum lower-bound claims retain their original scope.

C2.justification: v2 interprets Figure 5 as evidence that initialization-based beta and beta-prime estimates capture the benchmarks' native difficulty separation. It extends the earlier interpretation of favorable difficulty and budget regimes to the new benchmarks and explicitly frames Table 4's exclusions as focusing on measurable curriculum effects. The original mechanism explanations remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix D.2 supplies benchmark prompt templates, GSM8K split sizes, round-partition rules, selected DeepMind modules, and experiment-specific budgets. Table 8 documents benchmark fine-tuning hyperparameters, including weight decay of 0.0001. The original graph implementation details remain under reorganized Appendix D.1, substantially expanding the documented experimental procedures.

E1.justification: v2 adds GSM8K word problems and numeric-answer DeepMind Mathematics tasks to the retained synthetic shortest-path coverage. Experiments include an aggregate of nine easy modules and curriculum evaluation using native easy/medium/hard partitions in algebra, arithmetic, and numbers.

E2.justification: Fixed uniform-mixture training remains the comparator for easy-to-hard curricula, including rho=0 in v2 Table 4. The additional Llama and Qwen checkpoints are base-model configurations using the same self-improvement procedure; no competing self-improvement algorithm is newly evaluated.

E3.justification: Section 6.2 and Appendix D.2 introduce six base-model configurations, three-round benchmark protocols, official GSM8K test evaluation, new question/answer-budget grids, module-selection rules, and rho-controlled curriculum mixtures. Appendix D.1 also removes tolerance qualifiers from synthetic class-balancing requirements, a reported specification revision that does not establish that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the analyses: Tables 1–2 examine self-improvement across model-relative difficulty regimes, Table 3 tests question and answer budgets on GSM8K, and Table 4 tests curriculum strength on native mathematics difficulty splits. Figure 5 additionally checks how estimated difficulty-separation parameters track rho. The original graph analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five-seed averaging for Figures 3–4 and standard errors across 15 initializations in Figure 4(b). New Table 4 extends the existing standard-error reporting convention to additional results, without specifying a new run count or statistical estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Figures 1–4 retain their plot data, while v2 adds substantial benchmark results. Examples include Qwen3-8B improving from 27.52% to 30.67% on GSM8K (Table 1), Qwen3-32B declining from 97.89% to 96.69% on selected easy mathematics modules (Table 2), and an arithmetic/add_sub_multiple curriculum gap of 17.08 percentage points at rho=0.8 (Table 4). M1.justification: The reward-filtered maximum-likelihood update in Section 3 and curriculum versus fixed-mixture procedures in Section 5.1 are retained. The added model checkpoints and rho-controlled task mixtures instantiate this framework for new experiments; they do not revise its learning algorithm.

P1.justification: Section 6 is reorganized into synthetic and standard-benchmark subsections, each separating setup and results. Appendix D similarly groups the retained graph material and adds a benchmark subsection. The synthetic setup paragraph is rewritten and validation summaries are updated, while most existing prose and the theoretical narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds model-trajectory tables, paired budget panels, a module-by-rho table with standard errors and underlined maxima, Figure 5's two-panel difficulty plot, and hyperparameter Table 8. Existing appendix Tables 1–3 become Tables 5–7. Figure 2 is relocated, and Figures 3–4 receive task-specific captions while retaining their plots.

R1.justification: v2 adds a brief discussion of Yang et al.'s budget-allocation work, plus references for GSM8K, DeepMind Mathematics, Qwen2.5, and Qwen3. Existing cited works and the principal positioning around finite-sample, task-centric curriculum analysis are retained.

T1.justification: The main assumptions, bounds, propositions, and definitions/proofs in Appendices A–C are retained. The limited mathematical addition is Section 6.2.2's explicit sampling-matrix definition W=(1-rho)U+rho I, formalizing interpolation between fixed-mixture and fully staged benchmark curricula. No new theorem or proof accompanies it.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical validation depended on simulations and a bespoke graph task. v2 substantially strengthens the theory's empirical relevance by testing difficulty, budget, and curriculum predictions on standard mathematics data, multiple model sizes, and native difficulty partitions, with supporting implementation details. Selected-module reporting and unspecified run counts for the new benchmarks limit generality and statistical assessment, but the targeted new evidence, including negative outcomes, provides a substantial benefit while preserving the original theory and results.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, theoretical framework, and retained experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete Appendices A–D support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds original GSM8K and DeepMind Mathematics experiments, including model trajectories, budget sweeps, and curriculum comparisons in Tables 1–4 and Figure 5.

before.justification: v1 reports original Monte-Carlo simulations in Figures 1–2 and Llama-based shortest-path experiments in Figures 3–4, with experimental details in Appendix D.

results.title: A Task-centric Theory for Iterative Self-Improvement with Easy-to-Hard Curricula

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same principal claims about finite-sample self-improvement, acceptance feedback, conditions favoring easy-to-hard curricula, and empirical validation. The revised corollary does not rewrite those overarching claims.

C2.justification: Remark 5.7.3 qualifies the optimal-difficulty interpretation to finite intervals. New Appendix E explains the clean-verification limitation, requirements for extending the analysis to noisy rewards, and why the current bounds do not directly apply to other test-time training objectives or update rules.

D1.justification: Appendix D retains the prompt templates, graph-generation procedure, CP-SAT data selection, training instructions, and settings in Tables 6–8. No new implementation or resource-access information is supplied.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic shortest-path task, GSM8K, and DeepMind Mathematics modules and difficulty levels. The noisy-reward and test-time settings discussed in v3 are not evaluated.

E2.justification: The fixed uniform-mixture comparator and the evaluated Llama and Qwen model roster remain unchanged. The newly cited test-time methods do not participate in the reported comparisons.

E3.justification: Section 6 and Appendix D retain the same Pass@1 evaluation, data splits, model sizes, question and answer budgets, iteration counts, and curriculum mixing settings.

E4.justification: Both retain the same analyses of initialization, task difficulty, question budgets, per-question answer budgets, and adjacent difficulty separation, including collapse and saturation observations. No new empirical robustness or supplementary analysis is added.

E5.justification: Appendix D.1 retains five-run averaging with different seeds for Figures 3–4. Figure 4(b)'s aggregation across 15 initializations and standard-error shading, and Table 4's standard-error reporting, are unchanged.

E6.justification: The empirical tables and plotted simulation/experimental results are unchanged. For example, both report Qwen3-8B's GSM8K trajectory as 27.52, 28.66, 29.75, and 30.67 in Table 1; Table 4 also retains all scores and standard errors.

M1.justification: Sections 3 and 5.1 retain the same generation, reward filtering, maximum-likelihood update, and easy-to-hard curriculum procedures. Appendix E discusses possible extensions without implementing a new method.

P1.justification: v3 presents Corollary 5.6 informally and places its formal statement in Appendix C.4, adds Appendix E, and clarifies the auxiliary infinite-limit argument. It also adds an ICML acceptance note and updates bibliographic text; the overall narrative and section order remain largely intact.

P2.justification: All five figures and eight tables are retained. Figures 4–5 and Tables 1 and 3 move earlier, with accompanying text and table reflow; the graphical content and captions remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Appendix E adds positioning relative to test-time computation through citations to SETS, Learning to (Learn at Test Time), and Test-Time Training Done Right. Most other reference changes update publication metadata for existing works.

T1.justification: Corollary 5.6, formalized as Corollary C.4 in v3, replaces the global unique-optimizer guarantee with a guarantee on qualified finite intervals [0,B], with B-dependent smallness conditions. It changes the large-difficulty threshold scaling from Θ(2^(-β'/2)) to O(2^(-β')). Appendix C.4 substantially revises the supporting arguments and adds strict-convexity and moment-inequality proofs in Lemmas C.10–C.11.

improvement.justification: v3 resolves an important inconsistency: v2's Lemma C.7 derives an O(2^(-β')) upper bound but concludes Θ(2^(-β'/2)). The revision retains the compatible bound, confines the optimizer guarantee to controlled finite intervals, and adds convexity and moment arguments. These changes substantially improve the mathematical support for a central curriculum conclusion, despite narrowing its scope. The empirical evidence is preserved, and Appendix E clarifies applicability.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including the revised proofs and new Appendix E in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains the original simulation and model-training results reported in Figures 1–5 and Tables 1–4.

before.justification: v2 reports original Monte-Carlo simulations and LLM self-improvement experiments on synthetic shortest-path tasks, GSM8K, and DeepMind Mathematics.

results.title: A Task-centric Theory for Iterative Self-Improvement with Easy-to-Hard Curricula

C1.justification: The abstract and four contribution statements retain the same substantive claims about CPRD, BT representability, KL projection, and margin/connectivity bounds. The new experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine the central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands practical interpretation: Section 7.6 explains dataset rankings through domain mismatch and the margin/connectivity tradeoff; Section 8 discusses conditional-independence diagnostics and difficulties testing them in high dimensions. Appendix D.3 explains linear connectivity as a proxy for richer hypothesis classes, and D.2 qualifies estimator reliability at extreme sampling parameters.

D1.justification: v2 adds model and labeler identifiers, the real-data connectivity calculation, and implementation details for synthetic perturbations. Appendix D.4 specifies randomly oriented three-cycles, at most 20 cycles per context, and validation/test sizes of 2048. Existing synthetic implementation details remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates finite synthetic contexts and responses. v2 adds HH-RLHF, PKU-SafeRLHF, SHP, and UltraFeedback training data with a common UltraFeedback test set, extending coverage to real language-model preferences. Section 7.5 also introduces a synthetic scenario that violates BT representability.

E2.justification: The original-score versus rank-normalized and uniform versus optimized sampling comparisons are retained. The added experiments compare data conditions using BT; Llama supplies embeddings and Skywork supplies labels, without adding a competing learning method.

E3.justification: New protocols use 10K pairs per real dataset, a linear reward head on frozen Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct embeddings, and a common Skywork-relabeled test set. The non-BT experiment introduces controls preserving comparison mass and the projection target, plus RMSE and probability-MAE evaluation. Appendix D.3 adds connectivity evaluation for general test comparisons; the original Section 7.1 settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 7.5 and Appendix D.4 add a controlled misspecification analysis testing whether BT recovers the same projection target despite altered preference probabilities. Appendix D.2 adds an analysis of connectivity estimates' sensitivity to stochastic optimization. The original margin and connectivity analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions already report standard errors over five seeds for the original experiments. New Table 3 reports ten connectivity estimations per alpha, aggregated across five seeds, with mean, standard deviation, and relative standard deviation. This adds targeted uncertainty reporting without establishing an increase in the original experiments' run counts.

E6.justification: Figures 1–4 retain their results, while Tables 1–3 add substantial new findings. At n=131072, Table 1 reports probability MAE of 0.02754 for BT data and 0.06618 for non-BT data. Table 2 reports 82.170% accuracy for UltraFeedback training versus 78.380% for SHP, although SHP has higher connectivity. Table 3 adds estimator-stability results.

M1.justification: The generative and BT learning objectives, rank normalization, and alternating connectivity optimization remain unchanged. The added experiments use the existing BT learner with new data and an additional linear-head configuration.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and section ordering are retained. v2 adds experimental and appendix subsections, expands the discussion, and adds acknowledgements. It also changes the displayed author name from Maria-Florina Balcan to Nina Balcan and replaces the preprint footer with conference publication information.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the empirical displays with three new tables covering misspecification, real-dataset comparisons, and estimator stability. Figures 1–4 retain their curves and captions but change plot typography. The overall two-column main text and single-column appendix layout remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds Balcan et al. (2016) on combinatorial comparisons and references supporting UltraFeedback, SHP, PKU-SafeRLHF, Llama, and Skywork. The existing related-work discussion and central novelty positioning remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The main theorems are retained, but Appendix D.3 adds a general-test-distribution connectivity definition and Proposition D.1 with its eigenvalue proof. Appendix D.4 derives a zero-flow condition and cycle perturbations preserving the BT projection target. v2 also corrects sigmoid and cross-entropy derivative signs around Equation 81.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical grounding of the paper's diagnostic claims. Beyond v1's small synthetic setting, it tests misspecification with a controlled projection target, demonstrates connectivity on real preference data, and quantifies estimator stability. Supporting derivations make these additions assessable. The real-data evidence remains limited to frozen linear heads and one relabeled test distribution, but the combined gains meaningfully strengthen the paper's credibility and practical relevance.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work and contain readable main text, equations, figures, and appendices. The retained material and v2 additions can be reliably matched.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original results on non-BT preferences, real preference datasets, and connectivity-estimation stability in Tables 1–3.

before.justification: Section 7 and Appendix D report original synthetic experiments on margin, connectivity, sampling optimization, and accuracy on small-margin pairs.

results.title: What Does Preference Learning Recover from Pairwise Comparison Data?

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the empirical validation claim to language models trained from scratch at 100M/200M scales. The introduction revises the claimed average vision accuracy improvement from +3.7% to +3.0% across revised comparisons. The central bounded-confidence synchronization contribution remains the same.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations of RoPE compatibility, the complementary role of compact local branches, and over-smoothing (D.2.4, D.4.4 and E.3). It also interprets the sink-token comparison as evidence for structural mitigation. Appendix A acknowledges pretraining experiments while retaining the limitation that language models still use standard attention.

D1.justification: New Table 14 documents pretraining budgets, optimizer settings, batching, sequence length, architecture, comparator-specific settings and H200 hardware. The ImageNet recipe is also revised and separated by model type in Table 11. These substantially expand the technical information beyond v2's vision, generation and LoRA recipes.

E1.justification: V3 adds FineWeb-Edu and WikiText-103 for language-model training, plus LAMBADA, CBT, Blimp, Hellaswag and ARC-Easy evaluation. It also introduces 21 LongBench tasks covering bilingual long-context evaluation. Existing vision, generation and LoRA benchmark coverage is retained.

E2.justification: V3 evaluates RoPE and top-k ViT comparators, introduces sliding-window, top-k, Longformer and Routing Transformer language-model comparisons, and directly compares against a learnable sink token (Tables 8, 17–19, 25 and 27). The Swin comparison already existed in v2 Table 14 and is moved to v3 Table 4.

E3.justification: V3 introduces 100M/200M pretraining protocols using 10B/20B tokens and 1024-token sequences, adjusts baseline layer counts for parameter matching, and evaluates LongBench at 8K context. Existing ImageNet settings also change: learning rates are revised and Krause sigma changes from 4.0 to 4.5/9.0 (v2 Table 9; v3 Table 11).

E4.justification: V3 adds targeted analyses of positional-encoding compatibility and LongBench sensitivity to window/top-k settings of 32/16 versus 512/256 (Table 26). Existing vision component ablations, generation ablations and Llama/Qwen hyperparameter studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without experimental seed counts, repeated-run information, confidence intervals or significance tests. The added experiments retain this reporting practice.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantial results for pretraining, LongBench, RoPE/top-k comparisons and sink-token comparisons. ImageNet Table 3 is revised: ViT-B-16/KViT-B-16 accuracies change from 72.19/74.50 to 75.85/76.75 under changed training recipes, so these are not same-setting gains. Existing generation and LoRA benchmark scores are retained.

M1.justification: The RBF affinity, local support, top-k selection and auxiliary language-model pathway remain unchanged. V3 adds a KViT variant replacing additive positional encoding with RoPE (Appendix D.2.4), constituting a limited architectural adaptation.

P1.justification: Editing is concentrated in empirical summaries and selected experimental passages, with most existing prose retained. The Swin discussion moves into Section 5.2, and former Appendices E and F become E.1 and E.2 under a broader heading. The publication notice also changes.

P2.justification: V3 substantially expands the table displays with pretraining, extended-baseline, LongBench and sink-token tables, adds RoPE rows to Tables 1–3, and restructures the ImageNet configuration table. The Swin table moves into the main text. Figure 2 corrects masking notation and clarifies its caption; Figure 6 removes LoRA-specific labels.

R1.justification: Appendix B adds substantive positioning against earlier distance-kernel attention, relative positional encoding, adaptive attention spans, Longformer, top-k attention and Routing Transformers. Appendix E.3 adds over-smoothing literature. These additions materially broaden discussion of closely related methods and theoretical perspectives.

T1.justification: The formal definitions, attention equations and Appendix C clustering arguments remain unchanged apart from punctuation and notation presentation. New Appendix E.3 discusses over-smoothing conceptually without adding a formal result or proof.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially addresses v2's limited testing against close alternatives and its reliance on LoRA-only language evidence. Pretraining experiments, parameter-matched comparisons, 8K LongBench tests and RoPE/sink-token controls strengthen empirical validation, while new recipes improve reproducibility. Results are not uniformly favorable—the sink-token baseline wins on MMLU-Pro—and uncertainty estimates remain absent. Nevertheless, the broader controls and explicit retention of the global-attention limitation provide a substantial net quality improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Krause Synchronization Transformers and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices. Retained, relocated and newly added material can be reliably distinguished.

after.justification: V3 retains these original experiments and adds language-model pretraining, LongBench evaluation and additional baseline comparisons.

before.justification: V2 reports original image-classification, autoregressive-generation and Llama/Qwen evaluation results, including component ablations and throughput measurements in Appendix D.

results.title: Krause Synchronization Transformers

C1.justification: The two central contributions and exchangeability-qualified risk claim remain. v3's conclusion explicitly adds deployment over existing judges without retraining. Its abstract also changes the retained 2.4× coverage comparison from 'naïve' to 'vanilla' baselines, although Table 3 supports the ratio against Naïve calibration and gives Vanilla full coverage.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations concerning continuous versus discrete confidence, critic-dependent verbalized confidence, conservative behavior under label noise, modest calibration budgets, and target-distribution recalibration. Section 6 removes v1's explicit warning that non-positional biases may persist. Some new interpretations overreach: Appendix H describes MT-Bench/Arena transfer as valid, although Table 12 reports Arena-to-MT-Bench risks of 0.122, 0.103, and 0.107 for the Qwen judges.

D1.justification: v3 documents additional baseline configurations, identifies the specialized critic checkpoint, and supplies corruption and calibration-size procedures. Figures 4–6 simplify the documented response delimiters, without establishing that earlier experiments were rerun. Existing logit extraction, greedy BPE inference, Transformers usage, and two A100 GPUs remain documented.

E1.justification: v3 adds JudgeBench and PKU-SafeRLHF to the three retained benchmarks. Appendix C evaluates reasoning-intensive comparisons across knowledge, mathematics, and coding, plus safety-focused preferences between harmful and safe responses, substantially extending represented data and task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds Swap-and-Aggregate to Table 1 across all four judges and three original benchmarks. Appendix D additionally evaluates Self-Consistency for Qwen-7B/14B across those benchmarks and Trust-or-Escalate for all four judges on MT-Bench. These are actual additional comparators; v1's original comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: The original 2,000-instance, 50/50 evaluation remains. New protocols include a Skywork-Critic-Llama-3.1-8B judge, Self-Consistency with five samples at temperature 0.7, calibration-label corruption with clean test labels, calibration sizes from 50 to 1,000 with remaining instances held out, and calibration/testing across different benchmarks. These substantially expand evaluation design without establishing reruns of the retained experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained risk-budget and judge-scale analyses, Appendices F–H add controlled tests of calibration-label noise, annotation-budget sensitivity, and distribution shift. They examine whether reliability survives corrupted labels, how coverage depends on calibration size, and when transferred thresholds violate the target risk.

E5.justification: The original 1,000-split averaging and standard-deviation bands remain. v3 specifies 500 random splits per cell for the new noise, calibration-size, and transfer studies. This adds experiment-specific repetition information; it does not report increased repetitions for the original results.

E6.justification: The original numerical entries in Tables 1–3 are unchanged, but v3 adds Swap-and-Aggregate scores and extensive results in Tables 4–12 and Figure 7. Examples include Skywork-Critic achieving 0.996 coverage with 0.094 risk on RewardBench, and cross-benchmark transfer reaching 0.203 risk at a 0.10 target. These are newly reported conditions, not improvements to the original scores.

M1.justification: Both versions average aligned forward/reverse preference probabilities, compute binary entropy, and select the largest threshold satisfying the same corrected linearized-loss constraint. The abstention fallback is unchanged. v3 clarifies the prediction rule and applies the existing method to a specialized critic without introducing a new component.

P1.justification: v3 shortens the abstract and conclusion, adds concrete introductory motivation, rewrites baseline lists into grouped prose, and expands explanations around prediction rules and calibration. It updates running headers and publication text. The main section order and most existing narrative remain, while new scientific material receives appendices C–H.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is substantially redrawn with clearer labels and an expanded caption. Table 1 gains comparator rows; nine additional tables and Figure 7 display the new evidence. Prompt figures are reformatted and relocated, and existing tables and plots are rearranged. Figures 2–3 retain their underlying content.

R1.justification: v3 adds a focused discussion distinguishing BPE from swapped/repeated judging and discrete self-consistency, with new citations including TrustJudge, Tripathi et al., Wang et al.'s Self-Consistency, and Lyu et al. It also cites the new benchmarks and critic, and introduces an explicit first-framework novelty claim in the Impact Statement. The broader conformal-risk-control positioning is retained.

T1.justification: Theorem 2.1 and its displayed mathematical conditions remain unchanged. v3 adds an argument that deterministic BPE preserves exchangeability and expands Appendix A.1's justification of Equation 13 using symmetry of the calibration rule. This is a limited addition to mathematical reasoning, without a new theorem or revised guarantee.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for BPE's distinct contribution through the bidirectional comparator in Table 1, and for SCOPE's practical limits through the noise, calibration-size, and transfer studies in Appendices F–H. These address important unanswered questions in v1, including exposing risk violations under distribution shift. The abstract's comparator error, overbroad transfer interpretation, and removed residual-bias caveat reduce precision, but the added comparative and diagnostic evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SCOPE and BPE, with matching authors, methodology, and original experiments. Text extraction and rendered-page inspection support comparison of the equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices: A–B in v1 and A–H in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and adds benchmark, comparator, specialized-critic, label-noise, calibration-size, and cross-benchmark transfer results.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on MT-Bench, RewardBench, and Chatbot Arena, including uncertainty metrics, selective coverage, and empirical risk across multiple judges and calibration/test splits.

results.title: SCOPE: Selective Conformal Optimized Pairwise LLM Judging

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the empirical claim from three to four benchmarks and introduce the Bench II result. Separating knowledge from outline structure and using graph-driven exploration remain the central contributions; the conclusion is substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: v1 interprets lower citation accuracy as a precision–coverage tradeoff; v2 attributes it mainly to independent-citation scoring, supported by joint evaluation. New discussions explain component contributions, criticize retrieval-oriented KG construction for gap detection, and qualify extraction-error risks through claimed self-correction. The cost–quality tradeoff also receives fuller treatment.

D1.justification: v2 adds module-level runtimes and quota-backfilling details. Conversely, it removes v1's explicit 10-query budgets for each graph, top-5 URL setting, and separate no-KG pseudocode. Backend identifiers, retrieval pipeline, and prompt templates are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds DeepResearch Bench II alongside the three retained benchmark datasets. This extends evaluation within text-based, long-form research; additional application domains, languages, or modalities are not documented.

E2.justification: WebWeaver and WebShaper become evaluated comparators in Tables 1–2. v2 also tests a LightRAG-based KG-construction variant and expands cost comparisons to other research systems. These additions substantially strengthen comparison with relevant alternative approaches; Graph-R1, GraphSearch, and GraphAgent remain discussion-only references.

E3.justification: New protocols include Bench II's rubric metrics, GPT-5 evaluations on DeepResearchGym/DeepConsult, fixed-five-round ablations with shared initialization, joint-citation scoring on 20 cases, and five-annotator review of 10 evaluation cases. These extend the evaluation design; the original benchmark judging models are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's KG/no-KG analyses, v2 tests enrichment, exploration, topology-based selection, and LightRAG construction separately (Figure 3). Appendices A.2, F, and G add citation-protocol analysis, an audit of 6,014 extracted triplets with a correction example, and human validation of LLM judging.

E5.justification: Appendix G introduces inter-annotator reliability estimation, reporting Gwet's AC1 of 0.95 alongside unanimous and individual agreement rates. Neither version reports repeated-run performance uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Existing headline scores, including 53.08 RACE, remain. v2 adds 41.48 Total on Bench II, GPT-5 scores of 96.52 on DeepResearchGym and 6.84 on DeepConsult, and new ablation/reliability results. Mean stopping iterations change from 3.20/3.81 to 3.23/3.88. Cost results are replaced with measurements on a specified 20-case subset, not an established same-setting cost increase.

M1.justification: The dual-graph workflow, search-chain scoring equations, report generation, and prompt templates remain unchanged. Added explanations of chain filtering, quota backfilling, and self-correction do not establish a changed implementation; the LightRAG substitution is an experimental variant.

P1.justification: The main section order and most existing prose remain. v2 makes localized wording, affiliation, and cross-reference corrections, expands appendix organization, and relocates the cost analysis, case trajectory, and unchanged prompt templates.

P2.justification: v2 adds the two-panel ablation Figure 3, Bench II Table 3, and extraction-error Table 7. It replaces the compact cost table with Tables 5–6, expands benchmark tables, and adds an Iter 1 column to the stopping table. Original Figures 3–4 are retained as Figures 4–5.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Bench II, LightRAG, Graph-R1, GraphSearch, and GraphAgent. Appendix A.4 sharpens the distinction between evolving graph-guided research planning and graph retrieval over fixed corpora. Other reference changes largely update publication metadata or consolidate duplicate entries.

T1.justification: New Appendix D defines candidate search spaces, derives cardinality/budget bounds, and argues for monotonic gap resolution and practical convergence. This is a limited formal extension beyond v1's retained scoring equations, without a proved convergence guarantee.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's broad KG/no-KG comparison: relevant direct baselines, component ablations, citation and extraction audits, and human checking address important weaknesses in attributing and trusting the reported gains. Expanded cost measurements clarify practical tradeoffs. These benefits outweigh the loss of explicit retrieval-budget settings, although the small human audit and heuristic convergence argument leave limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DualGraph research work. Their main text, tables, figures, equations, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original evaluations and adds benchmark results, component ablations, citation and graph-extraction analyses, and a human evaluation of judge reliability.

before.justification: v1 reports original DualGraph evaluations on three research benchmarks, iterative-outline ablations, and token-cost measurements.

results.title: A Tale of Two Graphs: Separating Knowledge Exploration from Outline Structure for Open-Ended Deep Research

C1.justification: The three-level measurement framework and SSR/SSR-D contributions remain. The abstract and introduction replace assured answer invariance with a response-abstracted skeleton designed to limit encoding, while OOD preservation/restoration becomes mitigation of degradation and improved robustness within the reported evaluations.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly limits the theoretical guarantee to the skeleton channel, acknowledges potentially large residual answer dependence, and explains why excessive invariance can remove useful guidance. Ironic monitoring becomes an unverified mechanistic hypothesis with proposed future tests. The teacher analysis also changes from smooth scaling to benchmark-dependent tradeoffs.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-access link, clarifies seed construction, teacher training and final student-distillation data flow, and documents how the training recipe extends across model sizes. Prompt instructions become more detailed. Conversely, v1's explicit 200k seed-trace count is omitted; the stated 100k final student traces concern a different pipeline stage.

E1.justification: Reported coverage remains LMArena-based reasoning generation and ArenaHard-v2.0, EQ-Bench 3, IFEval, MultiChallenge, GPQA-Diamond and AIME 2025 evaluation. The added subset comparisons, judged traces and conversational case study do not establish a new dataset domain or task coverage.

E2.justification: New Table 5 adds evaluated Native rollout and Best-of-3 rollout baselines under Qwen3-Max-Preview and Kimi2.5 settings. This substantially broadens comparison beyond the retained neutral and suppression-based RCG methods to strong forward-reasoning alternatives.

E3.justification: Lexical anchoring changes from ROUGE-L recall to IDF-weighted content-token recall; probabilistic anchoring changes from per-token information gain to a clipped fraction of baseline answer surprisal removed. The stated default SSR-D teacher changes from NBG-3.5-Pro to Qwen3-235B-Instruct-2507. Section 5.4 also introduces 16k-subset rollout comparisons and a 500-example, two-pass judge protocol. These reported revisions do not establish that the original experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds teacher/evaluator-dependence checks, validation using two external LLM judges, skeleton length/tag/transition/refinement analyses, and a conversational case study. The component ablation is retained, while the teacher-choice study expands from two to three teachers. These additions examine robustness, trace quality and structural behavior beyond v1's analyses.

E5.justification: New Tables 6 and 7 report sample variances alongside mean judge scores and explicitly identify the 500 judged examples. These describe variation across examples, not repeated-training uncertainty; v2 adds no corresponding seed counts, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 adds the results in Tables 5–7 and Figures 5–8 while retaining the printed values in main Tables 1–4. In the teacher study, NBG-3.5-Pro changes from 59.5/56.6/44.2 to 58.9/57.8/45.0 on ArenaHard/GPQA-D/AIME; the former triplet is now assigned to Qwen3-235B-Instruct-2507. Section 4.3 also corrects v1's description of NEU traces as primarily occupying the Reason zone.

M1.justification: The two-phase SSR procedure, functional tags and SSR-D objectives remain intact. However, the revised SSR prompt in Appendix I adds iterative skeleton deliberation, explicit encouragement of nonlinear reasoning and a developed paragraph explaining and checking each step, refining the reported generation procedure.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much existing prose remain. V2 edits grammar and terminology, revises selected abstract, interpretation and SSR-D passages, and rewrites the bounded theoretical discussion. It inserts Section 5.4, Appendix D, acknowledgements and an impact statement, with corresponding appendix renumbering.

P2.justification: V2 adds three validation tables and four figures showing skeleton distributions, tag positions/transitions, refinement comparisons and qualitative examples. It expands the teacher table and reflows the appendices. Original Figures 1–4 retain their graphics, although Figure 4's caption changes; the first-page Nanbeige logo is removed.

R1.justification: V2 adds faithfulness literature including Lanham, Bentham, Paul and Tanneru, discusses answer attribution through Wang et al. (2026), and distinguishes SSR from the constructed trajectories discussed by Yang et al. (2025c). The main research positioning remains intact. Lewis-Lim et al.'s publication update represents the same cited work.

T1.justification: Appendix C replaces marginal functional invariance and an unjustified conditioning inequality with sequential conditional-information assumptions and a matching chain-rule proof. It adds a variable-length skeleton bound accounting for length leakage and removes the formal monitoring-bypass proposition. Sections 2.1 and 2.3 also substantively redefine two anchoring metrics.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially improves rigor by repairing Appendix C's capacity argument and withdrawing unsupported guarantees about total anchoring and monitoring. Forward-reasoning comparisons, cross-teacher checks and external LLM-judge evaluations provide important additional support for trace quality, while narrower claims better reflect the evidence. These gains outweigh remaining reproducibility gaps, particularly the unexplained retention of original scores despite revised metric definitions and the changed teacher description.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SSR/SSR-D research. The complete 23-page v1 and 28-page v2, including their equations, figures, tables and appendices, support reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds rollout comparisons, external LLM-judge evaluations, structural analyses and a qualitative case study.

before.justification: V1 reports original anchoring measurements, downstream benchmark evaluations, component ablations and teacher-scaling results.

results.title: Measuring and Mitigating Post-Hoc Rationalization in Reverse Chain-of-Thought Generation

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction recast the central problem and measurement contribution around training–inference mismatch. V2's claim that suppression increases both entropic and probabilistic anchoring is narrowed to increased trajectory anchoring with probabilistic anchoring near neutral. The central SSR/SSR-D mitigation and downstream-performance contributions remain.

New Remark A.1 derives the two-step commuting probability; the dependent Lemma C.3 bound and several gradient indices are corrected.

results.title: On the Emergence of Implicit Curriculum in RLVR Learning Dynamics

Appendix J adds a distinct long-input scenario using RCW sequences extended from 4,000 to 8,000 and 12,000 timesteps.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. v2 makes localized abstract and reward-description edits, adds equal-contribution and publication/disclosure text, and extends the structure with a related-work subsection, Appendix E.1, and Appendices G–K. There is no extensive rewriting of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds seven tables, including resource-cost displays and paired region/tolerance-based localization tables. Figures 1–4 and the original tables retain their content, with several relocated through reflow; Table 3 now appears below Figure 4. The substantial change is the expanded tabular presentation.

results.title: Adaptive Time Series Reasoning via Segment Selection

Tables 5–12 add substantial comparison, stability, sensitivity, and efficiency results. These additions do not constitute improved scores for unchanged AG-REPA settings.

P1.justification: v3 substantially reorganizes the narrative: it expands practical-method explanations, adds a discussion/limitations section, moves main-text ablations into the appendix, consolidates definitions within experimental details, and organizes appendices around hazardous generation, jailbreaks, memorization and extended limitations. These changes exceed isolated language corrections.

P2.justification: The existing graphical content and tables are retained, with relocations and limited display edits. v2 Figure 2 becomes appendix Figure 3, and extraction Table 9 becomes Table 19. Algorithm 1 gains an explanatory caption, while Figure 5 and Table 8 correct their BERTScore direction guidance.

R1.justification: v3 adds Lee and Han's adaptive steering/remasking work and An and Han's DLM-SWAI, explaining how their steering signals differ from SAD's reference-based estimator. It also replaces the contrast between heuristic DiffuGuard and guaranteed SAD with the narrower statement that SAD derives from an exact identity. Most related work is retained.

T1.justification: v3 substantially revises the formal connection between practical SAD and the retained exact-denoiser identity. It withdraws v2's finite-N safety-guarantee assertion, states that no approximation bound is established, distinguishes learned from exact denoisers, and formally defines the relaxed, length-normalized estimator and logit update in Equations 8–11, acknowledging lost unbiasedness. No new safety proof is supplied.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses a substantial reproducibility deficiency by specifying the estimator actually used, and materially improves scientific reliability by withdrawing the finite-N guarantee and acknowledging the retained DIJA example's failure. These gains concern the paper's central method and safety evidence. The repair remains incomplete: the abstract still says 'provably safe', and the new pseudo-perplexity equation contradicts its accompanying description.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SAD research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results in the main text and reorganized appendices.

before.justification: v2 reports original hazardous-generation, jailbreak, throughput and WikiText-103 memorization experiments, including additional extraction results in its appendices.

results.title: The Safety-Aware Denoiser for Text Diffusion Models
